title: POU11011 — Short assignment: the blog post
section: What you are actually being asked to do
text:
What you are actually being asked to do
Take one concept from the module and use it to make sense of one real political situation.
That is the whole task. It is the core move of the discipline, and it is what the final essay asks you to do at greater length and with more at stake. This is the rehearsal.
Note what it is not. It is not a summary of a concept. It is not a news report with a bit of theory sprinkled over the top. The concept has to do work — it has to make you see something in the case that you would not have seen without it, and you have to show me the seeing.
Depth beats breadth every time. One concept, one case, 800 words. A post that gestures at power and the state and legitimacy will lose to one that takes the second face of power seriously for three paragraphs.

title: POU11011 — Short assignment: the blog post
text:
What a blog post is
This is a genre most of you have never written for marks, so here is the spec.
A blog post integrates your own perspective with evidence and analysis. It is less formal than an academic essay, and it lets you be creative with structure. In practice that means:

A hook. Open on the case, the puzzle, or a fact that should bother the reader. Not “In this blog post, I will argue…”. Never that.
Short paragraphs, headings, and bold text where they earn their place.
Links and images are welcome, and do not count toward the word limit. A link to the article you are analysing is worth more than a sentence describing it. Caption any image; do not decorate.
First person is fine. “I think the interesting thing here is…” is allowed, and often better than the passive constructions students reach for when they are nervous.
Referencing is still required. Informal register, formal citation. At least two module readings, cited properly, with a short reference list at the end. The list does not count toward the word limit.

Two things it is not: a personal opinion piece with citations bolted on, and an academic essay with subheadings inserted. If you can delete every heading and lose nothing, you have written the second one.
Good models to read before you start: the LSE blogs, The Conversation, Good Authority (the successor to the Monkey Cage). Notice how fast they get to the point, and how often the second sentence is already the argument.

title: POU11011 — Short assignment: the blog post
text:
A structure that works
Not a template you must follow — but if you are stuck, this shape gets a good mark with 800 words.

The hook (≈100 words). The case, concretely. What happened, and what about it is odd.
The claim (≈50 words). One sentence saying what you are going to argue. Put it early. Blog readers do not wait.
The concept (≈150 words). Name it, define it properly, cite where it comes from. This is the only stretch where you are allowed to sound like a textbook, and it should be the shortest part you are tempted to write.
The work (≈400 words). Apply it. Two or three moves, each with a specific detail from the case. This is where the mark is won.
The limit (≈100 words). What your concept does not explain about this case, or what the strongest objection would be. First-years skip this; it is the single cheapest way to move from a II.1 to a I.

title: POU11011 — Short assignment: the blog post
text:
The prompts
The prompt options are released roughly three weeks before the deadline, and they will be tied to whatever is actually happening in the world in October 2026. That is deliberate: I would rather you analysed something live than something safely settled.
The versions below are the standing concept-anchored forms, so you can start thinking now. The released versions will name specific cases.
[DECISION for Noah — the final prompt list is yours. Below are drafts anchored to the portable concepts from lectures 1–10. Pin each to a live case ~3 weeks before the deadline; last year’s prompts named the case in the question itself, which worked.]

Prompt A — Power
Pick a recent political decision or non-decision. Using the three faces of power, work out where the power actually lay. Which face best explains what happened — and how would somebody disagree with you?
The strongest versions of this take on the second or third face, where the evidence is hard. The weakest ones describe a vote.


Prompt B — The state
Choose a state in the news. Using state capacity — and distinguishing coercive, extractive and administrative capacity — explain one thing that state is failing, or managing, to do. What does the case show about why capacity is not one number?


Prompt C — Ideology
Take a live political controversy. Show what a liberal, a conservative and a socialist answer to it would actually be — not the caricatures, the serious versions — and say which one the policy on the table most resembles.


Prompt D — Regimes and measurement
Take a country that is genuinely hard to classify as democratic or authoritarian. Using one concept from the regimes lectures (polyarchy, competitive authoritarianism, or a specific index), argue for where it sits — and say what is at stake in the label.

title: POU11011 — Short assignment: the blog post
text:
How it is marked
Against the module rubric: argument · use of concepts · evidence · structure and writing · referencing, mapped to the Trinity marking bands. The full one-page rubric is in the marking rubric — read it before you write, not after you get the mark back.
For this piece specifically, the two criteria that separate the top of the pile from the middle are use of concepts (is the concept doing work, or being described?) and evidence (are there real specifics from a real case?).

title: POU11011 — Short assignment: the blog post
text:
Common failure modes
These are the ones that actually turn up, in rough order of frequency.

Describing the concept instead of using it. Two hundred words defining the three faces of power, then three hundred summarising a news story, and no point where they touch. This caps you in the II.2 range no matter how well written it is.
Too many concepts. See above about depth.
No case, or a case the size of a continent. “Democracy in Europe” is not a case. A single decision, election, protest, court ruling or piece of legislation is.
The essay in disguise. Formal register, no hook, headings bolted onto five paragraphs of continuous prose. You lose marks in structure and writing because the brief was a blog post.
Decoration mistaken for format. Bold on every third phrase, a stock photo of a ballot box, four headings for 800 words. Formatting has to earn its place.
Sources that are not sources. Two module readings, minimum, cited properly. A link to a newspaper is evidence about the case, not an academic source. And do not ask a chatbot for references — it invents them, and a fabricated citation is a fabricated citation regardless of where it came from.
Over the word limit. 800 words is a limit, not a target. Going over incurs a penalty of three per cent. State your word count at the top.

title: POU11011 — Final essay
text:
What this is for
The blog post asked you to run one concept over one case. This asks for something harder: a sustained argument, in answer to a question somebody else set, using the module’s toolkit across more than one case.
I am not looking for recall. A competent summary of what Lukes, Weber and Tsebelis each said is worth roughly what it costs to generate, which is now nothing. What I am looking for is the thing that is still expensive: you deciding what the question is really asking, taking a position on it, and defending that position against the strongest version of the other side.
Fifteen hundred words is short. That is on purpose. Short essays punish padding and reward people who know what their argument is before they start typing.

title: POU11011 — Final essay
text:
The questions
[DECISION for Noah — final question list is yours. Six drafts below, one per portable concept, deliberately spanning the whole term so that no student can answer having attended only half of it. Recommend releasing four to six. Each is written to require at least two cases, which is what makes the concept do comparative work rather than illustrative work.]
Answer one.

Power. “The most important exercises of power leave no observable trace.” Is this true, and if it is, how can political science study power at all? Answer with reference to at least two cases. (Portable concept: the three faces of power; measurement.)
The state. Why can some states do things that others cannot? Compare two states and argue whether the difference is best explained by capacity, legitimacy, or something else. (Portable concept: state capacity; monopoly of legitimate violence.)
Ideology and identity. Why do some social differences become political and most never do? Answer with reference to at least two cases, and be explicit about what would count as evidence for your explanation. (Portable concepts: thin vs thick ideology; primordialism vs constructivism vs instrumentalism.)
Regimes. Elections are held in states nobody would call democratic. Are these elections meaningless, or do they do real political work? Answer with reference to at least two authoritarian regimes. (Portable concepts: repression vs co-optation; the dictator’s dilemma; minimal vs substantive definitions of democracy.)
Institutions. “Paper constraints only bind when somebody powerful wants them to.” Assess this claim using the idea of veto players and at least two cases of constitutional or judicial constraint on an executive. (Portable concepts: veto players; constitutionalism; institutional erosion.)
Political economy and collective action. Why do democracies persistently under-supply things that most voters say they want — housing, or climate action, or both? Answer using a collective action or concentrated-interests argument, with at least two cases. (Portable concepts: median voter and why it fails; collective action.)

You may not answer a question you substantially answered in your blog post. If in doubt, ask me before the deadline.

title: POU11011 — Final essay
text:
How to write it
Most first-year essays lose marks in the same four places. Here is how to not do that.

Have an argument, and put it in the first paragraph
An argument is a claim that a reasonable person could disagree with. “Power has three faces” is not an argument; it is a summary. “The third face of power is real but unfalsifiable as usually stated, and political science should therefore treat it as a hypothesis about mechanisms rather than a claim about outcomes” is an argument.
Your introduction should say, in plain words: here is the question, here is my answer, here is how I will get there. Three or four sentences. No throat- clearing about how politics has fascinated humanity since the dawn of time.
A test. Cover everything except your first paragraph. Can a stranger say what you think? If not, rewrite it.


Answer the question that was set
The single most common way to lose a class of marks is to write a good essay about an adjacent topic. Both the LSE and TCD marking schemes say this explicitly: good answers that stray from the question set are normally capped at a lower band. Reread the question after your third draft and ask whether each paragraph is doing work for that question.


Use the concepts as tools, not as furniture
A concept earns its place if removing it would break your argument. If a paragraph defines something and then never uses it, cut the paragraph and buy yourself 120 words of analysis.
Comparison is where the marks are. Two cases treated together — where the comparison is the point — is worth far more than two cases described in sequence.


Take the other side seriously
Somewhere in the essay, state the strongest objection to your argument and answer it. Not a strawman. This is what “critical evaluation” and “independence of judgement” mean in the Trinity band descriptors, and it is the most reliable way to move from a II.1 into a first.


Structure
Not a template, but this shape works at 1,500 words:








Section
Words
Job




Introduction
~150
Question, answer, route


The concept
~200
Define what you are using and where it comes from


Case 1
~350
Apply it, with specifics


Case 2
~350
Apply it, and compare — do not just repeat


Objection
~250
The strongest counter-argument, and your reply


Conclusion
~150
What follows, and what you are still unsure about



Do not include a table of contents, an abstract, or subheadings unless they genuinely help. This is an essay, not a report.


Prose
Short sentences. Active voice. If you cannot say what a sentence means without reading it twice, neither can I. Spellcheck it. Read it aloud once — you will find three things you cannot hear yourself saying.

title: POU11011 — Final essay
text:
Sources and referencing

Use academic sources, not just the textbook. Heywood & Laing is where you start, not where you finish. The module readings, and the recommended readings, are the obvious next step; going beyond them is what a first-class essay looks like.
Any consistent citation style is acceptable — Harvard, Chicago, APA, pick one and hold to it. The TCD Library style guide will help.
Cite paraphrases, not just quotations. Careless note-taking is how honest students end up in plagiarism procedures.
An alphabetised bibliography at the end. It does not count toward the word limit.
Only cite what you have read. If a source appears in your bibliography and you could not say what its argument is, take it out.

Sloppy or inconsistent referencing costs marks under the referencing criterion of the rubric. Fabricated references are an academic integrity matter.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
How do we know?
We’ve made about a hundred confident claims this term. How many of them would survive you actually checking?

IMAGE — full-bleed cold-open background. A detective’s magnifying glass over a blurred newspaper or data-table texture, warm low-key lighting — sets the “political science as detective work” framing before a word is said. Stock photo (Unsplash/Pexels, search “magnifying glass newspaper” or “detective desk”). Use as ## How do we know? {background-image="w12-lec20-img/opener-detective.jpg"} with a dark overlay so the gold text stays legible.


Cold open, no admin, no “welcome back for the last one.” Let the question sit for a beat — genuinely pause. This is the last lecture; the energy should be “we’re finally asking the question underneath every other lecture,” not sentimental. Don’t announce it’s the last class yet — that’s the closing slide’s job.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Nineteen lectures of “wait, how do we know that?”
text:
Nineteen lectures of “wait, how do we know that?”

Lec 2: could you ever observe someone shaping what you want, not just what you do?
Lec 4: does “war made the state” hold up outside the one region it was built on?
Lec 7: does turning a box on a census form actually create an identity?
Lec 8: is ethnic violence “ancient hatred,” or something elites manufacture on purpose?
Lec 10: rich countries look more democratic — which way does the arrow run?
Lec 11: how do you find out what people in a closed society actually think?
Lec 12: is “elections are a strategic tool for autocrats” actually well evidenced?


Every one of those was this lecture, in miniature. Today we do the full version.

Move fast through the bullets — this is a highlight reel, not a re-teach. If you have time, ask the room which one they remember best; it’s a good gauge of what actually landed this term. The Lecture 2 one is the important flag forward: say explicitly “that live poll question from Week 1 — which face of power is most common in Irish politics — that’s exactly the kind of claim we’re about to learn to interrogate properly.”


This recap slide is built from a grep across the term’s actual “How do we know that?” section dividers (Lecs 2, 4, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12) so it reflects what’s really in the decks rather than an invented list — worth re-checking this list once all twenty decks are locked, in case any HDWKT segment gets cut or moved in editing.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Key term: causal inference

Causal inference: working out whether A actually causes B, rather than just A and B happening together (correlation).


The classic warm-up: ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise and fall together, all year — but summer causes both.

Control for season and the correlation between ice cream sales and drownings disappears entirely — that’s what a confound looks like: a hidden third variable driving two things that otherwise look causally linked. It’s an easy example precisely because the shared cause (the weather) is obvious; most confounds in political science hide a lot more artfully than that.


Everyone finds this example easy — good, that’s deliberate, it builds false confidence before the next two slides remove it. The whole lecture’s argument: political claims are almost never this obvious, and the “hidden third cause” is much harder to spot when it isn’t the weather.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Claim: democracy causes economic growth
You’ll hear this constantly — op-eds, aid debates, “why isn’t country X richer yet” takes.

The confound: rich countries also tend to democratize. Which way does the arrow run?

Look across the world and democracies are, on average, richer than non-democracies. That correlation is real and well documented — the open question is which way the arrow runs: does democracy cause the wealth, or does wealth cause the democracy?


IMAGE — chart, inline .absolute right side of the slide. Scatterplot of V-Dem electoral-democracy index (x-axis) against GDP per capita (y-axis), one dot per country — shows the correlation visually before the causal-direction question is posed. Source: Our World in Data “Democracy and GDP” chart, or build fresh from V-Dem + World Bank data. Place .absolute right, ~45% width, so it doesn’t crowd the fragment build.




Does democracy make you rich?
Does being rich make you democratic?
Or does something else — history, geography, luck — drive both?


Three live hypotheses. Democracy might cause growth because institutions protect property, so investment happens. Growth might cause democracy because a growing middle class demands a vote. Or some third factor — colonial history, geography, sheer luck — might drive both, with no direct causal line between them at all.



Decades of research, still contested — not a failure, an honest report on how hard this is.

Explicit callback: this is Lecture 10’s “richer countries look more democratic — which way does the arrow run?” question, now with the general method named. Don’t resolve it — the unresolved-ness is the point. Resist the urge to hand them an answer; the honest answer is “political scientists disagree, and here’s why that’s not a scandal.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Claim: contact between groups reduces prejudice
text:
Claim: contact between groups reduces prejudice
Comes up in every debate about integration, mixed schools, shared housing.

The confound is different in kind — selection, not reverse causation. People who choose contact might already have been less prejudiced beforehand.

This is a different flavour of confound from the democracy-and-growth case: not reverse causation (which cause is upstream) but selection — who ends up in each group in the first place, and why. Someone who chooses to live in a mixed neighbourhood, or send their kids to an integrated school, may already have been less prejudiced before that contact ever happened.



Compare the groups and you still can’t tell: effect of contact, or just who chose it?

Put differently: compare people who had contact to people who didn’t, find the contact group less prejudiced — is that an effect of contact, or just proof that less-prejudiced people were always more willing to have contact in the first place?



You need contact that isn’t a choice — exactly what a natural experiment gives you.

This is a different flavour of confound from the democracy/growth slide — deliberately paired so the room sees two distinct failure modes: reverse causation (which cause is upstream?) versus selection (who ends up in each group in the first place, and why?). Say that contrast out loud — it’s the pedagogical point of running two examples rather than one.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: When history runs the experiment for you
text:
When history runs the experiment for you
You can’t randomly assign countries to “be democratic.” But sometimes history does it for you — for free.

You can’t randomly assign countries to “be democratic” or people to “have contact with an out-group” — but sometimes history does something close to it for free: a lottery, a border, a rule with an arbitrary cutoff, splitting people into groups as if by a coin flip.


Regression discontinuity — near-identical people either side of a cutoff
Difference-in-differences — two similar places, one gets a policy, compare the drift
Instrumental variables — shifts your cause, no other route to the outcome


Regression discontinuity compares people just either side of an arbitrary cutoff — an age, a test score, a border — who are otherwise near-identical; differences between them isolate the cutoff’s effect. Difference-in-differences compares two similar places where one receives a policy change and one doesn’t, and tracks how far apart they drift afterwards. Instrumental variables works by finding something that changes your cause of interest but has no other plausible route to your outcome, letting you isolate that one channel.


None of these are perfect. All of them beat comparing two countries and assuming causation.

Keep this fast and conceptual — the payoff is the worked example on the next slide, don’t let this become a stats lecture. The point is just: these are the moves, roughly, that let you get closer to a real answer than a raw correlation ever could.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Worked case: the Vietnam draft lottery
text:
Worked case: the Vietnam draft lottery
The US drafted men for Vietnam using a birthdate lottery — dates drawn at random.

IMAGE — inline .absolute, top-right of the slide, ~40% width. Archival photo of the actual 1969 US Selective Service draft lottery drawing (the glass jar / capsules being drawn). Source: US National Archives or Wikimedia Commons (“Selective Service draft lottery 1969” — public domain).


That randomness is the gift — whether you served came down to a barrel, not your background.

Whether you served wasn’t about your politics, your class, or your family connections — it was your birthday, drawn from a barrel. That’s what makes it arbitrary, and that’s what makes it usable as a natural experiment.



Researchers compared “bad-number” men (drafted) to “good-number” men (not drafted) to isolate the real effect of service.

Because the lottery numbers were assigned at random, the two groups were, in every other respect, alike: same generation, same country, same starting point in life. Any later difference between them — in earnings, in political attitudes — can be attributed to military service itself, rather than to whatever kind of person chooses or avoids service. The randomness does the work a researcher would otherwise have to control for by hand.



That’s the detective move: find the place where chance, not choice, decided who got what — then compare.

Picked the draft lottery over rainfall-and-protest designs (which are closer to what Comp A’s institutions/development readings sometimes use) to keep clear water between the two courses — flag if you’d rather swap for a case with more direct relevance to something students have already seen this term (e.g. a lottery-based school-admissions natural experiment would tie back to nothing in particular but is a gentler, more relatable version). Angrist’s actual draft-lottery papers are the standard citation if you want to name one on screen.


This is the single cleanest natural experiment most first-years will ever meet — spend real time on it. The mechanism (an actual lottery machine) is vivid and easy to picture, which is exactly why it works as the one worked example rather than a menu of five.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: The full version of a method you’ve already met
text:
The full version of a method you’ve already met
Back in Lectures 11 and 14, you met the list experiment — a way to estimate privately held views people won’t admit to.

The mechanics:

Split your sample at random into two groups
Group A gets 4 boring items — “how many bother you?”
Group B gets the same list plus the sensitive item
The difference in averages estimates true support for it


Group A receives a list of four boring, non-sensitive items and is asked only for a count — “how many of these bother you?” — never which ones. Group B receives the exact same list plus the sensitive item, asked in the same format. Because assignment to A or B is random, the only systematic difference between the two groups’ average counts is the sensitive item — so the gap between the two group averages estimates true support for it, without anyone ever confirming or denying their own answer individually.


No one’s individual answer is ever exposed — the honesty only shows up once you subtract two averages.


Slow down here — this is genuinely one of the cleverer designs in the social sciences and it’s worth letting the mechanism land properly, not rushing to the next slide. If a student looks confused, walk the four numbered steps again with a concrete example: “does the government deserve your support?” as the hidden item.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Measuring what people hide, for real
text:
Measuring what people hide, for real
Russia, 2020–21. Four surveys. The question underneath: is Putin’s support real, or performed?

Half the sample is told his approval ratings are high. Half is told they’re low
Then both halves answer about support — some by list experiment, so nobody names a preference
The low frame lowers support. The high frame does nothing


So it isn’t only fear talking. Told he’s less popular, some Russians become less supportive.

The study is Buckley, Marquardt, Reuter & Tertytchnaya, “Endogenous Popularity: How Perceptions of Support Affect the Popularity of Authoritarian Regimes,” American Political Science Review 118(2), 2024. Design: four survey waves in Russia in 2020–21 — three nationally representative (two face-to-face, one online), one subnationally representative online sample large enough to carry a list experiment. Respondents were shown a frame presenting Putin’s approval as relatively high or relatively low, then asked about their own support. Pairing the framing experiment with a list experiment is what makes the result interpretable: if the frame only changed what people were willing to say, you would expect the effect to disappear once the list experiment removes the need to say it. It doesn’t. That points to genuine preference updating — people revising what they actually think — rather than preference falsification alone. The asymmetry is the striking part: telling people he is unpopular moves them; telling people he is popular does not.


Verified 2026-09-03 against the APSR listing (Cambridge Core) and the paper’s SSRN/UCL Discovery records: authors, journal, volume/issue and year as stated; four waves 2020–21; framing experiment paired with a list experiment on the subnational sample; the low-popularity frame reduces support, the high-popularity frame does not. No effect sizes are on the slide — I haven’t put numbers on screen that I can’t check against the published tables.


Noah: this is your paper and I’ve written it from the abstract and the public record, not from you. Three things to confirm before this goes up: (1) that this is the study you want on screen — the alternative is the police-corruption/bribery list-experiment work, which is more viscerally “measuring what people hide” but less clean to describe in ninety seconds; (2) the actual numbers, if you want any — I’ve deliberately left the slide numberless; (3) the sensitive item as it was actually worded, which is the detail a first-year room will remember. This slide is the payoff for the promises made in lec11, lec12 and lec14’s notes, so it needs to be real.


If this slide is still a placeholder on delivery day: fall back to a published list-experiment finding (support for an autocrat, or admitted bribe-paying) rather than leaving the slide empty — but the room will remember “my lecturer’s own study” far longer than any borrowed example.


IMAGE — either the paper’s title block / first-page header (a genuine journal article on screen is its own small teaching moment: this is what the output of the term’s method actually looks like), or a simplified redraw of the two framing conditions side by side. Not a photo of Putin — the slide is about the instrument, not the man.


Frame this as the payoff of the whole term’s measurement thread: Lecture 2 (can you observe the third face of power?), Lecture 4 (how do you measure state capacity?), Lecture 9 (how do you measure democracy?), Lecture 14 (how do you measure corruption?) — all of it building toward “here’s a real research design, built and run by the person standing in front of you.” Say that lineage out loud. Then the honest coda: the reason we bothered with the list experiment at all is that we did not trust our own first result. That’s the whole lecture, demonstrated rather than asserted. Worth naming the co-authors — it’s also the moment to say out loud that research is not a solo activity.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The replication crisis
An uncomfortable coda: redo a published study, and a striking share don’t hold up.


Publication bias — journals favour dramatic findings; null results go unpublished
P-hacking — run enough analyses on the same data, something looks significant by chance
Small, flashy studies — huge effects with 50 people often shrink to nothing with 50,000


Publication bias means journals favour dramatic, “statistically significant” findings; boring null results tend to get filed away and never published at all, which skews the published record toward the dramatic. P-hacking means running enough different analyses on the same dataset that something, somewhere, looks significant by chance — and it’s that version, not the other nineteen that found nothing, that gets written up. Small, flashy studies routinely produce effects that look huge with fifty participants and shrink to nothing once the sample grows to fifty thousand.


IMAGE — chart, inline .absolute beside the bullet list, ~40% width. The Open Science Collaboration (2015) “Estimating the Reproducibility of Psychological Science” summary chart — original vs. replicated effect sizes/significance rates across ~100 studies. Source: Science 2015, Fig. 1 (the widely reproduced summary graphic).



And our own discipline’s worst case: a 2014 Science paper found a 20-minute conversation with a gay canvasser durably changed minds on same-sex marriage. The data were fabricated. Retracted in 2015.

Michael LaCour and Donald Green published “When contact changes minds” in Science in December 2014: door-to-door conversations with gay canvassers appeared to produce large, lasting shifts in attitudes to same-sex marriage. It was celebrated — the effect was big, the design looked clean, and the finding was one people wanted to be true. In May 2015 two Berkeley graduate students, David Broockman and Joshua Kalla, tried to build on it, found the survey data could not have come from where LaCour said it did, and concluded that no such surveys had ever been commissioned. Green, the senior co-author, asked Science to retract; the paper was retracted on 28 May 2015, with LaCour not agreeing to the retraction. The coda is the part that matters for this lecture: Broockman and Kalla then ran the study properly, and in April 2016 published in Science a finding that roughly ten-minute conversations did durably reduce prejudice against transgender people. The original claim was fraudulent. Something close to it turned out to be true anyway — and the only reason anybody knows that is that two graduate students checked.


One honest slide, not a takedown of the whole discipline — the tone should be “here’s how science corrects itself,” not “nothing is real.” The LaCour story is the one to spend time on, and land the sequence in this order: celebrated finding → two graduate students try to build on it → the data don’t exist → retraction → and then they ran it properly and something like the effect was real. The people who caught it were students. Say that to a room of first-years, and pause. It also rhymes exactly with the contact-hypothesis slide earlier in this deck — same literature, and the natural experiment / careful design is what settled it.


Swapped 2026-09-03, acting on this slide’s own cc and FRESH-EYES §2 (“psychology, when your own discipline has better scandals”): power posing is out, LaCour & Green is in. Facts verified — LaCour & Green, “When contact changes minds,” Science, Dec 2014; irregularities identified by David Broockman and Joshua Kalla, May 2015; retracted 28 May 2015 at Green’s request, LaCour dissenting; Broockman & Kalla’s own study, Science, April 2016, found ~10-minute conversations durably reduced anti-transgender prejudice. Sources: Science news coverage (May 2015, April 2016); Slate, “Gay marriage study faked” (Jun 2015); Retraction Watch ten-year retrospective (Jun 2025). The old power-posing text is preserved in the addl block below.


Previous version of this beat, if you prefer the psychology example: “Power posing — stand like a superhero for two minutes, supposedly boosting hormones and confidence — the textbook cautionary tale: viral talk, huge splash, effect vanished.” With its note: the vanishing was confirmed by later, larger studies and, notably, by one of the paper’s own original co-authors, who later published a piece distancing herself from the claim.


Noah: the LaCour case is better than power posing for three reasons and worse for one. Better: it’s political science, it’s an experiment of exactly the kind this lecture has been praising, and the people who caught it were graduate students — i.e. people barely older than the room. Worse: it’s a fraud case, not a replication-failure case, and those are different diseases. If you want both diagnoses on the table, the honest one-liner is “one of these is somebody lying, the other is everybody being sloppy, and the second one is the bigger problem.” Your call whether to say it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The detective’s checklist
Next time someone tells you “X causes Y,” ask:

What’s the actual evidence? A study, or a vibe?
Correlation or causation? Could something else drive both?
How was it measured? Would a different measure change it?
Has it replicated? One flashy study isn’t a verdict.
What would change your mind? If nothing could prove it wrong, it isn’t science — it’s ideology wearing a lab coat.


None of this makes you right — just harder to fool, including by yourself.

Noah: this checklist is doing a lot of work but is fairly earnest/list-like — the “conspiracy board” meme two slides later is your comic release valve, so this one probably doesn’t need a joke. If it feels flat live, a quick self-deprecating aside works (“apply this to me too — I’ve been wrong about things on this course, ask me which ones after”) rather than a new bit.


Land this as a practice, not a personality trait — the goal is “believe things conditional on evidence, and change your mind when the evidence changes,” not performative cynicism. Point five is the Popperian falsifiability test from way back — if you used the phrase “ideology wearing state-costumes” in Lecture 4, this is a nice rhyme: “ideology wearing a lab coat.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Twenty lectures, four ideas
Everything else was scaffolding. These four kept turning up:

Collective action (Lecs 14, 18, 19) — rational choices, terrible outcomes
Veto players (Lecs 15, 18) — who can block change
State capacity (Lecs 4, 11, 17) — want vs. can actually do
Measurement (Lecs 2, 9, 14, 20) — never neutral


Collective action explains why individually rational choices can produce collectively terrible outcomes — the logic connecting corruption, the housing crisis, and climate change. Veto players are whoever can block a change from happening: the more of them there are, the more stable a system is against upheaval, but also the harder it is to get anything done. State capacity is the gap between what a state wants to do and what it can actually do — a state can want to collect taxes, register births, or enforce laws, and still fail if the capacity isn’t there. And measurement is the thread underneath all three: none of these tools mean anything until someone decides how to count it, and that choice of how to count is never neutral.


These work on political situations that haven’t happened yet. The facts on the rest of the slides won’t.

Slow down, let each bullet land with its own click, and resist making a speech about it — the content does the work. This is literally the “concept spine” from the course design (PLAN-MT2026.md §3) made visible to students for the first time; they’ve been building this toolkit without necessarily noticing the pattern until now, so the tone is “look what you’ve got”, not “look what I gave you”.

text:

You had a working answer: conflict, plus collective decision-making, under scarcity. Would you still give that answer today — or add “and here’s how I’d know if I’m wrong about it”?

Full-circle beat: ask this as a genuine question, not rhetorically — a show of hands on “would your Day 1 answer survive a term of scepticism training” is a good way to end the content portion of the module. title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Political economy II: inequality, redistribution, housing
text:
Political economy II: inequality, redistribution, housing
If the poor outnumber the rich, and everyone gets a vote, why isn’t there more redistribution?

IMAGE — full-bleed background for this title slide. A recognisable “tax the rich” protest image (e.g. an Occupy-style “We are the 99%” placard, or a Robin Hood-adjacent visual) to put a face on the puzzle before any theory shows up. title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Key term: the median voter theorem
text:
Key term: the median voter theorem

Median voter theorem: in a majority-rule election between two parties, the winning policy is whatever the middle voter prefers — because both sides need that voter to win.


Apply it to redistribution: the median voter is poorer than the average voter — so should always want to tax the rich and redistribute down.

Why the median voter is poorer than the average: a national income distribution has a long right tail — a small number of very rich people pull the mean well above the middle. That gap between mean and median is the whole engine of the theorem’s prediction: the further the tail stretches, the poorer the median voter looks relative to the average, and the stronger their theoretical incentive to vote for redistribution.


IMAGE — inline chart, a stylised income distribution with a long right tail, mean and median marked. Doesn’t need to be real data — the shape is the point (mirrors what the notes suggest drawing on the board). Use as a small .absolute figure beside or below the definition.


Walk through the logic slowly once — it genuinely is elegant. Draw a quick income distribution on the board if you like: long right tail, mean well above median. That gap is the whole engine of the prediction.


Noah: earnest theory slide, good spot for a beat of yours — a joke about how “the middle voter decides everything” explains an awful lot of Irish coalition politics, or a quick aside on how un-median-voter-like an actual authoritarian election is (no theorem needed when there’s only one name on the ballot).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The prediction

More inequality → bigger gap between mean and median income → the median voter is relatively poorer
A relatively poorer median voter should demand more redistribution, not less
So: more unequal democracies should redistribute more. Inequality should be self-correcting, politically.


Meltzer & Richard’s (1981) formal version of an old intuition — a beautiful theory.

Land the word “beautiful” — it sets up the reversal on the next slide. This is the kind of clean, falsifiable, mechanism-first claim political scientists love to build models around.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Does it hold up?
Take the most unequal rich democracy — the United States — and the most redistributive — somewhere Nordic.

If the theory were right, the US should have the most aggressive redistribution: highest inequality, poorest median voter, biggest demand to tax the rich.


It has close to the least.

Let this land as genuinely strange, not as a gotcha. This is what “how do we know that” segments are for: a clean prediction, tested against real cases, and it just doesn’t fit. Ask: “so either the theory’s logic is wrong, or something else is intervening between what the median voter wants and what policy delivers.” That’s the whole rest of the lecture.


Kept this evidence beat to two slides (not a full data dive) — the brief flags this lecture as HDWKT-as-autopsy rather than a separate opener, so I folded it straight into the median-voter arc instead of giving it its own labelled segment up top. If Noah wants real cross-national numbers on screen (Gini vs. social spending as % GDP, US vs. Nordic vs. UK), that’s an easy chart to drop in here — flagging as a build option rather than inventing numbers.


IMAGE — inline chart, Gini coefficient vs. social spending as % GDP, US / Nordic (e.g. Sweden or Denmark) / UK. Source: OECD Social Expenditure Database or World Bank Gini data. Makes the “US should be most redistributive, isn’t” claim visible rather than asserted. Use as .absolute chart beside the two comparison paragraphs.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
So what’s actually going on?
The median voter could demand more redistribution. In most rich democracies, they mostly don’t. Why not?

Pause here properly — let someone answer before the next slide. Don’t reward the first plausible-sounding guess too fast; there are genuinely several right answers coming, and the room should generate at least two of them before you reveal.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Four things breaking the prediction

Who’s organised — few, coordinated rich vs. many, diffuse poor. A collective action problem (Lec 14) underneath the vote.
Veto players — a majority isn’t enough; redistribution must survive every veto point, and money can lean on each one (Lec 15).
Beliefs about desert — bad luck or bad choices? That belief shapes the vote, independent of income.
Cross-cutting identity — race, region, or religion can outweigh income, splitting “the poor” apart (Lec 7–8).


None of these are exotic — tools you already own.

Four mechanisms break the median-voter prediction. Who’s organised: the rich are few and easy to coordinate, while the poor are many and hard to organise — a collective action problem (Lecture 14) sitting underneath what looks like a simple voting decision. Veto players: even a determined majority needs redistribution to survive every veto point in the system, and concentrated money can lean on each one along the way (Lecture 15). Beliefs about desert: whether people think poverty is the result of bad luck or bad choices changes what they vote for, independent of their own income. Cross-cutting identity: race, region, and religion can matter more to people than income, splitting “the poor” into groups that don’t vote together (Lecture 7–8).


Explicit callback script for delivery — say these out loud, don’t let them stay implicit: “Collective action — this is Lecture 14’s corruption logic, wearing a different costume: individually, organising to demand redistribution is costly and uncertain, even if the group would benefit.” “Veto players — this is Lecture 15’s tool: it’s not enough for the median voter to want something, it has to survive every actor who can block it.” “Cross-cutting identity — this is Lecture 7 and 8’s material: if class isn’t the only thing people vote on, a ‘poor’ coalition can be split by race, religion, or nation before it ever forms.”


This slide is the engine room of the lecture. Take your time. The “beliefs about desert” bullet is a good spot for a quick, non-loaded example: attitudes to welfare in the US are famously tangled up with race (Gilens’ work on this, if you want a name to drop lightly — don’t build a whole segment on it).


Noah: 76 words — dense, but maps onto a named callback structure (Lec 7/8/14/15), so splitting would break it. Left whole with .breathe. Same call on “Who benefits from scarcity?”, “Who are the veto players?”, “Every party promises housing” below.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The American puzzle, named
The US has high inequality and many low-income voters who oppose taxing the rich.

Part of the answer: most Americans (accurately or not) believe they might get rich, or that the poor could work harder. Redistribution looks like punishing a future version of yourself.

This is the “tunnel effect” intuition (Hirschman) if you want a name for it, though you don’t need to cite it explicitly. The point for first-years: beliefs about mobility, not just current income, shape redistributive preferences. Keep this to one beat.


Currency check: is there a sharper, more current (2026) polling data point on US attitudes to wealth taxes or redistribution than the general “belief in mobility” framing? Textbook stops ~mid-2024 — worth a fresher hook if one exists by delivery.


IMAGE — inline chart, Pew Research (or similar) polling on US attitudes to taxing the wealthy / belief in economic mobility, ideally a 2025/26 wave if one exists (see currency-check note above). Use as small .absolute chart, corner of the slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Three bets, all placed decades ago, all still running
text:
Three bets, all placed decades ago, all still running
Rich democracies chose different welfare states, and then couldn’t unchoose them:

Nordic — universal, generous, high tax, high trust that the state delivers
Continental (e.g. Germany) — built around work status: strong insurance for workers, weaker for outsiders
Anglo-American (US, UK, Ireland-ish) — targeted, means-tested, lower tax, more contested legitimacy


Not “better” or “worse” — different political settlements, locked in decades ago.

IMAGE — inline chart, social spending as % GDP by welfare regime type (Nordic / Continental / Anglo-American), e.g. OECD Social Expenditure Database — the classic Esping-Andersen “three worlds” comparison. This is the slide the brief flags as closest to a taxonomy; a chart does more work here than a fourth bullet would.


Three bullets, two minutes, do not let this become a taxonomy march — that’s exactly the failure mode the brief warns against. The only point worth landing: these aren’t natural categories, they’re the frozen outcome of political battles (which party had power, when, and for how long).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Start with the shape of it
text:
Start with the shape of it
Ireland is a high-capacity state: reliable tax collection, a functioning bureaucracy, services most of the world envies (Estonia-vs-Lebanon, Lec 4).

And it has spent a generation being unable to build enough homes.


When a capable state fails for years, capacity isn’t the constraint — something is choosing this outcome.

This is the direct payoff of the “capacity ≠ political will” line parked back in Lecture 4 — say the callback out loud, by lecture number, not just in spirit. This is exactly the beat that lecture teased and refused to resolve. Resolve it now.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Who benefits from scarcity?

Existing homeowners — two-thirds of households. Rising prices make them richer; new supply nearby threatens amenity and property value.
Local politicians — blocking a development is visible and popular now; the citywide gain is diffuse, later, and someone else’s credit.
Residents near a site — easy to mobilise against one project. Future renters aren’t in the room yet.


This is concentrated interests beating diffuse interests again — recognise it? Lecture 14’s collective-action logic, same mechanism, different stakes.

Three groups benefit from housing scarcity, and each has good reason to organise against new supply. Existing homeowners — roughly two-thirds of households — get wealthier as prices rise, and nearby development (height, density, apartments) can threaten local amenity and property value. Local politicians are elected locally: objecting to a specific development is visible and popular right now, while the diffuse citywide benefit of more homes accrues to someone else’s credit, later. Residents near a proposed site are organised, motivated, and easy to mobilise for a single planning objection — the renters who might live there in five years are, by definition, not yet in the room to argue for it.


IMAGE — inline photo, a “For Sale” or “Sold” sign outside a Dublin period house — a concrete visual for rising prices benefiting existing owners. Use as small .absolute image, corner of the slide.


COLLECTIVE ACTION CALLBACK, explicit: the canonical phrasing across this term is “concentrated interests beat diffuse interests” — a small, organised group with a lot at stake per head wins against a large group with little at stake per head, regardless of whether the concentrated side is pursuing a cost or a benefit. In Lec 14, a small group of corrupt actors (high stakes each) extracts from an unorganised public (low stakes each). Here it’s the same mechanism with the concentrated side defending a benefit instead of extracting one: a concentrated group (existing owners, local objectors) protects scarcity value and local amenity against a diffuse, badly organised group (future renters, people not yet resident) who would gain from change. Same tool, same asymmetry — say that explicitly.


Fixed per fresh-eyes review (2026-09-03, §1 item 5 / §7 item 2): this slide previously framed its case as “concentrated benefit, diffuse cost” and called it “the mirror image” / “flipped direction” from Lecture 14, which put it at odds with Lecture 19’s claim of “the same asymmetry” as this slide. Standardised on the canonical phrasing “concentrated interests beat diffuse interests” (organised minority with high per-head stakes beats a diffuse majority with low per-head stakes) so this slide, Lecture 14, and Lecture 19 describe one consistent mechanism rather than mirrored or contradictory ones — the housing example is unchanged.


Don’t moralise this slide — homeowners objecting to a development next door is not villainous, it’s rational individual behaviour given the incentives. The point is structural, not a morality tale. That’s what makes it a political science lecture and not a rant.


Noah: 75 words — dense, but a tight 3-item list, left whole with .breathe. Part of the housing set-piece density call (see “Four things breaking the prediction” above).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Who are the veto players?
Recall Lecture 15: change requires every veto player on board.

Local councillors — can vote down or slow-walk local area plans and individual developments
Planning objectors — one well-resourced objection buys years of appeals. Lecture 14’s tribunals lived on this exact choke point: a veto is the thing worth buying
Coalition partners — housing policy has to survive the usual multi-party arithmetic (Lec 15)
Homeowners as an electorate — the biggest, best-turnout bloc in the country


More veto players, more places to say “not here / not yet / not like that.”

IMAGE — inline photo, a planning-application notice pinned to a site hoarding or fence (the public-objection-period kind), or the An Bord Pleanála / An Coimisiún Pleanála building signage. Makes “veto player” concrete rather than abstract. Use as small .absolute image.


Fuller wording of the trimmed bullets, if you want it back: “Planning objectors — a single well-resourced objection can trigger years of appeals (An Bord Pleanála / An Coimisiún Pleanála).” “Coalition partners nationally — housing policy must survive Ireland’s usual multi-party coalition arithmetic (Lec 15’s ‘who can dismiss whom’).” “Existing homeowners as an electorate — the largest, best-turnout voting bloc in the country.”


Why Lecture 14’s tribunals belong on this slide. The Mahon Tribunal ran from 1997 to 2012 — fifteen years — investigating payments to politicians in return for planning decisions in the Dublin area. Its final report, published in March 2012, described corruption running through the planning process, and made findings of corruption against a former government minister, a developer, a former TD and eleven councillors. The point for today is not the scandal. It is why planning: rezoning a field is a decision worth an enormous amount of money to one identifiable person, taken by a small number of local officials with the power to say no. That is the textbook definition of a veto point — and a veto point is exactly what a bribe is for. Lecture 14 showed you people paying to move a veto. Today’s slide shows you the same veto being used entirely legally, by objectors and councillors, for free. Same choke point, two different ways of pulling the lever.


Source, checked 2026-09-03: Mahon Tribunal established November 1997 (originally the Flood Tribunal), final report published 22 March 2012 — RTÉ News, 22 Mar 2012; TheJournal.ie summaries of the final report, Mar 2012; Britannica entry “Mahon Tribunal”. Findings of corruption against Pádraig Flynn, Owen O’Callaghan, the late Liam Lawlor and eleven councillors; the report rejected much of Bertie Ahern’s evidence but did not make a finding of corruption against him — say it that way if you name him at all, it’s the detail that gets misremembered.


This is the slide to slow down on — make them name a real example if you have one to hand (a specific stalled development, a specific planning appeal that ran for years). A concrete local case lands far harder than the abstract list. Cold-call: “why would a government that says it wants more housing still find it this hard to build?” Then land the tribunal callback explicitly: “remember Lecture 14, the planning tribunals? Ask yourself why the corruption in this country kept turning up in planning and not somewhere else. It’s on this slide: planning is where the veto points are, and a veto is the thing worth buying.” Corruption and NIMBYism are the same structural fact, approached from two directions.


Noah: the tribunal callback is drafted from sources, not from you — check my facts, and decide how far you want to push it. The strong version of the claim is that Ireland’s planning corruption and Ireland’s planning paralysis are the same institutional feature seen twice, which is a genuinely good line if you believe it. I’ve written it as a printnote and a delivery note rather than putting it on the slide, so it’s yours to promote or drop.


Noah: this is the natural slot for a live, current example — a specific stalled Dublin (or other city) development, a live planning appeal, or a 2026 headline about housing delivery numbers missing target. Swap in whichever is freshest and most locally recognisable to your students at delivery time.


Noah: separately, 87 words — the densest slide in this set-piece. Left whole with .breathe (same call as the other housing-set-piece slides) rather than split.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Every party promises housing. Delivery stays hard.
text:
Every party promises housing. Delivery stays hard.
What this explains that “the state is incompetent” doesn’t:

Ireland can run a modern tax system and a national vaccine rollout (Lec 4’s capacity claim)
Every government since the crash has campaigned on housing and missed its own targets
The thread isn’t administrative failure — the losers from more housing are organised and vote; the winners are diffuse and don’t


Politics, not capacity, is the binding constraint. That’s the whole lecture in one line.

The common thread across housing failures isn’t administrative incompetence — Ireland proves elsewhere that it can run a modern tax system, a national vaccine rollout, a functioning bureaucracy. It’s that the people who lose from more housing nearby are organised, local, and reliably vote, while the people who would gain — future residents, people not yet living in the area — are diffuse, often not yet resident, and don’t vote on the issue at all.


IMAGE — inline chart, annual housing completions vs. government targets, Ireland, roughly 2016–2026 (source: CSO housing statistics, Department of Housing, or a Housing Commission / ESRI report figure). Makes “missed its own targets” a visible line, not just a claim.


This is the thesis sentence — say it slowly, maybe even repeat it. If you want a single sentence students remember from this lecture, it’s this one.


Noah: 78 words — dense, part of the housing-set-piece density call (see “Four things breaking the prediction” above). Left whole with .breathe.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Could it be different?
Some cities and countries have built their way out of a housing shortage. What would have to change here — about who has a vote on any given project, or how many veto players get one — for Ireland to look more like them?

Cold-call, and push back on purely technical answers (“build more,” “cut red tape”) — ask them to name the political change, not the policy change: who would need to lose a veto, or gain a voice, for the incentives to shift? Good candidates to steer toward if the room stalls: giving future/non-local residents a stake in local planning decisions, national override of local objections, changing what counts as a “material” planning objection. Don’t need a right answer — the point is to make them reason in veto-player terms unprompted.


Live poll: “Would you support giving central government the power to override local planning objections to increase housing supply — yes / no / depends?” Tool for live polling still undecided (per the running placeholder across the course) — question is ready, wire up once the tool is chosen.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Key readings this week
Required:

Heywood & Laing, Politics (2025), Ch. 7 — remainder (backlash against markets/globalisation; use lightly for today, the redistribution material is mostly outside the textbook)

Candidates — not yet confirmed, flagging rather than assigning:

Meltzer & Richard, “A Rational Theory of the Size of Government” (1981) — the formal median-voter model
Iversen & Soskice, Democracy and Prosperity (selections) — why some rich democracies redistribute more than others


Heywood ch7 doesn’t actually contain a median-voter or welfare-regime discussion in any depth — it’s mostly varieties-of-capitalism and globalisation backlash (which Lec 17 already used). I’ve kept the textbook reference honest (says “remainder,” doesn’t overclaim what’s in it) and flagged Meltzer & Richard / Iversen & Soskice as candidates rather than confirmed readings, per the brief’s instruction not to invent readings as fact. Worth deciding whether this lecture gets a non-Heywood required reading, since the textbook genuinely doesn’t cover its core content.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Next: collective action at planetary scale
text:
Next: collective action at planetary scale
Lecture 19 — Climate as a collective action problem
Collective action has failed twice at home — corruption (Lec 14), housing (today). Next: the hardest version — free-riders are entire countries, losers not yet born.

Read ahead: who are the “existing homeowners” of climate policy — who benefits from the status quo, and who’s too diffuse (or not yet born) to organise against it?
See you Tuesday

What this lecture argued. The median voter theorem is elegant and mostly wrong in practice: more unequal democracies do not reliably redistribute more. We autopsied why — collective action, veto players, beliefs about who deserves what, and cross-cutting identity all bend the prediction between what a majority wants and what policy delivers. Welfare states are not natural categories but political settlements, frozen in place decades ago by whoever held power at the time. And Irish housing is the case that puts it all together: a demonstrably high-capacity state, failing for a generation, because scarcity has organised beneficiaries and abundance does not. Politics, not capacity, is the binding constraint.


Clean handoff — the bridge is explicit: same collective-action logic, bigger stakes, longer time horizon. If it lands, students should be able to predict the shape of the climate lecture before you’ve said a word of it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
