See you Tuesday

POU11011: Introduction to Political Science · Dr Noah Buckley · Trinity College Dublin · MT2026 Slides and readings: noahbuckley.me/teaching/pou11011 · Submissions: Blackboard


Reading for next time is on the module page and Blackboard.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Rules that bind rulers
A constitution is just paper. What makes it real is people willing to defend it.

IMAGE — full-bleed background behind this opening quote. A weathered/torn page of printed constitutional text, or a photo of people physically rallying to defend a constitutional court (e.g. the 2015-16 Warsaw “Committee for the Defence of Democracy” protests). Something that visualises paper vs. people. Source: Wikimedia Commons / Reuters archive. Use as ## Rules that bind rulers {background-image="w10-lec16-img/opener.jpg" background-color="var(--week-title-bg)"}.


Cold open, no admin yet. Let the line sit for a beat. Today’s whole lecture is one question dressed up in different clothes: when does a rule written on paper actually stop a powerful person from doing what they want? Sometimes it does. Often it doesn’t. We’re going to work out why.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Today

A question we parked — Lecture 10’s unfinished business, cashed in
Constitutions as coordination devices — not sacred texts
Judicial review — where courts get the nerve to say no
Cases: Poland, Russia, Israel, the US — and Ireland’s very different route


The big question: do constitutions limit power, or do powerful people just ignore them?

Judicial review is the power of courts to strike down laws or executive actions as unconstitutional. Political scientists don’t just ask whether a court formally has this power — they ask how we’d measure whether it’s real: does the court actually use it, and does anyone comply when it does?


Revision log, 2026-09-03

Light-touch pass: .breathe added to 8 dense list/closer slides for whitespace
Added todo humour slot on “Judicial review” (incl. Russia Constitutional Court option)
Added todo wry-aside slot on “Why does Ireland ask the people instead?”
Left “Israel” case alone deliberately — needs careful, neutral framing, not a joke slot
No text cut, split, or moved between channels
Density: 47.8 → 47.8 w/slide (unchanged)

Content pass, 2026-09-03 (second sitting, FRESH-EYES §2/§3)

New Russia case, written as a real draft — “The paper constraint that didn’t bind” (1993 suspension; 2020 amendments), placed between Poland and Israel. This is the §3 priority-4 slot. Every date and number web-verified; sources in the cc under that slide.
Retitled four noun-phrase headings as questions/claims: “Constitutions as coordination devices”, “Judicial review”, “De jure vs de facto”, “Rights: paper vs enforcement, completed”.
Killed the “What we did today” recap (a teaser follows it); its five bullets moved verbatim to a printnote on the closing “Next up” slide.
Wrote final wording for both live polls (tool still Noah’s call).
Not done here: FRESH-EYES §3 lists “Institutions as constraints — for good and ill” as a flat title, but that heading is in lec15, not this deck.



Four items, keep it moving. Standard “plan for today” bookend. Flag once, lightly, that judicial review is genuinely new territory for almost everyone in the room — LC Politics & Society doesn’t cover it, so don’t assume anyone has a head start here, but also don’t over-explain; treat them as smart adults meeting a new idea, not a hard one.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The question we parked
Back in Lecture 10, we told a story about Weimar Germany’s 1919 constitution.

It also had an emergency-powers clause, Article 48
By 1933, that clause dismantled everything else using the constitution’s own rules
A right on paper is only as strong as whoever enforces it — parked for today


So: who enforces it? Usually, the answer people reach for first is courts.

Weimar’s rights charter included free speech, free assembly, and equality before the law — genuinely progressive for 1919, one of the most progressive in the world. Article 48 let the president rule by emergency decree, bypassing the legislature, in a crisis; it was meant as a safety valve. By 1933 it was the exact mechanism the Nazi government used to suspend civil liberties and rule without parliament — legally, according to the constitution’s own text. The lesson: a right nobody is willing to enforce when a government decides to ignore it is not really a right.


This is the explicit bridge — say “remember Weimar” out loud, don’t assume they’ll make the connection themselves. If anyone asks why we’re not just teaching this as one continuous lecture: it’s deliberate, this is the same pedagogical move as parking Tilly’s evidence base, or parking the “whose state is it” theories — plant the seed, let it sit, cash it in later so it actually sticks.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Key term: constitutionalism

Constitutionalism: the practice of limited government — government institutions and political processes actually constrained by constitutional rules, not just described by them.


Every dictator you’ve ever heard of had a constitution too. Having a constitution and practising constitutionalism are completely different things.

This is the distinction the whole lecture hangs off. The USSR had a beautiful constitution — free speech, free assembly, the works — and none of it constrained anyone. North Korea has one now. A constitution is a document; constitutionalism is a norm about whether anyone treats the document as binding, including when it’s inconvenient for the people in charge. That’s the real variable we’re chasing today.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: A constitution is a shared expectation, not a sacred text
text:
A constitution is a shared expectation, not a sacred text
So don’t read it as scripture. Read it as a bet about what everyone else will do.

A constitution works when everyone expects everyone else to defend it
Break that expectation once and get away with it, and it collapses fast
That’s why constitutional crises so often look like a test of nerve, not a legal argument


Same document, rock-solid in one country, meaningless in another. The politics does the work.

“Everyone” here means officials, judges, opposition, and the public — a constitution binds only when all of them expect all of the others to defend it if it’s violated. Why does that expectation collapse so fast once it’s broken? Because enforcement is costly for whoever attempts it, and nobody wants to be the one who pays that cost if they don’t expect anyone else to back them up. If everyone believes everyone else will defend the constitution, defending it is cheap — you’re not alone. If everyone believes nobody else will, defending it is expensive and probably futile, so nobody does. This is a coordination problem: the constitution’s real strength depends on what everyone believes everyone else believes. The text of the document barely changes this dynamic.


Deliberately light-touch on the “self-enforcing constitution” literature (Weingast and others sit behind this framing) — naming the idea, not the theorist, keeps this at intro-level and avoids a citation that means nothing to a room with zero prior exposure. If you want to name-drop, this is the natural spot, entirely your call.


Good spot for a quick everyday analogy: a constitution is like a house rule everyone in a shared flat has agreed to — it only works if breaking it gets you shunned by your flatmates, not just noted in the rulebook. If nobody enforces the “clean the dishes” rule, it stops being a rule.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Can a court overturn a law the voters’ representatives passed?
text:
Can a court overturn a law the voters’ representatives passed?
Depends where you’re standing. Three answers:

Strong review — courts can strike down laws as unconstitutional (US, Germany, Ireland)
Weak review — courts can interpret, but not veto outright (UK)
No review — parliament is sovereign, full stop


Noah flagged this in his own notes as “the dullest, most list-like slide in the deck” — good spot for a joke or meme (a judge in a robe blowing a referee’s whistle; or a quick aside about a country whose constitutional court you find funny/absurd — Russia’s Constitutional Court has some good material here if you want it). Placeholder only, your call.


If a court has review power, it becomes another veto player — same tool as Lecture 15.

The UK has no single codified constitution, so there’s no fixed text for courts to check legislation against — that’s why “weak review” fits: courts can flag that a law seems to conflict with, say, the Human Rights Act, but Parliament remains sovereign and can rewrite the law regardless. A veto player (Lecture 15) is any actor whose agreement is needed to change policy. A court with strong review power is a veto player on ordinary legislation: pass it however you like, if the court strikes it down, it’s dead — you now need to satisfy the court, not just the legislature.


IMAGE — inline .absolute photo of a courtroom in session (e.g. the interior of the US Supreme Court chamber, or Ireland’s Supreme Court/Four Courts) to anchor this taxonomy slide with something concrete — the dullest, most list-like slide in the deck. Source: Wikimedia Commons.


This is genuinely new material for almost everyone — LC Politics & Society doesn’t touch judicial review, so don’t rush past it assuming familiarity. Walk through the Irish case concretely: parliament passes a law, the courts find it unconstitutional, the law dies, full stop — compare to the UK, where courts can say “this seems to conflict with the Human Rights Act” but Parliament can, in principle, just rewrite the law anyway. Different systems, genuinely different amounts of constraint.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Where do courts get the nerve?
text:
Where do courts get the nerve?
Judicial review on paper is easy. Making it bite needs three things to hold:

Independence — real autonomy from the executive
Compliance — a ruling only works if the losing side obeys it
Legitimacy — seen as a referee, not a partisan actor with a robe on


Lose any one of those and the “check” on power quietly stops checking anything.

“Independence” on paper usually means a constitutional line guaranteeing judges’ tenure or removal-for-cause-only. That’s necessary but not sufficient — a court can be formally independent and still fold under pressure if judges fear for their careers, their budgets, or their safety. All three requirements recur through today’s three cases: keep them as a checklist while we go through Poland, Israel, and the US.


This is where backsliding (Lecture 13) comes back explicitly: the first move in the capture sequence was always “courts and the referees.” Now you know why courts are step one — control the referee and you control what “unconstitutional” even means going forward.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Every constitution on Earth says its judges are independent
text:
Every constitution on Earth says its judges are independent
Which tells you almost nothing. So what would you go and count instead?

De jure independence — what the constitution promises on paper
De facto independence — what actually happens in practice
The gap is what V-Dem tries to measure — same move as Lecture 9’s indices


Don’t trust the label on the box. Go and check what’s actually inside it.

De jure independence is written into the text: judges serve fixed terms, can’t be removed without cause, and their tenure is formally protected. De facto independence is about what actually happens in practice — whether appointments are made on merit or used to reward loyalists, whether the executive can quietly expand the bench to add friendly judges (“court-packing”), and whether the court’s budget or resources can be used as leverage. V-Dem (Lecture 9) builds exactly this kind of proxy measure for judicial independence, because “independence” itself can’t be directly observed — you have to go looking for things that correlate with it: turnover rates, packing episodes, whether adverse rulings actually get enforced.


CHART — V-Dem’s judicial/high-court independence index plotted over time for 2–3 contrasting countries (e.g. Poland vs. Germany vs. Hungary), to make the de jure/de facto gap visible as a line dropping while the constitutional text stays unchanged. Source: V-Dem dataset (v-dem.net) or Our World in Data’s V-Dem explorer.


Explicit measurement callback — say it out loud: “this is the same move as V-Dem scoring democracy in Lecture 9, or the tax-take proxy for state capacity in Lecture 4. We can’t directly observe ‘independence,’ so we go looking for something we CAN count — turnover rates, packing episodes, whether rulings against the government actually get enforced — that’s plausibly correlated with it.” Keep this to one beat; it’s a callback, not a new methods lecture.


Live poll — final wording: “Ireland’s courts are — (a) independent on paper and in practice, (b) independent on paper only, (c) neither, (d) no idea, and that’s my honest answer.” Option (d) is deliberate: it stops the room guessing and sets up the “so go and count something” move. Tool still undecided — TCDpolls/Vevox is institutionally available (2 Sep Blackboard session); wording is locked.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Poland: capture, then partial restoration

2015 onwards: the government packed the Constitutional Tribunal and reshaped judicial discipline
Same capture sequence as Lecture 13: courts first, referee control makes everything downstream easier
After 2023, a new government tried to reverse it — messy, still not fully resolved


Poland shows capture isn’t automatically permanent — reversing it is much harder than doing it in the first place.

The 2015–19 changes lowered the retirement age for judges (forcing out sitting justices), gave the executive more control over judicial appointments and discipline, and packed the Constitutional Tribunal with loyalists. After the October 2023 election, the new coalition government tried to undo this — but ran into a genuine puzzle: many of the disputed appointments were made “legally,” under rules the old government itself had changed. Some judges appointed under the contested system are still sitting. Undoing capture through the same legal channels that enabled it turns out to be much harder than doing the capturing in the first place.


IMAGE — the Polish Constitutional Tribunal building in Warsaw, or a documentary (not dramatic) photo from the 2023–24 protests over judicial reform. Source: Wikimedia Commons.


Direct callback to Lecture 13’s “courts and the referees” — cold-call: “who remembers what step one of the capture sequence was?” This is the completed example, capture AND (partial) restoration, which Lecture 13 didn’t have room to follow through to the end.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Russia: the paper constraint that didn’t bind
text:
Russia: the paper constraint that didn’t bind
Russia has had a Constitutional Court since 1991. Twice it mattered — twice it lost.

1993 — the Court ruled Yeltsin’s dissolution of parliament unconstitutional. He suspended the Court and its chairman, Valery Zorkin, was pushed out of the chair
2020 — asked whether resetting Putin’s term count was constitutional, the Court said yes. It took two days
Same amendments cut the bench from 19 judges to 11, and let the president ask the Senate to remove one


Independence, compliance, legitimacy — the checklist from three slides ago. Score Russia on all three.

The 1993 episode: in September 1993 Yeltsin dissolved a parliament that was refusing to pass his reforms. The Constitutional Court, under its first chairman Valery Zorkin, ruled the decree unconstitutional and grounds for impeachment. Yeltsin won the ensuing armed standoff, suspended the Court on 7 October 1993, and Zorkin resigned the chairmanship (he was restored to the bench in 1994 and — remarkably — chairs the Court to this day). The 2020 episode: parliament passed an amendment “zeroing” Putin’s previous presidential terms, and Putin said he would accept it only if the Constitutional Court found it constitutional. The Court reviewed the whole amendment package and issued its blessing within two days, declaring the ruling final and unappealable. The same package reduced the Court from 19 judges to 11 and gave the president power to initiate the removal of high-court justices through the Federation Council. Note what did not happen in either case: nobody tore up the constitution. Both moves went through it.


Sources, all checked 2026-09-03: 1993 suspension — Washington Post, “Yeltsin suspends top court”, 8 Oct 1993; RFE/RL retrospective on the October 1993 crisis; Zorkin’s removal and 1994 restoration — Novaya Gazeta Europe profile of Zorkin, 19 Jul 2023. 2020 review — ABC News, “Russia’s constitutional court clears proposal to let Putin stay in power”, Mar 2020; Meduza, “52 pages for 12 more years”, 17 Mar 2020 (the two-day turnaround). Bench cut 19→11 and presidential power to initiate removal via the Federation Council — ICJ briefing paper on the 2020 amendments (Mar 2020) and US Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor, 15 Jul 2020.


Noah: this is your case, written from sources rather than from you — check my facts and put your own angle on it. Two things I’ve deliberately left out because you’d tell them better: what it was actually like watching the 2020 vote happen, and whether you’d read Zorkin as a captured judge or a sincere one who talked himself into it. Also: the twist worth landing out loud is that the same man chaired the Court in 1993 and in 2020.


IMAGE — the Constitutional Court’s building in St Petersburg (the Senate and Synod building on Senate Square — the Court was moved there from Moscow in 2008, which is itself a nice detail about distance from power), or a documentary photo of Zorkin. Source: Wikimedia Commons.


Sharpen the contrast with Poland: Poland’s capture was contested at every step and is being partly reversed. Russia’s wasn’t contested at all by the end — the Court did the paperwork itself, on request, in two days. That’s what the end state of the process looks like when nobody defends the coordination expectation. Callback to the “coordination device” slide: 1993 is the moment the expectation broke; everything since is just the consequence. Keep it to about ninety seconds — Poland is the case you teach, this is the case you land.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Israel: the fight happening right now
text:
Israel: the fight happening right now

2023: the government tried to strip the Supreme Court’s power to strike down decisions as “unreasonable” — removing a check mid-fight
Triggered the largest sustained protest movement in the country’s history
The fight is genuinely unresolved — you’re watching this case develop in real time


Judicial review’s third requirement — legitimacy and compliance — playing out live.

The 2023 protests drew reservists, tech workers, and ordinary citizens out week after week — the largest sustained mobilisation in Israel’s history. The fight has been reshaped repeatedly by events since 2023; treat this as a live case study, not a closed one.


Currency check: Israel’s judicial-overhaul fight has moved a lot since 2023 and will likely have moved further by November 2026. Confirm the state of play close to delivery — what’s been passed, what’s been struck down, what the current flashpoint is — before this slide goes up.


IMAGE — photo from the 2023 mass protests (e.g. the weekly Tel Aviv/Kaplan Street demonstrations, or reservists protesting in uniform). Keep it documentary and crowd-scale, not a partisan symbol. Source: AP/Reuters archive or Wikimedia Commons. Confirm the specific photo close to delivery alongside the currency check above.


Careful, neutral framing here — this is politically live and personal for some students. Present it as an institutional puzzle (can a court survive an attempt to defang it while the fight is happening?), not as a verdict on the underlying politics. Good moment to ask: “what would you need to see to know whether the court ‘won’ this fight?”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: The US: courts vs the executive
text:
The US: courts vs the executive

A recurring feature of the current administration: executive actions challenged in court, injunctions issued
This is the “compliance” requirement from two slides ago, stress-tested in real time
US courts have strong judicial review on paper — whether that constrains power depends on compliance


Same question, different starting point: a judiciary tested on whether “formally powerful” survives pushback.

A ruling only constrains power if the losing side treats it as binding. US courts can issue injunctions blocking an executive action — but an injunction is only as strong as the executive’s willingness to comply with it, and to comply promptly rather than slow-walking or narrowly interpreting it. That’s the same compliance requirement from two slides ago, now playing out in a system everyone assumed had it locked down.


Currency check, high priority: this is fast-moving and highly current-events-dependent. Confirm the specific, most illustrative episode (a named case or ruling, not a vague “there have been disputes”) close to delivery, and keep the framing institutional rather than partisan — the teaching point is about compliance and constraint, not about any individual administration’s merits.


IMAGE — exterior of the US Supreme Court building, or a photo of the specific relevant case’s courthouse once the currency check above identifies the illustrative episode. Source: Wikimedia Commons.


Keep this descriptive and institutional — the point for the room is “formal power on paper doesn’t guarantee real constraint,” using the most currently uncontroversial framing you can find. Don’t let this turn into a partisan discussion; redirect to the analytic question if it starts to.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Why does Ireland ask the people instead?
text:
Why does Ireland ask the people instead?
Ireland doesn’t lean on courts to defend the Constitution the way most democracies do.

Direct amendment — changing the Constitution requires a referendum, not just parliament or the courts
Why? — built into the 1937 Constitution from the start, beyond any one government’s reach
Result — Ireland constitutionalises social questions — divorce, abortion, marriage equality, blasphemy — and settles them at the ballot box


Noah: natural spot for a wry aside about Ireland’s enthusiasm for referendums generally (we’ve voted on blasphemy, we’ve voted on the Seville Boycott… whatever’s freshest). Leave it loose for delivery rather than scripting it here.


Most democracies leave hard social questions to courts. Ireland puts them to the people instead.

Ireland has held over 40 constitutional referendums since 1937 — a rate almost no other democracy matches. Divorce (1995), the Good Friday Agreement (1998), marriage equality (2015), and the repeal of the Eighth Amendment on abortion (2018) were all settled this way rather than by courts or legislatures alone. The requirement is baked into Article 46: any amendment needs a referendum, full stop. That single design choice routes Ireland’s hardest political fights through direct democracy instead of judicial interpretation.


IMAGE — photo from a referendum count or campaign, e.g. the 2018 repeal referendum result celebration in Dublin Castle courtyard, or “Yes”/“No” campaign posters from any referendum. Source: Wikimedia Commons / RTÉ archive.


This is the Irish hook the plan asks for — deliberately not “how is the Taoiseach chosen” (LC-recycled civics), but why does Ireland constitutionalise social questions and settle them by referendum, and what does that tell us about courts vs the public as a constraint? Genuinely distinctive; neither Comparative nor LC touches this angle.


Contrast concretely: in the US, abortion went to the courts (Roe, then Dobbs — decades of judicial back-and-forth). In Ireland, it went to two referendums (1983, then repeal in 2018) — direct, binding, and settled by the electorate rather than nine judges. Ask the room: which feels more legitimate to you, and why? There’s no right answer, that’s the point.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: So who actually enforces a right?
text:
So who actually enforces a right?
Back to Lecture 10’s Weimar question — and today we’ve seen three different answers to it.

Courts — if they’re independent, obeyed, and seen as legitimate (three requirements, three slides ago)
The public — Ireland’s answer: the constraint doesn’t depend on nine judges holding their nerve
Neither — Weimar’s answer. A right nobody defends is not a right, it’s a sentence in a document


Same conclusion as the coordination-device slide: the paper never does the work. Somebody has to.

Restated from the previous section: “if the people themselves have to vote on it” — already established on the Ireland slide two back, cut here for redundancy.


Ireland’s answer works because the “who enforces it” question is decided directly by the people who’d otherwise have to trust courts to do it for them — there’s no gap between what the constitution says and what the public is willing to defend, because the public wrote the change themselves. That’s a genuinely different solution to the same enforcement problem Weimar failed to solve.


This is the slide that closes the loop — say explicitly “this is the answer to the question we parked in Lecture 10.” Don’t introduce new material here, just tie the threads: Weimar (nobody enforced it), Poland/Israel/US (courts, contested), Ireland (the public, directly). Three different answers to the exact same underlying question.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: What actually makes a constitution stick?
text:
What actually makes a constitution stick?
Is a constitution stronger if courts enforce it, or if the public would overturn a violation by referendum? What happens if neither one will actually defend it?

Live poll — final wording (if you run only one poll today, run this one): “A right you actually care about is under threat. Who would you rather had the final say — nine judges, or fifty-one per cent of the country?” Two options, no fence-sitting; the split is the discussion. Tool TBC (Vevox available).


Pause properly here, let people actually answer before moving on. Push on the third option — “what if neither one holds” — with an authoritarian-constitution example (a country whose constitution promises free elections that never happen). Make them land on: it was never really about the document.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Next up
Next lecture — Political economy I: states, markets, globalisation
We’ve spent four lectures on how power is organised and constrained — institutions, veto players, constitutions, courts. Now: what power actually gets used for, starting with the economy.

Read ahead: Heywood & Laing Ch. 7 (start), skim for “varieties of capitalism”
See you Tuesday

What this lecture argued. Lecture 10 parked a question — a right on paper needs somebody to enforce it — and today cashed it in. Constitutionalism is not the same thing as having a constitution: the question is whether the rules actually bind the people in charge. Judicial review is a court’s formal power to say no, but three things have to hold for that power to be real — independence, compliance, and legitimacy. Measuring whether they hold means looking at the gap between de jure and de facto independence, the same move as measuring democracy in Lecture 9 or state capacity in Lecture 4. And there are at least three different answers to “who defends the rules”: contested courts (Poland, Russia, Israel, the US), the public voting directly (Ireland), and nobody at all (Weimar).


Signal the shift clearly: from how power is organised and checked (Lecs 3–16) to what power gets used for (Lecs 17–19). This is a genuine section break in the module — say so, it helps the “concept spine” hang together for them.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Corruption and state capture
When everyone does it, nobody can be the one who stops.

IMAGE — full-bleed cold-open background. Something visual and slightly noir for “envelope changing hands”: a close crop of cash/an envelope on a desk, or a dim corridor/office door, nothing cartoonish. Source: stock (Unsplash/Pexels, search “bribery” or “envelope money” turns up usable options) or a press photo with clear licensing. Use as ## Corruption and state capture {background-image="w09-lec14-img/opener.jpg" background-color="var(--week-title-bg)"} with the quote text kept in the yellow overlay style already on the slide.


Cold open. Don’t define anything yet — let the line sit. This is a lecture built to feel different from the last few weeks: less “here is a concept,” more “here is a trap, and you’re already in one somewhere in your life.” Corruption gets taught as scandal — a bribe, a resignation, a headline. We’re teaching it as structure: a collective action problem with a state attached.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Today

Principal–agent problems — why people in charge cheat the people they serve
Corruption as a collective action trap — first full outing of a tool you’ll see twice more this term
How do you count what people hide? — a short measurement beat, with a trick that’s actually mine
Cases — Ireland, Russia, Brazil (and FIFA, for fun)


Not a lecture about bad people — about incentives and institutions.

Corruption is often taught as a story about individual bad actors — a bribe, a resignation, a scandal. This lecture teaches it as a structural problem instead: “everyone does it” is self-sustaining because the incentives facing any one official make silence the individually rational choice, even when the outcome is worse for everyone collectively. That reframing, from bad people to bad incentives, is what makes it a much more useful thing to understand, because it tells you where the fix actually has to happen: in the structure, not in finding better people.


Guard-rail note, carried forward from the stub (per PLAN §3b, resolved — KEEP this slot): Comparative A&B runs a full Week 4 on corruption — definitions, grand vs petty, the macro-correlates literature (income, resource exports, regime type), and anti-corruption field experiments. It uses zero principal–agent framing, zero collective-action framing, and neither Ireland’s tribunals nor Lava Jato appear anywhere in its syllabus. So the lane here is real and doesn’t step on Comp’s toes: teach state capture as a collective-action trap, not corruption-in-general. I’ve kept measurement to the short beat the brief asks for rather than a section, and I’ve deliberately not used Comp’s studies (Peisakhin & Pinto, Ferraz & Finan) anywhere below — see the measurement slide for what I used instead.
One change from the old stub: I dropped the “Ukraine: the oligarch trap” case — it’s not in your current build spec (which names Ireland + Lava Jato + FIFA specifically). Update, 2026-09-03: Russia’s loans-for-shares has since been added as the second case, per FRESH-EYES §3, which makes four. If that’s one too many for fifty minutes, cut FIFA — it’s the “for fun” one, doing the least analytical work.


This is also, quietly, a “how do we know that” lecture in disguise — the measurement beat later on does that job (same move as Lecture 9’s democracy-measurement lecture: fold it into the substantive material rather than bolting on a separate segment).


Revision log, 2026-09-03

Added .breathe to five list-then-closing-statement slides (Today, principal-agent problem, measurement problem, list experiment, breaking the trap).
Principal-agent joke todo and Ireland Russia-slot todo already existed — not duplicated.
No text cut, moved, or split.
Density: 49.4 → 49.4 w/slide (unchanged).

Content pass, 2026-09-03 (FRESH-EYES §3, item 3)

Everything on the slide is from Daniel Treisman, “Loans for Shares” Revisited, NBER WP 15819 (2010): idea came from banker Vladimir Potanin; privatisation chief Anatoly Chubais agreed; 12 companies, ~$800m lent to the federal budget; first auction 3 November 1995 at Surgut, where the local airport closed for the day and the winner was the company’s own pension fund; loans unrepaid by September 1996, so creditors auctioned the stakes to themselves. Treisman’s revisionist finding is on the slide too, because it is the better teaching move: the largest discounts ($542m) went to incumbent Soviet-era managers at LUKoil and Surgutneftegaz, not to the famous oligarchs ($185m across Yukos, Sibneft and Norilsk Nickel).
Ireland slide upgraded and pointed forward to Lecture 18, per FRESH-EYES §3 (“planning corruption → planning veto points”). title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Picture this
You’re a customs officer. Your salary is modest. A shipping agent slides an envelope across the desk: wave the container through, no inspection, and this is yours.

Nobody’s watching closely enough to catch it every time. And here’s the thing — the officer next to you already does this. Has for years. So has the one before that.

IMAGE — inline .absolute photo, mid-slide. A shipping container yard or a customs checkpoint barrier, ideally with a uniformed officer waving a truck through. Source: Unsplash/Pexels (“customs checkpoint,” “shipping containers”) or a CBP/Revenue press photo with clear licensing. Keep it small and off to one side — this slide’s text is the anchor, the image just grounds it.


Concrete before abstract — this is the anchor scenario for the whole lecture, refer back to it. Ask the room: “would you take it?” Don’t shame anyone who says maybe — that’s the point of the lecture, the honest answer is usually “it depends who else is doing it.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Who’s actually working for you?
You hire someone to act on your behalf, with incentives you don’t fully control.

Principal — the public, the state, the taxpayer, the shareholder
Agent — the official, the officer, the politician, the CEO
The problem — the agent can profit by not doing what the principal wants


In a state, everyone is a principal to countless agents. That’s where corruption lives.

The principal usually can’t fully observe or verify what the agent is doing on their behalf — that information gap is what makes the relationship exploitable in the first place. In a state this problem multiplies: every citizen is a principal to a vast number of agents (officials, officers, regulators), and no single principal, and no oversight body, can watch all of them all of the time. That gap — the space where nobody is watching closely enough — is where corruption lives.


Close the loop back to the customs-officer example: principal = the state/taxpayers who want the tariff collected; agent = the officer; the problem = the officer profits by not doing the job, and the state can’t watch every crossing every day.


Noah: retitled from “The principal–agent problem” (2026-09-03) — its own todo called it the driest slide in the deck and the noun-phrase heading wasn’t helping. Still the natural slot for a wry aside about your own principal–agent problems (supervising, TAs, marking), or a quick “this is also just… your landlord” line, before it scales up to the state.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Key term: state capture

State capture: when private interests — business, organised crime, oligarchs — gain control over the state’s decisions, not through winning elections, but through bribery, intimidation, or quietly rewriting the rules in their favour.


It’s not “corruption” writ large. It’s the state working for the private interest instead of the public one.

Second contrast point (cut for length, restore if there’s time): “and it’s not ordinary lobbying either” — capture isn’t just naked self-interest lobbying, since lobbying at least runs through open, legal channels.


IMAGE — this is the driest slide in the lecture (a definition), and the best candidate for a visual anchor. A photo of an imposing state institution — a courthouse, a regulator’s headquarters, a parliament building — used inline .absolute, small, bottom corner. The point is just to give “the state’s decisions” a face before the cases arrive. Source: Unsplash/Pexels or Wikimedia Commons.


State capture is easy to confuse with two neighbouring ideas, and it’s worth keeping them separate. It isn’t “corruption” simply scaled up — a single bribe can be corrupt without leaving any lasting mark on who the state answers to, whereas capture changes the state’s decision-making on an ongoing basis. And it isn’t ordinary lobbying either, which operates in the open through legal channels; capture works through bribery, intimidation, or quietly rewritten rules, and its whole point is that it isn’t supposed to be visible.


Distinguish carefully from Lecture 13. Backsliding is regime erosion — courts, media, elections getting hollowed out on purpose by whoever holds power. Capture is different: the machinery keeps running, elections still happen, but who it’s actually working for has quietly changed hands. Say explicitly: “backsliding can create the conditions for capture — a captured judiciary is easier to build once courts are already weakened — but capture happens in perfectly normal-looking democracies too.” Brazil is your example of that: no coup, no backsliding, just an entire tier of politics and business bought.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The trap
Go back to the customs desk. Alone, you’re the outlier — easy to spot, easy to fire.

But if everyone on the shift takes it, for the same reasons — something changes.

Nobody can report it without confessing to it themselves
A code of silence forms — not organised, just the only rational move once everyone’s already in
Someone has to break first — meaning turning in your colleagues, your boss, maybe your whole department


Restore the rhetorical triple if you want it back: “…easy to spot, easy to fire, easy to make an example of.”


The logic scales beyond the customs desk. A single deviant is easy to isolate and remove — that’s what makes lone corruption fragile and rare in equilibrium. But once a norm of taking the envelope is shared across an entire shift, reporting it stops being an act of integrity and becomes an act of self-incrimination: nobody can name the practice without naming themselves as part of it. No one organised this silence — it emerges because, once everyone else is already implicated, staying quiet is each individual’s best available move, even though the group as a whole would be better off if the practice stopped.


Let the “someone has to break first” line land — pause before moving on. This is the emotional core of the lecture: it explains why decent people sustain corrupt systems without any of them being especially evil. Ask: “who here would be the one to break first?” Nobody answers honestly and that’s fine — that’s the trap working on the room in real time.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Key term: collective action problem

A situation where what’s individually rational for each person makes everyone worse off collectively — and no individual, acting alone, can fix it.


This is the first full outing of a tool that comes back twice more this term — remember this shape, you’ll recognise it wearing different clothes.

Portable concept — flag it out loud on the slide, not just in notes. The economist Mancur Olson is the name behind this if you want to drop it, but keep the definition doing the work, not the citation — first-years don’t need the Olson reading to get the logic. Say explicitly where it returns: Lecture 18 (why voters don’t get the redistribution the median-voter theorem predicts they’d support) and Lecture 19 (climate change — the same trap at planetary scale, farmers and free-riders instead of officers and envelopes). Per the concept spine in PLAN §3.


The reframe to land here: corruption isn’t sustained by everyone being greedy. It’s sustained by an incentive structure where whistleblowing is individually suicidal even when it would be collectively good. That’s why the fix has to be institutional, not “find better people” — swap out every corrupt customs officer for an honest one and the same structure produces the same outcome within a few years, because the structure is the problem.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Not just corruption — state capture
Same trap, whole institution instead of one customs desk.

Judges who won’t rule against a certain developer. Regulators who won’t fine a certain bank. Procurement officials who all know which firm “wins.”


Same silence, same “someone has to break first” — at state scale.

An organisation answering to almost nobody is the common ingredient across all four cases. This is the same collective-action logic as the customs desk, just scaled up from an individual transaction to an institution’s whole pattern of decisions. Instead of one bribe changing one outcome, the institution’s decision-making itself becomes bent around a private interest — every ruling, every fine, every contract quietly tilted the same way, over and over, until “capture” is a more accurate word than “corruption” for what’s happening.


This is the bridge slide between the individual-level collective action logic and the case studies coming up, all of which are capture at scale, not one-off bribery.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The measurement problem
You can’t just ask “have you taken a bribe?” Nobody who has says yes on a survey.

Indirect measurement — follow the money: wealth that outgrows salary
Perception surveys — how corrupt a country feels — reputation, not the thing itself
List experiments — the trick that actually gets closer to the true number


Same underlying problem as Lecture 2’s “how do you observe the third face of power” — the thing you want to measure is designed to be invisible.

Each of these methods has a real weakness — and the people most worth asking about corruption have the most reason to lie about it. Indirect (“lifestyle”) measurement catches only corruption that shows up as visible, traceable wealth — it misses officials who are careful, or who take non-monetary favours instead of cash. Perception surveys are easy to collect at scale, but what they measure is reputation: a country can be perceived as more corrupt than it is because of media coverage or stereotype, or less corrupt than it is because bad practices are simply well hidden. List experiments (next slide) come closest to an actual estimate, because they never ask anyone to confess to anything individually.


Explicit callback: measurement is a recurring thread (Lecture 2, Lecture 9’s democracy indices, this lecture, and the methods finale in Lecture 20). Say the thread out loud — “this is the third time we’ve hit this problem, and it won’t be the last.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: The list experiment, in one slide
text:
The list experiment, in one slide
Split your sample in two.

Control group — four ordinary statements (“I own a car,” “I’ve voted before”…); reports how many are true, never which
Treatment group — same list plus one sensitive item (“I’ve paid a bribe”); same count-only report
Nobody admits the sensitive item — but the average count is higher in the treatment group, by exactly that share


You never learn who did it. You do learn how many did.

The logic works because the treatment group’s extra reported item is anonymous by construction — no one outside the respondent knows whether their count went up because they voted, own a car, or paid a bribe. What lets you recover an estimate is comparing group averages rather than individuals: if the treatment group’s average count is 0.5 higher than the control group’s, and the only difference between the two lists is the sensitive item, then roughly 50% of respondents must have that item be true for them. Nobody is ever asked to confess anything, and yet the researcher walks away with a genuine estimate of how common the behaviour is — which is exactly the number a straight yes/no survey question could never get you.


Noah: this is the slot for your own list-experiment work — swap this generic walkthrough for your actual design and (if you’re comfortable sharing) your actual results. First-years respond really well to “the person teaching you this ran this exact study” — don’t undersell that you’re not just describing a technique, you’re describing your own research. Full version of this material returns in Lecture 20 (the methods finale) — this is the trailer, that’s the feature.


IMAGE — simple two-column built diagram (not a photo): “Control: 4 items, avg. reported = 2.1” vs “Treatment: 5 items, avg. reported = 2.6” with a bracket showing the 0.5 gap = estimated bribe-paying rate. Build directly in Keynote/Quarto rather than sourcing a photo.


If time is short, this is a compressible slide — the previous slide’s three-bullet summary can carry the beat alone and you can do the full walkthrough live on the board instead (chalkboard tool is wired for this deck).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Ireland: the planning tribunals
Not the Ireland they expect. Two tribunals — Flood/Mahon (planning), another on payments to politicians — spent over a decade on how Dublin land got rezoned, and who got paid.

Developers paid for favourable rezonings — worth enormous sums to whoever held the right land
1997 to 2012. €250–300 million. The longest, dearest inquiry in the state’s history — and it still only got part of the picture
Never one dramatic bribe: decades of small, deniable decisions


The verdict: corruption “affected every level of Irish political life.”


Hold onto planning permission. It comes back in Lecture 18 as a veto point.

IMAGE — inline .absolute photo, mid-slide. Dublin city/development skyline, or a photo evoking the tribunal era (Dublin Castle, where several tribunals sat, is a clean, recognisable option). Source: Unsplash/Pexels/Wikimedia Commons.


The two Irish tribunals referred to here are the Flood/Mahon Tribunal (planning corruption, running 1997–2012) and the Moriarty Tribunal (payments to politicians, particularly Charles Haughey and Michael Lowry). The planning tribunal sat from 4 November 1997 to 22 March 2012 — fourteen years, the longest and most expensive public inquiry ever held in the state, at an estimated €250–300 million — and its final report concluded that corruption “affected every level of Irish political life.” Together the two tribunals are widely judged to have established only part of the true picture — many of the people most centrally involved died, moved abroad, or simply declined to cooperate before the full story could be pinned down. What makes the Irish case pedagogically useful is that there was no single dramatic bribe anyone could point to as “the scandal” — the pattern was hundreds of individually small, individually deniable rezoning decisions, spread across decades and dozens of officials, that only looked like a system once you added them all up.


This is the deep case — the local one, and less familiar to them than they’d guess (they know Ireland-the-democracy, not Ireland-the-tribunal-country). Land the “small decisions, not one big bribe” point hard — it’s the collective-action logic made concrete: no single rezoning looked scandalous on its own, which is exactly why nobody broke the silence for so long.


Deliberately not naming individual politicians/developers on the slide to keep this a structural story rather than a scandal-tour — your call live whether to name names (Ray Burke is the standard reference point if you want one on record). Worth a currency check: is there a live planning-corruption story in 2026 worth a one-line update?
Dates, cost and the “every level of Irish political life” quotation verified 2026-09-03 against RTÉ’s report on the final report (22 Mar 2012) and the tribunal’s own publication date. The forward pointer to Lecture 18 is per FRESH-EYES §3: this is the module’s cleanest single link between the corruption block and the housing set-piece, and it was going unused.


The forward pointer is the line to say out loud, not just show: “the reason a developer paid for a rezoning is that planning permission is worth an enormous amount of money — and the reason it’s worth that much is that somebody can stop you getting it. Hold that thought. In three weeks we’ll ask why Ireland can’t build houses, and the answer will be the same institution seen from the other side.” That’s the corruption block and the inequality block welded together in two sentences.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Russia: how to buy a country in fourteen months
text:
Russia: how to buy a country in fourteen months

The Russian state is broke. An election is coming that the Communists are expected to win.


A banker, Vladimir Potanin, has a fix: we lend you money, you post shares in twelve state companies
~$800m lent. First auction, Surgut, 3 Nov 1995 — and the local airport closes for the day
The state doesn’t repay. The lenders auction the shares. To themselves


Nobody broke a law. That’s the point.

The scheme was proposed by the banker Vladimir Potanin and agreed to by Anatoly Chubais, then in charge of privatisation. Under it, the government handed usually-minority tranches of shares in twelve large state-owned corporations — including the oil companies Yukos, Sibneft, LUKoil, Sidanko and Surgutneftegaz, and the nickel producer Norilsk Nickel — to selected businessmen to manage in trust, in return for loans to the federal budget totalling about $800 million. If the loans were not repaid by September 1996, the creditors could auction the shares and keep 30% of any profit. The loans were not repaid, and the creditors sold the stakes, mostly to themselves, with competition minimised by careful rigging: winning bids came in barely above the starting price, rival bidders were disqualified on technicalities, and the very first auction, held on 3 November 1995 in the remote Siberian town of Surgut, took place on a day the local airport chose to close. The two-stage design was political as much as fiscal: the loans were made before the June 1996 presidential election and the share auctions happened after it, which gave every participant a direct financial stake in Boris Yeltsin defeating the Communist candidate Gennady Zyuganov. Yegor Gaidar, the former prime minister, later acknowledged that without the scheme Zyuganov’s chances “would have been substantially better.”


This is the Lecture 13 arc closing: the people who were made rich here are the same milieu the “vertical of power” spent 2000–2006 disciplining. Say that link out loud — the two lectures are one story told from opposite ends. The single best beat is the airport closing: it’s absurd, it’s specific, and it’s the exact opposite of a dramatic bribe. And the sting is the last line — the scheme did not require anyone to break a law, because the people writing the terms and the people bidding were the same small group.


Every figure verified 2026-09-03 against Daniel Treisman, “‘Loans for Shares’ Revisited,” NBER Working Paper 15819 (2010), https://www.nber.org/papers/w15819 — a good source precisely because Treisman is sceptical of the standard morality tale, so nothing here is borrowed from the polemical version.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: How do we know it was corrupt?
text:
How do we know it was corrupt?
Everyone knows loans-for-shares was the great robbery. Treisman went back and checked.

The execution was corrupt — rigged auctions, disqualified bidders, the airport
But the biggest discounts went to Soviet-era managers buying their own firms: $542m, against $185m for the famous oligarchs
The stakes were 8–10% of the stock market — not “the crown jewels”


The scandal is real. The story everyone tells about it is partly wrong. Both things.

Treisman’s re-examination concurs with the critics that the scheme’s execution appeared corrupt, but finds the conventional wisdom wrong on several counts: the stakes involved represented a relatively small fraction of the market (about 8–10% of total Russian stock-market capitalisation at the time); the pricing in most cases was in line with international practice once the companies’ enormous debts and the political risk of a Communist victory were factored in; the largest beneficiaries were entrenched Soviet-era industrial managers rather than the famous oligarchs; and the firms that ended up under oligarch control subsequently performed considerably better than comparable enterprises that stayed in state hands. For comparison, Treisman notes that roughly $2.5 billion of Gazprom stock was given away for privatisation vouchers around the same period, at least $1 billion of it to that company’s own management and workers — a larger transfer, attracting far less attention.


This is the deck’s second “how do we know that” beat and it’s worth the ninety seconds: it teaches scepticism about a story students are inclined to believe, which is much harder and more useful than scepticism about one they’re inclined to reject. The move to name: a scandal being real doesn’t make every claim about it true. Treisman didn’t defend the scheme — he checked the numbers and found the famous version overstated in specific, checkable ways.


Noah: check my facts / add your own angle. Treisman’s revisionism is contested, and you’ll have a view on how far to push it in front of first-years. If you’d rather run the standard account and skip this slide, the case above stands on its own — this slide is the optional sharpener.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Brazil: Lava Jato
“Operation Car Wash.” Started as a money-laundering probe at a Brasília petrol station. Became the biggest corruption case in Latin American history.

Petrobras (state oil) and Odebrecht (construction giant) ran contracts-for-kickbacks — routed through slush funds to politicians
Spread to eleven countries — Odebrecht had a dedicated internal division for paying bribes abroad
Over $13 billion implicated, hundreds of indictments, a sitting president impeached, a former president jailed


IMAGE — chart, priority slide. A simple map or bar chart of the eleven countries implicated in the Odebrecht bribery network, sized by amount paid — the original source is the DOJ/Brazilian federal prosecutors’ plea agreement data, widely reproduced (e.g. Reuters, ICIJ graphics). Use inline .absolute, right-hand side.


Operation Lava Jato (“Car Wash”) began in 2014 as a small money-laundering investigation and grew into the largest corruption probe in Latin American history. Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled oil company, and Odebrecht, its largest construction conglomerate, ran a system in which public contracts were routinely awarded in exchange for kickbacks, funnelled through slush funds to politicians and party officials across the political spectrum. The bribery wasn’t confined to Brazil — Odebrecht maintained a dedicated internal division, complete with its own budget and staff, whose job was structuring bribes to officials in other countries. The investigation eventually implicated more than $13 billion, produced hundreds of indictments, led to the impeachment of a sitting president, and put a former president in jail.


“$13 billion, eleven countries” is the number that makes them sit up — let it land. The word “division” is doing work: Odebrecht literally had an internal bribery department with its own budget and staff, like any other corporate function. That’s capture as organisational routine, not personal weakness — reinforces the whole lecture’s frame.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
FIFA, for fun
2015: FBI agents arrest FIFA officials in a five-star Zurich hotel, at dawn, over breakfast.

Votes for World Cup hosts, broadcast rights, sponsorships — allegedly bought and sold for decades.


Same shape as the others — fewer ministries, more tracksuits. Capture doesn’t need a state. Just an institution worth paying off, and nobody watching the watchers.

IMAGE — inline .absolute photo. The Baur au Lac hotel in Zurich (site of the 2015 dawn arrests) is a clean, recognisable, well-photographed building; alternatively a FIFA headquarters exterior shot. Source: Wikimedia Commons/press photo with clear licensing.


This is the light one — keep it fast, it’s the “and here’s the punchline” case, not a full worked example. Good place for a laugh line if you want it (“world football’s governing body ran itself like a Bond villain’s side hustle”). Don’t spend more than 90 seconds here.


Noah: with Russia added, this is now the fourth case and the deck’s obvious overflow valve. It does the least analytical work of the four — if you’re behind the clock, cut it here rather than trimming Ireland or Russia. Keeping it because “fewer ministries, more tracksuits” is one of the best lines in the module.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: What all three have in common
text:
What all three have in common
None of these were one bad actor. Each took years to run, involved dozens of participants who all knew, and only broke open when someone finally talked.
What made that person different from everyone else who stayed quiet?

Let this sit — don’t answer it immediately, it’s the pivot into “fighting back.” If you want a cold call: ask what it would take for THEM to be that person in their own future workplace. That’s also the seed for the closing “why should a first-year care” slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Breaking the trap
If the problem is the incentive structure, fix the structure — not just the people caught in it.

Reduce the payoff — transparency in procurement, less discretion for officials
Make breaking the silence survivable — whistleblower protection, independent prosecution
Change who’s watching — term limits, outside audits


It can be broken — usually by making honesty rational again, not by finding better people.

IMAGE — chart. Transparency International’s Corruption Perceptions Index, showing a country’s score over 10-20 years (Brazil post-Lava Jato is a good choice — score dips then partially recovers) to make “it can be broken, but it regenerates” visible as a real trend line, not just an assertion. Source: transparency.org CPI data, or Our World in Data’s CPI series.


Each of the three levers targets a different part of the incentive structure. Reducing the payoff makes the corrupt option less lucrative in the first place — transparent, competitive procurement and less discretion in officials’ hands both shrink the value there is to capture. Making the silence survivable addresses the collective-action trap directly: whistleblower protection, credible independent prosecution, and a press that can actually publish all lower the cost of being the one who breaks first, so that “someone has to break first” stops being such a costly move. Changing who’s watching increases the odds that any given act gets seen at all — term limits, rotation of officials, outside audits, and investigative journalists with nothing to lose all prevent the kind of long-tenured, unobserved relationships that let capture set in undetected. None of this is permanent: capture is a trap that regenerates if you stop watching, because the underlying incentive structure resets the moment vigilance lapses, which is why anti-corruption work is maintenance, not a one-time cure.


Close the loop to the principal–agent framing from early on: all three of these are ways of realigning the agent’s incentives with the principal’s interest, or making it easier for the principal to actually observe the agent. That’s the whole lecture in one sentence if you need it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Why should a first-year care?
You are going to work inside institutions — firms, hospitals, startups, maybe government — where “everyone already does it” will show up, long before it looks like Lava Jato.
How do you see the trap forming, and what does it cost to be the one who says something?

Make this land as personal, not abstract. Internship expense reports, a “everyone fudges the numbers a bit” culture, a professional norm nobody questions because questioning it is career-costly. Cold-call for examples if the room’s warm enough; if not, tell a version of your own “picture this” story from the top of the lecture as a bookend.


Live poll: “Have you ever gone along with something you thought was mildly wrong because everyone else was doing it too (cheating on a group project, splitting a bar tab unfairly, anything low-stakes)?” — yes/no, anonymous. Polling tool still undecided (Slido? Mentimeter? in-house?) — spec the question now, wire up the tool once decided. This is the one live-poll slot for this deck.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Dictatorships II: Elections, Information & Succession
Vladimir Putin has been in charge of Russia for 27 years. Nobody actually knows what happens the day he isn’t.

Cold open, no admin. Let it sit for a second — this is a genuinely unresolved, live fact about a huge, nuclear-armed state. Don’t over-explain, just let the strangeness land: we’re so used to democracies having a boring, guaranteed answer to “who’s next” that it’s easy to forget most of the world’s autocracies don’t have one at all.
Say the arithmetic precisely if anyone asks, because a first-year will: prime minister from 9 August 1999, acting president from 31 December 1999, president from May 2000. That’s 27 years as of August 2026 — including the four years, 2008 to 2012, when the job title on the door said “prime minister” and nobody seriously thought that changed who was in charge. The title swap is itself worth ten seconds: it’s the succession problem being postponed, not solved.


IMAGE — full-bleed background behind the cold-open title text. Vladimir Putin, formal/official portrait, or a shot of an empty Kremlin corridor — something that reads “power without a visible successor.” Source: kremlin.ru official photo bank (reusable) or Wikimedia Commons. Use as {background-image="w08-lec12-img/putin.jpg" background-color="var(--week-title-bg)"} on this title slide, with a dark overlay so the yellow quote text stays legible.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Today

How do we know that? Autopsying Lecture 11’s “elections are a strategic tool” claim — what’s the evidence?
Puzzle 1: why hold elections you could cancel?
Puzzle 2: the dictator’s dilemma — why does nobody tell the autocrat the truth?
Puzzle 3: succession — why does the whole system wobble when the leader ages?


Four items, say them fast, this is the recurring bookend. Signal explicitly: “one lecture, three puzzles, all about the same underlying weakness” — the through-line is that concentrating power to avoid being challenged is exactly what makes information and succession so hard.
