title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Last time: “elections are a tool of rule”
text:
Last time: “elections are a tool of rule”
Lecture 11’s claim: elections signal strength, distribute spoils, gather information, and act as a safety valve.

What would actually count as evidence for that claim?

Spoils should flow disproportionately to loyalists — not randomly
Opposition figures should genuinely believe they had a shot
Electoral autocracies should behave differently from non-electoral ones


Cold-call: “who remembers the four reasons autocrats hold elections from last time?” before revealing. The point of this segment generally: convert a plausible-sounding claim into a checklist of what you’d need to actually believe it — same move as Lecture 4’s Tilly autopsy.


Lecture 11 argued that autocrats hold elections because elections do real work for the regime: they signal strength to potential challengers, distribute spoils to keep elites bought in, gather information about where support is weak, and act as a safety valve that lets frustration vent through a ballot rather than the street. That is a strong claim, and it is worth asking what would actually count as evidence for it, rather than just a plausible-sounding story. Three things would need to be true: spoils would need to flow disproportionately to election loyalists rather than randomly; opposition figures would need to genuinely believe they had a shot, not just be going through the motions; and autocracies that hold elections would need to behave differently from ones that do not — more responsive to public opinion, less purely repressive.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Does it hold up?
Political scientists test this by comparing electoral vs. closed autocracies, and tracking regimes over time.

Finding, roughly: electoral autocracies last longer, and show co-optation (loyalists rewarded, “wrong”-voting regions starved).


But — the hinge for today — these elections sometimes blow up in the autocrat’s face.

Keep this compressed, one beat. Don’t cite specific studies by name here (that’s Comparative’s job with the full Boix & Svolik / Geddes literature) — the point is methodological: the claim survives comparison, but it has a failure mode, and that failure mode is where today’s lecture goes.


Political scientists have tested the “elections are a tool of rule” claim in two main ways: by comparing autocracies that hold elections against ones that don’t, and by tracking individual regimes over time as they introduce or abandon elections. The finding, roughly, is that electoral autocracies do last longer on average than closed ones, and do show the patterns of co-optation the theory predicts — loyalists rewarded with jobs and contracts, regions that vote “the wrong way” seeing less investment. But the same elections that deliver all these benefits sometimes blow up in the autocrat’s face, and that failure mode is where the rest of today’s lecture goes.


IMAGE — chart. Average regime duration/survival for electoral vs. closed autocracies, or a V-Dem “Electoral Democracy Index” style plot distinguishing autocracies with vs. without multiparty elections. Source: V-Dem Institute (v-dem.net) public data, or Our World in Data’s democracy/autocracy series. Use as an inline .absolute chart beside the text, not full-bleed.


Deliberately not naming the specific studies (Blaydes on Egypt, Magaloni on Mexico, etc.) to avoid drifting into Comparative’s Week 5 reading list. If you want a named citation here for credibility, Svolik’s The Politics of Authoritarian Rule is the standard cite but is also heavily used by Comparative — your call whether that’s a collision worth avoiding.


Noah: currency, and it’s a gift. Russia’s Duma election is scheduled for 18–20 September 2026 — about six weeks before you give this lecture. That makes “why hold an election you could cancel?” a question about something the room can still remember reading about, not a hypothetical. Worth one live slide: what was the reported turnout, what was the reported result, and what did it actually buy the regime? Confirm the official figures before delivery.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Puzzle 1: why hold elections you could cancel?
text:
Puzzle 1: why hold elections you could cancel?
If you control the army, the courts, and the television stations — why bother with a ballot box at all?

Short answer from Lecture 11: because they’re useful. But “useful” cuts both ways.

This is a genuine recap-as-launchpad slide — not new content, just resetting the puzzle so the dilemma in the next section lands as a twist on something they already accepted, not a new idea from nowhere.


Schedler’s framing (the “menu of manipulation” — autocrats don’t choose between clean elections and no elections, they choose how to rig: which stage of the process to manipulate) is Comparative’s assigned reading. Using the idea lightly here (elections aren’t binary rigged/clean, there’s a menu of dials an autocrat can turn) without building a slide around Schedler by name or citation.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The dictator’s dilemma
Elections serve autocrats by gathering information about support and co-opting elites.
But there’s a trap: the more honest the count, the more dangerous the information.

This is the spine of the lecture — slow down here. Set up the trap, then move to the next slide for the causal chain. The name for this — “the dictator’s dilemma” — is the portable concept; say the phrase itself out loud, it’s doing double duty as a study term.


Portable concept: the dictator’s dilemma (information that’s useful to gather is also dangerous to have). This is the lecture’s headline term — flag forward explicitly to Lecture 20, where the same information-asymmetry logic reappears as a general feature of politics, not just autocracy.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The spiral

An autocrat holds elections expecting to win comfortably — say, 70%
The actual result comes in lower — 65%, or worse
Now the autocrat knows the opposition is stronger than they thought
The next election is riskier — which tempts them to rig it harder
Which convinces the opposition the game is fixed, so it stops playing by the rules
Which makes the “safety valve” from Lecture 11 useless


Result: a spiral toward either much heavier repression, or losing control of the process entirely.

Walk the causal chain on the incremental build, one line at a time, and ask after step 2: “so what does the autocrat do now?” before revealing the rest.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: When the dilemma goes wrong: the electoral surprise
text:
When the dilemma goes wrong: the electoral surprise
Sometimes the miscalculation is too big to absorb — the election accidentally ends the regime.

The autocrat calls the election confident of victory, or the fraud staying hidden
The result — or the fraud needed to fake it — is undeniable, even to the regime’s base
Security forces or elites, watching the result, decide the game is up and stop enforcing it


The information the election was supposed to safely extract turns out public and impossible to walk back.

This is the “surprise” pattern — the dilemma isn’t hypothetical, it periodically actually breaks regimes. Good place to slow down and let the case example do the work.


Noah: drop in the specific case here — the classic candidates are the Philippines 1986 (Marcos), Serbia 2000 (Milošević), or Georgia 2003 (Rose Revolution) — any one where the electoral result or the visible ballot-stuffing was the actual trigger for collapse. Pick whichever you can narrate in under two minutes with a concrete detail (a photograph, a phrase, a specific vote count) — that’s what makes it stick for first-years.


IMAGE — crowds in the street reacting to a contested vote count, tied to whichever case Noah picks in the todo above (Manila 1986, Belgrade 2000, or Tbilisi 2003 all have strong photo archives). Source: AP/Getty editorial archive or Wikimedia Commons. Use as an inline .absolute image, right-hand side of the slide — visual anchor for “the information got out and couldn’t be put back.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Puzzle 2: nobody tells the autocrat the truth
text:
Puzzle 2: nobody tells the autocrat the truth
An autocrat surrounded by loyalists lives inside an information bubble — bad news gets filtered before it reaches the top.

So how does an autocrat ever find out what people actually think of them?

Let them sit with this before revealing anything. Answers involve: elections (risky, as just covered), purges/reshuffles to test loyalty, competing intelligence services, and the inner family circle. All are partial and all are dangerous in their own way — that’s the point of the next slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Why nobody tells you

Sycophancy — good news travels fast; bad news gets buried on the way up
The loyalty-testing problem — you can’t tell loyalty from competence, so you purge and reshuffle constantly, just in case


Both of these are people problems. The next two are worse: they’re built into the machinery.

Two bullets, then the hinge line. Don’t rush — the “you can’t tell loyalty from competence” point is genuinely interesting and students haven’t met it: the better an official is at their job, the more they look like a threat.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
And the numbers lie too

Competing agencies — military, secret police and party all report to the autocrat, and all shade the truth to protect their own budgets
Falsified statistics — officials report the numbers their boss wants; the distortion compounds at every level up the chain


The paradox: autocrats end up less informed than democratic leaders, despite having far more power.

The falsified-statistics bullet is the connective tissue to the reporting example on the next slide — don’t let it feel like a throwaway, it’s doing real work. The final line is the payoff — more power, worse information — let it land as a genuine paradox, not just a summary.


Split from a single four-bullet slide (2026-09-03) that was the deck’s densest. The break is at the people/machinery join, which is also the pedagogically useful one: the first two mechanisms are about individuals behaving rationally, the second two are about a system producing bad numbers even when nobody is lying on purpose.


Four mechanisms explain why the truth struggles to reach an autocrat. Sycophancy: good news gets reported quickly, while bad news gets softened, delayed, or buried entirely before it reaches the top. The loyalty-testing problem: it is genuinely hard to tell whether an official is loyal or merely very good at performing loyalty, so autocrats respond by purging and reshuffling constantly, just in case. Competing agencies: the military, the secret police, and the party all report to the autocrat, all compete with one another for standing, and all have reasons to shade what they say. The falsified-statistics problem: local officials report the growth numbers, harvest yields, or case counts their superiors want to hear rather than the real ones, and the distortion compounds at every level up the chain. Put together, the paradox is that autocrats often end up less informed about their own country than democratic leaders, despite having vastly more power over it.


IMAGE — diagram. This is the most taxonomy-like slide in the deck and would benefit most from a visual: a simple pyramid or funnel showing “truth” narrowing as it moves up through layers labelled local official → agency → inner circle → autocrat, getting thinner (more filtered) at each level. Likely custom-built in Keynote/PowerPoint rather than sourced — no existing chart does this well.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: The numbers get better every step up the chain
text:
The numbers get better every step up the chain

Local officials are evaluated — sometimes punished — based on the numbers they report upward
So they have every incentive to report good numbers, true or not
Multiply that up a chain of provinces and ministries, and the number reaching the top can be badly wrong


Several authoritarian states’ early COVID-19 reporting is argued to illustrate this: local pressure to look competent, distorting what the centre sees.

Keep this generic-but-concrete rather than pinning it on one named country in the delivered version if you’d rather not — the mechanism (falsified statistics compounding up a hierarchy) is the point, the specific country is a todo below for you to firm up or swap.


Local officials are typically evaluated — and sometimes punished — based on the numbers they report upward, whether that’s economic growth, harvest yields, or public health data. That gives them every incentive to report good numbers whether or not the numbers are true. Multiply that incentive up a chain of provinces, ministries, and regions, and the figure that finally reaches the centre can be badly wrong. Several authoritarian states’ early COVID-19 case-count reporting is argued to illustrate exactly this dynamic: local pressure to look competent, distorting the picture the centre actually receives.


IMAGE — chart. Officially reported vs. independently estimated figures for some autocratic-state statistic where the gap is well documented (e.g. excess-mortality estimates vs. official COVID death counts, or official vs. independent GDP growth estimates). Source: The Economist’s excess-mortality tracker, WHO, or the original paper behind whichever case Noah settles on in the todo above. Use as an inline .absolute chart.


Noah: decide whether to name a specific country/case for the COVID reporting example, or keep it as the generic mechanism. If you want to name one, this needs a source you’re comfortable defending live — flagging rather than asserting a specific country’s numbers as fact.


Currency check: any 2026-fresh example of a government’s own statistics turning out to be wildly off from independent estimates would work here too, and would land better with a live class than a 2021 COVID reference. Swap if you find one.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: How do you ever find out what people really think?
text:
How do you ever find out what people really think?
If elections are risky and the bureaucracy filters truth out, what’s left?

Family and inner circle — candid talk might happen, but power’s main qualification becomes blood, not competence
Security services as a check — but they can lie too, protecting their own budget
Watching indirect signals — protest size, informal economic activity, out-migration — proxies harder to fake than a survey


Every option here trades off getting the truth against staying safe.

If elections are too risky to use as a truth-detector and the bureaucracy filters honest reporting out before it arrives, what options does an autocrat actually have left? The family and inner circle is one place candid talk might happen, but ruling through relatives means the main qualification for power is blood, not competence. Security services can act as a check, but they can lie too — reporting “we have it under control” protects their own budget and standing whether or not it’s true. A third option is watching indirect signals: protest size, informal economic activity, migration out of a region — proxies for discontent that are harder to fake than a survey response. Every one of these options is a compromise between getting the truth and staying safe.


This is Noah’s own research territory — preference falsification and how researchers try to get around exactly this problem is his area. Good spot to gesture forward: “this is basically the same puzzle I run into in my own research — how do you find out what people in an autocracy actually think, when saying it honestly could get them in trouble?”


Noah: this is the natural spot for a one-line teaser of your own list-experiment work (full version lands in Lecture 14/20) — even just “I actually design surveys that try to solve exactly this problem, more on that later in the term” would seed it nicely without derailing the lecture.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Puzzle 3: what happens when I’m gone?
text:
Puzzle 3: what happens when I’m gone?
An autocracy built on personal rule has no built-in answer. And the leader can’t safely build one — because anyone credible enough to inherit is credible enough to replace you early.

Let the trap land before you give them the routes out. This is the flip side of the information problem, and it’s the same root: concentrating power to avoid being outmanoeuvred is exactly what leaves no institution standing that could manage your exit.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Three routes out, all bad

Institutional — “the deputy takes over.” But why would rivals with tanks accept that?
Competitive — rivals fight it out openly; the strongest wins, often violently
Family — power passes to a relative. Clear, if they can build a credible claim to rule


When a succession does go smoothly, it’s because rivals found a way to credibly commit to the outcome.

Flip side of the information problem, and say so explicitly: autocrats concentrate power because they’re worried about being outmanoeuvred — but that same concentration is exactly what guarantees a crisis when they leave. This is the lecture’s second portable concept.


Autocracies built around one dominant, personalist leader have no good built-in answer to a basic question: what happens when that person is gone? There are three broad routes. Institutional succession, where a rule specifies that a deputy or designated heir takes over — but this only works if rivals who control tanks and loyal officers actually accept it, which they have no guaranteed reason to do. Competitive succession, where rivals fight it out openly and the strongest wins; this often means real instability and violence. And family succession, where power passes to a son, daughter, or other relative — which buys a clear answer to “who’s next,” but only if that person can build a credible claim to actually rule, not just a hereditary one. Most successions are fraught precisely because none of these routes is automatic. When they do go smoothly, it is usually because rivals have found some way to credibly commit to accepting the outcome in advance.


IMAGE — a concrete family-succession case for the third bullet: a photograph of a dynastic power transfer (e.g. Kim Jong-un’s succession in North Korea, or a Gulf monarchy’s crown-prince investiture). Source: state media stills via Wikimedia Commons, or AP/Getty editorial. Use as an inline .absolute image beside the bullet list.


Callback to Lecture 8’s credible commitment problem (used there for ethnic power-sharing) — same underlying mechanic: rivals can’t trust a promise when there’s no institution to enforce it if the new leader breaks it. Naming the callback explicitly on the slide, per the brief’s “concept callbacks said out loud” rule.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Why democracies don’t have this problem (as badly)
text:
Why democracies don’t have this problem (as badly)

Noah: earnest, flat slide by design (it’s a short bridge) — natural spot for a quick aside or joke about how boring Irish/Western succession fights look by comparison, if you want one before the Russia slide that follows.

Democracies “solve” succession through elections: boring, regular, and — crucially — everyone agrees on the rule in advance.

Autocracies rarely have an equivalent everyone trusts. Which is why many destabilise not when the leader is strong, but the moment they’re visibly ageing, ill, or gone.

Good spot for a rhetorical beat: “notice that the boring, repeatable, faintly annoying thing about democracy — you have to have an election again in four years whether you like it or not — is also its biggest structural advantage over autocracy.” Ties back to any “democracy is inefficient” framing from earlier lectures if you’ve used it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: The live case: Russia’s succession question
text:
The live case: Russia’s succession question
In charge since August 1999 — 27 years, as of this August — with no mechanism he and Russia’s elites visibly trust for what comes next.

No strong single institution (party, legislature) sits above personal loyalty to him
No successor has been allowed to build enough independent standing to inherit power safely
Elites face exactly the credible-commitment problem from two slides ago: whoever comes next might turn on them


Not a prediction of collapse — personalist regimes can engineer orderly-looking transitions too. It’s a description of why the question stays genuinely unresolved.

Be careful with tone here — this is live political analysis about a real, powerful, currently-ruling head of state, not a historical case study. Keep it descriptive (why the mechanism is absent) rather than predictive (what will happen). Good moment to note explicitly that plenty of informed people disagree about how this resolves — that’s honest, not evasive.


Vladimir Putin has led Russia, as either president or prime minister, continuously since August 1999 — 27 years as of November 2026, four of them (2008–2012) spent formally as prime minister under President Medvedev without anyone seriously believing that changed who was in charge — with no clear constitutional mechanism that both he and Russia’s elites visibly trust to govern what happens after him. Three things compound the problem: no strong single institution, whether a party or a legislature, sits above individual loyalty to him personally; no obvious successor has been allowed to build enough independent standing to inherit power safely, since a credible rival is also a threat; and the elites around him face exactly the credible-commitment problem introduced two slides ago — whoever comes next might turn on the people who backed the old guard. None of this is a prediction of collapse; personalist regimes can and do engineer orderly-looking transitions. It is a description of why the succession question stays genuinely, currently unresolved.


IMAGE — Vladimir Putin, a recent official photograph (2025-26), or a Kremlin exterior/interior shot suggesting concentrated, opaque power. Source: kremlin.ru official image bank (reusable) or Wikimedia Commons. Use as an inline .absolute image, upper-right of the slide.


Currency check (September 2026): this whole slide needs a freshness pass before delivery — anything material changed about Putin’s health, an named successor, constitutional changes, or actual succession-adjacent events since the textbook’s mid-2024 cutoff should be folded in here.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: What makes a succession actually stick?
text:
What makes a succession actually stick?
When an autocrat does die or step aside and the state doesn’t collapse — what made it work?

(Hint: not charisma, not bloodline alone — institutional design, and a bargain among the elites who stayed.)

Let them guess before revealing. Point toward: a ruling party or institution that’s genuinely stronger than any one leader, some kind of pre-agreed (even if informal) succession procedure, and a credible signal that the new leader will honour existing elite deals rather than purge everyone who backed a rival.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Two contrasting cases

A monarchy with clear succession rules (e.g. a Gulf state): the ruling family functions as the institution — everyone already knows whose turn is next
A one-party system with internal rules (e.g. China or Vietnam): power passes through party institutions, not just to whoever seizes the palace — messier behind closed doors, but not a pure vacuum


Both are still autocracies — but both have found something that functions like an institution, even without elections.

Two cases show what “something that functions like an institution” can look like short of elections. In a monarchy with clear succession rules — a Gulf state, for instance — the ruling family itself functions as the institution: everyone already knows, and broadly accepts, whose turn is next, which removes most of the guesswork that plagues personalist regimes like Russia’s. In a one-party system with internal rules — contemporary China or Vietnam’s party structures, for example — power formally passes through party institutions rather than simply to whoever seizes the palace. It is messier and more contested behind closed doors than it looks from outside, but it is not a pure power vacuum either. Both remain autocracies, but both have found some substitute for the “boring, agreed-in-advance” mechanism that elections give democracies.


IMAGE — two small inline images side by side: (1) a Gulf monarchy succession/investiture ceremony (e.g. a crown-prince photograph), and (2) a Chinese or Vietnamese Communist Party Congress hall shot. Source: state media / Wikimedia Commons / Getty editorial. Use as paired .absolute images, one per case, so the contrast reads visually as well as textually.


The point isn’t “monarchies and one-party states have solved succession” — it’s that some kind of institution, even a thin or informal one, beats having none at all. Contrast implicitly with the Russia case just covered, which currently lacks either.


Kept both cases generic/structural rather than naming a single dramatic transition (e.g. a specific succession crisis) to stay inside the “Russia and Gulf monarchies are free, China is Comparative’s” guard rail — the China reference here is deliberately about party structure, not the censorship/control material Comparative owns, but flagging in case you’d rather cut it and keep this to Gulf monarchies alone.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Same root, three puzzles

Elections that could inform and legitimate you can also expose and doom you
Loyalists who could tell you the truth have every reason not to
Rivals who could inherit power peacefully have every reason not to trust the deal


Every one of these traces back to the same thing: concentrating power to avoid being challenged is exactly what makes it impossible to trust anyone else with information, or with the succession.

This is the lecture’s closing insight, said explicitly rather than left implicit — the brief’s own note that this deck is “droppable” makes it more important, not less, that the underlying logic is stated clearly in one place in case Noah trims elsewhere. Land this slowly.


Flex note (from the plan): this lecture is marked droppable in PLAN-MT2026.md if the two-lecture autocracy block feels indulgent once the term is running. If cut, the material that MUST survive into Lecture 11 is: the dictator’s dilemma (one slide) and a one-line mention that succession is unsolved in personalist regimes — everything else here (the electoral-surprise case, the information-filtering mechanisms, the Russia deep-dive, the two-case succession comparison) can go. That reclaims the slot for the identity block (Lecture 7–8 area), per the plan’s note that dropping this buys back “identity III.”


Guard rail — from PLAN-MT2026.md §3b: Comparative’s Week 5 is a full week on autocracy, assigning Schedler’s “menu of manipulation,” Morgenbesser, Pepinsky, Magaloni on the PRI, Geddes/Frantz/Wright, Boix & Svolik, Levitsky & Way, King/Pan/Roberts, and Greitens. Intro stays conceptual: the dictator’s dilemma and the succession problem as puzzles, not a literature review. Cases here are Russia and Gulf monarchies (free); Mexico/PRI and China-censorship belong to Comparative — the one Chinese reference on this deck (party succession structure) is deliberately about institutional form, not the censorship/information-control material Comparative owns, and is cc-flagged above for Noah to cut if he wants a cleaner boundary.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Live poll

Live poll — question written, tool still undecided (TCDpolls/Vevox is the presumed answer; Noah decides). Run it immediately after “The spiral,” before the electoral-surprise slide.
“You’re the autocrat. Your pollsters privately tell you your real support is 55%. What result do you announce?”

55% — the truth
65% — comfortable, believable
85% — unambiguous, nobody challenges it
99% — total

Then show the distribution and work backwards: every answer above the truth costs you information, and every answer near the top tells your own officials that honest numbers are unwelcome — which is the dictator’s dilemma arriving in the room rather than on a slide. Cheap, fast, and it makes the abstraction personal.


Keep this to three minutes. The teaching move is the debrief, not the vote: whatever the room picks, ask what that number does to the next person who has to report bad news upward.

Heywood & Laing, Politics (2025), Ch. 5 — remainder (personalist regimes, electoral authoritarianism, succession)

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
For next lecture
Lecture 13 — Democratic backsliding
Think about: Lectures 11–12 showed why autocracy is fragile — bad information, no clean succession rule. Now flip the question: what happens when an elected leader decides, slowly and mostly legally, to stop respecting the rules that would let voters remove them?
Reading: on the module page and Blackboard.
See you Tuesday

Bridge line to say out loud: “we’ve spent two lectures on how dictatorships are built and how they wobble — now we ask the reverse question: how do democracies quietly turn into the thing we’ve just been describing?” That’s backsliding: not a coup, a legal-looking hollowing-out, one institution at a time.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Democracy: Why It Emerges, Why It Survives
text:
Democracy: Why It Emerges, Why It Survives
If democracy is just a set of rules, they should be easy to switch off whenever an autocrat gets fed up. Most of them don’t get switched off. Why?

Cold open, no admin. Last lecture (9) was definitions and measurement — what democracy IS. This one is why it happens and why it lasts. Let the question sit a beat before moving.


IMAGE — full-bleed opener background. Long queues of voters on election day — the classic 27 April 1994 South African election photos work well (crowds stretching for blocks, first democratic vote), and quietly seeds today’s central case before it’s named. Source: AP/Getty archival or IEC South Africa archives (rights-check before use). Use as {background-image="w06-lec10-img/opener.jpg"} on this slide; keep the gold question text overlaid on top.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The plan for today

How do we know that? Richer countries look more democratic — which way does the arrow run?
Why does democracy emerge — two families of answer, in outline
Why does democracy survive — where we spend most of today
The unfinished business: rights on paper vs. rights that hold


Revision log, 2026-09-03
Content pass, 2026-09-03 (FRESH-EYES §2/§3)

Split the elite-bargains slide (its own todo called it the densest in the deck): mechanism on one slide, the “I won’t jail you if I win” payoff as its own quote slide.
Added Russia 1993 as a drafted case slide — decree 1400, the shelling of the White House, the December constitution — answering the standing todo that asked for a post-Soviet case and noted a failed bargain would teach better than a third successful one. All facts web-verified; sources in the cc.
Confirmed the Moncloa fix stands: the slide describes the Pacts as the October 1977 economic and social package, with the amnesty law and 1978 constitution as separate later steps. Correct as written; no change.

Killed “What we did today” (a teaser follows); bullets moved to printnote on “Next up”.

Earlier this day

Trimmed on-slide text on 6 overweight slides (elite bargains, “only game in town”, armies staying home, institutions sticky, two faces, rights enforcement) — cut clauses already covered in printnote, none deleted
Added reading-week logistics + delivery note to “Next up”
Density: 48.8 → 47.0 w/slide (22 → 22 slides)



Four items, read fast. Flag out loud that today is deliberately survival-heavy — say “we’re going to go quickly through why democracy shows up, and slowly through why it sticks around, because that second question is the more interesting one and the one your textbook undersells.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Richer countries look more democratic
GDP per capita vs. democracy score (V-Dem, from last lecture), every country on earth: rich countries cluster near the democratic end.

So: does wealth cause democracy? Or does democracy cause wealth?

Plotting GDP per capita against a country’s V-Dem democracy score — the same measure introduced in Lecture 9 — produces a real empirical pattern: richer countries cluster toward the democratic end of the scale, poorer countries toward the non-democratic end. The relationship isn’t perfect (there are rich non-democracies and poor democracies) but it is strong enough that political scientists have spent decades arguing over what it means.


IMAGE — chart. A scatterplot: GDP per capita (x-axis, log scale) vs. V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index (y-axis), one dot per country, visible upward-sloping cloud. Source: build from V-Dem + World Bank data, or adapt an Our World in Data chart (ourworldindata.org has a near-identical one on its democracy topic page). Doesn’t need to be fancy — the point is “look, there’s a pattern,” not a publication-quality figure. Use full-width, replacing the current text-only slide body.


Explicit callback: this is the SAME “which way does the arrow run?” question from Lecture 3’s McCombs & Shaw segment (did the news set the public’s agenda, or follow it?). Say so out loud — the measurement/causation thread is deliberate and pays off fully in Lecture 20. Then ask the room: give me a story for wealth-causes-democracy, then a story for democracy-causes-wealth (secure property rights, courts that enforce contracts, less looting by rulers who can be voted out). Both are plausible. That’s exactly the problem.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Does money make democracy, or does democracy find money?
text:
Does money make democracy, or does democracy find money?

Wealth causes democracy: richer societies produce citizens who demand a say (modernization theory — next)
Democracy causes wealth: elected governments can’t just expropriate you, so growth follows
Political scientists have fought this for seventy years — still not settled


We’re parking the full fight. Today: what does political science, not economics, add to the story?

Political scientists have argued over the direction of this causal arrow for decades, with steadily better data, and the debate is still not fully settled. Second-year Comparative Politics spends two full weeks on exactly this argument, working through Przeworski, Inglehart, and the wider literature in detail. This lecture parks the fight deliberately — not because it doesn’t matter, but because a different question is a better use of today’s time: whatever the direction of the wealth–democracy arrow, what does political science specifically add to the story — the actual mechanics of how power changes hands?


Say the parking-lot line out loud — it’s honest, not a cop-out. The pivot: even if we can’t settle the direction of the arrow, we CAN look at the political mechanics of how a country actually moves from “ruled by one group” to “ruled by whoever wins an election.” That’s what’s coming.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Getting one is not the same as keeping one
text:
Getting one is not the same as keeping one

Why emergence? Why would a ruling class ever voluntarily open elections that might unseat them?
Why survival? Once elections start, why don’t winners just cancel the next one?


Same underlying tool for both: credible commitment — a promise that sticks even though you could break it. Callback to Lecture 8.

“Credible commitment” is the problem of making a promise stick when the person making it could renege the moment it becomes convenient, and everyone involved knows it. Lecture 8 used the concept to explain why rival armed groups agree to stop fighting each other (“we’ll stop fighting”); here the same logic explains why a ruling elite voluntarily accepts the risk of losing power through elections rather than holding onto all of it by force (“I won’t jail you if I lose”). In both cases, the promise only works if there is some way to make breaking it costly.


Name Lecture 8 explicitly here — same intellectual move, different application. In L8 the question was why rival groups stop fighting each other; here it’s why a ruling elite stops trying to hold all the power. Both need some way of making a promise credible when the person making it could renege the moment it’s convenient.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Story one: get rich, get democratic
text:
Story one: get rich, get democratic
The classic mid-century answer: as countries get richer, democracy tends to follow.


The mechanism: an educated, propertied middle class starts wanting a say
The correlation is real (see the scatterplot) — the mechanism is contested
Counter-example: Singapore is rich and not fully democratic


The modernization thesis — the classic mid-twentieth-century answer to why democracy emerges — holds that as countries get richer, more urban, and better educated, an educated, propertied middle class develops and starts wanting a say in how it is governed, and eventually gets one. The correlation between wealth and democracy is real, visible in the scatterplot from the earlier slide. What’s contested is the mechanism: whether wealth really produces this effect, and through which channel.


Second counter-example: several poor countries are nonetheless long-standing democracies (India, Botswana, Costa Rica). Cut for time since Singapore alone makes the point on-slide; restore if the room wants both directions of counter-evidence.


Keep this to outline level — genuinely light touch. Don’t build a set piece: no Przeworski’s GDP-per-capita threshold, no Inglehart-Welzel post-material values sequence, no exogenous-vs-endogenous distinction. Second-year Comparative does all of that at full depth in weeks 1–2 (Tilly, stationary bandits, Przeworski & Limongi, Inglehart & Welzel). Say one sentence — “richer countries are more likely to end up democratic, though nobody fully agrees why” — and move to the mechanism that actually does the work below.


Guard-rail per BUILD-NOTES: this is the heaviest Comparative overlap in the whole block. Comp A Week 1 Thursday runs the full modernization sequence (Przeworski & Limongi’s ~$6,000 GDP-per-capita threshold, Inglehart-Welzel’s endogenous post-materialism story, Acemoglu-style elite-under-pressure formalization) — I’ve read that dump and deliberately kept this slide to two sentences and one bullet list, no numbers, no named-theorist deep dive. If this still feels too close, the fix is to cut it to one line and fold it into the HDWKT segment above.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Nobody gives you democracy. Somebody settles for it.
text:
Nobody gives you democracy. Somebody settles for it.
Not wealth producing a demand for votes — competing elites cutting a deal, because neither can win outright.


Before: rival elites fight for total control
The trigger: a stalemate — nobody can win, and the costs keep climbing
The deal: losing an election has to be safer than losing a civil war


Deliver this as a mechanism, not a citation list. The next slide is the whole thing in one sentence — set it up, then let it land on its own.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: The whole deal, in one sentence
text:
The whole deal, in one sentence

“I won’t jail you if I win, and you won’t jail me if you win.”


Say it slowly and stop talking. This is the sentence they should be able to reproduce in the exam, and it is the sentence lecture 11 breaks: dictatorship is what you get when nobody can make that promise credibly.
Callback: this is lecture 8’s credible-commitment problem, one level up. Name the lecture.


2026-09-03: split off the old “elite bargains” slide, which FRESH-EYES and its own todo flagged as the densest in the deck (~68 words). The mechanism is now one slide, the payoff line is its own quote slide — Noah’s standard “one big line, set large” move.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Case: South Africa’s negotiated transition
By the late 1980s, neither the apartheid government nor the anti-apartheid movement could defeat the other — sanctions and unrest were grinding the state down, and the ANC couldn’t win militarily either.

The deal (1990–94): free elections for a black majority government, in exchange for guarantees — no mass prosecutions, property protections, a government of national unity in transition.

Neither side could win outright: international sanctions and internal unrest were grinding the apartheid state down, but the ANC had no realistic path to military victory either. That mutual stalemate produced the negotiated deal between 1990 and 1994 — free elections delivering a black-majority government, in exchange for guarantees to the outgoing regime: no mass prosecutions for apartheid-era officials, protection of existing property rights, and a government of national unity during the transition. F. W. de Klerk and Nelson Mandela shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize for the negotiation — a joint prize for a joint bargain.


This is the clean, vivid version of the bargain — mutual guarantees, explicitly negotiated, both sides visibly better off than continued conflict. If the room needs a hook: F.W. de Klerk and Nelson Mandela shared the 1993 Nobel Peace Prize for this — literally a joint prize for a joint bargain.


IMAGE — Mandela and de Klerk at the CODESA negotiations, or the joint 1993 Nobel Peace Prize ceremony — something that visually says “two former enemies, same table.” Source: AP/Getty archival photo (rights-check before use) or South African History Online. Use as inline .absolute image beside the deal text.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: And it’s not the only shape the bargain takes
text:
And it’s not the only shape the bargain takes
Spain, 1977–78: after Franco’s death, the old regime’s reformists and the opposition struck a matching bargain in stages — the Moncloa Pacts (October 1977), a package of economic and social reforms that traded wage restraint for promised political and fiscal reform, followed separately by an amnesty law and the 1978 constitution — reform managed from within, not a reckoning with the dictatorship’s past.

Different history, different cast — same underlying logic: both sides needed the other to believe the deal would hold.

Keep this to 45 seconds — it’s the “more than one case” requirement, not a second full case study. The point is that the shape of the bargain (mutual guarantee, negotiated exit) recurs even though South Africa and Spain have almost nothing else in common.


Fixed per fresh-eyes review (2026-09-03, §1 item 5): the slide conflated the Moncloa Pacts with “mutual amnesty and a new constitution.” The Moncloa Pacts (25 October 1977) were specifically economic and social-policy agreements (wage restraint, tax and fiscal reform, in exchange for promised political reforms) signed by the government, parties and unions to manage Spain’s economic crisis during the transition — the 1977 Amnesty Law and the 1978 Constitution were separate, later agreements in the same transition, not part of the Moncloa Pacts themselves. Reworded to describe the Pacts accurately and keep the amnesty/constitution as distinct steps. Source: web search (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moncloa_Pacts and related summaries of the 1977 Agreement on the Programme of Sanitation and Reform of the Economy).


Noah: this is a natural spot for a personal or research-adjacent case if you have one that lands better with a Dublin first-year audience than South Africa/Spain — e.g. a post-Soviet transition case from your own work, if one fits the “elite bargain” shape rather than the “collapse into personalism” shape (careful: many post-Soviet cases are better examples of bargains failing, which might actually be a stronger teaching moment — your call).


IMAGE — Adolfo Suárez signing the Moncloa Pacts, October 1977 (or a photo of the negotiating parties at the table). Source: Spanish government archives / Wikimedia Commons. Use inline .absolute, small, bottom-right — this slide is deliberately brief.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: When does the deal never get made?
text:
When does the deal never get made?

No real stalemate — one side is strong enough to just win outright
Weak enforcement — the deal exists on paper, but nothing makes either side keep it
The other side looks existential — if losing means losing everything, there’s no incentive to accept defeat


Notice: two of those three are about survival, not emergence — where we’re going next.

A bargain fails to form for a few recurring reasons. Sometimes there is no real stalemate — one side is strong enough to simply win, so there is nothing to negotiate over. Sometimes the deal exists on paper but nothing enforces it: no courts, no army, no impartial party willing to hold either side to its promise. And sometimes one side comes to see the other as an existential threat rather than a rival — if losing genuinely means losing everything, there is no incentive to accept defeat gracefully rather than fight on. Notice that two of these three reasons are really about whether a bargain, once struck, can be trusted to hold — a question about survival, not emergence.


Compressed from the stub’s four-point list — external intervention folded out, since it’s a smaller factor and this slide is already doing the job of bridging emergence into survival. The bridge line at the end is the important part: say it out loud, it’s the pivot to the next section.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Russia, 1993: what “no stalemate” looks like
President against parliament, deadlocked over who ran the country. No mutual guarantee was available — so one side simply won.

21 September — Yeltsin dissolves a parliament he has no constitutional power to dissolve
4 October — the army shells the parliament building. 147 dead by the prosecutor-general’s count
12 December — a new constitution, written by the winner, hands the president enormous power


The loser wasn’t at the table. Thirty years later, that presidency is still the one you read about.

The 1993 constitutional crisis ran from Yeltsin’s decree No. 1400 of 21 September, dissolving the Congress of People’s Deputies and Supreme Soviet — which he had no constitutional authority to do — through to the storming of the parliament building, the White House, on 4 October, after Yeltsin ordered the army to shell it. The prosecutor-general’s official figure is 147 dead; other official counts give 187, and higher estimates circulate. On 12 December a new constitution was approved by referendum, granting the president extraordinarily strong powers relative to the legislature.
Put beside South Africa and Spain, the contrast is the lecture’s argument in one case. In those transitions neither side could finish the fight, so both sides wrote guarantees into the deal. In Russia one side could finish the fight, so there was no deal to write — the winner wrote the constitution alone, and the institution he designed for himself was still there, considerably strengthened, for his successors. Bargains are not made because elites are decent. They are made because neither side can afford not to.


Two minutes, and it is the pivot into the survival half of the lecture. The teaching point is comparative, not moral: don’t do “Yeltsin bad.” Do “no stalemate, therefore no bargain, therefore a constitution with one author.”
Good moment to flag that Western governments at the time largely applauded the shelling — which is a useful, uncomfortable complication for anyone who thinks democratisation has obvious good guys.


Source check, 2026-09-03: decree 1400 of 21 September 1993; the shelling and storming of the White House on 4 October 1993; prosecutor-general’s official toll of 147 (other official figures give 187; higher estimates exist and are contested); the constitution approved by referendum on 12 December 1993 creating a strongly presidential system (RFE/RL, Carnegie Endowment, National Security Archive).
Written this pass to answer the standing todo on the Spain slide, which asked for a post-Soviet case and correctly guessed that a failed bargain would teach better than a third successful one. It also gives “When the bargain doesn’t happen” an actual case instead of three abstractions.


Noah: check my facts and take this over — it is squarely your material and I have written it as a comparativist would, not as someone who knows the period. The death toll is contested; say so or don’t, your call. Also: is 1993 the right post-Soviet case, or would you rather use Ukraine 2004, where a bargain did form (round table, election re-run traded for constitutional reform)?


IMAGE — the White House burning, 4 October 1993 (the black-scorched facade shot is the iconic one). Widely reproduced; check licensing on the specific frame. Full-bleed would carry real weight here, coming straight after two handshake photos.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The real puzzle
An elected government wins fair and square. It controls the army, the courts are stacked with its own appointees, and it has the votes to change the rules.
Why doesn’t it just cancel the next election?

Pause on this properly — let someone answer before moving. The honest answer many first-years reach for is “because voters wouldn’t let them,” which is not the whole story and is worth gently puncturing: plenty of voters have gone along with exactly that, historically and recently. The real answer is structural, not just moral.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
“The only game in town”

“Democracy becomes the only game in town when… the overwhelming majority of the people believe that any further political change must emerge from within the parameters of democratic formulas.” — Juan Linz & Alfred Stepan


Democracies survive not because incumbents are virtuous, but because enough other people have a stake in the rules continuing that breaking them gets expensive.

The full Linz & Stepan line: “Democracy becomes the only game in town when… even in the face of severe political and economic crises, the overwhelming majority of the people believe that any further political change must emerge from within the parameters of democratic formulas.” “Stake in the rules continuing” is doing real work in that sentence, and it’s worth unpacking concretely: coalition partners who expect their own turn in power later; a business class that wants predictable rules more than it wants a permanently friendly government; a bureaucracy and a military that would rather not be implicated in a power grab if it fails. The phrase “the only game in town” is quotable on purpose; it recurs conceptually all the way to Lecture 13, on democratic backsliding.


Unpack “stake in the rules continuing” concretely: coalition partners who expect their turn later, a business class that wants predictable rules more than a permanently friendly government, a bureaucracy and military that would rather not be implicated in a power grab. The Linz & Stepan phrase is quotable and worth having students write down — it recurs conceptually all the way to Lecture 13 on backsliding.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Armies staying home
A government’s ability to cancel an election runs through who controls force — the strongest predictor of democratic survival is a military that doesn’t intervene.

Chile, 1988: Pinochet lost a plebiscite. The military stood down.


Egypt, 2013: an elected government was removed by the army within a year. Same tool, opposite outcome.

A government’s ability to cancel an election ultimately runs through who controls force, which is why one of the strongest predictors of whether democracy survives is whether the military simply stays out of politics. Chile in 1988 and Egypt in 2013 make the pairing vivid: in Chile, Pinochet lost a plebiscite on extending his own rule, and after real internal argument the military stood down and let the result hold. In Egypt, an elected government was removed by the army within a year of taking power. Same institution, same basic power, two completely different choices — the point being that nothing about “having elections” automatically guarantees the military stays home. What differs is whether the military is professionalized and has something to lose from being seen as a coup-maker, or is already deeply embedded in politics and economic interests.


The pairing is the point — same institution, two completely different choices, which shows this isn’t automatic or guaranteed by “having elections” alone. Good moment for a show of hands: “what do you think made the difference?” — professionalized, non-politicized militaries with something to lose from being seen as coup-makers vs. militaries already deeply embedded in politics and economic interests.


POLL (Vevox/TCDpolls — tool still Noah’s decision). Question text, ready to go:

“Could you imagine the Irish Defence Forces refusing to hand over control after an election?” — Yes / No / I have genuinely never thought about it

The third option should win by a mile, and that is the lesson: most Irish eighteen-year-olds have never had to ask the question, which is what “the only game in town” feels like from the inside. Say that out loud when the bars come up.


IMAGE — split image: a Chilean “NO” campaign poster/rally from the 1988 plebiscite, paired with a photo of the July 2013 Cairo crowds around the army’s removal of Morsi. Sources: Chilean National Library archives (1988 plebiscite); Reuters/AP archival photo (2013, rights-check before use). Use as two inline .absolute images side by side.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Institutions get sticky
Once elections, an opposition, and independent-ish courts exist long enough, other people build their lives around them — hard to remove after that.


Opposition parties expect a turn eventually
Investors and foreign partners price in “this country follows predictable rules”
Courts, civil servants and media protect their own reputations



The elite bargain’s payoff, in reverse: too many people now have something to lose if it breaks.

Once elections, an opposition, and reasonably independent courts have existed for long enough, other people build their lives around them, and that is what makes them hard to remove. Opposition parties expect their own turn eventually — cancel elections and you have made a permanent enemy of everyone who was ever going to lose one. Investors, businesses, and foreign partners price predictability into their decisions; a country that “follows the rules” is a safer bet than one that doesn’t. Courts, civil servants, and the media develop independent institutional reputations that they have their own reasons to protect, separate from whoever currently holds office. Put together, this is the elite bargain’s payoff working in reverse: the deal that got democracy started in the first place is what keeps it running, because by now too many people have something real to lose if it breaks.


Explicit callback: name it as the same bargain logic from the emergence half of the lecture, just now sustaining rather than launching democracy. This is also the direct setup for Lecture 13 (backsliding): backsliding is what happens when this stickiness erodes gradually rather than all at once.


Portable concept for the spine: elite bargains as a foundation for institutional durability. It recurs at Lecture 13 (backsliding — what happens when the stickiness fails) and Lectures 15–16 (institutional design, veto players). Name the lecture number each time it comes back, per the course’s own convention.


IMAGE — a courthouse or parliament building with visible permanence and weight (e.g. the Constitutional Court of South Africa, or a generic marble-columns institutional building), inline .absolute, small, bottom corner. Point: institutions are physical, durable things people build their lives around, not just rules on paper. Source: any stock/CC building photo — doesn’t need to be a specific court.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: A right nobody enforces is a wish
text:
A right nobody enforces is a wish
Most constitutions promise a long list of rights. That doesn’t mean those rights actually hold.

Weimar Germany’s 1919 constitution had one of the most progressive rights charters in the world — free speech, free assembly, equality before the law. It also had an emergency-powers clause, Article 48. By 1933, that clause dismantled the rest.

The standard “types of rights” typology — civil, political, social — isn’t the point here; the real question is enforcement. A right on paper is only as strong as whoever is willing to enforce it when a government decides to ignore it. Weimar Germany’s 1919 constitution is the clean, vivid illustration: a genuinely rights-rich document, containing one of the most progressive rights charters in the world, dismantled from the inside using its own emergency-powers clause, Article 48.


This is the LC upgrade the plan calls for — skip the standard “types of rights” typology entirely (civil, political, social — they’ve seen it), and go straight to the enforcement question: a right on paper is only as strong as whoever is willing to enforce it when a government decides to ignore it. Weimar is the clean, vivid version — a genuinely rights-rich constitution, dismantled from inside using its own rules.


IMAGE — the front page of the 1919 Weimar Constitution document, or a photo of Hindenburg signing the 1933 Reichstag Fire Decree (the Article 48 emergency decree). Source: German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv) / Wikimedia Commons. Use as inline .absolute, right side of slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: So who actually enforces a right?
text:
So who actually enforces a right?

Not the constitution itself — a document can’t stop anyone from anything
Courts — willing and able to say no to the government, and have that ruling matter
Same “stakeholders with something to lose” logic as survival, applied to judges


Full version — “when do courts have the nerve to say no?” — is Lecture 16.

A constitution cannot enforce itself; a document cannot stop anyone from doing anything on its own. Enforcement runs through courts — specifically, whether courts are willing and able to say no to the government, and whether that ruling actually matters in practice. That’s the same “stakeholders with something to lose” logic used earlier for democratic survival generally, now applied specifically to judges: courts hold the line when they have their own institutional reputation and independence to protect. The full version of the question “when do courts actually have the nerve to say no?” is parked here on purpose — it’s Lecture 16’s material in full.


Say the park explicitly, same convention as elsewhere in the module. This is the bridge that closes the loop for today: democracy survives because enough people have a stake in it, and rights survive (or don’t) for exactly the same reason, one institution at a time.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Next up

Where we got to today. Emergence: modernization versus elite bargains, with the bargain doing most of the work (South Africa 1990–94, Spain 1977–78) — and Russia 1993 as the case where no bargain was needed, because one side could win. Survival: democracy lasts when it becomes “the only game in town” — armies stay in barracks, institutions get sticky because too many people have built their lives around them, and rights on paper only bind when somebody enforces them.

Lecture 11 — Dictatorships I: How Autocracies Work
Think about: if democracy is an elite bargain — a promise that losers won’t be jailed — what happens when that bargain never forms, or breaks down entirely? That’s dictatorship.
No lectures next week — study/review week. Back Tuesday 3 November. The short assignment is due around then [DATE PLACEHOLDER] — details on Blackboard.
See you after reading week

Clean handoff. Lectures 9–10 established what democracy is and why it emerges and sticks; 11–12 flip the question entirely: what does it look like when that bargain isn’t there? The credible-commitment thread runs through both — dictatorships persist partly because rivals can’t credibly commit to sharing power, and the autocrat can’t credibly commit to not being overthrown either. That insecurity is the whole engine of Lecture 11.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
When Does Difference Become Conflict?
Most diverse societies, most of the time, have no ethnic violence. That fact alone should wreck the “ancient hatreds” story.

Cold open. Don’t define anything yet — let the claim sit. Last lecture we asked where identities come from (primordial, constructed, or instrumental). Today’s question is different and harder: identities exist everywhere, so why does violence only happen sometimes? Land that distinction before you move to the plan slide.
