title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The puzzle: why not conflict?
One count finds 822 ethnic groups making up 1% or more of the population, across 160 countries. Almost none of those neighbours are shooting at each other right now.


Switzerland — four languages, Catholic/Protestant split. Last civil war: November 1847, 26 days, 93 dead
Tanzania — over 120 ethnic groups, decades of relative peace
Rwanda — two labels, colonially hardened. April–July 1994: ~800,000 dead in 100 days



Same raw material. Wildly different outcomes.

So difference itself can’t be doing the explanatory work. (Restates the line above in more analytical language — cut for pace, restore if the room needs it said twice.)


The 822 figure is Fearon’s (2003) count of ethnic groups that make up at least 1% of their country’s population, across 160 countries. Language counts run far higher — Ethnologue lists about 7,160 living languages — which is itself a first lesson: “how many ethnic groups are there” has no answer until you say what counts as one. Hold onto that; it is the same problem as measuring democracy in Lecture 9.
Switzerland’s last civil war, the Sonderbund War, ran from 3 to 29 November 1847 and killed about 93 people — a religiously and linguistically divided state that has not had an internal war since. Rwanda’s genocide ran from 6 April to 16 July 1994; the UN estimate is 800,000 dead, the Rwandan government’s own figure is 1,074,017, and the true number is contested.
The comparison above is not a coincidence of case selection. Switzerland, Tanzania, and Rwanda share the underlying condition that every account of ethnic conflict has to explain: linguistically or religiously distinct populations living within a single state. What varies is not the presence of difference but what happens to it — whether it is politically activated, and whether institutions exist to manage the activation safely. That is the puzzle the rest of the lecture works through.


IMAGE — inline .absolute chart alongside the case list, or a small full-width strip. A world map or bar chart showing the number of distinct ethnic groups by country (Ethnologue country profiles), to make “7,000–8,000 groups, under 200 states” visually concrete. A heat map reads better here live than a data table.


The Tanzania/Rwanda pairing is the spine of the lecture — same continent, same colonial overlay of “tribes,” opposite outcomes. Don’t resolve it yet, just plant it. You’ll come back to this exact pair later as the payoff comparison.


Source check, 2026-09-03: replaced an unverifiable “7,000–8,000 distinct ethnic groups” claim (that number is the count of living languages, not ethnic groups) with Fearon, “Ethnic and Cultural Diversity by Country”, Journal of Economic Growth 8 (2003) — 822 groups at the 1% threshold in 160 countries. Sonderbund War dates and the ~93 dead from the Swiss National Museum and standard accounts of the 1847 war. Rwanda: 6 April – 16 July 1994; UN estimate 800,000, Rwandan government estimate 1,074,017 (contested — say “estimates run from 800,000 to over a million” if pressed).
One line for the cross-national literature, deliberately NOT built into a set piece: large-N studies of civil war onset generally find that ethnic diversity itself is a weak predictor — diverse countries are not systematically more war-prone than homogeneous ones. This is Fearon & Laitin’s and Posner’s territory (Comparative’s spine, Week 8) — say the finding, don’t teach the paper, don’t put either name on screen. If a student asks “isn’t there a famous study on this,” you can say so verbally and point them to second year.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: “Ethnic conflict” is a description of the banner, not the cause
text:
“Ethnic conflict” is a description of the banner, not the cause

Ethnic conflict: political violence organised along lines of perceived shared ethnicity, nationality, or religion.


“Ethnic” here is an analytical category — how the combatants frame the fight — not a biological fact. And what the conflict is actually about is usually power and resources; identity is the banner people fight under.

This definition is doing real work: it stops students treating ethnic violence as natural or inevitable (“they’ve always hated each other”). It’s organised, it’s political, and — callback — it’s the same “socially constructed” move from Lecture 7’s constructivist answer to where identity comes from. Say that connection out loud.


Noah: earnest, definitional slide — good spot for a wry aside once the definition lands. A Russia beat works well here: Putin’s framing of the war in Ukraine as defending “Russian speakers” is a textbook case of a leader declaring who counts as “our” ethnic group, on the fly, for a political purpose — the room will recognise it from the news even if they’ve never heard the term “ethnic conflict.”


IMAGE — inline .absolute photo, small, corner-placed so it doesn’t crowd the quote box. A non-graphic photo of a political rally with flags or banners — crowd energy around a symbol, not violence — to make “identity is the banner people fight under” concrete before the case studies arrive. Generic stock search: “political rally flags crowd”.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Elite instrumentalisation
Identity doesn’t mobilise itself. Someone has to pick it up and use it.

IMAGE — full-bleed divider background. A politician mid-speech at a podium, crowd with flags in the foreground — generic enough not to pre-empt either case in the contrasting-pair todo below. Source: any stock/Unsplash “campaign rally speech” search. Use as ## Elite instrumentalisation {background-image="w05-lec08-img/rally.jpg"}.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: How do you turn a difference into a weapon?
text:
How do you turn a difference into a weapon?
Politicians and other elites activate an identity boundary — “us” vs. “them” — when it helps them win or hold power.


They don’t invent the identity from nothing — they reach for materials that already exist (language, religion, a colonial-era label)
Activation makes “us” feel more cohesive and “them” feel more threatening — an outgroup to be guarded against, not just a neighbour
This is a strategic choice, not a psychological compulsion — elites do it because, in the right conditions, it works



The hard question isn’t “why would a leader do this” — it’s: what turns this from a campaign tactic into mass killing?

Stress the strategic framing — this is your own research wheelhouse, and it’s the lecture’s real payload. Elites are rational actors reaching for a tool that’s reliably effective, not cartoon villains. The spiral into violence needs more than a speech: it needs institutional collapse and mutual fear, which is where credible commitment comes in later in the lecture.


Noah: a contrasting pair works well here — one case of a politician activating identity for electoral gain that stayed electoral (rhetoric, no violence), one where it escalated. The contrast is more persuasive live than the mechanism alone. Your call on cases — something recent and legible to first-years would land better than a historical one.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Case: Rwanda — the label came first
text:
Case: Rwanda — the label came first
“Hutu” and “Tutsi” started as social/economic categories — cattle-owning vs. farming. Belgian colonial administrators fixed them into racial identities, with ID cards to prove it.

The genocide wasn’t ancient hatred erupting. It was elites — decades later, facing collapse — activating a colonially manufactured boundary.

Before colonial rule, “Hutu” and “Tutsi” functioned largely as social and economic categories tied to occupation — cattle-owning versus farming — rather than as fixed ethnic or racial groups. Belgian colonial administrators formalised the distinction, classifying the population by which category their ancestors had belonged to, issuing identity cards that recorded the classification, and building an entire administrative system — access to education, government jobs, and political representation — around it. The 1994 genocide was not the eruption of an age-old hatred between two peoples. It was organised by political elites who, decades later, facing a civil war and a collapsing hold on power, activated this colonially manufactured boundary and organised mass killing along it.


This is the callback to Lecture 7’s constructivism, made concrete and consequential: an identity boundary that a colonial state built for administrative convenience became, sixty years later, the organising line for genocide. Handle this case as political history, not as spectacle — the room may include students who’ve encountered this material before and students for whom it’s entirely new. Don’t linger on the violence itself; the analytical point is what matters.


IMAGE — a still from RTLM-era Rwanda (a period photo of the radio station, or a map of FM signal coverage — see the “How do we know” slide below for why the signal-coverage angle matters). Keep it documentary, not graphic; avoid anything showing violence.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
How do we know that?
Testing “ancient hatreds” against actual evidence.

Section divider. This is this week’s evidence-autopsy segment — note in your delivery that it’s testing THIS lecture’s own central claim (elite instrumentalisation), not a claim from last time, because the claim under test is the spine of today’s argument.


IMAGE — full-bleed divider background. Silhouette of an FM radio transmission tower against open sky — foreshadows the radio-signal study two slides on, and reads as “evidence,” not spectacle. Source: any stock/Unsplash “radio tower silhouette” search. Use as ## How do we know that? {background-image="w05-lec08-img/radio-tower.jpg"}.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
What would “ancient hatreds” even predict?
If ethnic violence really were the automatic release of age-old hatred, you’d expect it to break out roughly evenly wherever Hutu and Tutsi lived side by side — hatred doesn’t care about radio reception.

If it’s elite-organised, violence should track something engineered and controllable — like whether local militia leaders could actually reach people with an incitement message.

Set up the test before revealing the study. Make students predict: which pattern would you expect under each theory? Then give them the answer.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The radio test
Rwanda’s hate-radio station, RTLM, broadcast explicit incitement before and during the genocide. Hilly terrain meant FM signal strength varied by village — for reasons that had nothing to do with local tension.

Researchers compared villages with strong reception to villages with weak reception, otherwise similar. Villages that could actually hear RTLM saw significantly more participation in the killing.


That’s not what “ancient hatred, always simmering” predicts. It’s exactly what “elites need a channel to organise mass violence” predicts.

RTLM (“Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines”) broadcast explicit calls to violence in the lead-up to and during the 1994 genocide. Rwanda’s hilly terrain meant that FM signal strength varied considerably between villages for reasons entirely unrelated to local ethnic tension — hills blocked the signal in some places, valleys caught it clearly in others. That geographic randomness is what lets researchers treat exposure to incitement almost like a natural experiment: it separates the effect of hearing the broadcast from the effect of how much ethnic tension already existed locally.


IMAGE — chart. Bar chart or scatter plot from Yanagizawa-Drott (QJE 2014) showing participation in killing by RTLM signal strength/reception — the paper’s core figure (check which figure number in the published version). If the original isn’t cleanly reproducible, a simplified two-bar “strong reception vs. weak reception” redraw works.


This is Yanagizawa-Drott’s radio-signal study (QJE, 2014) — you don’t need to name-drop it heavily for first-years, but it’s worth naming once as “a real study, not an illustration I made up.” The methodological point to land: terrain-driven signal variation is close to a natural experiment — it lets researchers isolate the effect of exposure to incitement from the effect of pre-existing local tension, because signal strength wasn’t chosen by anyone. This is a good early seed for the natural-experiments material that gets its full treatment in Lecture 20 — say so explicitly if time allows.


Deliberately choosing the radio-signal study over interview/testimony evidence or media-content-coding approaches (also real angles) because it gives the cleanest, most vivid “here’s what would distinguish the two theories” story for a 50-minute first-year lecture. If you want a second evidentiary angle in reserve for questions, comparative work on power-sharing institutions that did/didn’t prevent violence (Lebanon’s confessional system vs. Yugoslavia’s collapse) is the natural one — happy to build it out if you want a backup slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Credible commitment
Why can’t enemies just agree to stop?

IMAGE — full-bleed divider background. Two hands almost touching but not quite (a visual echo of credible-commitment hesitation), or a demilitarised-zone/checkpoint photo if a more concrete image reads better live. Source: stock/Unsplash “handshake hesitation” or “DMZ checkpoint”. Use as ## Credible commitment {background-image="w05-lec08-img/commitment.jpg"}.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Why can’t willing enemies just make peace?
text:
Why can’t willing enemies just make peace?
Suppose two groups — even ones who both want the killing to stop — try to make peace. Group A agrees to disarm first.

Group B’s problem: how does A know B won’t attack the moment A is defenceless?



If neither side can guarantee it won’t exploit the other’s vulnerability, both sides have an incentive to stay armed — or strike first
Peaceful cooperation might make everyone better off, and it can still fail, because nobody can credibly promise to keep the deal



This is the same shape as a collective action problem — everyone would prefer the cooperative outcome, but nobody can make the promise stick.

Slow down here — this is the harder idea in the lecture. The everyday version: it’s not that people don’t WANT peace, it’s that peace requires trusting someone who has every short-term incentive to betray you the moment you’re vulnerable. Ask the room: “what would make you trust the other side enough to disarm first?” Let a few answers land before the next slide (courts, outside guarantors, power-sharing rules).


Portable concept: credible commitment. Flag this out loud — it recurs when we ask why dictators can’t just promise reform (Lectures 11–12) and why constitutions need outside enforcement to mean anything (Lectures 15–16). Naming it here is the first of three planned outings.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: What actually makes a promise credible?
text:
What actually makes a promise credible?

Independent enforcement — courts or monitors neither side controls
Power-sharing rules — guaranteed seats, vetoes, or offices that don’t depend on winning every election
An outside guarantor — a third party with the will and the credibility to punish whoever breaks the deal


Without something in that list, the safest strategy is often to trust no one — which is exactly how a fragile peace collapses back into violence.

Keep this to three bullets, don’t taxonomy-march it. The point is just: credible commitment isn’t a feeling, it’s a set of concrete institutional fixes, and the next slide shows one that actually worked.


IMAGE — inline .absolute photo, small. International monitors or observers at a ceasefire line (OSCE monitors, UN peacekeepers, or a similar generic “outside guarantor” image) — ties directly to the third bullet. Source: any UN/OSCE press photo, credited.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Case: Northern Ireland — building the promise
text:
Case: Northern Ireland — building the promise
Decades of violence (“the Troubles,” c. 1968–1998) between a Protestant/Unionist majority and a Catholic/Nationalist minority, organised — like Rwanda — along an identity line elites on both sides actively mobilised.

The Good Friday Agreement (1998) built the guarantees in — not trust: mandatory power-sharing, cross-community consent rules, and external guarantors (the UK and Irish governments, the US in the background).


Peace didn’t require identity to stop mattering. It required making commitments credible enough that nobody needed to strike first.

The Good Friday Agreement, signed in 1998, did not ask either community to simply trust the other’s goodwill. It built the guarantees into the institutions themselves: mandatory power-sharing arrangements between unionist and nationalist parties in the Northern Ireland Executive, cross-community consent rules requiring cross-community majorities for major decisions, and external guarantors in the form of the British and Irish governments, with the United States playing a supporting role in the background.


This is the direct contrast case to Rwanda: same underlying mechanism (elite mobilisation of a real, salient identity divide), opposite outcome, because institutions eventually supplied the credible commitment that Rwanda’s collapsing state could not. Don’t present Northern Ireland as “solved” — it’s fragile and contested — but it is a genuine case of institutions doing the trust-building work.


IMAGE — documentary and non-graphic: a photo from the Good Friday Agreement signing (1998), or the Stormont power-sharing chamber, rather than imagery of the Troubles itself.


Noah: if you have a stronger personal or research angle on Northern Ireland or a comparable power-sharing case, this is the natural slot for it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Back to the puzzle: Rwanda vs. Tanzania
text:
Back to the puzzle: Rwanda vs. Tanzania

Rwanda: bipolar divide, colonially hardened, activated by elites facing collapse, no institutions left to guarantee safety → genocide
Tanzania: 120+ groups, no majority, deliberate nation-building (shared language, common identity) → no equivalent violence


Neither outcome was written into the demographics. Both were political choices.

Full version of the comparison: Rwanda’s bipolar identity divide, colonially hardened into fixed categories, was activated by elites facing a collapsing power base, with no functioning institutions left to guarantee anyone’s safety — the result was genocide. Tanzania’s ethnic landscape — over 120 distinct groups, with no single group close to a demographic majority — created a structural obstacle to “us versus them” politics: there was no natural majority group for a demagogue to mobilise against a minority. This was reinforced by a deliberate post-independence nation-building project under Julius Nyerere, which promoted Swahili as a shared national language and cultivated a common Tanzanian national identity layered on top of, rather than replacing, existing ethnic identities. Neither outcome was written into the demographics. Both were the product of political choices: what elites did with the identities available, and whether institutions existed to make cooperation safe.


This is the lecture’s thesis slide — say it plainly. “Diversity” was never the variable. Elite strategy plus institutional capacity to guarantee commitments is the variable. If you want a live callback, this is also implicitly a state-capacity point (Lecture 4) — Rwanda in 1994 was a state that had lost the capacity to guarantee anyone’s security.


Noah: compressed the on-slide bullets to core clauses and merged the full explanation into one printnote rather than splitting into two slides — the payoff line needs both cases visible together. Worth a look live to confirm it doesn’t feel rushed.


IMAGE — inline .absolute, split/side-by-side. Left: Kigali Genocide Memorial exterior (Rwanda, documentary not graphic). Right: an ordinary Tanzanian street or market scene (Dar es Salaam or Zanzibar). The visual contrast does the “same continent, opposite outcome” work without narration.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
When does difference become conflict?
Identity, elite mobilisation, and broken credible commitment are each necessary. None is sufficient alone.
What’s still missing from this picture? (A trigger event? A demographic shift one side reads as a threat? A war next door spilling across the border?)

Let the room debate for a minute before you answer. The point: conflict is contingent, not inevitable — Rwanda could have gone otherwise if the civil war hadn’t reignited elite fear, if institutions had held. That doesn’t make violence predictable, but it does make it a political failure to explain, not a natural disaster to shrug at.


POLL (Vevox/TCDpolls — tool still Noah’s decision). Question text, ready to go:

“Which of today’s ingredients does the most work in explaining ethnic violence?” — Activated identity / Elites who benefit from activating it / No credible commitment / A trigger event

Run it, show the split, then say the honest thing: the discipline doesn’t agree either, and the research design for settling it is Lecture 20’s problem.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
For next lecture
Lecture 9 — Democracy: What It Is & How You’d Measure It
Think about: democracy — elections, independent courts, the peaceful transfer of power — is itself a giant credible-commitment machine. How do you tell the real thing from the appearance of it?

If conflict happens when groups cannot make credible commitments to each other, then democracy itself can be understood as a giant credible-commitment machine: regular elections, independent courts, and the peaceful transfer of power are all mechanisms that make political promises credible over time. The hard question for next lecture is how you would actually measure whether that machine is real, or just for show.

See you Tuesday

Clean bridge: today’s credible-commitment idea is about to reappear at the level of an entire political system. Democracy’s core promise — “you can vote me out, and I’ll actually go” — is a credible commitment problem writ large. Say that connection explicitly; it sets up why measurement (next lecture’s centrepiece) matters so much.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Last time, quickly
Liberalism, conservatism, socialism all answer the same question: who should get what, and who decides?

Today’s five don’t play that game. Each one changes the question.

Nationalism asks: who counts as “us”?
Fascism asks: what do you do once “us” has an enemy?
Feminism and green ask: what counts as political in the first place?
Populism doesn’t ask a new question at all — it just tells you who to blame


This slide is the hinge from lecture 5. Say explicitly: “these aren’t a random extra five isms, they’re doing something structurally different from Monday’s three.” That framing is the spine of the whole lecture — don’t let it just be a list.


Noah: fairly earnest bridge slide as written — a quick joke or a Russia aside (e.g. “Putin has, at various points, been called a nationalist, a conservative, and a populist by people who all think they’re disagreeing with each other”) would loosen it up before the taxonomy starts.


Noah: if you use the Putin aside here, note lec05’s “Marx’s diagnosis” slide also reaches for a Russia/USSR example — that’s two Russia mentions in one week if you take both. Keep one, cut the other, or swap one for a different case.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Nationalism: who counts as “us”?

A nation — people bound by shared identity, history, homeland — ought to govern itself.


Sounds obvious. It wasn’t always.

Civic — the nation is whoever accepts the shared laws. (France’s official self-image.)
Ethnic — the nation is shared blood, language, ancestry. (Often the lived reality underneath.)



Politics lives in that fuzz.

Before nationalism, most people were ruled by empires, dynasties, and churches that never asked whether you shared their “identity” at all — your ruler’s religion or bloodline had nothing to do with yours, and nobody treated that as strange. Nationalism as a mass political force is roughly 200 years old.
The civic/ethnic line is a first cut, not a clean binary. Ask who gets to naturalise, and who gets called a “real” Irish/French/German person, and you are already watching the fight — it does not stay theoretical for long.


Ground this historically before the two flavours — nationalism is younger than most students assume. That’s the setup for lecture 7’s “why do people die for nations that are 200 years old?” — don’t answer it here, just plant it.
Don’t resolve the civic/ethnic fuzziness; that’s the point. Flag out loud: “nationalism is both an ideology, which is today, and an identity, which is next week’s whole question.” Say civic/ethnic is a first cut, or a sharp student will say it for you.


Portable concept flagged for callback: civic vs ethnic nationalism. Name lecture 6 explicitly when lecture 7–8 revisit this — the brief calls this out as the gateway.
2026-09-03: this slide is the old “Nationalism” + “Two flavours of who’s the nation?” slides merged (content pass: one slide per ism). Nothing lost — the historical framing and the naturalisation example moved to printnote.


Noah: a live 2026 example where civic and ethnic nationalism visibly collide — a naturalisation-policy fight, or a “who is really Irish” media moment — would land well here. Currency-check before September.


IMAGE — two inline .absolute images side by side, under the bullets. (Left) a French civic ceremony — Bastille Day, or a naturalisation ceremony — for civic nationalism. (Right) an ethnic-nationalist rally or “blood and soil” banner (e.g. a National Rally or AfD rally crowd shot) for ethnic nationalism. Source: press agencies via Wikimedia Commons. Keep captions minimal — the visual contrast is the whole point.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Is fascism just conservatism turned up loud?
text:
Is fascism just conservatism turned up loud?
No. Conservatism reveres tradition, gradual change, law. Fascism reveres the leader, the movement, and the rupture.

Four ingredients:

Rights and rational debate rejected
The leader embodies the nation’s will
Struggle and violence glorified
An enemy — it needs one



Never “is X literally fascist.” Ask how many of the four show up.

Students routinely file fascism as an extreme point on the same line as conservatism. It is a different line. Conservatism wants to conserve; fascism wants rupture — to tear down and rebuild.
Fascism’s clearest historical form was the interwar period of the 1930s and 40s, but applying the word to a later case isn’t about finding an exact replica of that moment. It’s about counting how many of these four ingredients are present, and how strongly, before the label starts to fit. Linz and Paxton are the standard anchors.


This contrast is the whole teaching point — get it exactly right, don’t hand-wave. One line distinguishing fascism from generic authoritarianism is worth it: authoritarian regimes mostly want to be left alone to rule; fascism wants to mobilise you, march you, remake you. That pays off directly in lecture 11 — not every non-democracy is fascist, most aren’t.
Give them the checklist as a diagnostic, not a label game. Resist naming a current politician fascist from the podium; let students argue application themselves. Productive in tutorial, dangerous from the lectern.


Noah: your call on whether to name a current case explicitly, or keep this deliberately historical and let students apply the checklist themselves. Either is defensible — flagging the decision rather than making it for you.


2026-09-03: “Fascism: not just very conservative” and “What fascism actually holds” merged into this one slide, and the noun-phrase title became a question. The dropped prose is in printnote.


IMAGE — full-bleed or large inline .absolute: the 1934 Nuremberg Rally (Leni Riefenstahl’s famous mass-formation shot; Bundesarchiv, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons). A sea of bodies in formation reads instantly as mobilisation, not tradition — put it up before the bullets build.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
“The personal is political”
Feminism says power runs through the home, the workplace, and language itself — not just parliament. Do you buy it?

Direct callback to lecture 1’s “is THIS politics?” montage — say that out loud: “remember the montage in lecture 1, where we asked whether a couple arguing about housework counts as politics? Feminism has an answer, and it’s yes.” Let the room actually argue both sides for a minute before moving on — good energy, good tutorial seed. Don’t resolve it from the podium.


This is doing more work than the slide title suggests — it’s not just “feminism cares about gender,” it’s a methodological claim: if power runs through places you weren’t counting, then any analysis that only counts parliament and elections is incomplete. Worth making that move explicit if time allows.


POLL (Vevox/TCDpolls — tool still Noah’s decision). Question text, ready to go:

“A couple arguing about who does the housework is politics.” — Agree / Disagree / It depends

Run it before you say anything. Show the split, don’t resolve it; the next two slides are the argument for “agree”, and the room will have taken a side already.


IMAGE — inline .absolute protest photograph: Ireland’s Repeal the 8th march (Dublin, 2018) for a local, close-to-home case, or a Women’s March crowd shot with signs if a more international image is preferred. Source: press photos, several available under CC on Wikimedia Commons. Run it full width behind or beside the question text — let the sea of signs make the “power runs through more than parliament” point visually before you say a word.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Feminism disagrees with itself

Liberal — equal rights and access within existing institutions: vote, pay, representation
Socialist — women’s subordination is welded to capitalism and the household economy
Radical — patriarchy is the deepest structure, older than class and older than the state


Three diagnoses of one problem. That’s what having an ideology means.

An ideology is not a single answer but a whole theory of what is wrong and why — which is exactly what these three schools show. They diagnose the same problem three different ways. Feminism disagreeing with itself as much as it disagrees with everyone else is normal for a real ideology, not a weakness of it.


Three clean bullets, under three minutes. This is the one taxonomy-shaped moment left in the lecture — resist adding a fourth or fifth sub-school.


2026-09-03: noun-phrase title (“Feminism: not one thing”) became a claim; bullets tightened.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Ireland, 2016–18: an ideology with institutional teeth
text:
Ireland, 2016–18: an ideology with institutional teeth

Oct 2016 – Apr 2017 — a Citizens’ Assembly, 99 people picked at random, five weekends on the Eighth Amendment
It votes 79–12 that the Eighth should not stand, and hands the question back to the Oireachtas
25 May 2018 — the referendum carries 66.4% to 33.6%


An argument about where power runs, ending as constitutional text.

The Eighth Amendment (1983) gave the unborn a right to life equal to that of the pregnant woman. The Citizens’ Assembly, chaired by Ms Justice Mary Laffoy, met over five weekends between October 2016 and April 2017, heard legal and medical evidence, and voted by 79 to 12 that the Eighth should not be retained in full — recommending that the Oireachtas be allowed to legislate rather than writing the rules into the Constitution. A Joint Oireachtas Committee reported in December 2017; the Thirty-sixth Amendment was carried at referendum on 25 May 2018 by 66.4% to 33.6%.
The point for today is not the abortion question itself. It is that “the personal is political” is a claim about where power runs, and here you can watch that claim travel from an argument, through a deliberative body, into the text of a constitution. Ideologies are not just opinions people hold. Sometimes they are machinery.


This is the payoff of “the personal is political” two slides back — say the callback out loud. Handle it straight and unsentimentally: you are teaching the machinery (assembly → committee → referendum → constitutional text), not relitigating the substance. Some of the room were 10 years old in 2018 and remember the posters; some have families who voted the other way. Name the process, not a side.
If short on time this is the slide to compress, not cut — the three dates alone make the point.


Noah: check my facts, and add your own angle — you were in the country for this and I wasn’t. The Citizens’ Assembly is also the obvious hook for a “is this how you’d design a democracy?” aside, which is free foreshadowing for lecture 9. Also: does the Repeal image belong here rather than on the question slide two back?


Source check, 2026-09-03: Citizens’ Assembly dates and the 79–12 vote from the Citizens’ Assembly (Ireland) record and Carnegie UK’s case study; referendum date and the 66.4%/33.6% result from the Thirty-sixth Amendment record. Added this pass — FRESH-EYES §3 flagged that lec06 had no Irish case at all and that Repeal was sitting unused as an image cue.


IMAGE — the Dublin Castle result announcement, 26 May 2018 (the crowd in the upper yard), or a Repeal mural. Press photos; several CC-licensed versions on Wikimedia Commons. Full-bleed background would work here — this is the emotional high point of the deck.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Green ideology: ideology, or just a policy area?
text:
Green ideology: ideology, or just a policy area?


“We should care about the environment” is a policy preference — every ideology can hold it
Green as a full ideology goes further — it questions growth itself, and brings the non-human world into politics


Liberals, conservatives, and socialists can all sign up for a climate policy without changing anything else about what they believe. Caring about the environment, on its own, isn’t yet an ideology — it’s a plank anyone can bolt on. Green as a full ideology is a different, bigger claim: it’s not just a policy preference bolted onto an existing worldview, it asks politics to answer to something beyond human interests altogether.



Deep ecology — nature has value independent of humans — is the radical end. Eco-modernism is the mainstream end.

Most “green” politics in Ireland and Europe — carbon taxes, EV subsidies, biodiversity targets — sits much closer to the eco-modernist, mainstream end than students assume. Genuinely radical deep-ecology politics, of the kind that questions growth and human centrality outright, is rare in practice.


This is the genuinely interesting intellectual question in the slide, not a rhetorical one — let it hang for a second before the incremental bullets resolve it. First-years tend to underrate feminism and green as “not real ideologies” (compared to the heavy hitters like socialism); make the case that both actually redraw the whole map rather than just adding a policy plank.


IMAGE — split image: (left) a rewilding or “rights of nature” case for deep ecology (e.g. a European rewilding project, or the Whanganui River personhood case); (right) a centre-right party’s climate-policy launch or carbon-tax announcement for eco-modernism. Inline .absolute, side by side under the definitions. Keep it visual and light — this shouldn’t turn into a climate-policy lecture, that’s lecture 19’s job.


Noah: one green thought provocateur quote would land well here (deep ecology has some genuinely startling lines about human centrality). Your call on which.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: They’re not arguing on the map. They’re redrawing it.
text:
They’re not arguing on the map. They’re redrawing it.
Notice what these two don’t do: they don’t mainly argue about markets vs the state, which is the classical three’s turf.

They add new axes to the fight — gender, the non-human world — that the old liberal/conservative/socialist map has no room for.

This slide is the payoff of the previous two — say it plainly: you can’t slot feminism or green cleanly onto a single left-right line, because they’re not answering the same question the line was built to measure. That’s a genuinely sophisticated idea for week 3 of first year — don’t rush past it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Populism doesn’t have a worldview. It borrows one.
text:
Populism doesn’t have a worldview. It borrows one.

Populism: the claim that power rightly belongs to the “true people” — and that a corrupt elite has stolen it from them.



It is not a complete worldview like liberalism or socialism — on its own it has almost nothing to say about markets, family, or environment
It’s a frame that attaches to other ideologies: populist socialism, populist nationalism, even populist conservatism
The one fixed move: us (the people, homogeneous and good) vs them (the elite, corrupt and self-serving) — everything else is borrowed


This is Mudde’s “thin ideology” framing (also in Freeden) — the anchor concept for the whole slide. Emphasise: thin doesn’t mean fake or unserious, it means structurally incomplete — it needs a host ideology to fill in the actual policy content. That’s what makes it able to show up on the left AND the right, which surprises students who file “populist” as a synonym for “far right.”


Portable concept: thin vs thick ideology. This is the payoff line of the whole lecture — worth stating explicitly as a callback anchor, since nothing later in the term names it again by title (unlike collective action or veto players, which recur on-slide elsewhere).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Same frame, opposite hosts

Left-wing / egalitarian populism — the people defined in class terms: the poor and squeezed-middle against a rich elite. (Chávez’s Venezuela; Syriza in Greece.)
Right-wing / national populism — the people defined in ethnic or cultural terms: the “true” nation against elites and outsiders alike. (Orbán’s Hungary; Le Pen’s National Rally.)


Same accusation, completely different targets — because populism doesn’t decide who counts as the people. Its host ideology does.

The core populist accusation — that a corrupt elite has stolen power from the true people — never changes. What changes is who gets to count as “the people” in the first place, and that’s decided not by populism itself but by whatever ideology it’s attached to.


This is the slide that makes “thin ideology” concrete rather than abstract — two real cases, same structural move, opposite politics. Peronism (Argentina) is a nice extra example if you want a third: a genuinely contradictory blend of nationalism, socialism, and conservatism under one populist banner, sometimes called “right-wing socialism” — good for showing populism doesn’t even require internal consistency in its host.


Noah: swap in current 2026 exemplars if Chávez/Orbán feel dated by September — Milei (Argentina) is an interesting complication since he’s populist AND fits a very different economic host (libertarian) than the classic left/right pair above.


IMAGE — split image under the two bullets: (left) a Chávez rally, red shirts, Venezuela; (right) an Orbán or Le Pen rally crowd. Source: press photos via Wikimedia Commons. The visual point: the crowd/rally aesthetic looks structurally similar even though the politics are opposite — same form, different content.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Meloni: what the thin ideology does once it wins
text:
Meloni: what the thin ideology does once it wins
Fratelli d’Italia — populist frame, national-conservative host. Governing since October 2022.


Pragmatic where the host had no strong view: pro-Ukraine, pro-EU, orthodox on the budget
Radical where it did: offshore processing in Albania, surrogacy abroad made a crime
Courts blocked Albania; her judicial overhaul then lost a referendum, 53.75% No


Giorgia Meloni became Italy’s first female prime minister in October 2022; by September 2026 her government was the longest-serving uninterrupted administration in postwar Italian history. The useful thing about her, for today, is the split. On the questions where her host ideology had no committed position — Ukraine, the EU, fiscal policy — she governed as an unremarkable European conservative. On the questions where national-conservatism does have a position — migration and the family — she moved hard: the November 2023 agreement with Albania to process asylum seekers offshore, and the October 2024 law making surrogacy abroad a crime for Italian residents.
Italian courts repeatedly blocked the Albania detentions. The government’s response was a constitutional overhaul of the judiciary (the “Nordio reform”: separating the career paths of judges and prosecutors, splitting the judicial council in two). It went to a confirmatory referendum on 22–23 March 2026 and was rejected, 53.75% No to 46.25% Yes, on turnout near 59%.
Which is the lesson: the populist frame tells you who the enemy is — here, unelected judges standing between the people and their government. It does not tell you what to do about the budget. The host does that.


This is the slide the title of the lecture has been promising. Two minutes, not five.
The teaching move: make them predict. “She ran as an anti-establishment nationalist. Guess what she did about the EU.” Then show the split. Populist frame + national-conservative host explains the pattern that otherwise looks like hypocrisy.
The referendum is the best beat — she used the classic populist accusation against the judiciary and lost at the ballot box. Don’t editorialise; the facts are enough.


Source check, 2026-09-03: longevity record and the pragmatic/radical characterisation from AP, 3 Sep 2026 (“Italy weighs the results as Giorgia Meloni’s government sets a longevity record”); Albania protocol Nov 2023 and the court blocks from Euronews/Reuters reporting Oct 2024–Jan 2025; surrogacy law Oct 2024; referendum date and 53.75%/46.25% split from the 22–23 March 2026 confirmatory referendum record (JURIST, Euronews, Univ. of Padua human rights centre).
Written this pass to answer FRESH-EYES §2: “lec06 promises Meloni, Milei, Le Pen and the AfD on its title slide and analyses none of them.”


Noah: check my facts and add your own angle. Also your call whether Meloni or Le Pen is the better lead case for an Irish first-year audience in autumn 2026 — I picked Meloni because she has actually governed, which is what makes the frame-vs-host split visible.


IMAGE — Meloni at a European Council press conference (institutional setting, suit, flags) beside a 2022 campaign-rally shot. The visual argument of the slide in one pair: same politician, two registers. Press photos via Wikimedia Commons / European Council audiovisual service (the latter is reusable with attribution).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Milei: same frame, a third host
text:
Milei: same frame, a third host
Elected December 2023 with a chainsaw as a prop: the people against the caste — on a libertarian host.


18 ministries cut to 8
Monthly inflation 25.5% at handover; about 1.9% by mid-2025 — poverty rose first
Midterms, October 2025: ~41%, and 37 lower-house seats become 101



The frame travels. The content never does.

Javier Milei took office on 10 December 2023, having campaigned with a chainsaw as a stage prop and a single enemy: la casta, the political caste. Structurally this is the same accusation Chávez made and the same one Le Pen makes — a corrupt elite has stolen power from the true people. The host ideology, though, is neither socialist nor nationalist but libertarian, so the programme is austerity and deregulation rather than nationalisation or immigration control.
In office: ministries cut from eighteen to eight, tens of thousands of public-sector jobs removed, and the fiscal balance flipped to surplus. Monthly inflation was 25.5% in the month he inherited (annual inflation for 2023 was 211%); by mid-2025 monthly inflation was around 1.9%. Poverty rose sharply first and then fell back to roughly 31.6%. At the October 2025 midterms his coalition took about 41% of the national vote and went from 37 to 101 seats in the lower house.
So: three cases, three hosts — Chávez (class), Le Pen and Orbán (nation), Milei (market) — and one shared frame. That’s what “thin ideology” means, and it is why “populist” is not a synonym for “far right.”


Fast — 90 seconds. This slide exists to break the reflex that populism means the nationalist right. Milei is populist and libertarian, which most of the room will not have a box for.
Don’t get drawn into whether the economics worked; that’s lecture 17–18’s territory and you’ll lose ten minutes. If pushed: inflation down sharply, poverty up then down, and the argument is live.


Source check, 2026-09-03: inauguration 10 Dec 2023; 25.5% monthly inflation at handover and 211% for 2023; ministries 18→8 and 30,000+ public-sector layoffs (CNN, Dec 2024); ~1.9% monthly inflation and ~31.6% poverty by mid-2025; October 2025 midterms ~41%, 13 of 24 contested Senate seats, lower-house bloc 37→101 (Reuters/NBC/Euronews, 27 Oct 2025). Figures move — recheck the 2026 numbers before delivery.


Noah: currency check needed. These figures are good to mid-2025 / Oct-2025; by November 2026 the inflation and poverty numbers will have moved and there may be a fresher story worth telling.


IMAGE — Milei with the chainsaw at a campaign rally. It is the single most useful image in the deck: a literal prop for “tear down the elite,” on a politician whose actual programme is a spreadsheet. Press photos via Wikimedia Commons.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Why does populism keep winning?
Partly because elites are sometimes corrupt. Partly because “it’s not your fault, it’s theirs” is one of the most intoxicating sentences in politics.

Let this land as a genuine question, not a rhetorical one — populism’s appeal isn’t irrational, and treating it as a symptom students should simply diagnose and dismiss undersells it. Good moment to note: populist rhetoric is often responsive to a real grievance even when its diagnosis of why is wrong or oversimplified.


IMAGE — inline .absolute, understated: a closed-shopfront/“to let” high-street photo, or a queue tied to a cost-of-living grievance. The point is to make “elites are sometimes corrupt, and the grievance is real” visible rather than purely rhetorical — keep it low-key, this is a discussion beat, not a big visual moment.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
How do we know that?
If populism is a style more than a policy programme, how would you ever measure “how populist” a party or leader actually is?


Text-as-data: run a party’s manifestos and speeches through a “populism dictionary” — count how often it uses people-vs-elite language, homogeneous “the people” framing, anti-pluralist rhetoric
The measure is only as good as the dictionary — miss the right words, or count sarcasm as sincerity, and the score is noise


Keep this to one slide, ~2 minutes — it’s a light methods beat, not a full “how do we know” segment like lecture 4’s Tilly autopsy. The point: measuring an ideology that’s defined by rhetorical style rather than policy content is a genuinely different measurement problem from, say, measuring left-right position by survey. Flag it as a teaser for lecture 20, where measuring hidden/hard-to-observe things gets the full treatment.


Candidate citation: Hawkins’ or Rooduijn’s populism text-scaling work — confirm which before this goes in front of students; light touch, one slide, don’t build it out further.


IMAGE — chart. A populism-score bar chart by party or leader, e.g. from the Global Populism Database (Hawkins et al.) or the Manifesto Project’s populism scaling. Source: the original paper’s figure, or V-Dem’s populism indicator if simpler to source. Inline .absolute, right-hand side, next to the text-as-data bullets — a real chart makes “how would you measure this” concrete rather than abstract.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Two caveats before you go
Every ideology here is a teaching-device pure type — real parties are hybrids.

Real parties and movements are almost always hybrids — a bit of nationalism here, a populist frame there, a green plank bolted on top. Treat each of today’s five as a pure type built for teaching, not a box any real party fits into cleanly.


Today was about the ideas — not protest, media, or mobilisation. That’s Alex’s territory later in the module.

This wasn’t a lecture about protest movements, or about how ideas spread through media and mobilisation — that’s a distinct part of the module, taught later by Alex. Today’s job was narrower: understanding the ideas themselves, before we look at how they move and spread.


Two jobs in one slide: (1) the standard “pure types are simplifications” caveat that should follow any ideology taxonomy, and (2) a boundary-marking line so students don’t wander into thinking today covered protest/participation, which is Alex’s material. Keep this brief — it’s a closing caveat, not new content.


Guard-rail from the build notes: Alex owns media/participation and social movements — this slide exists specifically to draw that line without spending real time on it.

Mudde, “The Populist Zeitgeist” — or Müller, What Is Populism? (selected pages). TODO in _course.yml: choose one before this goes on Blackboard, don’t leave both listed as live options.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
For next lecture
Lecture 7 — Where do political identities come from?
Nationalism today was an ideology — a theory of how power should work. Next lecture it’s also an identity — a feeling of belonging. Why do people die for nations that are barely 200 years old?

Where we got to today. Nationalism — civic vs ethnic, and why the line is fuzzy on purpose (setup for lectures 7–8). Fascism — a rupture with tradition, not an extreme version of it. Feminism and green — ideologies that redraw the map instead of arguing on it, and, in the Irish case, redraw a constitution. Populism — a thin ideology: same frame, opposite hosts, as Meloni and Milei both show.
How exactly an ideology (a theory of how power should work) and an identity (a feeling of belonging) interact is the open question lecture 7 answers — today just plants it.


Read ahead: think back to the civic/ethnic nationalism split from today — you’ll meet it again next week wearing different theoretical clothes (primordialist, constructivist, instrumentalist).

Clean handoff, explicit callback to the civic/ethnic slide — that repetition is deliberate, it’s the concept-spine method the whole module runs on. Say it out loud: “same distinction, different vocabulary — that’s not an accident, that’s how this module works.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Last time: “war made the state”

“War made the state, and the state made war.” — Charles Tilly


A great line. But it’s a causal claim about history — so what would you need to actually believe it?

A measure of war — how much fighting, over how long
A measure of state-ness — tax, bureaucracy, territory — before and after
Some reason to think war caused the state-building, not the reverse


Callback slide — don’t re-teach Tilly, just put the claim back on the table so we can interrogate it. Ask: “who remembers what Tilly’s argument actually was?” cold-call one or two people before revealing the bullets.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Does the evidence fit — everywhere?
Tilly’s story is built almost entirely on early modern Europe — centuries of war forcing rulers to tax and count their populations.

Herbst’s counter-case: much of post-colonial Africa got its borders from European negotiating tables, not war between rival states.


If war-making builds state capacity, and a whole continent’s states skipped that process — that’s not a footnote, that’s a test of the theory.

Tilly’s account is built almost entirely on the experience of early modern Europe: dense, competing states locked in centuries of war, with gunpowder warfare forcing rulers to tax and count their populations in order to survive. Herbst’s counter-case is that much of post-colonial Africa got its borders from European negotiating tables rather than from war between rival states — so the mechanism that supposedly built European states never actually ran for most African states. If war-making is what builds state capacity, and a whole continent’s states never went through that process, that is not a minor exception to Tilly’s theory — it is a real test of how far the theory travels beyond the cases it was built on.


Keep this to one beat, don’t turn it into a full Herbst lecture. The point is methodological: a theory built on one region’s history is a hypothesis about the world, not a law of it. This is also the pattern for “how do we know that” segments generally — find the scope condition.


Herbst (States and Power in Africa) is doing a lot of work in one slide — deliberately compressed to keep this an 8–10 min segment, not a second state-formation lecture. If you want to go deeper here later in the term, this is the natural anchor point. Also: this is the first explicit place a Comparative-adjacent case (colonial border-drawing) shows up — worth checking it doesn’t collide with anything Alex is doing with imperialism/colonialism content.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Same planet, wildly different states
Cases first. The concept comes after.

IMAGE — full-bleed divider background. Earth from space is the literal read on “same planet” and is free/public domain — a striking, simple choice. Source: NASA (nasa.gov/images, public domain). Use as ## Same planet, wildly different states {background-image="w03-lec04-img/earth.jpg" background-color="var(--week-title-bg)"}.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Estonia vs. Lebanon
Estonia: start a business online in 15 minutes, vote from your phone, get a tax return the state already pre-filled.

Lebanon: the state has struggled for years to guarantee more than a few hours of electricity a day in its own capital.


Same category of thing — “a state” — doing wildly different amounts of actual governing.

Estonia: you can start a business online in fifteen minutes, vote from your phone, and the tax authority pre-fills your return because it already knows what you earned. Lebanon: the state has struggled for years to guarantee more than a few hours of electricity a day in its own capital — households and businesses run private generators just to keep the lights on and the fridge running. Both are internationally recognised, sovereign, UN-member states. What differs is not statehood in the legal sense, but how much actual governing each state can do.


IMAGE — split composition, inline .absolute (two photos side by side). Left: Estonia’s e-Residency/digital ID interface (screenshot from e-resident.gov.ee, or a photo of the ID card/reader). Right: a Beirut generator/blackout scene (widely photographed since Lebanon’s 2019–21 crisis — Reuters/AP archives). Keep it visual, minimal caption, let the two photos do the contrast work.


This is the anchor pair for the lecture — refer back to it later (“remember Estonia vs Lebanon”). If you have a livelier or more current pairing by September 2026, swap it in, but keep the shape: one hyper-capable digital state, one state visibly failing at basic service delivery.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: It shows up everywhere you look
text:
It shows up everywhere you look

Tax take: Nordic states pull in 40%+ of GDP, reliably. Many can’t crack 10–15% — not low rates, can’t enforce collection.
Vaccine rollout, 2021: some governments texted every citizen an appointment. Others couldn’t say how many citizens existed.
The traffic-camera test: some states fine your car within days. Others can’t deliver a letter to that address at all.


Tax take as a share of GDP: Nordic states pull in 40%+ of GDP in tax, collected reliably. Many low-capacity states can’t collect much more than 10–15% — not because tax rates are set low, but because they cannot enforce collection. COVID vaccine rollout (2021): some governments could identify every citizen, text them an appointment, and track who had received their second dose. Others could not reliably say how many of their own citizens existed, let alone locate them. The traffic-camera test: some states can photograph your car mid-offence and post a fine to your registered address within days. Others cannot reliably deliver a letter to that address at all.


IMAGE — chart, inline .absolute in the corner or below the bullets. Tax revenue as % of GDP, bar chart, 4–6 contrasting countries (Nordic vs. low-capacity states). Source: OECD Revenue Statistics or Our World in Data’s “Tax revenues” dataset.


The traffic-camera line is a good laugh line if delivered dry — “some states can find your car faster than they can find a missing person.” Use it, don’t over-explain it.


Noah: swap in a 2026-current example if the vaccine-rollout comparison feels dated by September — anything with a similarly sharp “some states can do this instantly, others structurally cannot” shape works (e.g. a recent natural-disaster response contrast, a recent census/registration failure somewhere).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The puzzle, named
It’s not about being big, rich, or scary. Some poor states are highly capable; some rich ones surprise you with how little they can actually do.
What is the thing that’s varying here?

Pause properly on this slide. Let someone answer before you reveal the term on the next slide — “capacity” should feel like it’s being extracted from them, not handed down.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Key term: state capacity

State capacity: the ability of a state to actually implement its own decisions across the territory it claims to govern — to extract resources, deliver services, and enforce rules.


Not what the state wants to do. What it can do.

This is the term that pays off the whole term — say that out loud here, don’t wait for the closing slides. Flag explicitly: this concept comes back hard in the dictatorship lectures (a dictator’s capacity to control territory and information) and in the political-economy lectures (capacity to actually run redistribution, regulate markets, build things).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Capacity isn’t one number

Extractive — can it raise tax reliably, from its own population?
Administrative — can it run things: census, schools, roads, a bureaucracy?
Coercive — can it enforce its laws and control its territory?


A state can be strong on one axis and weak on another — that’s usually where the interesting cases live.

Keep this light, three bullets, don’t build a taxonomy march out of it. The point is just: “capacity” isn’t one number, it’s at least three different capabilities that can come apart. Don’t spend more than 2 minutes here.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
How would you measure this?
Same problem as Lecture 2’s “how do you observe the third face of power” — capacity is mostly invisible until you go looking for a proxy.

Tax revenue as % of GDP — the classic extractive-capacity proxy
Census quality — does the state even know who and where its citizens are?
“Can it deliver the mail?” — a genuinely used political-science heuristic for basic administrative reach


Every one of these is a proxy, and every proxy is arguable — exactly the kind of thing you should be sceptical of, not just accept.

IMAGE — chart/map, inline .absolute. A world map of a state-capacity proxy, colour-coded by country — e.g. V-Dem’s state authority/territorial control measure, or the World Bank’s Government Effectiveness index. Makes “capacity is invisible until you go looking for a proxy” concrete. Source: v-dem.net or Our World in Data’s governance indicators.


Explicit callback: “this is the same move as measuring the third face of power in Lecture 2 — we can’t observe ‘capacity’ directly, so we go looking for something we CAN count that’s plausibly correlated with it.” This is doing double duty seeding the methods/measurement thread that pays off in the “how do we know” lecture later in term.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Capacity ≠ regime type
The trap: assuming “democratic” means “capable,” and “authoritarian” means “weak.”

IMAGE — full-bleed divider background. Something that juxtaposes “capable” and “authoritarian” without resolving the tension — e.g. Singapore’s skyline, or the Beijing skyline/CBD. Source: Wikimedia Commons. Use as ## Capacity ≠ regime type {background-image="w03-lec04-img/singapore.jpg" background-color="var(--week-title-bg)"}.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Four boxes that break the assumption
text:
Four boxes that break the assumption




High capacity
Low capacity




Democracy
Denmark, South Korea
many fragile new democracies


Autocracy
China, Singapore
many personalist regimes




China can build a high-speed rail network across a continent-sized country in a decade. Some democracies can’t get a single metro line built in the same time.

IMAGE — inline .absolute, small, next to or below the table. A photo of Chinese high-speed rail (a CRH/Fuxing train, or a striking shot of the network map) — makes the rail claim concrete. Source: Wikimedia Commons (multiple CC-licensed photos).


Let this land — it’s genuinely counter-intuitive for students who’ve absorbed “democracy = good government” as a package deal. Don’t resolve the tension, just name it and point forward: “we’re going to spend two whole lectures later this term on how autocracies actually work — this is the setup for that.”


Deliberately using Singapore/China as the high-capacity-autocracy examples rather than getting into contested “is China really that capable” debates — keep this a clean illustrative 2x2, not a rabbit hole. If you want a sharper democratic-fragile-state example than “many fragile new democracies,” a named case (e.g. a specific state with weak tax collection and a functioning multiparty system) would land better — your call on which one to use live.


Noah: the Russia slide that used to be requested here is now written as the next slide — your wheelhouse, so it’s a draft, not a finished thing.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The case I know best
Russia is the cleanest evidence that capacity isn’t one number.

Extractive: strong. The 2001 flat income tax replaced a leaky progressive system; income-tax revenue rose sharply and collection actually improved. The state can find your money.
Coercive: strong. In 2016 the interior troops were reorganised into the Rosgvardia — a national guard of roughly 340,000, reporting directly to the president. The state can find you.
Administrative: patchy. GDP per head in the richest region ran more than 40 times the poorest; healthcare and service quality vary enormously by region.


A state that can tax you and police you, but can’t reliably run a hospital in Ingushetia the way it runs one in Moscow.

Brian Taylor’s State Building in Putin’s Russia (2011) is the study behind this: he separates state capacity from state quality — how officials actually behave toward citizens — and finds the coercive agencies were effective at political control and much less effective at the ordinary work of policing crime. That gap is the point. High coercive capacity does not buy you administrative capacity, and a state can be genuinely formidable along one axis while barely functioning along another.


IMAGE — either a Rosgvardia line in riot gear (Reuters/AP, widely available) or, better for the contrast, a two-photo split: a Moscow government building against a regional hospital or road. Noah: you may have your own photographs from fieldwork, which would beat any of this.


Noah: check my facts and take this over. This is your material and it should sound like it — the three-bullet skeleton is verified but flat. The obvious additions are yours: whatever you saw of this first-hand, and the wry version of “the state can find your money and it can find you, it just can’t fix the road.”


Verified 2026-09-03: the 13% flat personal income tax took effect 1 January 2001, replacing a 12–35% progressive schedule; personal income-tax revenue rose sharply in 2001 and the reform is credited with reducing evasion (IMF WP/05/16, Ivanova, Keen & Weichenrieder; IFS/CEPR summaries). Rosgvardia created by presidential decree, April 2016, from existing internal-security forces, reporting directly to the president; personnel estimates cluster around 340,000–400,000 (CSIS; Darczewska, OSW). Regional disparity: 2016 GDP per capita in Nenets AO was roughly 43× that of Ingushetia (European Parliament briefing, “Socioeconomic inequality in Russia”, 2018) — the slide says “more than 40 times” to stay safely inside the source. Health outcomes vary strongly by region (Kalabikhina et al., International Journal for Equity in Health, 2021). Qualitative claim about coercion vs quality: Taylor, State Building in Putin’s Russia (CUP, 2011).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Whose state is it, anyway?
Political theorists have spent two centuries arguing about who the state actually serves — five quick lenses:

Pluralist — a neutral referee, responsive to whoever wins the argument
Marxist — an instrument of the dominant economic class
New Right (Leviathan) — a self-interested bureaucracy that keeps growing itself
Feminist — a structure built on and reproducing patriarchy
Elite theory — captured by whichever small group actually runs it


Notice what these really are: ideologies, wearing state-costumes.

IMAGE — the dullest slide in the deck (a five-item taxonomy); the one that most needs a visual anchor. The classic “Pyramid of the Capitalist System” cartoon (1911, public domain, IWW) stages exactly this question — who does the state actually serve — and gives you something to gesture at while you run through the five lenses. Source: Wikimedia Commons. Use inline .absolute, small, corner of the slide.


Fifteen minutes MAX for this whole beat, one slide, do not give each theory its own slide-block — that’s the dry version of this material and it’s exactly what to avoid. Move fast, treat it as a taster, not a unit. The “ideologies wearing state-costumes” line is the exit line — say it, then move.
Then park it out loud: every one of those five lenses is a full ideology with its own answer to “who should get what,” and they get the proper treatment next week — liberalism/conservatism/socialism next lecture, then nationalism/fascism/feminism/green/populism the one after. One sentence, not a slide: “what is the state for?” and “what is politics for?” are the same question asked twice.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
What should states actually do?
Even once you know a state is capable, there’s a separate question: should it use that capacity here?

Rent controls — protects tenants now, or shrinks supply and quality later?
Pandemic lockdowns — protects public health, or overrides individual liberty?
Price caps on energy — shields households from a price shock, or blocks the market signal that would fix the shortage?


Notice: both sides of every argument assume the state is capable enough to act. Low-capacity states don’t get to have this argument at all.

In each of these cases, the argument for intervention and the argument against it both assume the state is capable enough to act in the first place. Low-capacity states do not get to have this argument — they cannot do the thing either way, so the whole debate about whether the state should act is a luxury of already having the capacity to act.


Good spot for a quick show of hands or live poll — “who’d support a rent freeze in Dublin right now, who wouldn’t.” Don’t resolve it, the point is to show the scope-of-the-state debate is live and contested, not settled by knowing the facts.


LIVE POLL — tool still Noah’s call; TCDpolls (Vevox) is licensed by Trinity and is the cheap default. Question: “Should the state cap rents in a housing shortage? Yes / No / It depends.” If you only want one poll this lecture, this is the one to keep.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The Irish twist
Ireland is a genuinely high-capacity state — it collects tax reliably, runs a functioning bureaucracy, delivers services most of the world would envy.

And it still can’t build enough houses.


That’s the tell: when a high-capacity state still can’t solve a problem, capacity isn’t the binding constraint. Politics is.

IMAGE — full-bleed or large inline. A Dublin housing-crisis image — construction cranes over the skyline, a “for rent” queue, or vacant-site hoarding. Source: a recent Irish Times/RTÉ news photo, or an original phone photo — this is the most locally-replaceable image in the deck and worth keeping current for September 2026.


This is the non-obvious Irish hook the brief wants — not civics-class Ireland. Land it and then explicitly park it: “who actually has the power to block housing — planning objectors, local politicians, existing homeowners with a stake in prices — that’s a full lecture on its own, and it’s coming in the political-economy block later this term.” Don’t try to resolve Irish housing politics in two minutes; the point is purely to show capacity and political will are different things.


Deliberately not naming specific veto players here (that’s Lecture 15’s “who can stop whom?” content and the housing-as-political-economy-problem gets its full treatment in Lecture 18) — this slide should feel like a teaser, not a spoiler. If it runs long in delivery, this is the easiest slide to trim.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Readings
Required:

Heywood & Laing, Politics (2025), Ch. 3 — remainder of “Politics and the State” (the role-of-the-state section)

Recommended:

A short, accessible piece on state capacity/governance — flagged below, needs confirming

Stretch:

Migdal, Strong Societies and Weak States, or Herbst, States and Power in Africa — selected pages


Recommended slot: something like Fukuyama’s “What Is Governance?” (2013) is the natural pick — short, accessible, directly about the extractive/administrative/coercive framing — but I haven’t verified it against your actual reading-list access/licensing, so flagging rather than committing. Confirm before this goes on Blackboard.


Live poll date/tool TBC — see the housing-slide poll above; if you only want one poll per lecture, that’s the one to keep and this readings slide doesn’t need its own.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Next up
Next lecture — Ideologies I: liberalism, conservatism, socialism
Who should get what, and who decides? The isms — but taught as competing answers to a real question, not a taxonomy to memorise.

Read ahead: Heywood & Laing Ch. 2 (start), and think about which of today’s five “whose state is it” lenses you found most persuasive — you’ll recognise it again next week wearing a different name.

Today, in five lines: we autopsied “war made the state” and found its evidence base is mostly European; we named state capacity — extractive, administrative, coercive — and asked how you’d measure something invisible; we established that capacity is not the same axis as democracy vs. dictatorship (China builds railways, some democracies can’t build a metro line); we ran five theories of whose state it is, and parked them for next week; and we ended on Ireland — a high-capacity state that still can’t build housing, which tells you politics, not capacity, is the binding constraint.

See you Tuesday

Clean handoff — the “five lenses” slide from earlier in this lecture is the bridge; call back to it explicitly (“remember pluralist, Marxist, New Right, feminist, elite — that’s liberalism, socialism, New Right politics, feminism, wearing state-costumes”). That repetition is deliberate and is the through-line of the whole “concept spine” of the course — name it.

See you Tuesday
