title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Power
Who actually decides?

IMAGE — full-bleed opening background. Something that visualises invisible influence rather than a podium/handshake cliché: an empty chair at the head of a boardroom table, or a single spotlight on an empty seat. Stock (Unsplash/Pexels, search “empty boardroom” or “empty chair spotlight”). Use as ## Power {background-image="w02-lec02-img/opener.jpg" background-color="var(--week-title-bg)"}.


Cold open, no throat-clearing. Don’t recap Lecture 1’s “is this politics?” beyond one sentence — get straight to the puzzle. Energy should be “here’s a genuinely hard problem,” not “welcome to a new topic.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The plan for today

A problem: power is everywhere in political talk, almost impossible to see
Three progressively harder places to go looking for it
The open question: how would you ever know the hardest one is real?
One line about why any of this is bearable: what makes power cheap


Keep this to 20 seconds. Four bullets, read fast, move on.


Revision log, 2026-09-03

Nothing changed — already at target density, no cramped slides found
Density: 50.1 → 50.1 w/slide (unchanged)

Content pass, 2026-09-03 (second)

Cut the authority/legitimacy/Weber block (4 slides) down to one stub, “Coercion vs authority — parked”. All the text is preserved in an addl block on that slide; Weber is taught in Lecture 3 anyway. The deck was carrying three faces + Gaventa + the feed + coercion + legitimacy + Weber + a poll on day two.
Kept “Legitimacy is what makes power cheap” as the stub’s payoff line.
Poll slot: actual question text written; tool still Noah’s call.
“Power isn’t always a bad word” retitled as the question it asks.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Here’s the puzzle
A minister changes her mind about a bill after a phone call nobody else hears.
A newspaper never runs the story it was pitched.
You want what everyone around you already wants, and it never occurs to you to ask why.

In none of these did anything visibly happen. No vote, no argument, no press conference.


So: how would you ever observe someone exercising power, when the whole point is that nothing observable happens?

This is the frame for the entire lecture — sell it as a measurement problem, not a “here are three cool concepts” list. If you only get one sentence to remember from this slide, it’s the last one. Say it slowly.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Who has power over this room, right now?
text:
Who has power over this room, right now?

Me. I set today’s agenda — what we discuss, what we skip, how long we spend on it.
The timetabling office. Decided you’d be here, this room, this hour, for 50 minutes.
Nobody in this room at all. Whoever wrote the module regulations that make this lecture compulsory.


Only one of those is visible right now. The other two are just as real.

Only one of these three is a person you can point at exercising power in front of you. The other two — the timetabling office and whoever wrote the module regulations — are just as real, but neither one is happening in the room, and neither is something you could watch occur.


IMAGE — inline .absolute. A photo of a lecture theatre seating chart or timetable noticeboard (something bureaucratic and slightly funny), positioned small in a corner so it doesn’t compete with the text. Own photo of a TCD noticeboard works fine. e.g. ![](w02-lec02-img/timetable.jpg){.absolute bottom="5%" right="5%" width="20%"}.


Concrete, low-stakes, funny-but-true. Let them laugh at “me” — good, that’s the hook. This is doing real work: it previews all three faces without naming them yet (decision I made in front of you / rule that shaped what’s even on the table / distant actor you never see). Don’t label the faces here — that’s the reveal to resist. Just let the puzzle sit.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
A starting anchor: Dahl’s definition

Power: A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something B would not otherwise do.

Robert Dahl, 1957 — deliberately minimal. Notice what it requires: someone visibly not getting their way.

Good enough for a lot of politics. Not good enough for everything on the last slide.

Anchor, then immediately flag its limit — don’t let it sit as “the” definition of power for more than 30 seconds. The whole lecture is about what this definition misses.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Face 1: the open fight
Look for: who wins when two sides visibly disagree and one of them gets what it wanted.

A minister wants a bill passed. Backbenchers object. It passes anyway. That’s power, and it’s easy to see.

There’s a vote, a result, winners and losers on the record. That visibility is exactly what makes Face 1 the easy case: anyone watching can point to who won.



This is Dahl’s world: power as winning observable fights. Robert Dahl did exactly this — traced who won on housing, education, and urban renewal decisions in New Haven, Connecticut (Who Governs?, 1961).

IMAGE — inline .absolute, top-right corner. A period photo of New Haven, CT (city hall or a 1950s–60s urban renewal / housing scene) to anchor Dahl’s actual case. Library of Congress or Yale University Library digital collections are the right source. e.g. ![](w02-lec02-img/newhaven.jpg){.absolute top="10%" right="5%" width="30%"}.


This face maps directly onto Dahl’s definition from two slides ago — say so out loud. Keep this one fast; it’s the easy case and the room already half-knows it. The point is to establish the baseline before complicating it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Face 2: the dog that didn’t bark
text:
Face 2: the dog that didn’t bark
Look for: which issues never even make it to a vote.

Bachrach & Baratz (1962): power isn’t just winning decisions — it’s controlling which decisions get made at all. They called the ones that never surface non-decisions.


Harder to observe than Face 1. You can’t point to a vote that didn’t happen — you have to notice an absence, and absences don’t announce themselves.

Emphasise the methodological jump: Face 1 you observe a winner. Face 2 you have to notice something that isn’t there, which is already a much harder empirical task. Set up the cold-call on the next slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Cold call: what won’t any Irish party touch?
text:
Cold call: what won’t any Irish party touch?
Name an issue that stays off the table in Irish politics — not because anyone lost a vote on it, but because no mainstream party will put it up for one.

IMAGE — full-bleed or large inline background. The Dáil chamber, or Leinster House’s front steps — grounds the “Irish politics” prompt in an actual place. Source: Oireachtas.ie press images or Wikimedia Commons. e.g. ![](w02-lec02-img/dail.jpg){.absolute top="0" left="0" width="100%" opacity="0.15"} behind the text, or as a plain corner inset.


Actually cold-call someone here, don’t just rhetorical-question it. If the room goes quiet, have two in your back pocket — pick genuinely contestable ones, not obvious gimmes: something like agricultural emissions targets, or property-tax reform tied to home values, tends to work without being a culture-war landmine. Don’t let anyone answer with something that’s actually been voted on and lost — that’s Face 1, not Face 2. The test is: has it never even reached the floor?

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Face 3: wanting what suits them
Look for: cases where B never even wants to fight — because A shaped what B wants in the first place.


“Is it not the supreme exercise of power to get another or others to have the desires you want them to have — that is, to secure their compliance by controlling their thoughts and desires?”
— Steven Lukes, Power: A Radical View (1974)



This is the one nobody has an easy method for. No vote to watch, no absence to notice — only a preference that looks, from the inside, completely freely chosen.

Slow down here. This is the payoff slide. Let the quote sit for a beat before moving on — don’t rush past it into the next slide’s discussion. The ~5% who’ve met Lukes before have never actually had to sit with “what would count as evidence” — that’s the genuinely new ground, coming up next.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: So — how would you ever know?
text:
So — how would you ever know?
Face 3 claims someone’s preferences were shaped by power. What evidence would ever let you say that, rather than just “that’s what they happen to want”?

This is not a rhetorical question — it’s a real methodological problem, still contested among political scientists.

This isn’t just a puzzle for students meeting Face 3 for the first time. It’s an unresolved methodological problem among political scientists: what would ever count as evidence that a preference was shaped by power, rather than just being what someone happens to want?


Give this real air time — 2-3 minutes of room silence/discussion is fine. Don’t answer it yourself immediately; let a few hands go up first. The honest answer is “it’s genuinely hard and contested” — resist the urge to resolve it too quickly on the next slide. Gaventa (next) is an attempt, not a solved case.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
One serious attempt: Gaventa’s valley
John Gaventa, Power and Powerlessness (1980) — an Appalachian coal-mining valley in the US, one company dominant for generations.

Miners who were being badly exploited mostly didn’t organise, didn’t vote against the company, didn’t even talk about alternatives. Not because they were satisfied — not because they were coerced into silence on any given day.


Gaventa’s case: decades of Face 1 and Face 2 power — every open fight the company won, every issue it kept off the agenda — wore a quiet sense of “that’s just how it is” into the way people saw their own situation.


Notice the move. He doesn’t claim direct proof of Face 3 — he reconstructs it from a documented history of Faces 1 and 2, plus the observed absence of resistance that theory would predict. That’s an inference, not a photograph. Is it good enough?

IMAGE — full-bleed background or large inline. An Appalachian coal-camp / company- town photo (rows of company housing, a coal tipple, or a 1930s–70s mining valley shot). Library of Congress or West Virginia archives (many are public domain). Puts a face on “one company dominant for generations.” e.g. ## One serious attempt: Gaventa's valley {.smaller background-image="w02-lec02-img/appalachia.jpg"} with a dark text-scrim, or as an .absolute inset if kept as body background-color.


This is the closest thing to a worked answer to the previous slide, and it’s worth being honest that it’s an inference chain, not a smoking gun — that intellectual honesty is more useful to first-years than pretending the puzzle is solved. If you’d rather use a different empirical example you know better, swap it — the structural point (power’s history becomes internalised, and that’s the only kind of evidence available) is what has to survive the substitution.


Gaventa is the standard citation for a serious empirical attempt at Face 3 and fits the brief. Alternative if you want something more current/Irish-adjacent: media agenda-setting studies, or a shorter treatment of Lukes’ own worked example (non-unionised workers). Gaventa has the advantage of being a full book-length case rather than a stylised example, which suits “here’s what real evidence-gathering on this looks like.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
A live candidate: your feed
Advertising has always tried to do this. The newer version: algorithmic feeds that learn what keeps you scrolling and show you more of exactly that.

The Face 3 question, sharpened: if a feed shapes what you want and you experience that as just your own taste — is that power?

Longer framing of the same prompt, if the room needs it spelled out further: “What would you need to know to answer that, rather than just asserting it?” — it’s the same evidence problem as the Gaventa slide, just relocated to something in their pocket right now.


IMAGE — inline .absolute. A phone screen showing a generic infinite-scroll feed (blurred/anonymised, not a real person’s actual feed — a stock mockup or your own blurred screenshot). Positioned corner-inset, not full-bleed. e.g. ![](w02-lec02-img/feed.jpg){.absolute bottom="8%" right="8%" width="22%"}.


Keep this tight and analytical, not a moral-panic riff — the point is methodological (same “how would you know” problem as Gaventa, applied to something in their pocket right now), not “algorithms are bad.” If the room wants to go further with this, let one or two comments land and then move on — don’t let it become the whole lecture. Good bridge to media/misinformation material Alex covers later in term; don’t scoop that.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Could you run anything without it?
text:
Could you run anything without it?
A hospital, a household, a country — with no one having power over anyone. Could you?

Reframe before moving to authority. Power described this way can sound sinister — it’s worth explicitly saying it isn’t inherently so. Someone has to be able to make things happen collectively; the real questions are who has it, how they got it, and whether they’re answerable for it. That’s the bridge into authority and legitimacy.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Coercion vs authority — parked
A Garda directing traffic and an armed robber both get compliance. Only one of them is exercising authority.

Legitimacy is what makes power cheap.

Cut from the live deck, 2026-09-03. This lecture was carrying three faces + Gaventa + the feed + coercion/authority + legitimacy + Weber’s three types + a poll. Weber is taught properly in Lecture 3 (monopoly of legitimate violence) and legitimacy is re-anchored there, so the four slides that used to sit here are parked in addl below rather than delivered. Keep the two lines above — thirty seconds, as the bridge into Lecture 3 — and let Lecture 3 do the rest.


Parked slide 1 — Coercion vs authority

Coercion: you comply because you’ll be hurt if you don’t. The gun.
Authority: you comply because you accept the other side’s right to be obeyed. The badge.

Both the Garda and the robber get people to do things they wouldn’t otherwise do — that’s Dahl’s definition of power, satisfied by either one. What separates them isn’t the outcome, it’s whether the other side accepts the right to be obeyed.
Ruling by coercion alone is exhausting: you need to watch everyone, all the time, because nobody complies unless forced to. Legitimacy does that work for free.
Sharper version if wanted: Hannah Arendt, “On Violence” — violence is a sign that power has failed. “No government exclusively based on the means of violence has ever existed,” because even the most repressive ruler needs a base of organised support. Lots of violence is often evidence of weak power, not strong power. Pays forward to the dictatorship slots.
Parked slide 2 — Key term: legitimacy

Legitimacy: the belief, among the people subject to it, that an authority’s right to rule is genuine — that it ought to be obeyed.

Notice where legitimacy lives: in the eyes of the ruled, not in the ruler. It’s a belief, not a legal fact — you can have a perfectly legal government a lot of people don’t regard as legitimate, and vice versa. A regime can be stable and illegitimate (coercion is doing the work) or legitimate and unstable.
Parked slide 3 — Weber’s three types of legitimate authority

Traditional — “it has always been this way.” Monarchs, custom.
Charismatic — devotion to an extraordinary individual leader.
Legal-rational — obedience to rules and offices, not to the person holding them. The modern bureaucratic state.

Almost no real regime is purely one type. The typology returns when we ask why democracies hold together (Lectures 9–10) and how autocrats manufacture legitimacy they don’t have (Lectures 11–12). Charismatic is the unstable one: what happens when the founder dies?
Image cues from the parked slides, if any of this is ever restored: a Garda directing traffic; a triptych of crown / mass-rally leader / government office stamp.


Thirty seconds, tops. Say the Garda-and-robber line, say “legitimacy is what makes power cheap,” and tell them the machinery behind that sentence — Weber, the three types of authority — is Tuesday’s business. Do not start teaching Weber here; Lecture 3 opens on him.


Noah: if you’d rather keep the full authority block live, everything is in the addl block above, in order — but then Lecture 3 needs its Weber opening trimmed, or the room hears the same typology twice in a week.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Commit to an answer

LIVE POLL — tool still Noah’s call; TCDpolls (Vevox) is already licensed by Trinity, so it is the cheap default. Question, ready to wire up — single choice:

Which face of power matters most in Irish politics? 1. Face 1 — winning the open fight 2. Face 2 — keeping issues off the agenda 3. Face 3 — shaping what people want in the first place

Run it here, before the readings slide. The point is to make them commit to a claim now; Lecture 20 comes back and asks how they’d ever have known.


Read the room’s split out loud before moving on. If Face 3 wins, ask the winner what evidence they’d accept — that’s the Gaventa problem again, and it’s a good thirty seconds.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Key readings this week

Heywood & Laing, Politics (2025) — Ch. 1, “Faces of Power” and “Authority” sections (required)

Lukes, Power: A Radical View — selected pages, the three dimensions (required — PDF on hand)

Recommended: Dahl, “The Concept of Power” (1957)

Standard readings slide, back-load as usual. Confirm the Lukes page range before this goes on Blackboard — “selected pages” is a placeholder for the actual extract.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Next up
Lecture 3 — The state I: where does this thing come from?
Every face of power we discussed today assumed something: a state, with rules, courts, and a monopoly on legitimate force.

All of today’s fighting over agendas and preferences happens inside that assumption — a state that holds the monopoly on legitimate force. Take the state away and the whole discussion changes shape.


Think about it before next time: why does the state get to boss everyone around — and what happens where nobody holds that monopoly?
See you Tuesday

Seed Lecture 3 off the one legitimacy line you kept — Weber’s monopoly-of- legitimate-violence definition of the state is where Tuesday starts, and the three types of authority get taught there rather than here. Say “we’ll meet the man who wrote that sentence on Tuesday.” No admin beyond a one-liner if there’s a logistics update.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Module Description
This module introduces the central questions, concepts, and tools of political science. We start from the basics — what politics is, what power is, why states exist and why some of them work — then take on ideologies and political identity, democracy and dictatorship (and the grey zone between them), corruption, institutions, and who gets what in the economy. Throughout, the goal is not to memorise facts but to learn to think like a political scientist: to ask sharp questions, compare across cases, and use a small toolkit of portable concepts to make sense of a messy political world.

Learning Outcomes
On successful completion of this module, you will be able to:

Apply fundamental concepts and theoretical tools to understand problems in the world of politics
Identify the key questions and problems around which politics revolves
Use core analytical tools — power, the state, democracy, institutions, ideologies — to interpret political events
Compare political arrangements across countries and reason about why they differ

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Schedule
Week numbers follow Trinity’s teaching-week calendar (teaching week 1 begins 14 September); as a first-year module, this one starts lectures in teaching week 2.
Two lectures per week — Tuesdays and Thursdays at 11:00 — across ten teaching weeks: teaching weeks 2–6 (22 September – 23 October), then the College reading/review week (teaching week 7, w/c 26 October, no teaching), then teaching weeks 8–12 (3 November – 4 December). Twenty lectures in five parts.

Part I: Foundations


Teaching week 2 — Politics and power
Tue 22 & Thu 24 September

Big question: what is politics, and who actually decides?

Lecture 1: Is this politics? A rent freeze, a nurses’ strike, a viral post, a coup — what makes something political? Politics as collective choice under conflict.
Lecture 2: Power — who actually decides? The three faces of power, and the harder question: how would you ever observe the invisible kinds?
Readings: Heywood & Laing ch. 1; Lukes, Power: A Radical View (selected pages)


Teaching week 3 — The state
Tue 29 September & Thu 1 October

Big question: where do states come from, and why can some of them actually do things?

Lecture 3: Where do states come from? Weber’s monopoly of legitimate violence; war, taxes, and bureaucracy; Hobbes vs Locke.
Lecture 4: Why can some states actually do things? State capacity — why some states collect taxes, deliver vaccines, and hold territory, and others can’t.
Readings: Heywood & Laing ch. 3; Weber, “Politics as a Vocation” (selected pages)


Part II: Ideas & identities


Teaching week 4 — Ideologies
Tue 6 & Thu 8 October

Big question: what are the big answers to who gets what, and who decides?

Lecture 5: Liberalism, conservatism, socialism — three answers to who should get what, and who decides.
Lecture 6: Nationalism, fascism, feminism, green — and populism as a thin ideology that attaches to any of them.
Readings: Heywood & Laing ch. 2


Teaching week 5 — Identity
Tue 13 & Thu 15 October

Big question: where do political identities come from, and when does difference become conflict?

Lecture 7: Where do political identities come from? Why do some identities become political while most never do?
Lecture 8: When does difference become conflict? The real puzzle: most diverse societies, most of the time, have no ethnic violence.
Readings: Heywood & Laing chs. 6 & 8 (selected sections); Fearon, “What Is Identity?”


Part III: Regimes


Teaching week 6 — Democracy
Tue 20 & Thu 22 October

Big question: what is democracy, how would you measure it, and why does it survive?

Lecture 9: Democracy — what it is, and how you’d measure it. Minimal vs substantive definitions; V-Dem, Freedom House, and the grey zone.
Lecture 10: Why democracy emerges, and why it survives.
Readings: Heywood & Laing ch. 4; Schmitter & Karl, “What Democracy Is… and Is Not”


Teaching week 7 — reading week (no lectures)
No lectures, no tutorials. (Monday 26 October is a public holiday.) Catch up on the readings and work on the short assignment.
Teaching resumes with teaching week 8 on Tuesday 3 November.
Short assignment due — [date TBD], via Blackboard


Teaching week 8 — Dictatorships
Tue 3 & Thu 5 November

Big question: how do dictatorships actually work — and why do they bother holding elections?

Lecture 11: How autocracies actually work. Repression vs co-optation.
Lecture 12: Elections, information, succession. Why hold elections you could cancel? Why does nobody tell the autocrat the truth?
Readings: Heywood & Laing ch. 5


Teaching week 9 — When regimes go wrong
Tue 10 & Thu 12 November

Big question: how do democracies rot — and how do you count something everybody hides?

Lecture 13: Democratic backsliding. Not a coup — a slow, legal-looking hollowing-out: courts, media, electoral administration, universities.
Lecture 14: Corruption and state capture. Why “everyone does it” is self-sustaining — and how you count something everybody hides.
Readings: TBD


Part IV: Institutions & political economy


Teaching week 10 — Institutions
Tue 17 & Thu 19 November

Big question: who can stop whom — and when do rules on paper actually bind rulers?

Lecture 15: Who can stop whom? Executives, legislatures, and veto players — one tool you can carry to any country.
Lecture 16: Rules that bind rulers. Constitutions and courts — and when paper constraints actually hold.
Readings: Heywood & Laing chs. 13–15 (selected sections)


Teaching week 11 — Political economy
Tue 24 & Thu 26 November

Big question: who gets what in the economy — and why doesn’t more inequality produce more redistribution?

Lecture 17: States, markets, globalisation.
Lecture 18: Inequality, redistribution — and Irish housing as a political-economy problem, not a policy-detail problem.
Readings: Heywood & Laing ch. 7


Part V: Closing


Teaching week 12 — Zooming out
Tue 1 & Thu 3 December

Big question: why do we fail at long-horizon problems — and how would we ever know we were right?

Lecture 19: Climate as a collective action problem. Why democracies under-supply long-horizon goods.
Lecture 20: How do we know? Political science as detective work — how political scientists get fooled, and how they try not to be.
Readings: TBD

Semester 1 teaching ends Friday 4 December; the College assessment session runs 11–22 December 2026. The final essay deadline is [TBD].

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Module description
This module introduces you to the big questions in politics and to the conceptual, theoretical, and analytical tools that political scientists use to answer them. It is designed both for students who intend to study politics for the rest of their degree and for those taking a single, standalone introduction to the discipline.
We start from the basics — what politics is, what power is, why states exist and why some of them work and others don’t. From there we take on ideologies and political identity, democracy and dictatorship and the grey zone in between, corruption and state capture, political institutions, and the question of who gets what in the economy. We close on the two things that make political science a science: collective action problems, and how you would ever know whether a claim about politics is true.
The goal is not to memorise facts. It is to learn to think like a political scientist: to ask sharper questions, compare across cases, and carry a small toolkit of portable concepts into political situations you have never seen before.

Aims
The module has two aims: (1) to give you a basic knowledge of the key problems and questions around which politics revolves; and (2) to equip you with the fundamental conceptual, theoretical, and analytical tools used in the consideration of political questions.


Learning outcomes
On successful completion of this module, you should be able to:

Identify and understand the key problems and questions around which politics revolves.
Employ the fundamental conceptual, theoretical, and analytical tools used in the consideration of political questions.
Critically engage with and analyse contemporary national and global political events and issues using the tools and frameworks of political science.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
How the module works

Lectures
There are twenty lectures — two a week, Tuesdays and Thursdays at 11:00 — across ten teaching weeks. Attendance is not taken and there is no penalty for missing a lecture, but the lectures are where the module actually happens. Material will be covered in lecture that is not in the readings, and the slides are a prompt for what I said, not a transcript of it. You will not be able to reconstruct a lecture from the slides, and tutorials are not a place to catch up on lectures you missed. To do well here you need to do the readings, come to the lectures, and take part in tutorial discussion.
Lectures are participatory. I will ask the room what it thinks, and I would like an answer. Some lectures may be recorded, but you should not count on recordings being available, and access is not automatic.
Slides are posted on the course website after each lecture.


Tutorials
There are four tutorial sessions across the term, run in small groups of around twenty students by our teaching assistants. Tutorials are not weekly, and they are not repeat lectures: they are where you ask questions, argue with the readings, put a view to the room, and hear what your classmates make of it. Tutorial group assignment appears in your timetable.
Attendance at tutorials is compulsory and is linked to assessment (see below).
You do not sign up for a tutorial group. The department allocates groups and they appear in your my.tcd.ie timetable before teaching starts. If no tutorial group appears in your timetable by the end of teaching week 3, email your TA — not me — and we will sort it out. [TBD: confirm with the department that allocation is automatic via timetable and that there is no sign-up step this year.]
Tutorial dates: [TBD — four dates, confirmed once timetabling is complete]. With only four sessions, missing one costs you a quarter of the component, so put them in a calendar the day they are published.
Tutorials are a place for open, warm, and sometimes contentious discussion. People in the room have different backgrounds, experiences, and personal stakes in these questions. Engage seriously with the arguments and generously with the people making them.


Readings and the textbook
The core text is:

Andrew Heywood & Matthew Laing, Politics, 6th edition (Bloomsbury, 2025).

Chapter numbering is unchanged from the 2019 5th edition, so an older or second-hand copy is entirely fine — do not buy the newest edition on my account. A copy is provided in the Textbook item on Blackboard.
Each week has a small number of required readings you should complete before the relevant lecture, plus recommended readings for going deeper, for the assignments, and for your own interest. Additional readings beyond the textbook are provided via Blackboard. The reading list in the schedule below is indicative and may be adjusted during term; Blackboard and the course website carry the current version.
Two optional books, useful if you want a second angle on the regimes and institutions material: Patrick O’Neil, Essentials of Comparative Politics (Norton); and, pitched a level up, Clark, Golder & Golder, Principles of Comparative Politics.


Where things live

Blackboard — official notices, the textbook, readings, and all assignment submissions (via Turnitin). Anything time-sensitive or submission-related is here.
Course website — lecture slides, posted after each lecture, and the reading list.

Check both.

Discussion points and tutorial attendance (10%)

You are not being asked for polished analysis. You are being asked to raise something worth twenty minutes of argument, so that your TA can build the session around what the room actually wants to fight about.

Points attach to tutorials 2, 3 and 4; tutorial 1 is orientation. Deadlines: [TBD: three dates, set once tutorial dates are confirmed.]

Full mechanics — what to write, what does not count, excused absence, the GenAI line — are in the discussion points handout.


Short assignment — blog post (30%)
An 800-word blog post taking one concept from the module and using it to make sense of one real political situation. It is deliberately lower-stakes practice at the core move of the discipline — applying a tool to a case — before the final essay.

Length: 800 words. References, links and image captions do not count. State your word count at the top. Going over incurs a penalty of three per cent.
Style: rigorous but less formal than an academic essay. Headings, short paragraphs, bold text, links and images are all welcome; a real argument underneath is required. It is not an opinion piece with citations bolted on, and it is not an essay with subheadings.
Sources: cite at least two academic readings or materials from the module.
Prompts released: [TBD — roughly three weeks before the deadline], tied to what is actually happening in the world at the time.
Due: [TBD: deadline, expected around the study/review week, 23:00].

The genre spec, a structure that works, the prompt options and the failure modes that cost most marks are in the short assignment handout. Marking bands are in the rubric.


Final essay (60%)
A 1,500-word essay answering one of several set questions, drawing on the concepts, tools and cases from across the module. I am looking for more than recall: take a position, compare across cases, and reason with the module’s toolkit.

Length: 1,500 words, excluding references and footnotes (unless a footnote carries substantive content). State your word count at the top. Going over incurs a penalty of three per cent.
Questions released: [TBD: date — about a month before the deadline].
Due: [TBD: deadline, in the College assessment session, 11–22 December 2026, 23:00].

There is no examination. Questions, how to structure an argumentative essay at this level, citation expectations and the GenAI permissions for this piece are in the final essay handout; marking bands are in the rubric.


Written work: format requirements
In line with department guidelines, written work for this module must:

state the final word count, and observe the word limit;
be submitted to Blackboard in Word or PDF, with the Assignment Submission Form as page 1;
use consistent citation and referencing (the TCD Library style guide will help);
include an alphabetised bibliography;
be spellchecked.

Back your work up, and submit early enough to survive a technical problem. Keep your submission receipt. Computer crashes, corrupted files, and internet problems are not grounds for late submission.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Policies

Excused absence from tutorials
If you need an absence from a tutorial excused for certified medical reasons, your College Tutor must contact both your TA and me to make the request. Only requests from College Tutors are considered. If you want module credit for that tutorial, the discussion points must still be submitted — at or before the next tutorial, or within one week of the end of term if it relates to the last tutorial. It is your responsibility to make sure your College Tutor knows the correct procedure.


Late work
All late work, unless excused in advance by me, is penalised at 5 marks per day or part thereof, up to a maximum of 20 marks. There are many good reasons a student cannot submit on time and I am happy to make reasonable accommodations. What is not reasonable is getting in touch after the deadline, or a few hours before it. Do not leave requests until the last minute. Department policy does not allow extensions to be granted retrospectively except in exceptional medical circumstances. Requests for extensions go through your College Tutor; late submission on medical grounds requires a medical certificate. Work is not accepted after it has been marked and returned to other students, or after the end of teaching term — in those cases the mark is 0.


Academic integrity and plagiarism
Do not plagiarise. Academic dishonesty is a serious matter with serious consequences, up to and including no credit for the assignment, failure of the module, and expulsion. It is never permissible to submit work containing other people’s ideas without acknowledgment, and careless note-taking is not an excuse: put direct quotations in quotation marks, and reference paraphrases too. Trinity’s guidance is at libguides.tcd.ie/plagiarism, and if you have not already completed the Library’s Ready, Steady, Write tutorial, do that before your first submission. You must also submit only new work — not work submitted previously for another module.


Generative AI
These tools exist, you use them, and you will use them in whatever you do after this degree. Pretending otherwise would waste both our time. But this module is not assessing whether you can obtain a competent paragraph about political science — that is now free, and worth roughly what it costs. It is assessing whether you can read an argument, find its weak point, and put your own case in your own words. That capacity is built by doing the work, and it does not survive being outsourced. So the line I draw is this: use these tools to help you think and to help you fix your prose; do not use them to do the thinking or produce the prose. Where exactly that line falls differs by assignment, so it is set out below assignment by assignment. Disclose what you did on the submission form. I am not interested in policing you, and I am not going to run your work through a detector and accuse you on that basis — the detectors do not work well enough for that. I am interested in you being straight with me, and in you being able to think when there is no model in the room.
Permissions are set for each assessment separately, in the vocabulary of the School of Social Sciences and Philosophy Assignment Submission Form, so that the words in this syllabus and the boxes you tick on the form are the same words. “Permitted” means you may do it and must tick the corresponding box. “Not permitted” means doing it is an academic integrity matter, whether or not you disclose it.

Discussion points (10%)







Submission-form category
This assessment




No GenAI used
This is the expected answer.


Brainstorming
Not permitted. The point of the exercise is that you had a reaction to the reading.


Research/learning assistance
Permitted for one thing only: clarifying a term or passage you could not follow after genuinely trying. Not for summarising the reading — asking a model what an article says instead of reading it defeats the entire component, and your TA will be able to tell.


Writing assistance
Not permitted. These are one page, ungraded on style, and written for your TA. Spellcheck is fine.


Direct AI content inclusion
Not permitted.



These are low-stakes and frequent, so honesty matters more here than polish. A rough, obviously human page is worth more than a smooth one.


Short assignment — blog post (30%)



Submission-form category
This assessment




No GenAI used
Always fine. No penalty and no advantage — this is not a virtue signal.


Brainstorming
Permitted. Explore angles, argue with it about your thesis, generate objections to argue against.


Research/learning assistance
Permitted, with a warning. Use it to unpack a concept or a hard passage — then verify against the module readings. Do not ask it for references: it invents them, and a fabricated citation is a fabricated citation regardless of origin.


Writing assistance
Permitted, slightly wider than for the essay. Register is part of what this assignment practises, so you may ask for feedback on tone and blog-style structure, and may have it rework passages you wrote. The argument, the case, and the analysis must be yours from the start. Substantially revise and fact-check anything it hands back — you own every word you submit.


Direct AI content inclusion
Not permitted in the body of the post. Exception: if the AI output is itself your object of analysis, you may quote it, in quotation marks, cited per the Library guide, and flagged on the form.


Other use
Describe it on the form. If in doubt, ask me before the deadline; asking is never held against you.





Final essay (60%)







Submission-form category
This assessment




No GenAI used
Always fine.


Brainstorming
Permitted. Explore angles, argue with it about your thesis, generate counterarguments to argue against.


Research/learning assistance
Permitted, with a warning. Use it to unpack a concept — then verify against the module readings. Do not ask it for references. Sources must be ones you have actually read.


Writing assistance
Permitted only for text you have already drafted yourself — tightening, grammar, clarity, structural critique of your own draft. Generating a section from a prompt and then editing it is not “writing assistance”; that is the next row. This is deliberately narrower than the submission form’s own wording of this category, which is why it is spelled out here. If you use it, add a one-line note in an appendix saying which tool and what you used it for.


Direct AI content inclusion
Not permitted. No AI-generated text in the submitted essay, quoted and cited or otherwise. In a 1,500-word essay every sentence is supposed to be your reasoning.


Other use
Describe it on the form, or ask me before the deadline.





The examination
There is no examination in this module. [TBD: Noah to confirm this line stays accurate — the assessment table above says no final exam.]


The Assignment Submission Form — required on every submission
Every piece of written work submitted for this module must have the School of Social Sciences and Philosophy Assignment Submission Form attached as its first page. The form is on Blackboard in both Word and PDF. Complete it in full, including the plagiarism declaration and the GenAI disclosure — tick every category that applies to what you actually did, and use the Other use box if none of them fits.
A written submission received without a completed form is not accepted. It is returned to you unmarked, and the work is treated as not submitted until you resubmit it with a completed form attached — accruing the late penalties set out under Late work above for every day in between. This is a departmental requirement and applies across the module.
The form does not count toward your word limit. Ticking a box that the policy above permits carries no penalty of any kind.
[TBD: Noah to confirm two things — (a) whether the form is required for discussion points as well as the two graded assignments (this syllabus currently implies yes; recommendation is to exempt them explicitly), and (b) whether TAs give a 48-hour penalty-free window to supply a missing form before late penalties start running.]


If something looks wrong
Detection software does not settle this. Turnitin’s own documentation concedes a false-positive rate, and detectors misflag writing by people who learned English as a second language far more often than they misflag anyone else. I will not accuse anyone on the basis of a detector score, and no mark in this module will be reduced because software produced a number.
What actually happens: if something in a submission does not add up — an argument that does not match your other work, sources that do not exist or do not say what they are cited as saying, a disclosure that does not fit what is on the page — I will ask you to come and talk about it. That conversation is not a disciplinary hearing. Bring your notes, your drafts, your reading. Most of these conversations end there.
If the conversation does not resolve it, the matter goes through Trinity’s normal academic integrity route — the College Academic Integrity Policy and the associated procedure for suspected misconduct — and out of my hands. Submitting AI-generated content as your own work is plagiarism under College policy, and so is undisclosed use. That route is the same one that has always applied to plagiarism; nothing about it is AI-specific.
The baseline is Trinity’s Statement on Generative AI, the Library’s GenAI guide, and the College GenAI hub. Where this syllabus is stricter than the baseline, this syllabus governs.



Contacting us
Check the FAQ first — extensions, missed tutorials, readings, mark queries, and GenAI questions are all answered there.
There are around five hundred of you and one of me, so email has an order.
Start with your own TA. Anything about module content, readings, tutorials, your discussion points, or how an assignment works goes to the teaching assistant who runs your tutorial group. They are closest to your work and they are happy to meet on request.
Come to me second, and only for things a TA cannot settle — extensions, serious personal difficulty, a mark you believe is wrong after you have already discussed it with your TA, or a question about the module as a whole. When you do, copy your TA so we are not answering you separately.
The TAs and I will do our best to reply within two business days. Emails sent at midnight before a deadline will not be answered before it.
Please do not email either of us to ask: when something is due, where the slides are, what the word limit is, whether the lecture was recorded, what the reading is this week, or whether you can have an extension without going through your College Tutor. All of that is in this document, on Blackboard, or on the course website. Check there first — it is faster than we are, and it keeps the inbox clear for people with real problems.
For substantive questions about the material, come to office hours (by appointment — email to arrange). I will not be able to fill you in on a lecture you missed, but I am glad to talk through anything you are uncertain about.


Disability
Students with a disability liable to affect their ability to participate fully in this — or any — module are encouraged to register with the University’s Disability Service, which exists to make sure appropriate accommodations are in place.


Keeping up with current events
Read the news. Any serious source you like, national and international. Half the value of this module is having something concrete in your head when a concept turns up, and the other half is noticing that a concept explains something you read last week.
I reserve the right to modify this outline as necessary during term. The current version is always the one on the course website and Blackboard.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Schedule
Week numbers follow Trinity’s teaching-week calendar (teaching week 1 begins 14 September); as a first-year module, this one starts lectures in teaching week 2.
Twenty lectures across ten teaching weeks, in five parts. Readings below are indicative; confirm against Blackboard. “H&L” = Heywood & Laing, Politics, 6th ed.
Each week is motivated by a big question. The lectures are two attempts at it; the readings are the evidence. Where I know a reading is hard or short, I have said so.

Part I — Foundations

Teaching week 2 · Tue 22 & Thu 24 September

Big question: what is politics, and who actually decides?


Lecture 1 — Is this politics? A rent freeze, a nurses’ strike, a viral post, a coup. Politics as collective choice under conflict.
Lecture 2 — Power: who actually decides? The three faces of power, and the harder question: how would you ever observe the invisible ones?

Readings. H&L ch. 1 — the textbook at its most readable; start here. Lukes, Power: A Radical View (selected pages) — short, and the argument is the whole point. Read the third face twice.


Teaching week 3 · Tue 29 September & Thu 1 October

Big question: where do states come from, and why can some of them actually do things?


Lecture 3 — The state I: where do states come from? Weber’s monopoly of legitimate violence; war, taxes and bureaucracy; Hobbes against Locke.
Lecture 4 — The state II: why can some states actually do things? State capacity — coercive, extractive, administrative — and why it is not one number.

Readings. H&L ch. 3. Weber, “Politics as a Vocation” (selected pages) — a century old and still the best definition anybody has written; dense in places, so give it time.



Part II — Ideas and identities

Teaching week 4 · Tue 6 & Thu 8 October

Big question: what are the big answers to who gets what, and who decides?


Lecture 5 — Ideologies I: liberalism, conservatism, socialism. Three serious answers to the distribution question, run against one live case.
Lecture 6 — Ideologies II: nationalism, fascism, feminism, green — and populism as a thin ideology that attaches to any of them.

Readings. H&L ch. 2 — a long chapter; skim the ideologies you think you already know and slow down on the ones you don’t. [TBD: Mudde or Müller on populism — short.]


Teaching week 5 · Tue 13 & Thu 15 October

Big question: where do political identities come from, and when does difference become conflict?


Lecture 7 — Where do political identities come from? Why do some identities become political while most never do?
Lecture 8 — When does difference become conflict? The real puzzle: most diverse societies, most of the time, have no ethnic violence.

Readings. H&L chs. 6 and 8 (selected sections). Fearon, “What Is Identity?” — long and a little philosophical; read the opening and the section on identity categories, and don’t get stuck in the middle.



Part III — Regimes

Teaching week 6 · Tue 20 & Thu 22 October

Big question: what is democracy, how would you measure it, and why does it survive?


Lecture 9 — Democracy: what it is, and how you’d measure it. Minimal against substantive definitions; V-Dem, Freedom House, Polity, and three indices that disagree.
Lecture 10 — Democracy: why it emerges, why it survives.

Readings. H&L ch. 4. Schmitter & Karl, “What Democracy Is… and Is Not” — short and sweet, and the clearest ten pages on democracy you will read all term.






Teaching week 7 — reading/review week, w/c Monday 26 October. No lectures, no tutorials. (Monday 26 October is a public holiday.) Teaching resumes with teaching week 8 on Tuesday 3 November. The blog post deadline sits around here — [TBD].





Teaching week 8 · Tue 3 & Thu 5 November

Big question: how do dictatorships actually work — and why do they bother holding elections?


Lecture 11 — Dictatorships I: how autocracies work. Repression against co-optation.
Lecture 12 — Dictatorships II: elections, information, succession. Why hold an election you could cancel? Why does nobody tell the autocrat the truth?

Readings. H&L ch. 5.


Teaching week 9 · Tue 10 & Thu 12 November

Big question: how do democracies rot — and how do you count something everybody hides?


Lecture 13 — Democratic backsliding. Not a coup: a slow, legal-looking hollowing-out — courts, media, electoral administration, universities, in that order.
Lecture 14 — Corruption and state capture. Why “everyone does it” is self-sustaining, and how you measure a thing people lie about.

Readings. [TBD: backsliding reading.] [TBD: corruption / state-capture reading.]



Part IV — Institutions and political economy

Teaching week 10 · Tue 17 & Thu 19 November

Big question: who can stop whom — and when do rules on paper actually bind rulers?


Lecture 15 — Who can stop whom? Executives, legislatures and veto players — one framework you can carry to any country.
Lecture 16 — Rules that bind rulers. Constitutions and courts, and when paper constraints hold.

Readings. H&L chs. 13–15 (selected sections) — institutional detail; read for the argument, not the country lists.


Teaching week 11 · Tue 24 & Thu 26 November

Big question: who gets what in the economy — and why doesn’t more inequality produce more redistribution?


Lecture 17 — Political economy I: states, markets, globalisation.
Lecture 18 — Political economy II: inequality, redistribution, housing. Irish housing as a political-economy problem, not a policy-detail problem.

Readings. H&L ch. 7. [TBD: non-Heywood reading — ch. 7 does not cover the median voter or welfare regimes.]



Part V — Closing

Teaching week 12 · Tue 1 & Thu 3 December

Big question: why do we fail at long-horizon problems — and how would we ever know we were right?


Lecture 19 — Climate as a collective action problem. Why democracies under-supply long-horizon goods.
Lecture 20 — How do we know? Political science as detective work: how political scientists get fooled, and how they try not to be.

Readings. [TBD: collective action / climate politics reading.] [TBD: accessible causal-inference reading.]
Semester 1 teaching ends Friday 4 December 2026. The College assessment session runs 11–22 December 2026.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Is this politics?

POU11011 — Introduction to Political Science

IMAGE — full-bleed opening montage, five images in a 2-row grid (see the commented .absolute layout above for placement): a “for rent” sign with a red slash, a heated dinner table, a hospital/union picket line, a phone mid-scroll, a tank outside a parliament building. No captions yet — let the room guess before you tell them what each one is.


Do NOT open with your name, the syllabus, or Blackboard. Open with this slide up and silent for a beat, then: “Here are five things that happened somewhere in the world this year. I want you to tell me which of them are politics.” Let the room shout answers before you say anything else. This is the whole lecture — five cases, one payoff.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Case 1: the rent freeze
A government caps how much a landlord can raise the rent. A landlord says it’s confiscation and stops maintaining the property. A tenant says it’s the only thing standing between her and homelessness. Neither of them is lying.

IMAGE — photo of a “To Let” sign, or an Irish rent-pressure-zone news clip. Noah: swap in whatever the live rental-market story is in September 2026 — this one ages fast.


Don’t editorialise about who’s right. The point is that both sides have a case, and somebody has to decide whose case wins. That’s the seed of “collective choice under scarcity” — there isn’t enough affordable housing to go around, and a rule has to be made about who gets what.


Revision log, 2026-09-03

Replaced “One thing we’re not doing today” with “Politics vs political science” — positive claim slide, pitch moved to printnote
“What do all five have in common?” — dropped .smaller, added .breathe for vertical space
“Reading for next time” — added parting line for Thursday
Density: 45.0 → 45.0 w/slide (unchanged)

Content pass, 2026-09-03 (second)

“Six questions we’ll spend the term on” was a wall of six bold numbered questions — split into two slides of three (“Three questions before study week” / “And three after it”) and rewritten shorter and blunter. The veto-player printnote moved to the second slide.
Poll slot: actual question text written (below); tool still Noah’s call.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Case 2: the family row
Sunday dinner at home. Someone brings up the Occupied Territories Bill — should Ireland ban trade with illegal settlements? One cousin thinks it’s basic decency. Another thinks it’s virtue-signalling that will cost jobs. Nobody’s vote is being counted. Nobody’s a politician. Voices are raised anyway.

Noah: currency check needed before delivery — confirm in September 2026 whether the Occupied Territories Bill has passed, stalled, or been amended since this was drafted (mid-2026). If the news has moved on, swap in whatever the live “kitchen-table foreign policy row” is that week — Ireland’s neutrality debate is a reliable backup.


IMAGE — a Sunday-dinner-table photo (generic stock, not staged as this specific family), or a shot of the Dáil chamber mid-debate, to signal “the same argument, but in the room where it’s supposed to happen.” Use as an inline .absolute image, not full-bleed — this slide should stay text-forward.


This is the case that’s supposed to needle the “politics = government” assumption. No state institution is anywhere near this room. Ask: is this politics, or is it just an argument? Push them — what would have to be true for it to count?

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Case 3: the nurses’ strike
Nurses walk out. Patients’ appointments get cancelled. The union says pay hasn’t kept pace with the cost of living. The HSE says there’s no more money to give. Someone, eventually, has to decide who bends.

IMAGE — photo of an INMO picket line or similar. Noah: your call whether to use a real recent Irish nurses’/teachers’ dispute or keep this generic.


Good moment to note: this one looks more like “politics” to most people than Case 2 did — there’s an institution, a negotiation, a strike. Ask why it feels more obviously political. Banked for later: collective action comes back properly in Lecture 19 (climate) and 14 (corruption).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Case 4: the viral post
Someone posts something. It gets four million views by lunchtime. A politician is forced to respond. A policy that wasn’t on anyone’s radar yesterday is on the evening news tonight.

IMAGE — screenshot-style graphic of a generic viral post (blurred/fake handle — don’t use a real person’s actual post without checking it’s still the live example you want in September). Noah: pick something current closer to the time.


Ask: who has power in this story? The poster? The algorithm? The politician who has to respond? Don’t resolve it — flag that “who has power and how would you ever prove it” is the whole of Lecture 2.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Case 5: the coup
Soldiers surround a parliament building. The president is placed under house arrest. State television starts playing military marches. By morning there’s a new government and nobody voted for it.

IMAGE — photo of soldiers/tanks outside a government building. Noah: pick a real, current example close to delivery — there is depressingly rarely a shortage of these.


This is the one everyone will call “obviously politics” without hesitation — good, use that. Ask: what’s actually different between this and Case 1? (Scale, violence, who’s deciding — not the underlying structure.) That’s the pivot into the next slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Quick poll: which of these is politics?
text:
Quick poll: which of these is politics?

LIVE POLL — tool still Noah’s call. TCDpolls (Vevox) is already licensed by Trinity as a Blackboard tool, so it is the cheap default; pick one before Week 1 and standardise it for the term.
Question, ready to wire up — multiple choice, select all that apply:

Which of these five is politics? 1. The rent freeze 2. The family row 3. The nurses’ strike 4. The viral post 5. The coup

Expect a big spread on 2 and 4, near-unanimous yes on 5, and an argument about 1 and 3. The spread is the finding — use it.


The point of running this live rather than just asserting it: the spread of answers is the lecture’s first finding. If everyone agrees on everything, skip ahead. If there’s real disagreement (there will be, on the family row especially), that’s your opening for the next slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: What do all five have in common?
text:
What do all five have in common?

Somebody wants something somebody else doesn’t want to give.
There isn’t enough of it to go around — money, respect, land, power, the right to be listened to.
Eventually, some outcome happens. A decision gets made, even if that decision is “nothing changes.”


That’s it. That’s the core of politics: conflict, plus collective decision-making, under scarcity.

Land this slowly — this is the one idea you want them to leave the room with. Every case, however different, had those three ingredients. The rent freeze and the coup are the same shape of problem at wildly different scales and levels of violence.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
A working definition

Politics: the process by which people decide, collectively, how to handle the things they disagree about — who gets what, who’s bound by the outcome, and whether that outcome sticks.


Notice what’s not in that definition: parliaments, elections, politicians. Those are one place politics happens. They are not the only place.

This is the pivot away from the “politics = government” instinct most of the room walked in with. Don’t apologise for the abstraction — they’ve just spent five cases building the intuition, this just names it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Four ways people have defined it
text:
Four ways people have defined it
Political scientists have argued about this for a while. Roughly:

The art of government — what happens in cabinet rooms and parliaments. (Narrow.)
Public affairs — anything in the public sphere, stops at the front door.
Compromise and consensus — a method: settling disagreement by negotiation rather than force. (Crick’s view — next slide.)
Power — anywhere one person or group gets another to do something they wouldn’t otherwise do. (Broadest.)


Each definition draws the line around “politics” in a different place, and each one excludes something. “The art of government” is the narrowest — it excludes four of today’s five cases, everything except the coup. “Public affairs” gets further, but still stops at the front door: it excludes Case 2, the family row, because that happened in a private home. “Compromise and consensus” is Bernard Crick’s view, covered on the next slide. “Power” is the broadest of the four — broad enough to include your family, your flatmates, and all five of today’s cases — which is exactly why it turns out to be the most useful definition for a course that wants politics to be everywhere, not just in parliament.


IMAGE — this is the flattest, most taxonomy-shaped slide in the deck; it needs a visual more than any other slide does. Simplest fix: a 2x2 grid of small photos behind or beside the four bullets — a cabinet-room table, a newspaper front page, a handshake across a negotiating table, a boss talking to an employee — one per definition, unlabelled. Use as .absolute images, not full-bleed.


This compresses what used to be a four-slide march in the prior version of this course (and in Heywood himself) into one slide, per the plan — the taxonomy is background, not the lecture. If you want to spend real time on any one of these, “power” is the one that pays off directly: it’s the whole of Lecture 2.


Don’t dwell. Thirty seconds each, tops. The only one worth flagging forward is “power” — tell them explicitly “we come back to this properly on Thursday.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Why bother defining it at all?
text:
Why bother defining it at all?
Because how you draw the line decides what counts as a political problem — and what gets waved away as “just personal,” “just private,” “just the market.”

Good place for a short example if you want one: domestic violence was “private” for most of legal history until feminist political theory insisted it was political. The line moves, and moving it is itself a political act.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Bernard Crick’s defence

“Politics [is] the activity by which differing interests within a given unit of rule are conciliated by giving them a share of power in proportion to their importance to the welfare and the survival of the whole community.”
— Bernard Crick, In Defence of Politics (1962)


Crick’s real point isn’t the definition. It’s the defence: politics — messy, slow, compromising — beats the alternatives.

IMAGE — small portrait of Bernard Crick, or a cover shot of In Defence of Politics, placed .absolute in a bottom corner so it doesn’t compete with the quote. Both are easy to find on Wikimedia Commons or the publisher’s page.


Spell out the alternatives explicitly: naked force, one faction crushing another, “efficient” technocratic rule by people who don’t have to persuade anyone. Crick’s wager is that a society that argues its way to a compromise is better off than one that doesn’t have to. Ask: do they believe him?

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The payoff

Politics is not the noise that gets in the way of solving problems.
Politics is how societies solve problems they can’t solve by force or by unanimous agreement — which is most problems.
Every case today was politics working (or straining, or breaking). None of them were an aberration.


That’s the argument this whole module is built on. Everything from here is “so — how does that actually work?”

This is the emotional high point of the lecture. Don’t rush it. It’s also the answer to the cynic in the room who thinks politics is just people shouting — the reply is: yes, and that’s better than the alternative.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Three questions before study week

Where do states come from — and why can some of them actually run a country while others can’t?
What are people on the left and the right actually arguing about?
Why do a few identities become battle lines, and most never do?


This is the tour, not the syllabus grid — don’t put the 20-slot table on screen, it will read as a wall of admin. Deliver each line as a genuine question and let one land per click. Three now, three on the next slide; resist the urge to gloss each one.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
And three after it

Democracy or dictatorship — and would you notice the moment one turned into the other?
Who can stop whom? Constitutions, parliaments, planning objectors: who actually holds a veto?
How do we know any of this is true — and how do political scientists get fooled?


Same toolkit, twenty different rooms.

Question 5 is doing more work than it looks like. “Who can stop whom” is the veto-player question — and it turns out to explain a huge amount of comparative politics that “who’s officially in charge” doesn’t. A president who can’t get a budget past a hostile legislature and a prime minister with an obedient majority can hold the identical formal title and produce completely different policy. That gap — between who holds office and who can actually block things — is the thread that runs from constitutional design all the way down to why a housing policy dies in committee.


Land question 6 hardest: it’s the one that separates this from following the news. “Same toolkit, twenty different rooms” is the closing line — say it, then move to the next slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Politics vs political science
Not opinion, not punditry: systematic comparison, evidence over anecdote, “how would you know that?” asked out loud — starting properly in Lecture 3, every few weeks from there.

By Lecture 20 we turn the toolkit on itself: how political scientists get fooled, and how they try not to be. Hold onto your answer from today — we’ll ask whether it survives.

Political science means treating claims about politics the way you’d treat any hard empirical question: state the claim precisely, ask what evidence would confirm or kill it, compare cases rather than trusting one vivid anecdote, and stay genuinely willing to be wrong. “How do we know that?” segments are where that habit gets built — they take the big empirical claim from the previous lecture and interrogate it: what study is it actually based on, and what would have to be true for that study to be wrong? The first proper one runs in Lecture 3.


Don’t turn this into a philosophy-of-science lecture — one slide, move on. The point is just to plant that this isn’t the squishy study of politics people expect from the news; it’s a discipline with a method. First proper “how do we know that?” segment starts around Lecture 3. Lecture 20 is the payoff — flag it now so the promise lands later.


Noah: your own line here on why “science” and not “studies” — this is your call to make out loud, not mine to fabricate. (Comparative method? Falsifiability? Just “because we test things”?) One sentence is plenty.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Who am I?

From Minneapolis, Minnesota.
Lived in New York, Abu Dhabi, and Moscow before Dublin.
My own research: Russian politics, authoritarianism, corruption — when and why mayors get arrested, why some autocracies are more corrupt than others, how ordinary people decide whether to protest.


IMAGE — small photo strip or pin-map of Minneapolis / New York / Abu Dhabi / Moscow / Dublin, placed .absolute down one side of the slide. A real personal photo from one of those cities beats a generic map if Noah has one to hand.


Noah: personalise this. Your Comparative Politics version of this slide has more specific research questions (rally-round-the-flag effects, protest attitudes) — decide whether first-years get the same level of detail or a lighter version. This is also a natural slot for one concrete anecdote (a Moscow story, a “why I ended up studying this” story) if you want to open with something more personal than a bullet list.
