title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The state
A line on a map that can tax you, draft you, and lock you up — and mostly, you let it

IMAGE — full-bleed background behind the title slide. Something concrete that makes “a line on a map” literal: a border checkpoint/customs gate, a passport-control queue, or a boundary marker in open landscape. Source: Unsplash / Wikimedia Commons (CC). Use as background-image="w03-lec03-img/border.jpg" with a dark overlay so the gold subtitle text stays readable.


Cold open, no logistics. Ask the room: name one thing you did this morning that didn’t touch the state. Phone network licence, currency, the road, the college itself. Give them 20 seconds, take two answers, then say: that’s the whole lecture — the thing so total it’s invisible.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Last time, and today

Lecture 2 asked who actually decides — the three faces of power
Today: the biggest, most invisible power-holder of all — the state. What is it, and where did it come from?
Next time: fine, we have states — why can some do things, and others can’t?


Lecture 2’s quiet third face — the one that shapes what people want before they ever get to choose — was the hardest of the three to see, and the main reason that lecture took as long as it did.


Revision log, 2026-09-03

Reordered ending: Readings before Next time; added parting line to Next time
Applied .breathe to 8 list-then-statement slides (whitespace only)
Existing todo/cc flags (Weber aside, causal-chain aside, Irish cc on “Test it”) reviewed — still open, left as-is
Density: 52.9 → 53.0 w/slide (unchanged)

Content pass, 2026-09-03 (second)

Wrote the Irish case slide (“Apply it to this state”) that the previous pass flagged as too hot and left as a cc — the post-1921 state and the contested monopoly of violence. Facts verified; the go/no-go decision is flagged to Noah on the slide.
Retitled three noun-phrase headings (“Before the state” → “What did people have instead?”; “Two very different questions” → “Two questions people keep mixing up”; “The causal chain” → “War → capital → taxes → bureaucracy”).
Poll slot: tool named (TCDpolls/Vevox as the default), question text already existed and was left as written.



Keep this to 30 seconds. The throughline is “power” — the state is just power that got organised and made permanent. Don’t over-explain, they’ll see it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
How do we know that?
A recurring feature: 8–10 minutes on the actual evidence behind a claim from last time.

Each time, the pattern is the same: name the claim, then interrogate the study behind it — the design that produced it, and what would have to be true for the finding to be wrong. That last step, falsifiability, is the actual training on offer here, dressed up each week as a case study.


Today’s claim: the “second face” of power — agenda-setting, the power to decide what even gets talked about. Fine theory. How would you ever see someone exercising it, when the whole point is that nothing happens?

Say explicitly this is a recurring feature so they know to expect it — first time only, spend 20 seconds on the format itself, then never again. This slide plus the next one is the whole segment; keep it to 8–10 minutes, it’s not a tangent, it’s methods training in disguise.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Measuring the invisible: who sets the agenda?
text:
Measuring the invisible: who sets the agenda?
McCombs & Shaw (1972), Chapel Hill, North Carolina — measuring agenda-setting, not just asserting it.

The puzzle: everyone “knows” the media shapes what we think matters. How would you show it?
The design: code what the news covered; ask undecided voters what mattered most; compare the rankings.
The finding: the rankings matched almost perfectly. The media didn’t tell people what to think — it told them what to think about.


What would falsify it? Which way does the arrow run? That question — correlation vs. causation — is Lecture 20’s whole job.

The uncomfortable possibility the correlation alone can’t rule out: maybe the news wasn’t shaping what voters cared about at all — maybe it was just covering what they already cared about. A correlation this clean is consistent with both stories; only the direction of the arrow tells you which one is true, and McCombs & Shaw’s design can’t settle that on its own.


IMAGE — chart. McCombs & Shaw’s rank-order comparison (media issue-salience rank vs. voter issue-salience rank), redrawn as a simple two-column ranked bar chart, or a modern equivalent (e.g. Pew’s News Coverage Index against a Gallup “Most Important Problem” ranking). Use as a small inline image beside or below the incremental list, not full-bleed. Source: recreate from McCombs & Shaw (1972) Table 1, or Pew/Gallup for a current version.


Chose the McCombs & Shaw agenda-setting study here rather than Gaventa, because lec02 already gives Gaventa two slides as its Face-3 evidence attempt — this way week 1 covers face 3’s evidence problem and week 2 covers face 2’s, no repeat. The dangling “which way does the arrow run” is deliberate — it seeds the causal inference thread that pays off in Lecture 20.


Cold-call candidate: “how would YOU test whether the media sets the agenda, rather than follows it?” Let a couple of answers land before the design reveal. The falsifiability beat matters more than the study details — this segment is methods training in disguise.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Okay. So what is a state?
text:
Okay. So what is a state?
You’ve never lived a day without one touching you. Could you actually define it?

Let this sit for a beat — genuinely useful discomfort. Most will reach for “government” or “country,” which is exactly the confusion the next stretch untangles.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The weird thing we’re explaining
What a state actually is, stripped of familiarity:

A line on a map, mostly agreed on, rarely moved by force
An organisation that can tax you, conscript you, jail you
Almost everyone, almost all the time, just… goes along with it


That second bullet undersells the scale: the state can do all three to millions of people it has never met and never will — no personal relationship, no negotiation, just the claim of authority. That impersonality is part of what makes it strange.


Why does this exist? Why would anyone let an organisation have that much reach over them?

This is the puzzle-setting slide — don’t rush it. The oddness is the point: students have total, lifelong familiarity with states, which is exactly why they’ve never had to ask why one exists at all.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Weber’s answer

The state: a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.
— Max Weber, Politics as a Vocation (1919)


IMAGE — inline .absolute portrait of Max Weber (public-domain photo, Wikimedia Commons), placed small in a corner so the quote stays the visual focus. Alternative: a single stark image evoking “monopoly of legitimate force” — a police line, a military honour guard — if a straight portrait feels flat.


Put this on screen and just leave it a second before unpacking. This is the single most load-bearing definition of the term, and one of the most useful sentences in the whole module — say that out loud.


Noah: this slide is dead earnest by design (the quote should just sit there), but you might want a one-line aside ready for right after — something wry about how often “monopoly of legitimate force” gets asserted rather than actually held. A Russia line would land here too (a state that very much wants the monopoly and spends a lot of effort pretending it has it).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Unpack every word

Monopoly — not “mostly.” The only one allowed to.
Legitimate — force people accept as rightful. Same tool as Lecture 2
Territory — a state’s writ runs here, and stops there


Monopoly: anyone else who uses force — a militia, a gang, a vigilante — is, by definition, breaking the state’s rule, not competing with it on equal terms. There’s no such thing as a state that mostly holds the monopoly.
Legitimate: legitimacy is what lets power operate without constant visible coercion — a state that has to fight for every square metre every day isn’t really holding a monopoly at all, it’s just the biggest gang in the fight.
Territory: no territory, no state — just an authority claim with nowhere to land. That’s the difference between a state and, say, a church or a multinational company.


Put together: the state isn’t defined by what it’s for — it’s defined by what it controls: legitimate force, in a bounded space.

The “legitimacy” bullet is the one to slow down on — it’s the direct callback to Lukes/legitimacy from Lecture 2, make the link explicit out loud (“same tool as last lecture”). Students will want to jump to “but is it a force for good” — park that, it’s ideology territory (Weeks 5–6), not today.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Test it

A private security firm patrols a gated estate — force, not the monopoly
A cartel taxes a town’s market stalls, and the police don’t go there
A paramilitary polices “its” community, and the state can’t or won’t stop it


Why the security firm doesn’t count as a rival monopoly: it operates under the state’s licence and law, and the state can revoke it at will — delegated force, not competing force. The cartel is the harder case: by Weber’s test taken literally, the cartel is closer to holding the local monopoly than the state is, because the state’s writ has actually stopped running there. That’s not a flaw in the definition — it’s the definition doing its job, telling you something true and uncomfortable about where state power actually reaches.


IMAGE — concrete case, small inline .absolute: a gated-community security checkpoint for the private-security example, or a photo evoking informal territorial control for the cartel example (choose something that doesn’t sensationalise). Source: Wikimedia Commons / Unsplash. Place beside the relevant bullet.


Weber’s definition isn’t a description of well-behaved cases — it’s a test for the messy ones, including parts of your own country’s history.

The Irish version of this test is now written as its own slide, next — it was flagged here as “too hot to write” in the previous pass and the fresh-eyes review called it the strongest unused idea in the first seven decks. Written dry and factual; the call on whether to deliver it is on that slide.


Don’t let “test it” slide turn into a debate about whether any state ever fully has the monopoly — that’s true and fine, the definition is a benchmark, not a pass/fail. If the Irish example lands, let it; if the room goes quiet, move on.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Apply it to this state
Treaty signed, December 1921. Irish Free State established, December 1922.

June 1922 – May 1923: the new state fights a civil war against the anti-Treaty IRA — men who denied its right to exist at all
It ends not in surrender but in an order to “dump arms”: go home, keep the guns
Decades later, paramilitaries were still claiming the right to use force in the name of an Irish republic


Weber’s test, applied honestly: the monopoly is something a state wins, loses, and has to keep winning. Not something it gets at independence.

The dates: Anglo-Irish Treaty signed 6 December 1921; the Irish Free State formally established 6 December 1922; the Civil War ran from the shelling of the Four Courts on 28 June 1922 to Frank Aiken’s “dump arms” order of 24 May 1923. The point is not that Ireland was unusual — it is that the ordinary condition of a new state is a contested monopoly, and that the definition you just learned is what lets you say that precisely rather than vaguely. Every state on the map has a version of this in its past; Ireland’s is just close enough to see clearly.


IMAGE — the Four Courts, Dublin, shelled and burning, June 1922. Public domain / National Library of Ireland; widely reproduced. One image, full width, no caption needed — the room will recognise the building.


Noah: your call whether this runs in Lecture 3. Two questions I can’t answer for you: (1) is a lecture hall of Irish first-years in week 3 the right room for the Civil War and the Troubles, delivered by an American in ten sentences? (2) if yes, do you want the third bullet at all, or does the deck stop in 1923? Also please check my facts — dates and the “dump arms” order are sourced in the cc below, but the framing is the part that needs an Irish reader.


Facts verified 2026-09-03: Treaty signed 6 Dec 1921; Free State established 6 Dec 1922; Civil War 28 June 1922 – 24 May 1923, ended by Frank Aiken’s “dump arms” order rather than a negotiated surrender. Sources: Britannica, “Irish Civil War”; theirishstory.com overview; Wikipedia “Guerrilla phase of the Irish Civil War” (all consistent on dates and on the dump-arms order). Written deliberately without adjectives and without assigning blame to either side.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
What did people have instead?
For most of human history, “who’s in charge here” had a different answer:

Empires — authority radiating out from a centre, thinning at the edges
City-states — sovereignty, but tiny and local
The Church — in medieval Europe, overlapping authority with kings


Empires had no fixed border where authority just stopped — control faded gradually rather than ending at a line. City-states like Athens or Venice held real sovereignty, but never claimed anything continent-spanning. And in medieval Europe, your king and your bishop could both plausibly claim to be in charge of you — two competing authorities, no clean division of territory between them.


No one of these looked like a bounded territory with one monopoly on force. That shape had to be built.

Keep this to a minute — one slide, not a tour. The point is only: the modern state is a historically weird invention, not the default setting for human organisation. Peace of Westphalia (1648) — mention in passing as the rough “paperwork” moment states, don’t dwell, it’s not the causal story.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Charles Tilly brings the heat

“War made the state, and the state made war.”
— Charles Tilly


IMAGE — full-bleed or large inline: early modern European warfare — massed pikemen and cannon, or a period painting of a siege (e.g. Thirty Years’ War). Makes “war made the state” visually literal. Source: Wikimedia Commons (public-domain paintings — search “Thirty Years War siege painting”). Use as .absolute behind or beside the quote.


Ten minutes, one causal chain. This is the historical story of how the modern European state got built.

Tell it as a story, not a literature review — no stationary bandit, no modernization theory, that’s second-year Comparative’s Week 1 and they’ll do it properly. Here it’s in service of Weber’s definition: how does a “monopoly of legitimate violence” actually get assembled?

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
War → capital → taxes → bureaucracy

Rival rulers, competing for the same territory → constant war
War (guns, cannon, standing armies) needs capital
Capital requires taxation — knowing who your people are and what they have
Taxation and war both require bureaucracy
To make any of this stick, you need a monopoly on violence


Step 4’s bureaucracy means, concretely, record-keepers, tax collectors, administrators — the unglamorous staff who make taxation and war-fighting possible at scale. Step 5 is the one that closes the loop: no rival lord, bandit, or city can be allowed to tax or fight on their own account, or the whole chain unravels. And the payoff of the sequence — the bureaucratic state, the boring, permanent, record-keeping apparatus most people picture when they picture “government” — wasn’t the goal any ruler set out to achieve. It was scaffolding built to win wars, that outlasted the wars themselves.


IMAGE — chart/diagram: the five-step causal chain redrawn as an actual arrow diagram rather than a numbered list, or a chart of early-modern European fiscal/military capacity growing over time (e.g. from Tilly’s own figures, or Karaman & Pamuk’s fiscal-capacity series). Use full-width, inline, below or beside the list. Source: recreate from Tilly (1990) or Karaman & Pamuk (2010).


Follow the chain back: the modern bureaucratic state was built as a side effect of war-making, not designed on purpose.

This is the whole payoff of the Tilly beat — the state as an accidental by-product of rulers just trying to win wars. Tilly’s more provocative line — “banditry, piracy, gangland rivalry, policing, and warmaking all belong on the same spectrum” — is a good one to drop if time allows, but cut it first if running long.


Noah: this is the driest slide in the deck (a five-step numbered chain) — a joke or a concrete aside would help it land. Olson’s “stationary bandit” line pairs naturally with Tilly’s “banditry and warmaking on the same spectrum” quote in the notes, and this is a very findable spot for a Russia example (a state built the same way — war, extraction, coercion — with the bureaucracy arguably still catching up).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Two questions people keep mixing up
text:
Two questions people keep mixing up

Philosophers ask: why should we want a state? — a justification, worked out from first principles
Historians and sociologists ask: how did we actually get states? — Tilly’s answer, worked out from evidence


Here’s the fun part: these two stories don’t agree. The philosophy is about legitimacy; the history is about war and money.

No ruler ever actually sat down, reasoned from a state of nature, and designed a state on paper — that isn’t what the historical record shows happened. The two accounts aren’t rival descriptions of the same event; they’re answers to two different questions, and the confusion starts the moment you treat one as evidence against the other.


This slide is the hinge of the lecture — flag explicitly that we’re switching registers, from “what happened” to “how would you defend it.” Don’t let students assume Hobbes/Locke are describing history; they’re doing moral philosophy.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Hobbes: the case for an absolute state
text:
Hobbes: the case for an absolute state
Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651). What are people actually like, underneath the rules?


Without a common power to keep us all in awe, life is a war “of every man against every man” — “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.”



His fix: everyone hands all their rights to one absolute sovereign — the Leviathan — in exchange for order.

Harsh, and Hobbes knows it — his argument isn’t that this is a good bargain, only that it beats the one alternative he actually cares about: a world with no common power at all, where life is “solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short” for everyone, all the time.


IMAGE — the Leviathan frontispiece (1651), the famous engraving of the giant sovereign body made of tiny citizens. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons. Ideal as a large inline image or even a full-bleed background — it is one of the most recognisable images in political theory and does real explanatory work on its own.


Ask: “is Hobbes right that people are naturally like this?” Don’t resolve it — flag that this is a live, contested assumption, not a proven fact. It’s doing a lot of work for his whole argument.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Locke: the case for a limited state
text:
Locke: the case for a limited state
John Locke, writing decades later. Same starting move — state of nature, social contract — very different ending.

People have natural rights — life, liberty, property — before any state exists
The state’s only job is to protect those rights
Because the state can threaten those rights too, citizens need protection against the state itself


In practice, “protection against the state itself” means limited, representative government — checks on power, elections, courts that can rule against the sovereign — not a blank cheque handed to whoever holds the seat of power, the way Hobbes’s Leviathan gets one.


IMAGE — portrait of John Locke (public domain, Wikimedia Commons), inline .absolute, sized and placed to visually pair with the Hobbes portrait two slides back if Noah wants a matched set across the two slides.


Same tool, opposite conclusion: Hobbes gives up almost everything for order; Locke keeps a leash on the state.

This is a genuine intellectual fork worth naming out loud: it’s the ancestor of the whole liberal/authoritarian spectrum in political thought, and it recurs all module (ideologies in Weeks 5–6, “rules that bind rulers” later in the institutions block). Don’t resolve who’s “right” — that’s the point of teaching both.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Justification vs. history — hold both

Tilly explains how states actually got built: war, taxes, bureaucracy, coercion — nobody’s rights were “protected” along the way
Hobbes and Locke explain why we should accept a state once it exists — or what it owes us in return


Neither one is wrong — they’re answering different questions. Watch for anyone, including textbooks, who slides from one to the other.

Good place for a 30-second show-of-hands: “closer to Hobbes or closer to Locke?” Don’t spend more than a minute on it, just a temperature check, keep moving.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Three words people use interchangeably. They shouldn’t.
text:
Three words people use interchangeably. They shouldn’t.

State — the permanent apparatus: courts, army, civil service, tax office. Outlasts every election
Government — whoever is currently running it. Changes on a Saturday in February
Nation — people who feel they belong together. Doesn’t need a state


What makes a nation, in practice: a shared culture, language, and story people tell about who they are — none of which requires a state to back it up. A stateless nation (the Kurds) and a multinational state (the UK, and arguably Ireland’s own relationship to Northern Ireland) are the two clearest illustrations that “nation” and “state” aren’t the same word wearing different clothes.


Ireland test: the state outlasted three governments; the government changed in most recent election; the nation — who counts as “Irish” — is older, and far more contested.

IMAGE — inline .absolute photo: Leinster House (the Dáil) for “state,” or Government Buildings on Merrion Street for a sharper state-vs-government visual contrast. Source: Wikimedia Commons. Keep it small and corner-placed so it doesn’t compete with the Ireland-test text.


Fill in the actual most recent government-change date/event closer to delivery — keep it current rather than dated by September 2026.


This is the single most common student confusion in this material — spend real time here, not a rushed afterthought. A stateless nation (Kurds) and a multinational state (the UK, arguably Ireland’s own relationship to Northern Ireland) are both good one-line examples if time allows, but don’t open the North’s status as a live discussion in a 50-minute lecture — flag it and move on rather than let it run.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Readings
Required

Heywood & Laing, Politics — Ch. 3, “Politics and the State” (definitional and origins sections)
Weber, Politics as a Vocation — selected pages (the state and legitimate violence)

Recommended

Tilly, “War Making and State Making as Organized Crime” — provocative and worth it


LIVE POLL — tool still Noah’s call; TCDpolls (Vevox) is the licensed default. Question: “Which is closer to the truth: Hobbes (people are naturally dangerous, order needs an absolute state) or Locke (people have rights before the state, order needs limits)?” — run at the Hobbes/Locke hinge slide or here as a wrap-up; either works, your call on pacing.


Flag the poll placement decision to yourself before delivery — mid-lecture keeps energy up, end-of-lecture works better as a clean segue into Lecture 4’s “but why do some states struggle” hook. Either is fine.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Next time
Fine — we’ve got states. A line on a map, a monopoly of force, built out of war and bureaucracy, justified after the fact by philosophers.

Lecture 4: why can some states deliver vaccines, collect taxes, and control their own territory — and others can’t, even when they want to?
See you Thursday

The teaser line is doing real work — say it, don’t just show it. This is the “state capacity” concept that the module will keep returning to; plant it clearly so Lecture 4 has something to land on.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Ideologies I
Who should get what — and who decides? Your answer isn’t yours alone. It has a name, a history, and rivals.

Cold open, no admin. Don’t over-explain the question yet — let it sound like a real provocation aimed at them personally. This is the distribution question that structures the whole lecture; you’ll come back to this exact phrasing at least three times today.


IMAGE — full-bleed background for the cold open. A visibly divided crowd shot — an election count, a big demonstration, or a packed rally with competing signs — something that reads as “many different answers to who gets what, all in one room.” Source: Getty/Reuters wire photo, or an Irish general election count (RTÉ/Irish Times archive). Use as ## Ideologies I {background-color="var(--week-title-bg)" background-image="w04-lec05-img/opener.jpg"}.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The plan for today

Last week’s leftover: the five “whose state is it” lenses were a preview — today we open them up properly
What ideology actually is, and why your opinions come in packages
How do we know that? — can you actually measure something that lives in someone’s head?
Three rival answers: liberalism, conservatism, socialism


Four items, read fast, move on. The framing to hold onto: this is not a vocabulary list, it’s three competing answers to one hard question, and by the end they should be able to generate any of the three positions themselves from first principles rather than memorising labels.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Same five lenses, different name
Last lecture: pluralist, Marxist, New Right, feminist, elite — five answers to “whose state is it?”

The exit line was: these are ideologies, wearing state-costumes.


Today we take the costumes off. Three of those five lenses are actually the three oldest, biggest ideologies in politics — you already met them, you just didn’t know their real names yet.

This is the explicit bridge the brief asks for — say it exactly like this, don’t paraphrase it away. Pluralist → liberalism, Marxist → socialism, New Right → conservatism. Feminism and elite theory are parked again — feminism gets its full treatment next lecture, elite theory doesn’t map cleanly onto a classic ideology at all (flag that explicitly, it’s a good “not everything fits the pattern” moment).


Deliberately front-loading this bridge rather than saving it for later, per the brief. If it runs long, it’s compressible to the two sentences in bold — the payoff matters more than the walkthrough.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Key term: ideology

Ideology: a more-or-less coherent set of ideas about how society is, how it should be, and how to get there.


Three moving parts: a picture of the world, a vision of the good society, and a plan for getting from one to the other.

Stress the neutral, analytic sense — Heywood’s move. Ideology isn’t a slur and it isn’t something only other people have. Everyone in this room has one, whether they’ve ever named it or not. That’s the whole hook for the next slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Why do your beliefs come in packages?
text:
Why do your beliefs come in packages?

You have views on markets, equality, tradition, change, how much the state should do
Notice: your view on markets tends to predict your view on tradition — they are not independent
Nobody hands you a rulebook that says “if you believe X, you must also believe Y”


So where does the glue come from?

Plant the mystery properly — this is the engine of the whole lecture. Good cold-call moment: ask someone their view on a totally unrelated pair of issues (e.g. immigration and inheritance tax) and watch the room notice the correlation is real but nobody designed it. The answer, coming next: each ideology is a package deal — a bundle of answers to the same underlying questions.


Noah: a live, low-stakes example lands better than my abstract pairs — something from your own experience of student political attitudes, or a genuinely cross-cutting Irish case, would sell this harder than “markets and tradition.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Can you even measure this?
Power (Lecture 2) and state capacity (Lecture 4) were both things you can’t see directly — you had to go looking for a proxy.

Ideology is the same problem, but worse: it lives entirely inside people’s heads.


The standard fix: just ask people. Most large surveys ask respondents to place themselves on a single line, from 0 (left) to 10 (right).

Explicit thread callback — say the words “same move as Lecture 2” and “same move as Lecture 4” out loud. This isn’t officially on the course’s headline measurement chain (2→9→14→20) but it’s doing the same work, so name it anyway — more repetition of the pattern is good, not confusing.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
What does a “5” actually mean?

A “5” in Ireland and a “5” in the United States are not describing the same set of beliefs — the whole scale has shifted
Two people can both say “7” and mean completely different things by it: one is thinking about tax, the other about immigration
The same self-reported ideology can predict different policy positions in different countries


So the single left-right number is a real, useful measure — and it’s also a compression that throws information away.

That’s not a flaw unique to the left-right scale. It’s the price every measurement in political science pays: turning something as rich as a person’s whole set of political beliefs into one number always throws information away, even when the number is genuinely useful for comparing people, parties, and countries.


This is the payoff of the segment: not “surveys are bad,” but “here’s exactly what a widely-used measure buys you and exactly what it costs you.” That’s the methodological lesson that recurs through the whole term and lands fully in Lecture 20. Good moment to ask: “if not a single number, what would you measure instead?” — accept multi-dimensional answers (economic axis + social axis) if someone offers one, but don’t require it.


Live poll: “Where would you place yourself, 0 (left) to 10 (right)?” — then reveal the room’s distribution and ask what a “5” in this room actually means to different people who picked it. Tool for live polling still undecided; question is ready to wire up once decided.


IMAGE — chart. Left-right self-placement distributions by country, side by side (e.g. Ireland vs. the US), showing the scale sits in a different place in each — makes “a 5 in Ireland isn’t a 5 in the US” visible rather than asserted. Source: European Social Survey or World Values Survey left-right item, plotted as a histogram per country.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Three questions, three answers
Each ideology below answers the same three questions — just differently:


Who should get what? Markets and merit, or a floor everyone stands on regardless?
What is human nature like? Rational and self-interested, flawed and needing guidance, or fundamentally social?
How should change happen? Fast, slow, or resisted?


This is the portable frame — flag it as a tool they’ll reuse. When identity, regimes, and political economy show up later in term, the same three-question skeleton is underneath. Say that out loud now so the callback in later lectures actually lands.


Portable-concept callout: name this explicitly as a tool, the way state capacity and power got named as tools. If you want a single memorable phrase for it, “who gets what, who decides, how fast” is the compressed version.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Ireland built more houses last year than in any year since 2011
text:
Ireland built more houses last year than in any year since 2011
36,284 new dwellings completed in 2025 — the highest since the series began. CSO

In July 2026, 17,527 people were living in emergency accommodation, including 5,659 children. Both numbers are records. Dept of Housing


So: what should be done? Everyone in this room has an instinct about that. Where did your instinct come from?

The two numbers are not in tension by accident — supply rising and homelessness rising at the same time is exactly the kind of fact that different ideologies read in opposite directions. One reading: we are building, it just hasn’t caught up yet, so build faster and get out of the way. Another: building faster into the same market does not house the people at the bottom of it, because the market was never going to. Which reading you find obvious is the thing this lecture is about.


Figures verified 2026-09-03. Completions: CSO, New Dwelling Completions Q4 2025 — 36,284 in 2025, up 20.4% on 30,147 in 2024, highest since the series began in 2011. Homelessness: Department of Housing monthly report for July 2026 — 11,868 adults and 5,659 children, 17,527 total (reported in the Irish Times, 28 Aug 2026). Deliberately only two numbers on the slide. Both will be stale by September 2026 — refresh from cso.ie and gov.ie before delivery.


Do not editorialise yet. Put the two numbers up, let the room sit with the fact that both are records at once, then ask the question. You want instincts in the room before any of the three labels exist — the whole lecture is the reveal that their instinct is a package deal with a name on it.


Noah: your call on whether to cold-call here or run it as a poll (there’s already a left-right poll earlier in the deck — two might be one too many). Also: if you have a sharper Dublin number by delivery — rents, vacancy, planning objections — swap one in. Keep it to two.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: What would you actually do on Monday?
text:
What would you actually do on Monday?
Not “what do you believe.” What would you do — and what does that commit you to about markets, human nature, and how fast things should change?

Take three answers, no more. Write them on the board if you can; you’ll point back at them three times in the next twenty minutes. The predictable spread is: build more and clear the planning system out of the way / protect what’s there and go slowly / the state should build it directly. Those are your three ideologies, said by first-years without the vocabulary. That’s the design.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Liberalism’s answer
Who gets what? Whatever you earn through free exchange — the state’s job is to referee, not redistribute (in its classical form).

Human nature? Rational, self-interested, capable of working out your own best interests better than anyone else can.


Change? Progress through reason and debate — society gets better as ideas compete and the best ones win.


On housing: it’s a supply problem. Clear the obstacles to building and let the market clear. Rent caps make it worse — they shrink what gets built.

Deliver this as the trio’s opening statement, not a dictionary entry. The structural move — same three questions, liberal answers — should feel like a pattern clicking into place, since you just told them to expect exactly this.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Locke’s move

“Life, liberty, and property.” — John Locke’s answer to what government is for


Locke wasn’t describing government as it existed. He was attacking absolute monarchy and building the case for limited government, answerable to the people it governs.


Thomas Paine’s later verdict: the state is a “necessary evil.” Necessary — you need it for order. Evil — every bit of power it has is power taken from you.

Locke is the founding figure worth naming; don’t build out the full Enlightenment cast. The “necessary evil” line is a genuinely quotable, spicy one-liner — put it big on screen and let it sit for a beat.


IMAGE — inline portrait, .absolute (top-right, small). John Locke, the Godfrey Kneller portrait (c.1697) — public domain, Wikimedia Commons. Caption: “John Locke, 1632–1704.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Same word, two opposite politics

Classical liberalism: minimal state, free markets, “negative” liberty — freedom means being left alone.
Modern liberalism: the state can enlarge freedom — welfare, regulation, “positive” liberty — freedom means actually having a real shot at a good life.


Same starting value (the individual), wildly different conclusions about what the state should do.

That’s why “liberal” means almost opposite things depending where you are. In the United States, “liberal” usually means the modern, big-government version — welfare, regulation, an active state. In Europe, “liberal” often still means the classical, small-state version. Same root word, different politics — useful to know before you read American news coverage.


Worth flagging explicitly: in the US, “liberal” = modern liberalism (big government); in Europe, “liberal” often still means the classical, small-state version. This is a genuinely useful bit of cultural translation for a first-year who will otherwise be confused by American politics coverage.


2026 currency check: a live example of a self-described liberal party or figure governing right now — European liberal parties (Renew-family), or a US “liberal” policy debate, would both work. Confirm which lands better with September 2026’s news cycle.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Conservatism’s answer
Who gets what? Roughly what tradition and hierarchy already allocate — with a duty of care from the privileged toward the less fortunate.

Human nature? Limited, imperfect, security-seeking — people need stable structures more than they need abstract freedom.


Change? Only when it’s forced on you, and even then: change to conserve, not change for its own sake.


On housing: ownership is what makes people stakeholders. Help buyers, build in scale with the places that already exist, don’t bulldoze the settlement you have. Slowly.

Keep the same three-beat rhythm as the liberalism slide — that repetition is deliberate, it’s what makes the “same questions, different answers” frame stick.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Burke’s warning

“A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.” — Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790)


Burke wasn’t against reform. He was against reform built on abstract ideas — liberty, equality, fraternity — instead of on what history has actually tested and proven to work.

Fixed factual error flagged in the fresh-eyes review (2026-09-03, §1 item 5): the slide previously quoted Burke as saying “change in order to conserve,” but that exact phrasing is not a Burke quotation — it’s a popular paraphrase (often mis-cited) of his actual line, “A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation” (Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790). Swapped in the real quotation and demoted the paraphrase to a plain descriptive sentence in the previous slide. Source: text of Reflections (widely reproduced, e.g. via Project Gutenberg / Bartleby editions).



His target was the French Revolution: tear down every inherited institution overnight, in the name of pure reason, and see what happens.

Burke is doing the same “founding figure” job Locke does for liberalism — one thinker, one quote, don’t build out a reading list of conservative theorists. The useful nuance for first-years: conservatism isn’t “no change,” it’s “change slowly, and only the kind that doesn’t uproot what already works.”


IMAGE — inline, .absolute (bottom-right, medium). The storming of the Bastille, 14 July 1789 — the event Burke was reacting against. A period painting or engraving, public domain, Wikimedia Commons (search “prise de la Bastille”).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Which conservatism are we talking about?
text:
Which conservatism are we talking about?

Paternalistic / One-Nation: the privileged owe a duty of care downward — “reform from above, not revolution from below.”
New Right: a 1970s–80s break — neoliberal on the economy (shrink the state, free markets), neoconservative on everything else (traditional morality, law and order, the nation) — two different logics fused into one label.


That split is why “conservative” can mean either “protect the welfare state” or “shrink the state” — same label, very different economics.

The New Right’s own combination looks like a contradiction if you don’t say it out loud: a small state on the economy, but a strong, activist state on crime, immigration and morality. It isn’t an accident or a mistake — it’s a real, long-noted tension inside the New Right coalition (get government out of markets, keep it firmly in bedrooms and borders), and it’s worth naming as a tension rather than smoothing it over.


Fixed per fresh-eyes review (2026-09-03, §1 item 5): the slide stated the New Right pairs anti-state economics with social traditionalism but never flagged the apparent tension between “shrink the state” and “traditionalism” (which usually requires state enforcement) — read as an accidental self-contradiction. Reworded the bullet as neoliberal-economics + neoconservative-social-agenda and added a printnote naming the tension explicitly as a real, teachable feature of the New Right rather than a slip. Standard characterisation (e.g. Heywood’s Political Ideologies, ch. on conservatism/the New Right).


The qualifiers matter. The paternalistic tradition wants to protect the welfare state cautiously, from a position that still trusts the state to look after people; the New Right wants to shrink the state aggressively, trusting markets instead. Same word, opposite instincts about what the state is for.


This is the moment to flag that conservatism is arguably the most internally split of the three — worth a sentence acknowledging that, then move on rather than building a sub-taxonomy. New Right pairs nicely forward to Lecture 6’s populism material (Meloni, Milei) — you can tease that connection here if time allows.


2026 currency check: a live conservative or New Right figure/party as the carrier example — this is a natural point to gesture forward to Lecture 6’s populist-right slot without stealing its content. Confirm which figure is most current in September 2026.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Socialism’s answer
Who gets what? Distribution should track need, not just what the market happens to pay you.

Human nature? Fundamentally social — “no man is an island” — shaped by community, not born a self-sufficient competitor.


Change? Depends who you ask: revolution (overthrow capitalism) or reform (tame it through elections and welfare).


On housing: shelter is a need, not an asset class. The state builds it, on public land, and rents it with security of tenure. The market had its go.

Same three-beat rhythm again — third and final time, the pattern should now feel completely automatic to the room. The “depends who you ask” line sets up the revolutionary/reformist split on the next slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Marx’s diagnosis

“From each according to his ability, to each according to his need.” — Karl Marx


Marx’s claim wasn’t just “inequality is unfair.” It was that capitalism structurally requires exploitation: profit comes from paying workers less than the value they create.


His prediction: capitalism’s own contradictions eventually cause its collapse — not because socialists win an argument, but because the system breaks itself.

Give Marx the same weight the other two got a founding figure — but flag clearly that “Marxism” and “socialism” are not synonyms; Marx is the most influential socialist thinker, not the only one.


Noah: this slide is pretty earnest as written — a wry aside would help (e.g. the gap between “workers of the world unite” and how few states that ever called themselves Marxist actually got there by revolution, or a dry one-liner about the USSR claiming the label). Your call on the joke and whether a Russia/USSR mention belongs here or is better saved for lecture 12.


Noah: if you use the Russia/USSR aside here, note lec06’s “Last time, quickly” slide also reaches for a Russia/Putin example — that’s two Russia mentions in one week if you take both. Keep one, cut the other, or swap one for a different case.


IMAGE — inline portrait, .absolute (top-right, small). Karl Marx, the standard 1875 photographic portrait — public domain, Wikimedia Commons. Caption: “Karl Marx, 1818–1883.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Revolution or reform?

Communism (Lenin, the Bolsheviks): capitalism has to be overthrown — reform just delays the inevitable.
Social democracy (the reformist branch): tame capitalism through elections, welfare, redistribution, and regulation — no revolution required.


Most socialist parties governing in Europe today sit in the second camp — reform, not revolution.

That’s part of why “socialist” can sound almost synonymous with “generous welfare state” rather than “overthrow the market” in everyday usage. It’s also why the same label gets applied to very different things — a Nordic coalition government and a revolutionary vanguard party both get called “socialist,” even though they agree on almost nothing about how change should actually happen.


This split matters for their political literacy generally — “socialist” gets thrown around loosely in Irish and international media covering everything from Nordic welfare states to Venezuela, and those are not remotely the same thing. Worth saying that tension out loud.


2026 currency check: a live social-democratic governing example (Nordic coalition, a European social-democratic party in government) as the carrier — confirm currency in September 2026. Avoid drifting into a full Sinn Féin/Irish-left discussion here; that material belongs to Lecture 6’s populism slot, not this one.


IMAGE — inline, .absolute, next to the Communism bullet. A photo from the October Revolution, 1917 (Bolshevik Red Guards, or the storming of the Winter Palace) — public domain, Wikimedia Commons.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
So that’s the pattern
Back to Monday morning in Dublin. The three answers you gave me:

Get out of the way and build — that’s a claim about markets, merit, and rational people. Liberalism.
Protect what’s here, go carefully — a claim about flawed people needing stable structures. Conservatism.
The state should just build it — a claim about need over price, and society over the individual. Socialism.


Nobody in this room read a manifesto this morning. The packages showed up anyway.

The same three ideologies, set out against the three questions, as a table — this is the version to have in front of you when you revise:










Liberalism
Conservatism
Socialism




Who gets what
What you earn
What tradition allocates
What you need


Human nature
Rational, self-interested
Flawed, needs guidance
Social, cooperative


Change
Reason and progress
Slow, only if forced
Revolution or reform


Dublin housing
Clear the obstacles, let it build
Support owners, change slowly
The state builds it



Three different starting premises about the individual and society — and the whole rest of each ideology follows from that first move. The housing row is not an extra: it is the test of whether the other three rows are doing any work. If you can predict someone’s housing position from their view of human nature, the package is real.


This is the payoff of the whole lecture — the room generated the three positions themselves twenty minutes ago without the vocabulary, and now they get the names. Point at the three answers you wrote on the board. The table is in the handout; do not put it on screen, it kills the moment.


Noah: a meme lands here better than anywhere else in the deck — the political-compass format, which they already know and half-believe, is the obvious one. Your call.


Restructured 2026-09-03 (fresh-eyes §2: “lec05 is the worst offender — the taxonomy march”). The Irish housing case now runs before the three creeds; each creed slide carries a one-line housing answer; this slide is the “so that’s the pattern” payoff, and the 3×3 table has moved into the printnote/handout with a fourth housing row added. Seeds Lecture 18.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Next up
Next lecture — Ideologies II: nationalism, fascism, feminism, green — and populism as a thin ideology
The classic trio doesn’t cover everything. What happens when an ideology puts the nation — or the planet, or gender, or “the people vs. the elite” — at the centre instead?

Read ahead: Heywood & Laing Ch. 2 (remainder). Which of today’s three answers did you find most persuasive? Next week’s ideologies scramble that picture.

Today, in four lines: we opened up the five “whose state is it” lenses from last week and found three of them are the classic trio; we defined ideology as a package deal rather than a random bundle of opinions; we asked whether you can measure something that lives inside people’s heads, and found the left-right number is useful and a compression — the same problem as measuring power and capacity; and we ran one real Irish argument, housing, through liberalism, conservatism and socialism to show that three answers to who-gets-what, human nature, and how-fast-change-should-happen will generate the whole position for you.

See you Thursday

As you read, think about which of today’s three answers — liberalism, conservatism, or socialism — you found most persuasive on all three questions: who gets what, what human nature is like, and how fast change should happen. Next week’s ideologies (nationalism, fascism, feminism, green politics) don’t answer these three questions the same clean way, which is exactly what makes them harder to place.


Clean handoff. Tease specifically that populism (Lecture 6’s centrepiece) doesn’t answer the three questions the way liberalism/conservatism/socialism do — it’s a thin ideology that can attach to any of them, which is exactly the twist that makes next lecture land. Don’t give away the punchline, just point at it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Where Do Political Identities Come From?
text:
Where Do Political Identities Come From?
You didn’t wake up one morning and decide to be Irish, Catholic, or working-class. So where did that come from — and why does it run your politics?

Cold open, no admin. Let it sit. The puzzle for today: people come to see themselves as members of categories they never chose. Today asks where those categories come from. Next lecture asks the harder question — why some of them turn into violence and most don’t.

Something that reads “many identities, one crowd” at a glance: a stadium or match-day crowd shot with national flags, club colours, and scarves visibly mixed together (Unsplash/Getty sports-crowd search). Use as ## Where Do Political Identities Come From? {background-image="w05-lec07-img/crowd.jpg"}.

Three rival answers to “where does identity come from” — primordial, constructed, deployed
Why the “natural and ancient” story feels right — and why that’s the problem

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Why die for something 200 years old?
text:
Why die for something 200 years old?
Ideology is what you believe. Identity is who you are. People have died by the millions for nations barely two centuries old — why would anyone do that for something that new?

Political identity: a shared sense of belonging to a group — nation, ethnicity, religion, language, culture — that shapes who people see as “us” and “them” in politics.
Identity and ideology are two different, sometimes independent, things. A person can hold the same ideology (liberalism) while belonging to totally different identity groups — Irish, Nigerian, Sunni, secular. And people in the same identity group vote completely differently. That independence is exactly what makes this lecture and the next one interesting.


Do the ideology/identity distinction as one spoken line, not a slide — 20 seconds. Then let the question hang for a beat. Don’t answer it.
It’s the thread the whole lecture pulls on: if national, ethnic or religious identity were just an ancient inherited fact of life, dying for it would need no explanation. The fact that it is mostly recent — and people still do it — is the thing that needs explaining.


Noah: this is where the personal aside goes, and it now has room for one because the flat definition slide is gone. Either the self-tag (“I’m a Weberian liberal who happens to be Irish, Catholic-raised, and from [X]”), or the Russia beat: Putin as the case where ideology (a loosely defined conservative statism) and identity (Russianness, Orthodoxy) get deliberately fused rather than kept apart — which foreshadows why the distinction matters politically.


2026-09-03: the old “Quick recap: identity ≠ ideology” slide — flagged in FRESH-EYES §2 as the flattest, most textbook-definitional moment in the deck, by its own todo — is folded into the opening line here, and merged with the old “The puzzle, live” question slide. The definition itself lives in printnote, so students still have it on paper. Two slides became one.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Inherited, built, or deployed?

Primordialism: identities are ancient, natural, almost biological — inherited like blood type.
Constructivism: identities are built, not discovered — real because people believe in them.
Instrumentalism: identities are tools, activated by leaders to win power or resources.





Each one captures something real. None of them, alone, is the whole story.

Each theory’s fuller claim, spelled out: primordialists say you inherit your nation, ethnicity, or religion the way you inherit a blood type — it’s just a fact about you. Constructivists say categories like “nation” or “ethnicity” are invented, socially and politically, and become real because enough people come to believe in them — invented does not mean fake. Instrumentalists say identities are tools: leaders and organisations activate one identity over another, strategically, to win power or resources. None of the three is the whole story on its own; the lecture takes each in turn and shows why you need all three moving together.


Preview the shape of the lecture: we’ll take each theory in turn, ground it fast with a case, and by the end show why you actually need all three moving together. This is the same “three lenses, not a menu” move as the ideologies lectures — don’t let this feel like round two of the taxonomy march they just sat through.


IMAGE — dullest/most taxonomy-like slide in the deck; a three-panel .absolute strip would break up the list. One small photo per theory: a family crest or coat of arms (primordialism — “inherited”), a 19th-century vernacular newspaper front page (constructivism — “built”), a politician mid-speech at a podium with flags (instrumentalism — “tool”). All easy stock/Wikimedia Commons finds. Position as three .absolute images along the bottom third of the slide, roughly 200px square each.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Primordialism: the seductive story
Most people experience their identity as natural and timeless — that’s the theory’s whole appeal.

Your nation feels ancient — language, customs, a kingdom on a map
Your ethnicity feels biological — “blood,” “roots,” “stock”
Your religion feels inherited — passed down, immemorial, just there


Some of it is old. But the political form worth killing or dying for is usually far more recent than it feels.

The “feels timeless” list in full: your nation feels ancient because you can point to language, customs, and a kingdom on a map; your ethnicity feels biological — “blood,” “roots,” “stock”; your religion feels inherited, passed down, immemorial, just there. Some of that genuinely is old. But the political form it takes today — the version worth killing or dying for — is almost always much more recent than it feels.


Push gently against the room’s own instinct here — most of them will feel their own identity as timeless. That’s not a mistake to correct, it’s the mechanism — primordialism persists because it feels true from the inside, even where the history says otherwise.


Noah: an Irish anchor lands hard here — Irishness as “ancient” (the Gaelic revival’s own mythology reaches back to Cúchulainn and the Celts) versus Irishness as a late-19th/ early-20th-century political project (Gaelic League, GAA, the language revival itself as a deliberate, dated act of construction). Both true at once — that’s the point, not a contradiction to resolve. Your call whether to tell it as a story or put dates on a slide.


IMAGE — concrete case, inline .absolute (bottom-right, ~35% width). A Gaelic League/GAA-era poster or photo (e.g. an early Gaelic League branch photo, or a GAA match crowd from the revival period) — pairs directly with the Irish-anchor todo above if Noah tells that story live. National Library of Ireland digital collections or Wikimedia Commons are the likely sources.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Constructivism: nations get built
Benedict Anderson’s move: nations are imagined communities — not fake, but constructed.

“Imagined” — you’ll never meet most of your fellow nationals, yet you’re sure you share something with them.


How does that feeling get manufactured?

Print — vernacular newspapers and novels, teaching millions of strangers to imagine reading the same thing together
Maps, census, statistics — the tools rulers use to make “the nation” countable and real
Schools, conscription, flags, anthems — the everyday machinery that manufactures nationals out of people


Anderson’s fuller point: a nation is “imagined” because you will never meet more than a tiny fraction of your fellow nationals, yet you’re sure you share something with all of them — that feeling has to be manufactured, not assumed. Print did this by putting newspapers and novels into vernacular languages rather than Latin, teaching millions of strangers to imagine themselves reading the same thing at the same time. Maps, censuses, and statistics gave rulers the tools to carve up space and population and make “the nation” countable and therefore real. Schools, conscription, flags, and anthems are the everyday machinery states use to manufacture nationals out of people who didn’t start out thinking of themselves that way.


Most of you will have met Anderson already on the Leaving Cert Politics & Society syllabus — so don’t re-teach “imagined communities” as a revelation. Move fast, then land the sharper follow-up question on the next slide: if you already knew this, why does it still feel wrong that your nation is “only” 200 years old?


This is the LC-overlap section (Anderson is literally on the P&S list). Per the plan: 10 minutes, not 50, and don’t present it as new information — the payoff is treating it as the baseline the room already half-owns, then building past it. If in practice most of the room turns out not to know Anderson, this is the easiest slide to slow down on live; the content survives either pace.


IMAGE — inline .absolute (right third). A 19th-century vernacular-language newspaper front page (the print-capitalism bullet) — something like an early Irish, Czech, or Hungarian-language paper front page works well since it visibly is not Latin or a colonial language. Wikimedia Commons / national library digital archives.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
“Imagined” doesn’t mean “fake”
If nations feel ancient but are mostly a couple of centuries old, constructed by print, schools, and census forms — what does that tell you?


More fragile than primordialism suggests — built things can come apart
More manipulable — if it’s built, someone can build a rival version
Still powerful — people who know their nation is “invented” still fight and die for it


The fuller version of each point: identity is more fragile than primordialism suggests, because it had to be built, and what’s built can also come apart. It’s more manipulable, because if it’s built, someone can build it differently, or build a rival version. None of that makes it less powerful — people who know full well that their nation is “invented” still fight and die for it. Anderson himself is clear that nations are not thereby fake: “imagined” is not “imaginary.”


This is the pivot from constructivism-as-history-lesson to constructivism-as-political theory. The point students usually miss: knowing an identity is constructed doesn’t disarm it. Anderson himself is clear nations are not thereby fake — “imagined” is not “imaginary.” Say that explicitly; it’s the line the LC syllabus sometimes leaves fuzzy.


IMAGE — inline .absolute (small, corner). A torn-and-mended or hand-stitched flag — visual shorthand for “built, therefore fragile, therefore repairable/manipulable.” Easy stock-photo search (“mended flag” / “stitched flag”).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Instrumentalism: identity as a lever
Elites don’t invent identities. They activate them — pull one forward, push others back.


You are, right now, several identities at once — national, religious, regional, class, generational — most dormant
A politician emphasises one to build a coalition — identity is a shortcut: pre-built trust and networks
Activating one identity deactivates others — “Irish first” at a match, “working-class first” at a picket line



Identity is real. Which identity gets to matter right now is strategic.

The mechanism in full: at any moment you hold several identities at once — national, religious, regional, class, generational — and most stay dormant. A politician emphasises just one of those to build a coalition, because shared identity is a shortcut: pre-existing trust, networks, a shared language to organise in. Activating one identity deactivates the others — the same person is “Irish first” at a match and “working-class first” at a picket line, depending on who’s doing the activating and why.


This is Chandra’s core move, stated without the citation apparatus: people hold multiple, simultaneous identities, and politics is largely a fight over which one gets switched “on.” Good moment for a quick show of hands: “who in this room identifies, depending on context, as Irish, as a Dub/culchie, as a student, as [county] — that’s not inconsistency, that’s normal.”


Full shortcut list (trimmed on-slide to “trust and networks”): a shared identity gives a politician pre-existing trust, ready-made networks, and a shared language to organise in. Restore the third element if the two-item version feels thin live.


IMAGE — inline .absolute, paired pair (two small photos side by side). One of a GAA/football match crowd (national/local identity switched on), one of a trade-union picket line (class identity switched on) — visualises the “Irish first at a match, working-class first at a picket line” line directly. Both easy stock/news-agency finds.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Testing constructivism: can you watch an identity get built?
text:
Testing constructivism: can you watch an identity get built?
Constructivism claims identity categories are made, not discovered — catch one being created, on paper, with a start date.

Exhibit: the United States census.

Before 1980, there was no “Hispanic” box on the US census form
Added as a bureaucratic decision — advocacy groups wanted the population counted, funded, and represented
Once the box existed, people who’d said Mexican, Cuban, or Salvadoran increasingly reported the new label instead — the category itself helped produce the identity it measured


The mechanism spelled out: this is a bureaucratic form, not a war or a revolution, creating a political identity category with a documented birthdate. Before 1980 there was no “Hispanic” box on the US census; people who might now report that label were split across “white,” “other,” and national-origin categories. Advocacy groups pushed for a single pan-ethnic box because being counted meant being funded and represented by the federal government. Once the box existed, people who would previously have described themselves by country of origin (Mexican, Cuban, Salvadoran) increasingly reported the new label instead — the measurement instrument itself helped produce the identity it claimed to measure. It’s a clean falsification-style example: if primordialism were simply true, a category invented by a government form in 1980 shouldn’t be able to become a core identity for tens of millions of people within a generation.


This is the constructivism test in miniature: a bureaucratic form, not a war or a revolution, creating a political identity category with a documented birthdate. It’s a clean falsification-style example — if primordialism were simply true, a category invented by a government form in 1980 shouldn’t be able to become something tens of millions of people report as a core identity within a generation. Emphasise the mechanism, not just the fact: the measurement instrument changed what it measured.


Deliberately using the US Hispanic-category case rather than Posner’s Zambia/Malawi chameleon-identity study — that’s Comparative’s example (their spine reading for the identity-and-ethnicity unit) and the plan flags it as territory to stay off. The census case makes the same methodological point — identity categories responding to institutional incentives/definitions — through a completely different empirical door, so there’s no overlap risk. If a fresher or more Irish-adjacent example turns up before September (e.g. Irish census questions on Traveller ethnicity, or Northern Ireland’s community-background question), it’s a strong swap-in — flagging as a candidate, not committing.


IMAGE — chart, inline .absolute (right half). US Census/Pew Research line chart: self-reported “Hispanic” population as a share of the US population, 1980–2020, showing the post-1980 rise the case makes. Pew Research Center or US Census Bureau historical tables have this pre-built; cite whichever chart is used as the source line under it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: What this does — and doesn’t — prove
text:
What this does — and doesn’t — prove

Strong evidence for constructivism: built categories get internalised as real identity
Not infinitely pliable, though — the census couldn’t invent “Hispanic” from nothing without shared language, migration history, and discrimination already there to hang it on
Exactly the primordialist-constructivist-instrumentalist blend from earlier: raw material already there, category built, advocacy groups had instrumental reasons to want it


The fuller version: this is strong evidence for constructivism — categories can be created administratively and then get internalised as real identity. But it does not mean identity is infinitely pliable. The census couldn’t have invented a “Hispanic” identity from nothing if there weren’t already shared language, migration history, and discrimination experiences to hang the label on. Which is exactly the primordialist-constructivist-instrumentalist blend from earlier at work on one case: the raw material (shared history, language) was already there; the category was built; and advocacy groups had instrumental reasons to want the box added.


Close the loop back to the three theories — this is the moment the lecture’s thesis (each theory captures part of the truth) gets its clearest demonstration rather than just being asserted. Don’t let this become “constructivism wins” — the honest version is all three mechanisms operating on the same case at once.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Why isn’t being left-handed political?
Everyone in this room has dozens of identities — nationality, religion (or lack of it), region, class, generation, favourite football club, eye colour, handedness.
Almost none of those become political. So: what makes some identities politically explosive and most others invisible?

Plant this, don’t answer it. This is the deliberate cliffhanger into Lecture 8. Make the point explicit: constructivism alone explains that identities exist and can be built, but not why some of them come to matter more than eye colour or being left-handed. Instrumentalism alone explains that elites can activate identities, but not why some activations catch fire and others fizzle. You need Lecture 8’s answer — which is about power, numbers, and conflict — to close the gap.


IMAGE — small icon row/collage, inline .absolute along the bottom. Simple icon set for the “dozens of identities” list: a flag, a football-club crest, a religious symbol, a graduation cap, a family-tree icon, an eye. Visual gag: most stay grey/inert, one lights up — reinforces “almost none of these become political.” Simple enough to build directly in Keynote/PowerPoint rather than sourcing photos.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Readings this week
Required:

Heywood & Laing, Politics (2025), Ch. 8 — identity sections
Fearon, “What Is Identity (As We Now Use the Word)?” (1999) — selected pages

Recommended:

Anderson, Imagined Communities — selected pages (you may already have met this on the Leaving Cert)


Fearon is deliberately not on Comparative’s reading list, so it’s genuinely fresh ground here — flag that if anyone’s worried about overlap with second year. It’s also the single best short piece on why the boundaries-vs-content way of defining identity (who counts as a member; what members are expected to be like) matters, which is the conceptual backbone under everything in today’s lecture even though it wasn’t put on screen as its own term.


Fearon 1999 gives a clean two-part definition of social identity — (1) the rules of membership (who’s in), (2) the expected content (what members are like/do) — which is useful scaffolding if you want a slide-level “key term” moment for identity itself before running the three theories. I left identity’s definition to the recap slide and kept this in reserve rather than adding a fifth content slide; happy to build it out if you want the Fearon framing explicit on-screen rather than just in the reading.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
For next lecture
Lecture 8 — When Does Difference Become Conflict?
Today explained where identities come from. Next time: when does difference turn into a political dividing line — and, more rarely, into violence?

Think about it before you come in: if identities are built and elites can activate them, why doesn’t every activation succeed? Why do some diverse societies stay peaceful for decades and others don’t?

Clean handoff, explicitly bridging structure. Today = supply side (where identities come from). Next time = demand side (when they turn political, and when that turns violent) — the puzzle framing for lec08 is that most diverse places, most of the time, do NOT have ethnic violence, so don’t let today’s lecture imply that built + activatable identities inevitably produce conflict. That’s the trap lec08 exists to correct.

See you Thursday

POLL (Vevox/TCDpolls — tool still Noah’s decision). Question text, ready to go:

“Which of your own identities is most likely to become politically activated in your lifetime?” — National / Religious / Class / Generational / Regional / None of these

Placement is a live call: it closes lec07 cleanly, but it opens lec08 even better, because the distribution of answers is lec08’s puzzle. Noah picks one; don’t run it twice.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Democracy: What It Is & How You’d Measure It
text:
Democracy: What It Is & How You’d Measure It
North Korea’s official name contains the word “Democratic.” So does the DRC. Even dictators want this word — which tells you the definition is worth fighting over.

IMAGE — full-bleed background behind the title text. North Korea’s Arirang-style mass parade in Kim Il Sung Square (or a DPRK propaganda mural reading “Democratic People’s Republic of Korea”) — the most recognisable “democratic” irony available. Source: Wikimedia Commons (several CC-licensed DPRK parade photos exist). Use as ## Democracy: What It Is & How You'd Measure It {background-image="w06-lec09-img/dprk-parade.jpg" background-opacity=0.4} so the yellow title text still reads.


Cold open, no admin yet. Let the North Korea/DRC line land before you move — it should get a laugh or at least a raised eyebrow. The point of today isn’t “is [country] a democracy” — it’s “which definition are we even using, and how would you know if you were right.” Don’t resolve anything on this slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Is Hungary a democracy?
It has held regular multi-party elections since 1990. It is a member of the European Union. Yes or no?

POLL (Vevox/TCDpolls — tool still Noah’s decision). Question text, ready to go:

“Is Hungary a democracy?” — Yes / No / I don’t know enough to say

The third option is the honest one and most of the room should take it. Show the split, then go to the next slide, which is three professional answers that also disagree.


Two minutes, and don’t answer it. Most of the room knows Hungary is “controversial” without knowing why. The job of the next slide is to show them that the disagreement is not a matter of opinion or of missing facts — three serious projects, looking at the same country with the same information, produce three different answers. That’s what makes the definition question worth an hour of their lives.
If nobody bites, name Orbán and ask again.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Three professional answers. They don’t match.
text:
Three professional answers. They don’t match.

V-Dem (thousands of country experts): Hungary is an electoral autocracy — and has been since 2019. Not a democracy at all.
Freedom House (analyst scores): Partly Free, 65 out of 100. Downgraded from Free in 2019.
EIU’s Democracy Index: a flawed democracy — 54th in the world. Still, on their reading, a democracy.


Same country. Same decade. Nobody is lying.

V-Dem (Varieties of Democracy, Gothenburg) reclassified Hungary as an electoral autocracy in its 2020 Democracy Report, covering 2019 — the first EU member state ever placed outside the democratic category. Freedom House downgraded Hungary from “Free” to “Partly Free” in Freedom in the World 2019, the first EU member to be downgraded; in the 2026 report Hungary scores 65/100 (political rights 24/40, civil liberties 41/60). The Economist Intelligence Unit’s Democracy Index places Hungary in its second tier, “flawed democracy”, at 54th in the world with a score of 6.51. The Polity series, the fourth big project, stopped in 2018 and so has nothing to say about any of this — which is its own lesson about relying on a single number.
Three answers, from three serious research projects, with access to the same facts. The disagreement isn’t sloppiness. It’s what happens when you operationalise three different definitions of the same word.


This is the engine of the whole lecture and it now runs from slide three. Say the punchline out loud: nobody here is lying, and nobody is missing information. They disagree because they defined “democracy” differently before they started counting.
Then ask the extraction question, and wait: what would each of them have to believe about the word “democracy” for their answer to be the right one? Push until someone gets close to “elections happen and can be lost” versus “elections plus everything that makes them mean something.” Those are the next two slides — you want them to have half-built them already.
Don’t editorialise about Orbán. The slide is about measurement, and it’s more powerful if you refuse to take a side.


Source check, 2026-09-03: V-Dem Democracy Report 2020 (Hungary reclassified electoral autocracy, first EU member); Freedom House Freedom in the World 2019 (Free → Partly Free) and the 2026 Hungary country report (65/100, PR 24/40, CL 41/60); EIU Democracy Index (flawed democracy, rank 54, score 6.51); Polity5 series ends 2018.
Restructure, 2026-09-03: FRESH-EYES §2 called this deck “the one deck that is a chapter march in disguise — etymology → two definitions → three models → Dahl → three indices,” with the good question not working until slide 10. The Hungary disagreement now opens the deck and the two definitions get extracted from it. The later “how each of them counts” slide is no longer a first introduction to the three projects — it now answers a question the room has already asked.


Noah: currency check before delivery — pull the current V-Dem Democracy Report, the latest Freedom House Hungary score, and the current EIU rank. The 2026 Hungarian parliamentary election falls in spring 2026, so there may be a much fresher story here by November; if the story has moved, the structure of this slide survives a straight swap of numbers.


IMAGE — the single most valuable chart in the deck: one panel per index, Hungary’s trajectory 2010–2026, with the classification threshold marked. V-Dem and Freedom House both publish reusable graphics; Our World in Data has V-Dem and EIU series in one place. Build once, reuse in lec13 (backsliding) with the same axes.

DPRK cold open stays; the deck now goes straight to “Is Hungary a democracy?” and three professional answers that disagree (V-Dem: electoral autocracy; Freedom House: Partly Free, 65/100; EIU: flawed democracy, 54th). The minimal and substantive definitions are now extracted from that disagreement rather than announced. The measurement question is live from slide 2 instead of slide 10.
