Four items, fast. Flag out loud that the measurement section is not a side dish today — it’s the centrepiece, and it’s also this week’s “how do we know that?” segment folded directly into the material rather than bolted on separately.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Can you vote the rascals out?
text:
Can you vote the rascals out?
This is the EIU’s answer, and it comes from Schumpeter, 1942 — writing in the shadow of fascism, setting the bar deliberately low:

“The democratic method is that institutional arrangement for arriving at political decisions in which individuals acquire the power to decide by means of a competitive struggle for the people’s vote.”


Strip that down: can you vote the rascals out? That’s it.

Schumpeter’s fuller point: this isn’t the rule of the people, it is the rule of whoever wins the competition for the people’s vote. That distinction matters — it makes the winning politician the ruler, not the electorate, and it is exactly why critics say minimal democracy sells the “rule by the people” idea short. His blunter line elsewhere: “democracy is the rule of the politician.”


IMAGE — small inline .absolute portrait, corner of the slide. Joseph Schumpeter, c. 1940s (public-domain photo). Not essential, but a face for the quote helps the room clock that this is one specific economist’s deliberately narrow definition, not a definition handed down from on high. Source: Wikimedia Commons (public domain, pre-1950s photo).


Name the extraction: “that’s what the Democracy Index needs to believe to call Hungary a democracy.” The word “democracy” comes from dēmos + kratos, rule by the people — half a sentence, say it in passing here if you want it at all; the Greek is the easy part and every word after “the people” is contested. Lincoln’s “of the people, by the people, for the people” is the better ad-lib: three different claims smuggled into one sentence.
This is the procedural/minimal pole. Emphasise how deliberately unromantic it is — Schumpeter isn’t being cynical for effect, he’s trying to build a definition you can actually check against evidence: did an election happen, was it competitive, could the incumbent lose? That checkability is exactly why this definition wins the measurement fight later in the lecture.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Is being able to vote them out enough?
text:
Is being able to vote them out enough?
Minimal democracy asks: can you vote them out?

Substantive democracy asks something harder: does the outcome look like self-rule — real equality, welfare, dignity, a genuine voice for people who aren’t rich, organised, or loud?


A country can nail every procedure and still leave huge numbers of people powerless. Is that a democracy?


V-Dem and Freedom House think the answer matters. The Democracy Index doesn’t ask.

“Every procedure” means clean elections, honest counts, a free press — the full minimal checklist, ticked. A country can have all of that and still leave huge numbers of people who aren’t rich, organised, or loud with no real power over their own lives. Whether that counts as a democracy is exactly the disagreement this lecture doesn’t resolve for you.


Don’t resolve this. Let them sit with the tension: minimal is checkable but morally thin (elections happening isn’t the same as people actually having power); substantive is morally richer but who decides what counts as “real” equality or a “genuine” voice? That’s a value judgement dressed up as a definition. This tension is the whole lecture’s engine — it’s why measurement turns out to be so hard later on.


Portable concept: procedural vs substantive definitions. This is the distinction the lecture is actually teaching — everything downstream (Dahl, V-Dem vs Freedom House, the grey zone) is a different way of trying to answer “which of these two are we measuring?” Worth saying that explicitly on screen, not just in your head.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
One word, three machines

Direct democracy — citizens decide themselves. Pure in principle, doesn’t scale.
Representative democracy — we elect people to decide for us.
Liberal democracy — representative plus rights and limits on what the majority can do to the minority.


“Liberal democracy” bolts two things together that don’t always get along: majority rule and minority protection.

Direct democracy has real examples — the Athenian assembly, Swiss cantonal referendums — but none at any real scale. Representative democracy, in some form, is what every modern democracy actually runs on. Liberal democracy adds rights, rule of law, and limits on the majority to the representative model.


IMAGE — small inline .absolute image, corner of the slide. The Pnyx in Athens — the actual hillside where the citizen assembly met, now just a stone platform and a view. Grounds “direct democracy” as a real place before the lecture moves to abstractions. Source: Wikimedia Commons (CC-licensed tourist photos of the Pnyx are plentiful).


Keep this fast — it’s vocabulary, not a taxonomy march. The liberal-democracy tension (majority rule vs minority protection) is worth 20 seconds of extra emphasis because it’s the thing that snaps in Lecture 13 (backsliding) — a government can win elections legitimately and still dismantle the checks that protect everyone who didn’t vote for it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Why not just direct democracy?
We all have phones. Why not vote on everything, all the time?

IMAGE — inline .absolute image. A Swiss Landsgemeinde — the open-air cantonal assembly where citizens vote by show of hands (Appenzell Innerrhoden or Glarus are the two still running). The one surviving real-world example of direct democracy at any scale, and it only works because the canton is tiny. Source: Wikimedia Commons (several CC images of the Glarus Landsgemeinde exist).


Cold-call this, don’t just answer it. Push for: scale (millions can’t literally gather), time (governing is constant work, not a periodic vote), expertise (most people are rationally ignorant on most issues, and that’s a sane response to limited time), intensity (passionate minorities can lose every single vote and eventually stop consenting to the system), manipulation (whoever controls the question controls the answer). Land on: direct democracy isn’t obviously worse, it’s just a different trade-off — and representative democracy exists mostly to dodge these costs, not because “the people” are untrustworthy.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Dahl ducks the argument
Robert Dahl looked at the procedural-vs-substantive fight and basically said: forget the ideal, tell me what real, working democracies actually have in common.

Two dimensions, which he called polyarchy (“rule by the many,” not rule by all):

Contestation — can you actually compete for power, and lose it?
Participation — how many people are let into the competition?


Polyarchy is the workhorse definition of the whole lecture — it’s the thing that turns “what is democracy” from a philosophy essay into something with two dials you can actually turn up or down, country by country. Everything from here to the end of the lecture is really just: how do we read those two dials off real countries?

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Almost nobody sits in the top-right corner
text:
Almost nobody sits in the top-right corner

IMAGE — Dahl’s 2×2 (or continuous scatter) — contestation on one axis, participation on the other. Plot a handful of recognisable regimes as dots: somewhere like Norway near the high-high corner, a closed one-party state near the low-low corner, a couple of contested/hybrid cases in the middle. This is the single most reusable image in the regimes block — build it once here, and it can be redrawn with the same axes in Lecture 11 (dictatorships) and Lecture 13 (backsliding) to show movement over time. Old week04 scaffold flagged this exact reuse.

Almost nothing sits in the perfect top-right corner. That’s not a flaw in the map — it’s the honest picture.

Let this land before moving on: if you plot real countries, you get a smear, not two clean clusters. That smear is the whole reason “is X a democracy” yes/no questions are usually the wrong question — which is exactly the pivot into the measurement section.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Nobody hands you a spreadsheet
Dahl gives you two ideas. Nobody hands you a spreadsheet with “contestation: 0.7” written on it.

Someone has to decide: what counts as evidence of contestation? Who codes it? From what sources? On what scale?


That’s not a footnote — it’s where three of the biggest projects in political science live.

Callback, say it explicitly: “This is the exact same move as Lecture 2’s third face of power — we can’t observe the concept directly, so we go looking for something we CAN count that’s plausibly correlated with it. Same problem, different concept.” This is the measurement thread’s second stop (2 → 9 → 14 → 20) — name the thread out loud.


Explicit portable-concept callback to Lecture 2 here in the notes — worth saying on-screen too if the timing allows (“this is the same move as Lecture 2”). The measurement thread returns in Lecture 14 (corruption — how do you count what people hide) and closes out in Lecture 20.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: So how does each of them actually count?
text:
So how does each of them actually count?
You’ve met all three already. Here’s what’s under the bonnet:

V-Dem — thousands of country-experts coding hundreds of indicators, aggregated into several separate democracy indices
Freedom House — analysts score every country on political rights and civil liberties, rolled into “Free / Partly Free / Not Free”
Polity — codes the institutions of executive power into a single –10 to +10 scale


V-Dem (Varieties of Democracy) codes hundreds of indicators — media freedom, judicial independence, clean elections, and more — into several separate indices: electoral, liberal, participatory, deliberative, egalitarian democracy. Freedom House scores every country 1–7 on political rights and 1–7 on civil liberties, rolled into “Free / Partly Free / Not Free.” Polity codes only the institutions of executive power — how constrained is the executive, how open is recruitment to office — into one –10 to +10 scale.


IMAGE — chart, inline or full-width beneath the bullets. Freedom House’s “Freedom in the World” map (countries shaded Free / Partly Free / Not Free) — or, to match the visual family of the divider just before this section, V-Dem’s regime-of-the-world map instead. This is the closest thing to a taxonomy list in the deck, and the one that most needs a picture to break it up. Source: Freedom House’s annual report page, or V-Dem’s Democracy Report — both publish reusable maps.


Don’t drown them in methodology. The point students need: these are three genuinely different operationalisations of “democracy” — different data, different coders, different aggregation rules, sometimes different underlying definitions (V-Dem is closer to substantive/thick, Polity is closer to pure institutional/procedural). That’s why what comes next isn’t a scandal.


Noah: this slide stays dense on purpose — three real measurement projects, no way to compress further without losing one. Flag if you’d rather cut Polity to a footnote and teach only V-Dem/Freedom House in depth.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The disagreement is the signal
Hungary was not a special case. No two of these measures agree perfectly, and some years they don’t agree on which direction a country is moving.

That disagreement is meaningful, not a bug — it’s what you’d expect when three projects are measuring three slightly different things, built three different ways.

IMAGE — chart/table: one or two countries’ V-Dem / Freedom House / Polity scores side by side over the same recent years, showing visible disagreement. Candidates worth checking closer to term: Hungary, Turkey, India, or the US — pick whichever shows the clearest divergence in the latest data (needs a 2026 currency check; don’t lock in numbers now).


This is the payoff slide of the “how do we know” segment. Resist the urge to adjudicate which index is “right” — the lesson is that the disagreement itself is informative: where the indices diverge is usually exactly where a regime is contested or moving. If someone asks “so which one should I trust,” the honest answer is “depends what question you’re asking” — and that’s a satisfying, not evasive, answer.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: A number that decides who gets aid
text:
A number that decides who gets aid
Whichever index you pick isn’t just an academic choice.


Aid and sanctions decisions get tied to democracy scores
Governments cite favourable scores to claim legitimacy, and dispute unfavourable ones as biased
Every academic claim you’ll hear this term — “democracy causes growth,” “democracy reduces war” — depends entirely on which measure the researcher used


This is the stakes slide — it stops the measurement discussion feeling like pure methods trivia. It’s also a direct plant for Lecture 20, where the same point gets made about causal claims generally: the measure you choose can quietly decide the answer you get.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Democracy isn’t a light switch
If you plot every country on Dahl’s two axes, most of them cluster in the messy middle — not fully open, not fully closed.

Political scientists call this the hybrid regime or competitive authoritarian space — elections happen, but the playing field is tilted so hard the incumbent basically never loses.

In a competitive authoritarian or hybrid regime, opposition parties are not banned — they exist, campaign, and sometimes even win individual seats. What they cannot do is win the thing that matters: government. The incumbent controls the referees (courts, electoral commissions, state media) closely enough that a genuine loss essentially never happens, which is what separates this from both a clean democracy and a closed one-party state.


Keep this to vocabulary and the shape of the idea — the deep dive on how these regimes actually function (repression, co-optation, managed elections) belongs to Lectures 11–12, which this slide is explicitly teeing up. Don’t build out a typology here; one clean sentence on what “hybrid” means is enough.


Deliberately light-touch on hybrid/competitive-authoritarian regimes — this is Comparative’s territory in more depth later in their degree, and it’s also exactly the setup for POU11011’s own Lectures 11–12 (dictatorships) and 13 (backsliding). This slide should feel like a trailer, not the film.


Noah: the divider image uses Orbán/Hungary, but you know this territory from research — if a quick Russia example (Putin-era elections: real ballots, real opposition candidates, outcome never in doubt) lands better live than Hungary, swap it in or add it as a second beat here. Either works as the canonical “hybrid regime” case.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Where does Ireland sit, and on whose scale?
text:
Where does Ireland sit, and on whose scale?
Not “is Ireland a democracy” — you’ve already settled that one before you got here. The more interesting question: where exactly does Ireland sit, and on whose scale?


IMAGE — chart/table: Ireland’s most recent V-Dem, Freedom House, and Polity scores, shown next to two or three contrasting countries (one clearly consolidated, one clearly hybrid, maybe one recent backslider) — same visual logic as the disagreement slide above, but grounding it in a case they know. Needs a 2026 data pull closer to delivery.

Ireland scores near the top on every index going — which makes it a boring case for this slide and a genuinely useful baseline for comparison.

This is the non-civics-class use of Ireland the brief wants: not “how is the Taoiseach chosen,” but Ireland as one calibration point among many on a spectrum most of the world doesn’t sit at the edge of. Keep it brief — Ireland isn’t the point, the spectrum is.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Readings this week
Required:

Schmitter & Karl, “What Democracy Is… and Is Not” (1991)

Recommended:

V-Dem Democracy Report (latest edition) — skim the overview and headline figures


Reading list pulled straight from _course.yml’s Lecture 9 slot — both were already TODO-confirmed there, so keeping them as-is rather than inventing alternatives. If you want a shorter/more current companion piece (an op-ed on the “democratic recession,” say), that’s an easy add and doesn’t need to replace Schmitter & Karl.


POLL (Vevox/TCDpolls — tool still Noah’s decision). Second poll of the deck; run it on “The disagreement is the signal”, not here. Question text, ready to go:

“Now that you know how each one is built — which measure would you trust most?” — V-Dem / Freedom House / The Democracy Index / None of them on its own

Two polls in one lecture is one more than the norm. If only one runs, run the Hungary poll at the front; this one is the optional bookend, and it is most satisfying if the room’s answer has visibly changed since slide two.


Noah: personal-touch slot — if you have a go-to line about watching a country you’ve studied get reclassified by one of these indices (or a story about V-Dem/Freedom House scores being cited, disputed, or weaponised in a real policy debate), it would land well right after the disagreement slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
For next lecture

Where we got to today. Two rival definitions — minimal/procedural (Schumpeter: can you vote them out?) versus substantive (does the outcome look like self-rule?) — and why the gap between them matters. Dahl’s polyarchy: contestation × participation, the working compromise everyone actually measures. V-Dem, Freedom House and the Democracy Index: three ways of turning “democracy” into a number, and why their disagreement is informative rather than a scandal. And the grey zone — most regimes live in the middle, not at either end.

Lecture 10 — Democracy: why it emerges, why it survives
Today defined democracy and showed you how to measure where a country sits. Next time: why do some countries get it, and why do some keep it while others slide back?
See you Thursday

That is the shift from a descriptive question (what is democracy, how do you measure it) to a causal one (what makes it happen, and what makes it last). Political scientists usually call the second half of that question “democratic consolidation” or, in reverse, “backsliding” — both come up over the next few weeks.


Clean handoff. Explicitly flag the spectrum image from today — “remember the polyarchy map, remember the grey zone — next lecture asks how countries move along it, and later, Lectures 11 through 13 ask what’s actually happening at the low end and in reverse.” That forward-pointer is doing real work: it’s the reason this lecture can stay descriptive/measurement-focused without feeling incomplete.

text:
See you Thursday

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Dictatorships I: How Autocracies Work
If you control the army, the police, and the courts — why bother pretending to be popular?

IMAGE — full-bleed background behind the title text. A military parade / show of hard power (e.g. Red Square Victory Day parade, tanks and troops) — the “tanks in the street” image the cold-open notes deliberately invoke, which the lecture then complicates. Source: Wikimedia Commons / press-agency archive (Reuters, AP). Use as {background-image="w08-lec11-img/parade.jpg"} on this slide.


Cold open, no admin. Let it sit. Don’t answer it yet — the whole lecture is the answer, and the shape of the answer (soft tools beat hard tools, most of the time) is genuinely counterintuitive to a room that’s picturing dictatorship as “tanks in the street.” Hold that image loosely; we’re about to complicate it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The plan for today

Two cases first: Russia and a Gulf monarchy — same label, very different machines
The autocrat’s two levers: repression and co-optation
How do we know what people in closed societies actually think? — a method, and a puzzle Noah works on himself


The stick alone doesn’t work as a governing strategy: pure repression is expensive to sustain, requires watching everyone all the time, and tends to signal that a ruler’s power has already started to fail rather than that it is strong. That is why almost every durable authoritarian regime pairs repression with co-optation — buying loyalty rather than only extracting compliance by force.


Three items, fast. Standard bookend — don’t linger on this slide. One extra beat first, since this is the first lecture back after reading week: “where we left off — Lecture 10 was about identity and division. Today we pivot to a new block: how power holds on once it has it.” One sentence, then move on.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Russia, 2026
Regular elections. A parliament. A constitution. Opposition parties on the ballot.

And: the outcome hasn’t been in doubt since 2000. Serious challengers jailed, exiled, or dead; independent media barely exists inside the country.

Since Vladimir Putin’s first re-election in 2000, no Russian presidential election has produced genuine uncertainty about the outcome. Serious challengers have been jailed, forced into exile, or in a small number of cases killed. State television reaches nearly the entire population, while independent media has largely ceased to operate inside the country — the apparatus of a competitive election survives; the competition does not.


IMAGE — inline .absolute image beside the bullet text (not full-bleed). A Russian polling station: ballot box, flag, queue — deliberately banal-looking — paired with a stat card reading “official result: ~87%”. Source: press-agency archive (TASS/Reuters) or Wikimedia Commons. Keep it dry, not editorialised; let the contrast between ritual and result do the work.


Don’t editorialise heavily here — let the facts sit. The point of this slide isn’t “Russia bad,” it’s “Russia goes to a LOT of trouble to look like something it isn’t.” That effort is the puzzle. Ask: why bother with the ballot box at all?


Noah: the freshest possible version of this slide. Russia’s Duma election is scheduled for 18–20 September 2026 — roughly six weeks before you deliver this. Whatever the reported turnout and United Russia’s reported share turn out to be, they are the live version of “the outcome hasn’t been in doubt.” Swap the numbers in, and you get a case the room watched happen. (Source for the date: Russian electoral calendar, third Sunday of September; confirm the official result before delivery.)

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
A Gulf monarchy
No elections for the head of state. No pretence of one. Power passes inside a royal family, full stop.

And yet: no serious opposition movement, low visible unrest, citizens who mostly aren’t reaching for the exits.

IMAGE — inline .absolute image, side of slide. A generic modern Gulf skyline at dusk (Dubai, Doha, or Riyadh — deliberately not naming one, matching the cc note below) as shorthand for oil-funded state capacity. Source: Unsplash / Wikimedia Commons, any CC-licensed Gulf skyline photo. Swap for whichever city Noah picks live.


Contrast deliberately: Russia performs democracy it doesn’t have; a Gulf monarchy doesn’t bother performing anything and is, by some measures, more stable. That’s the hook for “co-optation” — wait for the toolkit slide before resolving it. Pick your own preferred Gulf case live (Saudi Arabia, UAE, Qatar all work) — no need to commit to one on the slide.


Deliberately not naming a single Gulf state on the slide so you can pick live based on whatever’s topical in October 2026 — the mechanism (oil rents fund co-optation, no need for the electoral performance) is the same across most of them. Per the guard-rail, this is free territory — Comparative’s authoritarianism week doesn’t use Gulf cases.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The puzzle, named
Both of these are “authoritarian regimes.” One spends enormous effort looking democratic. The other doesn’t bother at all.
What explains the difference — and why does either strategy work?

Let it sit for a beat. Don’t resolve yet. This is the pivot into the toolkit.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Key term: authoritarianism

Authoritarian regime: a system in which power is not subject to meaningful electoral competition or accountability — rulers cannot be voted out.


Note the word meaningful. Russia holds elections. It just makes sure it can’t lose one.

Stress “meaningful” — that’s doing all the work in the definition. An election with a predetermined winner isn’t a constraint on power, it’s something else entirely. That “something else” is where the lecture is headed.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Callback: legitimacy, the hard way
Lecture 2: legitimacy is what makes power cheap. Autocrats mostly don’t have it freely given — so they build a substitute.

Traditional authority — Gulf monarchies lean here: “it has always been this way”
Charismatic authority — built around a leader, fragile the moment they’re gone
Legal-rational authority — the one autocracies fake hardest: constitutions, courts, elections


In Lecture 2, legitimacy was defined as what makes power cheap: when people believe a ruler’s right to rule is genuine, the ruler doesn’t need to watch everyone all the time to stay in charge. Autocrats mostly don’t inherit that belief for free, so they have to construct a substitute out of Weber’s other two forms of authority. Traditional authority rests on the sense that a form of rule has always existed and is legitimate simply because it is customary — the basis of dynastic and monarchical rule, and the reason Gulf monarchies barely need to perform anything else. Charismatic authority is built around the pull of an individual leader, and is correspondingly fragile once that leader is gone. Legal-rational authority is the form modern states claim: legitimacy flowing from properly constituted rules, procedures, and offices rather than from tradition or personal charisma — and it is the one autocracies without a traditional claim available to them, Russia included, tend to fake hardest: constitutions, courts, and elections that mimic rule-bound government without functioning as real constraints on power.


Russia’s elections aren’t a concession to democracy. They’re an attempt to borrow legal-rational authority’s costume.

This is the direct payoff of Weber’s typology from Lecture 2 — say so explicitly: “remember the three types of legitimate authority? Here’s where they earn their keep.” A Gulf monarchy barely needs the costume because it can lean on traditional authority instead; Russia has no traditional or hereditary claim available to it, so it reaches for the legal-rational props instead. That’s WHY the two cases look so different — same underlying problem (how do you rule without being loved), different available raw materials.


Portable concept in this slide: the menu of legitimacy isn’t the same for every autocrat. What’s available depends on history — a monarchy has traditional legitimacy on tap; a revolutionary or coup-born regime doesn’t, and has to build something from nothing. Worth a beat if time allows; cuttable if you’re behind.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Repression
The stick: censorship, surveillance, imprisonment, violence.

It works — in the short run. But it has a cost problem: you have to watch everyone, all the time.


Russia, one law, three years: 10,778 court cases for “discrediting the army.” Every one needs a police report, a prosecutor, a judge.


Hannah Arendt’s line, from Lecture 2: heavy violence is often a sign power has already failed, not a sign it’s strong.

Repression’s cost problem isn’t just financial. A ruler who leans on the stick has to watch everyone, all the time, and can never fully trust what people tell them — informants can lie, officials can exaggerate loyalty, and the ruler has no easy way to tell genuine support from fear-induced compliance. That surveillance burden is itself a form of weakness: the more a regime needs to watch, the less it actually knows. The Russian figure on this slide is a concrete measure of that burden: OVD-Info recorded 10,778 first-instance administrative cases under Article 20.3.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences — “discrediting the use of the Armed Forces” — between 24 February 2022 and 17 February 2025. Each of those is a police report, a prosecutor’s file, and a court hearing. That is what repression costs when you actually itemise it.


Source for the 10,778 figure: OVD-Info, “Three Years into the Full-Scale War” (data to 17 Feb 2025), https://ovd.info/en/antiwar_3_years. Verified 2026-09-03. OVD-Info is a Russian human-rights monitoring project, itself designated a “foreign agent” — worth one line out loud, since the fact that the count exists at all, and who had to leave the country to keep counting, is part of the point.


Noah: check my facts / add your own angle. If you’d rather use a figure you trust more, or one you can date to 2026, swap it — the slide needs a number here, not this one specifically.


Direct callback — say it out loud: “remember Arendt from Lecture 2? No government run purely on force has ever survived, because even the most repressive ruler needs a base of people willing to carry out the repression.” A regime that’s doing nothing but crack heads is usually a regime that’s already lost the argument. That sets up why co-optation is the more interesting half of the toolkit.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Why pure repression doesn’t scale
Two callbacks converging on the same point:

Lecture 2 (Arendt): violence is expensive and self-undermining — it signals weak power dressed up as strong power
Lecture 4 (state capacity): repression still needs capacity — secret police, prisons, surveillance, informants who don’t defect


So the smartest autocrats spend as little as possible on the stick and as much as possible on the other lever.

Repression is not free even for a ruler willing to use it without restraint: it requires a functioning secret police, a prison system, a surveillance apparatus, and informants who can be trusted not to defect. Weak states, which by definition lack strong bureaucratic and coercive capacity, often cannot repress efficiently even when their rulers want to — one more reason repression alone rarely holds a regime together for long.


This is the analytical heart of the lecture — make sure it lands before moving on. Both callbacks should be named on screen, not just implied; the brief wants callbacks said out loud, not left for students to infer.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Co-optation
The carrot: buy loyalty instead of extracting it by force.

Elites — cabinet posts, state contracts, control of a ministry or a company
The military — officer perks, budget, autonomy — the single most dangerous group to alienate, because they hold the guns
The public — subsidies, jobs, services, stability — “don’t rock the boat and life stays liveable”


IMAGE — inline .absolute image, corner of slide. A visual for “co-optation” in action — a state awards ceremony, a well-provisioned military parade, or a public-sector job fair. Generic, not country-specific. Source: Wikimedia Commons / press-agency archive.


Co-optation is expensive, but it’s expensive in a way that buys durability. Repression is expensive in a way that buys resentment.

With elites, the point isn’t just paying them off — it’s that the payoff has to stay visible. Cabinet posts, state contracts, and control of profitable ministries or companies work as co-optation only if everyone who might otherwise defect can see what loyalty currently buys, and can imagine losing it.


This is the workhorse slide — spend real time here. Ask students to guess, before you reveal, which lever they think is more common in practice. (Answer: co-optation does most of the day-to-day work in most surviving autocracies; repression is the backstop, used selectively and visibly rather than constantly.)

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Two cases, two co-optation strategies
Russia: co-opts elites directly — state contracts, control of strategic industries, deals revocable the moment loyalty wavers. The public gets modest stability plus a nationalist story (next slide).

Gulf monarchies: co-opt almost everyone, at scale, using oil revenue — public-sector jobs, free services, no income tax. Political scientists call this rentier co-optation: no tax, no need for consent.

IMAGE — two small inline images side by side (or one composite), one per case. Russia: a state-contract signing / oligarch boardroom photo. Gulf: a public- sector workplace or “no income tax” visual cue. Source: Wikimedia Commons / press-agency archive for both.


“No taxation without representation” runs in reverse for a rentier state: when a ruler’s revenue comes from oil in the ground rather than from citizens’ income, the ruler doesn’t depend on citizens’ buy-in the way a tax-dependent state does. In Russia the same logic operates at a smaller scale and more selectively — the state doesn’t need everyone’s consent, only enough elites’ cooperation, and it buys that with contracts and control of strategic industries rather than with revoked taxation.


“No taxation without representation” runs in reverse here — if the ruler’s money comes from oil in the ground, not from your paycheck, the ruler doesn’t need your buy-in the way a tax-dependent state does. This is a nice one-line bridge to the “why do states need consent at all” thread without turning into a rentier-state lecture — one line, then move on.


Rentier-state theory (Beblawi & Luciani, Ross) is the academic name for this if you want to point students toward it, but keep it a one-line namecheck — it’s a whole literature and not the point of today’s lecture.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: What is a Duma seat actually for?
text:
What is a Duma seat actually for?
United Russia was assembled in December 2001 — not to win arguments. To organise loyalty.

2021: 324 of 450 seats. A constitutional supermajority
A seat buys a salary, immunity from prosecution, and a place near whoever hands out contracts
Lose the party’s favour and you lose all three at once


Co-optation with a building attached: the parliament isn’t where power gets contested. It’s where loyalty gets paid.

United Russia was formed at a founding congress on 1 December 2001, out of a merger between the Unity bloc and the Fatherland–All Russia bloc — two rival groupings that had fought each other in the 1999 Duma election and then combined behind the new president. In the 2021 Duma election it took 324 of 450 seats, comfortably above the 300 needed to amend the constitution. The point for this lecture is not the arithmetic but what the seats are for. A Duma mandate carries a salary, parliamentary immunity from prosecution, staff, and proximity to the people who allocate state contracts and regulatory favours. All of that is revocable: it depends on remaining on the party’s candidate list. That combination — valuable, visible, and withdrawable — is what makes a dominant party an efficient co-optation machine, and it is why an autocrat who could rule by decree still bothers to run one.


This is the concrete version of the elite-co-optation bullet two slides ago — don’t teach it as “here is Russia’s party system,” teach it as “here is what the carrot physically looks like.” The revocability is the load-bearing bit: a benefit you can lose tomorrow disciplines behaviour far better than one you own outright. Ask the room what the equivalent would be in an institution they know — a club, a team, a job — where the thing keeping people in line isn’t a threat, it’s not wanting to lose a good position.


Verified 2026-09-03. Founding congress 1 Dec 2001 (merger of Unity and Fatherland–All Russia): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Russia. 324/450 seats, 2021: https://www.plenglish.com/news/2021/09/22/united-russia-wins-324-of-450-seats-in-state-duma/.


Noah: check my facts / add your own angle. You have twenty years of watching this machine and I have a paragraph — the seat-as-sinecure point is yours to make properly. Also: after 18–20 September 2026 the seat numbers on this slide are one election out of date. Swap in the new ones.


IMAGE — inline .absolute, right-hand side. A Duma plenary session from the gallery: full chamber, near-unanimous show of hands. The visual point is uniformity, not grandeur. Source: duma.gov.ru press photos or Wikimedia Commons.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Legitimation: the story
The third piece: the narrative that makes rule seem right, not just survivable.

Nationalism and a besieged-fortress narrative (“we’re surrounded by enemies, only I can protect you”)
Performance — economic growth, stability after chaos, “look what the alternative did to your neighbours”
Tradition — the monarchy’s oldest and cheapest tool: this is simply how it’s always been


Repression and co-optation are what an autocrat does. Legitimation is the story about why it’s okay that they’re doing it.

Legitimation sits underneath both of the other levers. Repression and co-optation alone would still leave a regime looking naked and cynical — purely transactional, purely coercive. The legitimating story is what lets elites and citizens tell themselves that going along with the regime is reasonable, even sensible, rather than simply the path of least resistance.


Don’t over-build this — it’s the third leg of the stool, not a fourth full unit. The point is that repression and co-optation alone would still leave a regime looking naked and cynical; the story is what lets elites and citizens tell themselves that going along with it is reasonable, even sensible.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: What kind of dictatorship is it?
text:
What kind of dictatorship is it?
Political scientists sort autocracies into rough families — shorthand, not a taxonomy to memorise:

Noah: retitled from “One slide of vocabulary” (its own todo called it the driest slide in the deck, and a noun-phrase title wasn’t helping). Still the natural slot for a one-line aside — e.g. something wry about how many of these labels Russia has cycled through in your own lifetime of watching it. Not required, just the obvious place for one.


Personalist — power concentrated in one leader’s hands, thin institutions (many post-Soviet and African regimes)
Single-party — one party controls the state, has its own internal succession rules (China, historically the USSR)
Military — the armed forces rule directly or from behind a civilian front
Monarchy — hereditary, traditional-authority-based (the Gulf states)


IMAGE — chart. A simple bar or stacked-area chart showing the global mix of autocracy types over time (personalist / single-party / military / monarchy), to make “rough families” visually concrete on the deck’s dullest, most taxonomy-shaped slide. Source: V-Dem Regimes of the World data, or the Geddes-Frantz-Wright autocratic regimes dataset.


Russia today reads mostly personalist. The Gulf case is the clearest monarchy type. Most real regimes blend more than one.

Russia today reads mostly as a personalist regime, though one built on top of a formally competitive-looking constitutional system — elections, a parliament, courts — rather than an openly one-man system. The Gulf case is the clearest monarchy type of the two cases covered today. In practice, most real-world autocracies blend more than one family — a personalist leader ruling through a dominant party, for instance — so treat these as ideal types to reason with, not boxes every regime fits neatly into.


Keep this to two minutes flat — it exists so students have the vocabulary, not so they can reproduce a typology. Comparative Politics runs the full Geddes/Frantz/ Wright deep dive on exactly this in their authoritarianism week — don’t compete with that, just hand over the words. If you’re running long, this is the easiest slide to compress on the fly.


Guard rail — PLAN-MT2026.md §3b: deliberately one slide, vocabulary only. Comparative owns the full typology treatment (personalist/party/military as a genuine analytical unit, Geddes-Frantz-Wright coding rules, regime survival statistics). If this slide starts growing subheadings, that’s the tell to cut it back down.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: The obvious problem with just asking
text:
The obvious problem with just asking
Want to know how popular an autocrat really is? Send in a pollster and ask.

Except: if telling the truth carries real risk, people don’t. They say what’s safe to say.


This is called preference falsification — publicly stating a preference you don’t privately hold, because the private one is dangerous to reveal.

The problem with direct surveys in a repressive setting isn’t that people lie randomly — it’s that they lie in a predictable direction, toward whatever answer feels safest to give a stranger who might report it. That predictable bias is what preference falsification names: publicly stating a preference you don’t privately hold, because revealing the private one carries real risk. A raw approval rating gathered this way tells you what people are willing to say, not necessarily what they think.


This term is doing real work — Timur Kuran coined it, but you don’t need to name- drop him for this room; the concept is what matters. Good prompt: “if a stranger knocked on your door in an authoritarian state and asked ‘do you support the government,’ would you answer honestly?” Let them sit with their own instinctive “no.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The list experiment
One clever workaround, and it’s simpler than it sounds:

Give half the sample 4 non-sensitive items and ask how many bother them — just the number, not which ones
Give the other half the same list plus the sensitive item (“the president”) and ask the same question


IMAGE — diagram. A simple two-box explainer: “Group A: 4 items → average count” next to “Group B: 5 items (+ sensitive) → average count”, with an arrow down to “difference = estimated support.” Build as a plain vector diagram (Keynote/ PowerPoint shapes), not a photo — this is the one slide that most benefits from a made-not-sourced graphic.


Walk through this slowly and concretely — it’s a genuinely elegant design and worth letting land rather than rushing. Set-up half; the payoff (why it works) is the next slide.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Why the list experiment works
The difference in average counts between the two groups estimates true support for the sensitive item — no individual ever admits to anything.

No individual answer reveals anything. The honesty shows up only in the aggregate.

Because no one ever answers a question about the sensitive item directly — everyone only ever reports a total count — no individual response can be traced back to a view on the president specifically. The sensitive information only becomes visible once you compare the two group averages, which is exactly what makes the design safe to answer honestly: honesty happens at the level of the aggregate, not the individual.


If you want a live-in-the-room version: this is exactly the kind of thing a poll tool could demonstrate directly (see placeholder below) rather than just describing in the abstract.


Live poll — question text written, tool still undecided (TCDpolls/Vevox is the presumed answer; Noah decides). Run an actual miniature list experiment on the room. Split the audience in half at random and ask each half “How many of the following are true of you? Report only the number, not which ones.”

Group A (control), 4 items: I have a driving licence · I have lived outside Ireland · I have a sibling · I have read any of this week’s assigned reading.
Group B (treatment), the same 4 plus one: … · I have handed in work I did not really write myself.

Show both group averages on screen and subtract. The difference, times 100, is the room’s estimated rate — and nobody in the room has admitted to anything. Best single “we just did research on you” moment available in the whole course; worth prioritising if the tool decision lands before this lecture.
Noah decides: the sensitive item above is the sharpest one available but it is about them, in a module they are being assessed in. Safer swaps if you’d rather: “I have taken something from a shop without paying” or “I have lied to get out of a social occasion.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Noah’s own research

Noah: this is your slot. Drop in your actual list-experiment work — the design, the country/context, and the headline finding (however much you’re comfortable sharing at this level). This is the single best “your lecturer actually does this for a living” moment available anywhere in the term — worth more than any borrowed example. A photo or screenshot of the actual survey instrument would land well here too.


The short version: this method reads genuine support (or fear) behind a regime’s official numbers — the exact gap the Russia slide opened with.

As scaffolding, if this slot isn’t filled in time: the list experiment matters because it offers an honest read on how much genuine support — or genuine fear — sits behind a regime’s official numbers. That is exactly the gap this lecture opened with on the Russia slide: an official result of roughly 87%, and no reliable way to know, from that number alone, how much of it is real.


If Noah doesn’t fill this in time, fall back to a generic worked example (support for Putin, or for a Gulf monarch, using published list-experiment estimates) — but flag clearly in delivery that a fuller, sharper version of this exact method returns twice more: once in Lecture 14 (corruption — what people hide about bribery), and once in Lecture 20 (the term’s methods finale, full causal-inference treatment). Say the callback forward out loud both times you get there.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Readings
Required:

Heywood & Laing, Politics (2025), Ch. 5 (part) — regimes and non-democratic rule


Recommended slot — pick one, don’t stack both: something short and readable on either (a) the repression/co-optation framing directly, or (b) preference falsification/list experiments as a method — Noah to confirm exact piece and licensing before this goes on Blackboard. Deliberately NOT assigning Levitsky & Way, Geddes/Frantz/Wright, Magaloni, or Schedler here — those are Comparative’s readings for the full authoritarianism week; duplicating them undercuts the “stays conceptual, second year goes deep” division of labour.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Next up
Lecture 12 — Dictatorships II: elections, information & succession
If elections are a useful tool for an autocrat — signalling strength, distributing spoils, gathering intelligence — what happens when that information turns dangerous?

Think ahead: what happens to a regime like this one when its leader gets old, or dies, with no agreed rule for who comes next?
See you Thursday

What today covered. Two regimes wearing the same label run very different machines: Russia goes to enormous trouble to perform a democracy it does not have, while a Gulf monarchy does not bother performing anything and is, by some measures, more stable. The autocrat’s two levers are repression and co-optation — the stick is expensive and self-undermining, the carrot is expensive but buys durability, and almost every surviving autocracy runs mostly on the carrot with the stick held in reserve. Legitimation is the third piece: the story that makes either lever look reasonable rather than merely brutal or merely transactional. And because honesty is risky under a regime like this, working out what people actually think requires indirect methods — preference falsification names the problem, and the list experiment is one good answer to it.


Clean bridge: today explained the toolkit (repression, co-optation, legitimation) and the method for reading through the toolkit’s propaganda (list experiments). Next lecture takes elections specifically and asks why an autocrat would ever hold one on purpose — plus the succession problem, which is where a lot of these regimes actually break. Both follow directly from today’s framework; say so.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Democratic backsliding
The modern danger isn’t the tank. It’s the lawyer.

Cold open, no admin yet. Let the line sit. Backsliding is how a liberal democracy turns into a competitive authoritarian regime — still elections, but they stop being a fair fight. The threat looks nothing like what students expect: not a coup, but a slow legal hollowing-out carried out by people who won an election.


IMAGE — full-bleed background behind the title text. An imposing courthouse/supreme-court facade — classical columns, low dramatic light — to visualise “the lawyer” as the instrument of backsliding, in contrast to “the tank”. Source: Unsplash/Getty (“courthouse columns”, “supreme court facade”). Use as ## Democratic backsliding {background-image="w09-lec13-img/courthouse.jpg" background-color="var(--week-title-bg)"} (keep the maroon as fallback/overlay tint).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The plan for today

How do we know that? Autopsying last time’s grey zone — is a country “backsliding,” or is that just politics?
The capture sequence: courts → media → electoral administration → universities, in that order — and why that order
Cases: Hungary (the completed example), Israel and El Salvador (live/fast versions)
Could it happen here? — the boiling-frog problem


Four items, fast, don’t linger. Flag out loud that this lecture completes the regimes arc: Lecture 9 gave you the spectrum, Lectures 11–12 showed you the bottom of it, today shows you the route down.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Last time: the grey zone
Lecture 9 ended with most of the world sitting in the messy middle of Dahl’s map — not fully open, not fully closed.

V-Dem score drifting down 0.03/year for a decade — at what point does that become “backsliding” rather than “a rough patch”?

Today’s question makes the grey zone concrete. Imagine a country whose V-Dem score drifts down by roughly 0.03 a year for a decade. At some point along that slow decline, “a rough few years of ordinary politics” stops being a fair description and “backsliding” becomes the right word — but there is no single year where that switch flips. Naming exactly when the line gets crossed is the methodological problem this whole lecture works through.


Callback slide, don’t re-teach Lecture 9. Cold-call: “who remembers what the grey zone actually was?” The point of this segment: erosion doesn’t announce itself with a threshold crossing. That’s the methodological problem the whole lecture sits on top of — flag it now, pay it off properly on the “boiling frog” slide near the end.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The measurement problem, named
Every year, a country passes one law that looks defensible in isolation — a media regulation here, a court appointment rule there.

No single year crosses a “this is now a dictatorship” line. So — is it noise, or a trend?


Not a footnote — same measurement problem as Lecture 9: no direct observation, so you chase a proxy.

This is the same measurement problem introduced back in Lecture 9, not a side issue: democracy, like most concepts this course works with, isn’t something you can observe directly, so you go looking for a proxy that moves when the real thing does. That’s exactly the judgment call V-Dem and Freedom House make every year — deciding whether that year’s law is background noise or the start of a trend — which is why serious measures publish an expert-coded score rather than a yes/no verdict.


Explicit callback to the measurement thread (2 → 9 → 14 → 20) — say the numbers out loud if the room needs the thread named. This slide is doing double duty: it’s the HDWKT autopsy and the frame for the whole lecture, so don’t rush past it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Key term: democratic backsliding

Democratic backsliding: the gradual, legal-looking erosion of democratic constraints by elected leaders — not a coup, but a creeping shift from liberal democracy toward competitive authoritarianism.


No single dramatic break. A sequence of moves, each one individually defensible in a courtroom.

Distinguish sharply from regime collapse — a coup, a revolution, tanks in the street. Backsliding is the in-office version: the people doing it were elected, are still popular, and are using tools every government legitimately has. That’s what makes it hard to stop and hard to even agree is happening.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The capture sequence
Backsliders follow a pattern. The order is the lecture’s whole argument:

Courts and the referees — neuter judicial independence first
Media — tilt the information environment
Electoral administration — redraw the boundaries of a fair fight
Universities and civil society — shrink the space that organises opposition


Ask why courts go first — everything after that is easier to defend in court once the court is yours.

This is the hook — go deep on the logic of the ordering, not just the list. Step 1 legitimises steps 2–4: once you control the referee, every subsequent move that gets challenged in court simply… doesn’t lose. That’s the mechanism, and it’s the thing Comparative’s Week 6 slot never actually breaks down — they name-check the countries, not the sequence.


This is the deck’s spine — everything downstream (Hungary, Israel, Bukele) is this sequence run at different speeds. Comp Wk6 assigns Levitsky & Ziblatt and Brownlee & Miao and name-checks Hungary/Turkey/Poland/US/Brazil/India, but their slides (checked against the Week 6 Monday dump) never build the courts→media→elections→universities mechanics — that gap is exactly this lecture’s angle, confirmed clear.


Noah: check my facts / add your own angle. This todo asked for the Russia example; it’s now drafted as three slides after Hungary (“Same list, different order: Russia, 2000–2006”). Two things are yours to settle. One: whether Russia or Hungary is the lead case — I left Hungary leading because the textbook carries it, but you can narrate Russia firsthand and it’s the faster story. Two: the slide deliberately keeps the awkward finding that Russia went media-first, not courts-first. I think that’s the better lecture. Say if you’d rather it were tidier.


IMAGE — inline .absolute, small, right-hand side. Photo of Hungary’s Kúria (Supreme Court) building, Budapest — a concrete anchor for “courts go first”, ahead of the Hungary case proper on the next slide. Source: Wikimedia Commons (search “Kúria Budapest”).

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The worked example: Hungary
2010: Orbán and Fidesz win a landslide. He governs well — popular, real delivery.


Courts (2011–13): new pro-government judges appointed, the constitutional court’s powers cut
Media: state media expands; laws let regulators punish “scaremongering” coverage
Electoral administration: districts redrawn in Fidesz’s favour
Universities and civil society: schools, NGOs brought under closer state oversight


The landslide followed the previous government’s credibility collapse — Fidesz didn’t seize power in a vacuum, they won it outright after voters had already lost faith in the alternative. And for years afterward, Orbán delivered: real economic management, generous pensions, tangible improvements people could feel. That context matters for everything that follows — this was never a story about an unpopular leader clinging to power against the public’s wishes.


IMAGE — inline .absolute, top-right corner. Portrait of Viktor Orbán, official/press photo. Source: Wikimedia Commons or European Council press photos (CC-licensed).


Walk this one slowly — it’s the “completed” example, run over roughly a decade, so students can see the sequence land in order rather than all at once. Note the uncomfortable part out loud: Orbán remains genuinely popular. Elections still happen, on schedule, and he keeps winning them. That’s the point — this isn’t a story about a leader who lost the public and clung on by force.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Hungary, the uncomfortable part
By the mid-2010s, Hungary was no longer fully free — but not an outright autocracy either.

Relatively open elections, most rights still on the books, real public support. A hybrid regime, sitting exactly in Lecture 9’s grey zone.


And the illiberal parts aren’t hidden from voters. Many voters know, and vote for it anyway.

By the mid-2010s, most serious observers — V-Dem, Freedom House, and independent scholars alike — had converged on the same judgment: Hungary could no longer be called a fully free democracy, but it also hadn’t become an outright autocracy. That in-between verdict is exactly the point.


IMAGE — chart, inline. Hungary’s V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index, 2010–present, showing the decline into “electoral autocracy” territory — the empirical backing for “hybrid regime, sitting exactly in the grey zone.” Source: V-Dem / Our World in Data, filtered to Hungary (ourworldindata.org/grapher/liberal-democracy-index).


This is the beat that should unsettle them, gently — it’s not “the people were fooled.” It complicates any story where backsliding is just elite deception. Good moment to ask: does it matter whether backsliding is popular? Does popularity make it more or less worrying?


Sourced from Heywood & Laing ch5’s Hungary box-out (p.131–134) — kept it close to the textbook’s own account since it’s genuinely good and this is the one case where Comp and Intro can legitimately overlap (reused for continuity, per the plan). The mechanics framing around it is what’s new, not the case itself.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Same list, different order: Russia, 2000–2006
Hungary took a decade and started with the courts. Russia took six years — and started somewhere else.

The referees, first — May 2000: the country carved into seven federal districts with presidential envoys; elected governors pushed out of the upper house
Then the media — Gusinsky arrested June 2000; NTV taken over April 2001; Berezovsky’s channel gone by the same year


Two moves, two years, and the two things that could have made noise about the rest were already gone.

The comparison is worth setting out carefully. In May 2000, within a week of his inauguration, Putin issued a decree (13 May) dividing Russia’s eighty-nine regions into seven federal districts, each with a presidential plenipotentiary, and introduced bills (19 May) removing elected governors from the Federation Council and replacing them with appointees. That is the federal-structure equivalent of the “referees” step: not the courts exactly, but the institutions that could have said no. The media step followed almost immediately. Vladimir Gusinsky, owner of the Media-Most group and the independent television channel NTV, was arrested on 13 June 2000 on fraud charges; the charges were dropped the following month after he signed over Media-Most to the state-controlled gas company Gazprom, an arrangement he later described as “shares for freedom” and repudiated once he had left the country. Boris Berezovsky, who controlled the ORT channel, left Russia in the autumn of 2000 and gave up his stake soon after. Gazprom completed its boardroom takeover of NTV on 3 April 2001 and took physical control of the building at 3:30 in the morning on 14 April, when the new management arrived with a court order; roughly thirty-five of the channel’s journalists resigned that day.


This is your firsthand case — narrate it, don’t read it. The single most useful teaching beat here is the order: everything the room has just learned says courts go first, and Russia didn’t do that. Ask them why not, and let them get there: you only need to capture the courts first if the courts are currently capable of stopping you. Russia’s weren’t. Hungary’s were. The sequence isn’t a law of nature — it’s what you do when there’s an obstacle in the way.


All dates verified 2026-09-03; sources listed in the revision log on the plan slide. Deliberately not smoothing the courts-first claim: Russia ran media and federal structure first, and the discrepancy is the pedagogically valuable part rather than an embarrassment for the framework.


IMAGE — inline .absolute, right-hand side. The NTV building on Akademika Korolyova street, or a still from the final Kiselyov-era broadcast interrupted on the morning of 14 April 2001. Source: Wikimedia Commons / press-agency archive.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
And then, slowly, the rest

Courts — Dec 2001: judicial-reform package; from 2002 the bodies that appoint and dismiss judges include presidential appointees
Electoral administration — Dec 2004: direct elections for regional governors abolished after Beslan; the president appoints instead
Civil society — Jan 2006: the NGO law, written in the shadow of the colour revolutions


The whole list, in six years, without a single tank on a single street.

The remaining steps ran on a slower clock. A package of judicial-reform laws was promulgated in December 2001 — the amendments to the Law on the Status of Judges were signed on 15 December — introducing disciplinary liability for judges; from 2002, representatives of the president and of the wider public were added to the qualification collegia, the bodies that select, discipline and dismiss judges. In September 2004, days after the Beslan school siege, Putin proposed abolishing direct elections for Russia’s regional governors; he signed the law on 13 December 2004, giving the president the right to nominate regional leaders for confirmation by regional legislatures, with the power to dissolve a legislature that refused twice. And on 10 January 2006 he signed the law amending the rules governing non-governmental organisations, in force from 15 April 2006 — a response, on most accounts, to the role NGOs had played in the colour revolutions in Georgia, Ukraine and Kyrgyzstan.


Keep this fast — three bullets, one date each, then the closing line. The point isn’t the legislative detail, it’s that the list is the same list. If you want one detail to linger on, the 2004 one is the strongest: a terrorist attack on a school produced a law abolishing regional elections, and the connection between problem and solution was never really explained.


Noah: check my facts / add your own angle — and this is the obvious slot for a firsthand line if you have one. The 2006 NGO law in particular is something you watched land on people you knew.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
So which order is right?
Hungary: courts, then media, then elections, then universities. Russia: media and the regions first, courts years later.
Same four targets. So what decides the order?

Answer to steer them toward, but let them try first: you capture first whatever is currently capable of stopping you. In Hungary the constitutional court was a real obstacle, so it went first. In Russia in 2000 the courts weren’t going to stop anything, but two television channels reaching the whole country might have — so they went first. The generalisable version, and the one worth writing on the board: the sequence follows the constraints, not a playbook. That’s a much more useful thing to know than a memorised list, and it’s the version that survives contact with a case neither of us has seen yet.


This slide exists to stop the four-step sequence hardening into something students reproduce as a checklist in an exam. The mechanism (capture the binding constraint first) is the portable part; the ordering is not.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Same sequence, faster: Israel and El Salvador
text:
Same sequence, faster: Israel and El Salvador

Israel, 2023 onward — a live fight over step one: the judicial overhaul targets the Supreme Court’s power to strike down laws. Still unresolved.
El Salvador, Bukele — the condensed version: all four steps in a few years — captured legislature, permanent state of emergency, packed courts, term limits reinterpreted away.


Same logic, different speeds. Hungary took a decade. Bukele took about three years — and stayed genuinely popular the entire time.

Israel: the government’s 2023 judicial overhaul aimed squarely at the Supreme Court’s power to strike down legislation — step one of the sequence, contested in real time rather than narrated after the fact. It triggered mass protests and a partial government climbdown, and the fight was still open as this deck was written. El Salvador: Bukele ran the condensed version of the same playbook — a captured legislature, a state of emergency that never formally ends, courts packed with loyalists, and his own re-election secured by reinterpreting a constitutional term limit rather than repealing it outright.


IMAGE — inline, paired with the Israel bullet. Crowd photo, 2023 judicial-overhaul protests outside the Knesset or on Tel Aviv’s Kaplan Street — mass scale, Israeli flags. Source: Reuters/AP via Wikimedia Commons.


IMAGE — inline, paired with the El Salvador bullet. Nayib Bukele portrait, or a CECOT (mega-prison) photo if the state-of-emergency angle should read visually rather than just in the bullet text. Source: El Salvador government press office (widely republished) or Reuters via Wikimedia Commons.


Israel is the live case — useful precisely because the outcome isn’t settled, so you can ask students to predict rather than just narrate history. Bukele is the “if you want to see step 4 arrive fast” case — his crackdown on gangs bought him the public support that made the rest of the sequence easy to sell.


Currency check needed closer to delivery (textbook data stops ~mid-2024): confirm where the Israeli judicial overhaul actually stands by October 2026 (resolved? stalled? escalated?), and whether Bukele has since consolidated further or hit a check. Update this slide’s verbs accordingly.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Poland: the sequence in reverse
Poland’s Law and Justice party ran a version of the same playbook on the judiciary from 2015.

Then, in 2023, they lost an election — and a new government has spent since then trying to un-capture the courts.


Worth sitting with: capture isn’t permanent — but it’s not easy to reverse either.

You can’t just un-appoint a judge because you don’t like how they got their seat — the same legal formalism that made capture possible in the first place makes reversal slow and contested. That’s exactly why Poland’s post-2023 government is still fighting this fight, not finished with it.


IMAGE — inline or full-width strip. Warsaw “Free Courts” protest, 2017–18 — a huge crowd outside the Supreme Court or Sejm, EU flags visible. Counterweights the Hungary/Bukele photos with a case where the public pushed back. Source: Reuters/AP via Wikimedia Commons.


Useful counterweight to Hungary and Bukele so this doesn’t read as a one-way ratchet. The reversal is genuinely difficult and contested — flag that the “how do you fix a captured court” problem is a live, unresolved one, not a clean success story.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Norms and the “two cultures” problem
Political scientists Levitsky and Ziblatt argue backsliding happens when two unwritten norms break down between rivals:

Mutual toleration — rivals stop treating each other as legitimate competitors, not enemies
Forbearance — leaders stop showing restraint with the legal tools they technically have


When both go, the constitution stops being a shared rulebook and becomes a weapon whoever holds power reaches for first.

IMAGE — small inline thumbnail. Cover of Levitsky & Ziblatt, How Democracies Die — the source of the mutual-toleration/forbearance argument on this slide. Source: publisher’s page or Wikimedia (book-cover thumbnail).


This is the meta-insight, and it’s the reason the capture sequence works at all: none of those four steps is illegal on its own. They only add up to regime change because the other side has stopped restraining itself, and the target has stopped being able to count on anyone enforcing the unwritten rules. Democracies are fragile because half of what holds them together was never written down.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Could it happen here?
What would the first sign look like in an established democracy — and who tends to notice it before it’s too late?

Don’t hand them a checklist immediately — let them generate answers first, cold-call a few. If it needs a nudge: rejecting the legitimacy of political rivals, tolerating or encouraging political violence, a willingness to curb basic civil liberties “just this once.” Keep it genuinely open and non-partisan — the exercise works precisely because reasonable people will disagree about where their own country sits.


Deliberately not naming a specific country here beyond the cases already covered — Irish, UK, or US current-events specifics will land better live and go stale fast in a written deck. This is the natural spot for whichever 2026-current hook feels sharpest when you’re actually delivering it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The boiling-frog problem
Go back to the HDWKT question from earlier: no single year crosses a threshold.


Each individual step is defensible, sometimes even popular
The people best placed to notice the pattern — journalists, judges, academics — are usually who steps 1–4 target first
By the time an outside observer agrees “yes, this happened,” reversing it is much harder than it would have been at step one



That’s why the order matters as much as the list — know what to watch before it’s obvious to everyone else.

The order matters as much as the list because it tells you where to look early. If you know courts go first, “watch the courts” is a usable instruction well before anyone would call what’s happening backsliding out loud — by the time it’s obvious to an outside observer, you’re already well past the point where reversal is easy.


This closes the loop on the HDWKT opener and gives students something usable, not just descriptive: the payoff of learning the sequence is that it tells you where to look early, not just what to call it after the fact.

Next up

Backsliding is elected power capturing the state. Next time: the state captured by private interests instead — and why “everyone does it” is its own trap.

See you Thursday

Backsliding is one way that elected power gets captured — a single actor or coalition using legitimate levers of state authority to entrench itself. Next lecture looks at a different failure mode: the state captured not by an elected leader consolidating power, but by private interests buying influence over specific decisions and contracts. “Everyone does it” is worth pausing on as a claim in its own right — it’s a common defence of corruption, and a trap for exactly the reason collective-action problems generally are.


Clean handoff. title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Who can stop whom?
The executive wants power. The legislature wants power. What happens when neither can win outright?

IMAGE — full-bleed cold-open background. A wide shot of an empty debating chamber (e.g., the Dáil chamber, or any national parliament) — benches facing each other, nobody home yet. Visually poses “who controls this room?” before the lecture answers it. Source: Oireachtas photo library / Wikimedia Commons. Use as ## Who can stop whom? {background-image="w10-lec15-img/empty-chamber.jpg" background-color="var(--week-title-bg)"}.


Cold open, no admin yet. Welcome to the institutions block — and say up front that this is deliberately NOT four lectures marching through constitutions, courts, executives, legislatures (that’s how this material is usually taught, and it’s the most forgettable part of any intro course). We’re doing it with one tool instead: veto players. By the end of 50 minutes they should be able to open a newspaper story about ANY country’s government and say “here’s who can block this.”

Today

Who’s the boss? Parliamentary vs. presidential vs. semi-presidential
What is a legislature actually for? — and the Duma vs. the Bundestag
Veto players — one portable tool for reading any political system
How do we know that? Do institutions actually matter, or do the same people just relabel?


Small tool. Huge payoff. You’ll use this one for the rest of the course.

Revision log, 2026-09-03

Light-touch pass: .breathe added to 8 dense list/closer slides for whitespace
Added todo Russia aside/joke slot on “Three ways to build an executive”
No text cut, split, or moved between channels

Added the legislatures segment — three slides. The deck previously never taught legislatures at all, despite Heywood ch15 being on the required list. Source: Ben Noble & Ekaterina Schulmann, “Not Just a Rubber Stamp,” in The New Autocracy (Brookings, 2018), figs. 3-1 and 3-2, PDF. Deliberately using their nuanced finding rather than a bare “rubber stamp” claim.
