Committee chairs are shared out in proportion to group strength, and the Budget Committee is chaired by an opposition MP by tradition (bundestag.de).

Drafted the Russia semi-presidentialism aside where the todo sat: on paper Russia is semi-presidential; under Art. 111, if the Duma rejects the president’s nominee for prime minister three times he may appoint anyway and dissolve the Duma (the 2020 amendments turned that duty into a discretion). Sources: Russian Constitution, ch. 6; IACL blog on the 2020 amendments.
Retitled four flat noun-phrase headings flagged in FRESH-EYES §3: “Three ways to build an executive” → “Who can fire whom?”; “The trade-off” → “Speed or stability — pick one”; “Two kinds of veto player” → “Some veto players are in the constitution. Some are just arithmetic.”; “Institutions as constraints — for good and ill” → “Count the players, don’t read the label.”
Live-poll question already written; left as-is (tool still undecided).



Fuller framing of item 1: where executive authority comes from — covered in two slides here, not the four lectures this topic usually gets.


Four items, keep it fast — this is the recurring bookend, don’t linger. Flag explicitly that veto players is the SECOND portable concept of the course (after collective action, Lecture 14) — say the word “portable concept” out loud, they should start recognising the pattern.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Who can fire whom?
The big design choice: where does the executive’s authority come from, and who can take it away?

Parliamentary — the executive is drawn from and answerable to the legislature. Lose a confidence vote, lose office. (Ireland, UK, Germany, Spain.)
Presidential — voters elect the executive separately, for a fixed term. (US, most of Latin America.)
Semi-presidential — both exist at once: an elected president and a prime minister who needs the legislature’s confidence. (France.)


Russia is semi-presidential too — on paper. The Duma “approves” the prime minister. Reject the president’s nominee three times and he appoints the man anyway, and dissolves the Duma.


Noah: check my facts / add your own angle. The Russia aside is now drafted on the slide (it was a todo asking you to supply one). Article 111: three rejections and the president appoints regardless — pre-2020 he was obliged to dissolve the Duma, since 2020 it’s his choice, which if anything sharpens the point. Yours to sharpen further, or to swap for the joke about countries that call themselves “presidential” purely for branding.


Verified 2026-09-03: Constitution of the Russian Federation, Art. 111; 2020 amendments changed the president’s obligation to dissolve into a discretion, and changed the Duma’s role from “consent” to “approval” — a nominally larger power attached to the same self-destruct button.


Noah: parliamentary vs. presidential vs. semi-presidential is likely half-known already (LC Politics & Society, general news) — flagging as a candidate for a faster live pass, spending the saved time on the veto-players payoff instead. Not cut — you said don’t delete substance, they’ve never seen the poli-sci framing.


Ask yourself one question about any system: who can dismiss whom? That answer tells you almost everything else.

The presidential case is the sharpest contrast with parliamentary systems: Congress cannot fire the president just for disagreeing with them, because the president does not depend on Congress’s confidence to stay in office — only voters, at the next fixed election, can remove them.


IMAGE — inline .absolute diagram. Simple side-by-side wiring diagram — three boxes (voters, executive, legislature) with arrows showing who elects/answers-to/can-remove whom, one panel per system. Drop in w10-lec15-img/systems-wiring.png.


Keep this to ONE slide of substance, not the old four-lecture march. The “who can dismiss whom” question is the exit line — it’s doing double duty: it’s also basically the first sentence of the veto-player definition, so it sets up the next section. Ireland is parliamentary: the Taoiseach is a TD, government needs the Dáil’s confidence, lose a vote and you can lose office. Don’t re-teach Irish civics mechanics (how the Taoiseach gets nominated) — they’ve had a lot of that; go straight to the trade-off.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Speed or stability — pick one

Parliamentary: fast to move, fast to fall — majority today, gone tomorrow.
Presidential: stable, but prone to gridlock — two elected branches, neither can fire the other.
Semi-presidential: interesting when president and PM are from different parties — cohabitation. (France, more than once.)


None of these is “better.” Each one trades speed for stability in a different place.

Parliamentary systems can move fast because the executive already commands a legislative majority — but that same majority can evaporate, costing the government office overnight. Presidential systems trade that instability for gridlock: two separately elected branches can both claim a democratic mandate, and neither can remove the other. Semi-presidential systems split the difference and can produce cohabitation, when the president and prime minister come from different parties — France has lived through this more than once, and it is often genuinely unclear who is in charge when it happens.


Resist the urge to declare a winner — students will want you to say parliamentary or presidential is “correct,” and the honest answer is that it’s a design trade-off, not a verdict. Cohabitation is a great “wait, what?” moment for first-years — France elected a president AND separately elects a National Assembly, and sometimes those disagree. Good spot for a show of confusion before you resolve it with the veto-player framework next.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Three jobs, and only one is famous
text:
Three jobs, and only one is famous

Legislate — make law. The one everybody names, and often the smallest part of the job
Scrutinise — drag the executive in and make it explain itself. Committees, questions, budgets
Represent — be the room where the country’s divisions have to be spoken out loud


Every legislature on earth claims all three. Whether it does any of them is a separate question — and it isn’t answered by reading the constitution.

Textbooks usually list a legislature’s functions as legislation, scrutiny (or oversight) of the executive, representation, and — in parliamentary systems — recruitment, since the government is drawn from the chamber’s own membership. The first is the most visible and frequently the least important in practice: in most parliamentary systems the overwhelming majority of laws are drafted by the executive, and the legislature’s real influence lies in what it can force the government to explain, amend, or abandon. That is why the comparison in the next two slides is between two chambers’ committee systems rather than between their voting records.


Keep this to a minute. Its only job is to give them three verbs so the next two slides have something to measure against. Resist listing recruitment as a fourth — it’s real (parliamentary governments are drawn from the chamber) but it dilutes the comparison, and they met it two slides ago under “who can fire whom.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Same institution, opposite function
Russia’s State Duma. 450 members, elections, committees, a constitution.

Executive-sponsored bills pass at roughly four times the rate of ordinary deputies’ bills
But deputies still submit about half of all bills, and the executive only about a fifth — this isn’t an empty room
Bills get rewritten between readings, sometimes beyond recognition. Just not in public


Not a rubber stamp exactly. A place where the fights happen with the door shut.

Ben Noble and Ekaterina Schulmann’s chapter “Not Just a Rubber Stamp” is the careful version of this. They show that the executive (president and government together) sponsors only around 20% of the bills submitted to the Duma, with deputies sponsoring around half; that executive bills, while overwhelmingly successful, do sometimes fail; and that bills are frequently and substantially amended between readings — in one case a two-hundred-word government bill about aircraft registration emerged as a ten-thousand-word law about taxation. Their argument is that “rubber stamp” is the wrong label, not because the Duma constrains the executive in the way a democratic legislature would, but because it is the venue where conflicts within the elite get resolved out of public view. That is a genuinely different function from either legislating or scrutinising, and it is the one the chamber actually performs.


The teaching move here is to refuse the easy answer. Students arrive expecting “Russia’s parliament is fake,” and the honest finding is more interesting: it’s busy, it amends things, it occasionally kills a government bill — it just does all of that as elite conflict management rather than as public accountability. Say the distinction out loud: the institution is real, the function has been swapped.


Verified 2026-09-03 against Noble & Schulmann, “Not Just a Rubber Stamp,” in Daniel Treisman (ed.), The New Autocracy (Brookings, 2018), figs. 3-1 and 3-2. The “four times” comparison is my rounding of their bill-success figure (executive bills climbing toward 80–90% by the fourth and fifth convocations against roughly 20% for deputies’ bills) — a range, not a single published statistic, so phrased as a ratio rather than a precise number.


Noah: check my facts / add your own angle. Noble is the obvious person to cite here and you’ll know how far to push the nuance with first-years. If you’d rather just say “rubber stamp” and move on, the Bundestag contrast still works — but I think the “real institution, swapped function” version is the better lecture and it’s the same point you make about Russian elections in Lecture 11.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
And the same institution, working
Germany’s Bundestag. Also elected, also has committees, also faces a government with a majority.

Committees mirror the ministries, and government MPs on them amend their own government’s bills in over half of cases
Committee chairs are shared out by party strength — opposition parties chair real committees
The Budget Committee is chaired by an opposition MP, by tradition. The people checking the money are the people who want the government gone


Same three jobs on paper. Wildly different amounts of actual scrutiny.

The Bundestag’s own description of its legislative process states that “very few Government bills are adopted by a majority of the Members of the German Bundestag without any amendments” — rather, members from the governing parties, who form the majority on every committee, examine their own government’s bill critically and introduce amendments in more than 50% of cases. Committee membership and the distribution of committee chairs reflect the relative strength of the parliamentary groups, which means opposition parties chair some committees despite the coalition’s numerical advantage; the chairmanship of the Budget Committee is by tradition given to an opposition member, precisely to underline parliament’s scrutiny of government spending. This is why German political scientists describe the Bundestag as a “working parliament” (Arbeitsparlament) in contrast to a “debating parliament” on the Westminster model: the decisive work happens in specialised committees rather than on the floor.


The budget-committee fact is the one they’ll remember, so land it slowly: the committee that scrutinises the government’s spending is chaired, on purpose, by someone whose job is to replace the government. Ask the room whether they’d expect that to work, and whether they can imagine the Dáil doing it. (The Public Accounts Committee chair going to the opposition is the closest Irish parallel — worth a one-liner if you want the local hook, though PAC audits spending after the fact rather than approving it.)


Verified 2026-09-03 against the Bundestag’s own English-language pages on committee recommendations and committee chairpersons (bundestag.de). Using the institution’s self-description is deliberate — it is a claim about design intent, and it is checkable.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: So what actually explains the difference?
text:
So what actually explains the difference?
Two chambers. Both elected, both with committees, both facing a government that has the numbers. One scrutinises. One doesn’t.
The constitution can’t tell you which is which. So what can?

Let them try. Steer toward: whether losing a committee fight actually costs the government anything — which depends on whether there is a route by which the government can be removed, and whether anyone outside the room ever finds out what happened inside it. That is the bridge straight into veto players, which is the next slide: an institution is a veto player only if its refusal has consequences. Say that transition explicitly.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Key term: veto players

Veto players: actors whose agreement is necessary for a policy to pass. Every veto player has to sign off — or the status quo holds.


Forget memorising “parliamentary vs. presidential vs. semi-presidential.” Ask instead: how many veto players does this system have, and who are they?

The status-quo point is the crux of it: changing a policy requires unanimous consent among the veto players, so any single one of them can freeze a policy exactly where it is. That is what makes the concept useful — it works whether you’re looking at a constitution’s formal structure or a coalition’s internal arithmetic.


IMAGE — inline .absolute photo. A closed gate, a padlocked door, or a level-crossing barrier — something that visually says “blocked” without a word of text, positioned next to the “who are they?” line. Source: any stock/Unsplash-style photo (CC0). Use as .absolute image, small, right-aligned.


This is the pivot of the whole lecture — say explicitly: “everything in the last two slides was actually just setup for this one idea.” Tsebelis’s framework (Veto Players, 2002) is the source if anyone asks, but don’t lecture the citation, use the tool. The power of the concept is that it works for ANY system, democratic or not — flag forward: “we’ll use this exact tool again in Lecture 18 when we ask who blocks housing policy in Ireland.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Some are in the constitution. Some are just arithmetic.
text:
Some are in the constitution. Some are just arithmetic.

Institutional veto players — built into the constitution: a second chamber, a constitutional court, a president with veto power. They exist whether or not anyone likes each other.
Partisan veto players — built by the arithmetic of who won: coalition partners, factions inside a governing party, a backbench rebellion that can cost you your majority.


Count both kinds before calling a government “powerful.”

This distinction is what separates a first-year-solid answer from a shallow one — a president who nominally has huge formal power can still be weak if they lack partisan veto players (a hostile legislature); a prime minister with a wafer-thin coalition majority can be weak despite having almost no institutional veto players in their way. Good moment to preview the coalition-arithmetic case coming up.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Veto players in action
Count the players whose agreement you need before anything changes:

Ireland (parliamentary) — the governing coalition + enough of the Dáil to survive a vote.
US (presidential) — president + Senate + House, and often the courts too.
France (semi-presidential) — president + prime minister + National Assembly.


More veto players → harder to change anything.

More veto players cuts both ways. It protects the status quo from a reckless majority, but it can also just mean nothing gets done — the same mechanism, judged differently depending on what you think should change.


Ireland — a three-party coalition means three sets of partisan veto players, not one (next slide). US — divided government means every one of them can block the others (US shutdown slide). France — in cohabitation, president and PM come from different camps, and both have real power (France slide).


IMAGE — inline .absolute graphic. A simple icon/bar chart comparing veto-player counts across the three cases (Ireland ≈ 3 coalition partners; US = 3, president/Senate/House; France = 2–3 depending on cohabitation). Build it yourself in Keynote/Figures rather than sourcing — it’s a synthesis of the lecture’s own numbers, not a citable dataset.


PORTABLE CONCEPT ANCHOR. This is the second major tool of the course after collective action (Lecture 14). Name it out loud and make it stick: “find the veto players, predict the gridlock.” Students will meet it again in Lecture 18 (who blocks housing/redistribution) and, per the plan, this is also exactly Tsebelis’s framework — they’ll see a much fuller version of it in Comparative Politics next year, so this is deliberately the light, portable, “carry this forward” version, not the full academic apparatus (agenda-setters, policy space dimensions, etc.).


Let them practise live: “Who are the veto players in Ireland’s current government?” Push past “the government” as an answer — get them to name the coalition partners specifically, and note that in a small majority, even a handful of backbench TDs become de facto veto players because losing them costs the government its majority. Concrete, close to home, no need for current-affairs currency-checking since the mechanism (not the party names) is the point.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Ireland’s coalition arithmetic
Ireland has had a coalition government continuously since 1989. That’s not an accident — it’s what PR-STV plus a small country produces.

Multi-party Dáil → no single party gets a majority on its own
Coalitions mean every partner is a veto player on anything contentious
A wafer-thin majority (say, 81 seats out of 160) makes individual TDs veto players too


What that buys you: broader buy-in, harder-to-reverse decisions. What it costs you: slower decisions, lowest-common-denominator policy.

Spelled out in full: coalition government buys broader buy-in and decisions that are hard to reverse once made, in exchange for slower decision-making and policy that gets watered down to whatever the most reluctant coalition partner will accept.


IMAGE — inline .absolute photo. A coalition government press conference or handshake photo (e.g., an Irish government-formation announcement), or a wide shot of the Dáil chamber in session. Source: Oireachtas / government press office. Use as .absolute image, mid-slide.


Electoral systems (why PR-STV produces multi-party Dáils in the first place) are Alex’s territory — Ch10, and Duverger’s law specifically is his to teach. One namecheck of PR-STV here as the cause of Ireland’s coalition habit is fine and arguably necessary for the case to make sense, but don’t build out the electoral-systems mechanics — that’s a boundary worth guarding carefully since it’s the most tempting overlap in this lecture.


Noah: running ~75-85 visible words, above the 44-52 target — treated as a deliberately dense single-case reference slide rather than split. Say if you’d rather this (and “France’s cohabitation”) split into a “setup” slide + a “trade-off” slide each.


This is the non-civics-class Irish angle the brief wants: not “how is the Taoiseach chosen” but “why does Ireland never get single-party government, and what does that structurally buy and cost.” If you want a concrete number, use whatever the current Dáil’s governing majority actually is in November 2026 — swap the “81 out of 160” placeholder for the real figure.


Currency check: confirm the actual size of the governing coalition/majority as of Nov 2026 before delivery — the “81/160” figure above is illustrative, not current data.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
France’s cohabitation
France elects a president and separately elects a National Assembly. Sometimes they disagree.

Cohabitation = president from one camp, prime minister (backed by the Assembly) from another
The constitution doesn’t clearly say who’s in charge when this happens
It’s happened more than once, and each time, French politics effectively runs on two rival veto players fighting over the ambiguous middle


Same country, same constitution — wildly different amount of executive power, depending purely on whether the president’s party also controls the Assembly.

In practice, the ambiguity tends to resolve along a rough convention rather than a rule: foreign policy stays presidential, domestic policy drifts to the prime minister. But even that split is negotiated case by case, not written down anywhere.


IMAGE — inline .absolute photo. A joint appearance by a French president and prime minister from opposing camps (a past cohabitation pairing), or the Élysée Palace exterior as a stand-in if a current photo isn’t available. Source: AFP / Wikimedia Commons. Use as .absolute image, mid-slide.


Currency check: French cohabitation is a live, recurring possibility rather than a fixed historical fact — confirm whether France is currently in a cohabitation-like configuration as of late 2026 before delivery, and swap in the current example if so.


Noah: running ~75-85 visible words, above the 44-52 target — treated as a deliberately dense single-case reference slide rather than split. Say if you’d rather this (and “Ireland’s coalition arithmetic”) split into a “setup” slide + a “trade-off” slide each.


Good moment for the “wait, so who’s actually in charge?” beat — let the ambiguity sit rather than resolving it too fast. The teaching point is that veto-player counts aren’t fixed by the constitution alone; they depend on election results layering on top of the constitutional design.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The US shutdown
The clearest gridlock case: Congress passes a budget, the president signs it — or money runs out.

President + House + Senate are all separate veto players
Divided government (different parties controlling different pieces) makes shutdowns more likely, not less
Nobody “wins” a shutdown — it’s what happens when veto players can’t agree and the system has no tiebreaker


This is what “more veto players” looks like when it goes wrong: not gridlock as an abstraction, but federal workers not getting paid.

No side “wins” a shutdown in the sense of getting its preferred policy through — a shutdown is simply what happens when veto players can’t agree and the system provides no tiebreaker. If any single veto player refuses to sign off, the government runs out of authorised money to spend, regardless of how reasonable anyone’s position is.


IMAGE — inline .absolute photo. A “closed due to government shutdown” sign (e.g., a National Park Service sign) — instantly recognisable, makes the abstraction concrete. Source: NPS / Wikimedia Commons (public domain). Use as .absolute image, mid-slide.


Shutdowns are a good visceral case because it’s not abstract “politics is slow” — it’s a concrete, headline-making consequence of veto-player deadlock. If there’s been a recent shutdown by delivery time, use it as the live example instead of a generic description.


Currency check: use whichever US shutdown is most recent/memorable by November 2026 as the concrete example — don’t let this go stale on a specific year.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Gridlock: bug or feature?
More veto players means change is harder. Is that a problem, or is that the point?

Don’t answer this one immediately — let them sit with it. Push toward: gridlock protecting a minority from a reckless majority is a feature (constitutional design often does this on purpose); gridlock blocking something a broad majority actually wants is a bug. The veto-player framework doesn’t tell you which is which — it just lets you SEE the mechanism. That distinction is the payoff of naming the tool.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Do institutions actually matter?
Juan Linz made a famous, provocative claim in 1990: presidential systems are more dangerous for democracy than parliamentary ones.

His mechanism: dual legitimacy (both branches can claim a mandate) plus fixed terms — makes presidential systems brittle in a crisis.

Dual legitimacy means the president and the legislature can both claim “the people chose me.” Fixed terms mean there is no way to remove a failing president short of impeachment or a coup. Together, Linz argued, these features make presidential systems structurally brittle in a crisis — a parliamentary system can swap out a failing government without breaking the constitution; a presidential one generally cannot.


IMAGE — inline .absolute image. Cover of Linz’s edited volume The Failure of Presidential Democracy (1994), or a portrait photo of Juan Linz. Source: publisher’s cover art / academic archive. Use as small .absolute image, corner placement.


Present this as a genuine, contested claim — not settled fact. Linz’s original evidence was mostly about Latin America’s coup-prone presidential systems compared to parliamentary Europe’s relative stability. Ask: is that a fair comparison, or is something else going on (e.g., which regions HAPPENED to adopt which system, alongside other risk factors)?

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The rival answer
Critics of Linz pushed back hard: maybe it’s not the institution that’s dangerous, it’s where presidentialism got adopted.

Most presidential systems are in Latin America and post-colonial states — places with other democracy-eroding pressures anyway (weak parties, inequality, military tradition)
Compare like with like: some presidential systems (US, Costa Rica) have been very stable; some parliamentary systems (Weimar Germany, interwar Italy) collapsed anyway
Maybe the “same people” just relabel the fight — a determined authoritarian will find leverage in either system


Political scientists still argue about it.

Framed as the standing question that opened this section: “do institutions matter, or do the same people just relabel?”


This IS the HDWKT segment — treat “does the type of system actually predict democratic survival” as the claim under autopsy: what’s the evidence, what would we need to see to believe it, what confound (region, colonial history, level of development) is doing unacknowledged work? Don’t resolve it — the honest answer is “contested,” and that’s a fine place to leave first-years, provided they see WHY it’s contested rather than just being told it is.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
What would settle it?
If you wanted real evidence — not just Linz’s intuition — what would you need to compare?

Push toward: matched cases (similar countries, one presidential one parliamentary, holding region/development/history roughly constant), or countries that SWITCHED system type and tracking what happened after. This is good methods scaffolding for Lecture 20’s full causal-inference treatment — flag that connection out loud if time allows, but don’t turn this into a Lecture 20 preview at length.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Count the players, don’t read the label
text:
Count the players, don’t read the label
The honest summary of today:

Institutions do shape outcomes — same voters, different rules, different governments
But institutions don’t fully determine politics — the same label can mean very different amounts of real power
The honest lesson: count the veto players, don’t just read the label off the constitution


On the first point: you’ve now seen three ways to wire an executive — parliamentary, presidential, semi-presidential — and watched veto-player counts swing wildly within the very same constitution, depending purely on who won the last election. On the second: “presidential system” is one label, but a president facing zero partisan veto players governs nothing like a president facing a hostile Congress — same constitution, same title, completely different amount of real power.

This is the recap/closing-arc slide before readings — bring the two halves of the lecture together explicitly: the label (“presidential,” “parliamentary”) tells you something, but the veto-player count tells you more. That’s the whole argument of the lecture in one line.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The story you’ve already heard
Something like this: after 1980, capital and firms crossed borders faster than states could regulate them. Sovereignty eroded.

That’s not wrong, exactly. It’s also not the interesting part of the story.

The fuller version of the story: from the early 1980s, financial deregulation and trade liberalisation let capital, goods and firms move across borders faster than any single government could write rules to keep up. International institutions — the IMF, the World Bank, the WTO — increasingly set the terms trade and lending had to meet, terms individual states had less and less power to resist. The result, on this telling, is a hollowing-out of national sovereignty: governments still hold formal authority, but substantive control over economic policy migrated upward to markets and international institutions.


This is the one-slide “received view” the plan and STYLE-BRIEF both flag: they’ve had globalisation-erodes-sovereignty with an IMF/WTO/World Bank flavour at Leaving Cert. Do NOT rebuild that lecture. State it, credit it, move past it in under two minutes — everything from here is the complication, which is where the actual content of the lecture lives.


Deliver this fast and slightly flat — you’re naming something they already know, not teaching it. The energy should visibly pick up on the next slide. If anyone looks smug that they’ve “done this already,” that’s fine — tell them: good, you’re ahead, now we complicate it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The complication: states never left
Here’s what the sovereignty-erosion story leaves out: markets don’t pre-exist states. Every market that crosses a border was built, rule by rule, by states.


Who can trade, and as what kind of legal entity — state decides (corporate law, licensing)
What counts as a binding deal — state decides (contract law, bankruptcy, property rights)
How much of it you keep — state decides (taxation, regulation, redistribution)


There is no pure, ungoverned market that globalisation somehow escaped. Before any good, service or unit of capital can cross a border, someone has to have already decided what counts as a legal transaction, who is allowed to be a party to it, and what happens if it goes wrong. Globalisation did not remove the state from that process — it just made the process operate at a larger scale.


This is the pivot of the whole lecture — everything after this slide is showing what it means for states to have choices even inside a globalised economy. Don’t let “the market” get talked about as a natural force in the room from here on; correct it gently if it comes up in questions.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Cases first: three democracies, three bets
text:
Cases first: three democracies, three bets

The United States — flexible labour markets, minimal welfare cushion, bet on dynamism
Germany — regulated labour markets, workers on corporate boards, strong social insurance, bet on stability
Ireland — deregulated and low-tax, yet backed by EU-level social protections and a large public sector — a genuine hybrid


None of these is “the market.” Each is a state deciding what kind of capitalism it wants to run.

Ireland doesn’t sit cleanly in either camp. On paper it looks like a liberal market economy — light labour-market regulation, a famously low corporate tax rate — but it also leans on EU-level social and regulatory protections, and runs a large public health and education system that a purely liberal model wouldn’t fund. It is not a clean fit for either pole, which is exactly why it’s the most interesting case in the room.


IMAGE — three small inline images (.absolute), one per case: a US factory floor or Wall Street trading floor; a German works-council boardroom or car-plant floor (codetermination); Dublin’s Grand Canal Dock tech campus. Source: Wikimedia Commons / Unsplash, one photo per bullet, positioned beside its text.


Don’t resolve which is “better” — that’s politics, and saying so out loud is itself the pedagogical point (echoes lecture 5’s “who decides” framing, coming next). Germany’s Mitbestimmung (codetermination — workers legally entitled to seats on supervisory boards) is a good concrete image if you want one extra beat: ask “who here thinks employees should get a vote on the board? now: should the law require it?”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Three words for what you just saw
text:
Three words for what you just saw

Embedded liberalism — open markets are a product of state power, not its absence. Varieties of capitalism — rich democracies never converged; they clustered (Hall & Soskice). LMEs (US, UK) coordinate through markets. CMEs (Germany, the Nordics) through unions and banks.


Quick to adapt and quick to bruise, or slow to adapt and slow to break. Pick one — you already did, by being born somewhere.

Embedded liberalism (the term is Ruggie’s; the idea is what matters) says open markets are sustained by rules, institutions and political bargains that states choose to make — and could choose to unmake. Markets need states as much as states are constrained by markets; it runs both ways. The EU single market is not “no rules,” it is thousands of pages of rules, every one of them state-negotiated. Deregulation is itself a regulatory choice. Varieties of capitalism (Hall & Soskice) is the observation that market democracies don’t converge on one model — they cluster into different, durable combinations of regulation, labour relations and social provision. The question isn’t “more capitalist or less capitalist”; it’s what your capitalism actually looks like. Liberal market economies — the US, the UK — coordinate mainly through competitive markets and formal contracts: hiring and firing is easy, welfare provision is comparatively thin, and capital and labour move quickly to wherever returns are highest. Coordinated market economies — Germany, the Nordics — coordinate through longer-term negotiated relationships with unions, banks and each other: job protection is stronger, welfare provision denser, and the whole system reallocates more slowly and predictably. Neither is a natural state of affairs; both are political settlements.


Compressed from three consecutive definitional slides (embedded liberalism / varieties of capitalism / the LME–CME poles) into one, per FRESH-EYES §2 — the full text of all three is preserved in the printnote above and now lands after the three cases rather than before, so the room meets the puzzle before the vocabulary. Nothing was cut.


Noah: flat by design — it’s the vocabulary slide, and it’s now the only one. Two beats worth having here if you want them: (1) a third pole neither Hall nor Soskice wrote about, where cronyism does the coordinating instead of unions or banks, which is your territory; (2) a dry line about how many varieties of capitalism a first-year has personally lived under. Roughly zero. They’ve been in school.


IMAGE — comparison chart. OECD Employment Protection Legislation (EPL) index, US/UK vs. Germany/Nordics, bar chart. Source: OECD.Stat EPL indicators. This is the slide closest to a bare taxonomy in the deck — the chart earns its place by turning “LME vs CME” from a label into a number.


Hand these over as tools, not as a theory to defend — you’re not asking them to litigate Hall & Soskice’s typology, you’re giving them a lens for the Ireland slide that comes next. Land the trade-off, not a value judgement. Good comprehension check: “if you lose your job tomorrow, which economy do you want to be standing in — and does the answer change if it’s your firm’s whole industry that’s dying, not just you personally?”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Ireland: the hybrid that shouldn’t work
text:
Ireland: the hybrid that shouldn’t work
Ireland doesn’t sit cleanly on either pole:

Liberal on paper — low corporate tax, light labour-market regulation, an economy wide open to foreign investment
Coordinated in practice — decades of national pay bargaining between unions, employers and government (social partnership), backstopped by EU-level protections
The result: one of the most FDI-dependent economies on earth — built on one political choice, a 12.5% tax rate, that drew in Apple, Google and Pfizer


Ireland has a long history of “social partnership” — national-level pay bargaining between unions, employers and government that coordinated wage growth and industrial peace for decades, much closer to the coordinated-market model than the “liberal” label suggests. On top of that, EU membership supplies a layer of social and regulatory protection — from working-time rules to state-aid limits — that a genuinely liberal, go-it-alone economy would have to build for itself.


Full company list as originally drafted: “Apple, Google, Pfizer, and dozens more.” Cut to three names on-slide for pace; restore the fuller list if a student asks who else is here.


IMAGE — Dublin’s Grand Canal Dock (“Silicon Docks”) skyline, showing the Google/Meta/LinkedIn campus, as an inline .absolute photo. Alternative/additional: the well-known Irish GDP-vs-GNI* divergence chart (“leprechaun economics,” post-2015 jump), source CSO Ireland or Eurostat — the single clearest chart in Irish political economy for showing how FDI-dependent the headline numbers are.


Currency check for Sept 2026: the EU/OECD 15% global minimum corporate tax deal has been reshaping this since 2023 — confirm where Ireland’s actual effective rate and political stance stand by delivery date, and whether there’s a fresher flashpoint (a specific firm relocating, an EU ruling, a budget announcement) to hang this on. This is the single fastest-moving fact in the whole deck.


This is the “Ireland as interesting hybrid” beat the brief specifically asks for — land it as a puzzle, not a boast: how does a small, liberal, low-tax economy also run one of Europe’s most extensive welfare states? Answer: it can afford to, because the tax-competition bet paid off spectacularly. That’s not guaranteed to keep working — flag forward to the corporate-tax pressure.


Noah: this is a strong slot for your own read on Irish tax politics if you want one — you’re better placed than the textbook to say whether 12.5% (or wherever the effective rate has landed) is still a going political bet or now under real threat.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Should Ireland raise its corporate tax rate?
text:
Should Ireland raise its corporate tax rate?
If the low-tax bet built the current welfare state, and international pressure keeps pushing the rate up — is Ireland’s model still the same model in ten years?

Live poll — final wording: “Ireland’s corporate tax rate should — (a) go up, (b) stay where it is, (c) go down.” Three ways, so nobody can sit on the fence, and the follow-up question is the real one: ask two people on opposite sides what they think the money is for. Tool still undecided (TCDpolls/Vevox is institutionally available); wording is locked.


Don’t resolve it. Good spot to note: whichever way this goes, it’s a political choice about what kind of capitalism Ireland wants to keep being — not a technical tax question. That’s the whole lecture in one sentence.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Money moved. Factories moved. People didn’t.
text:
Money moved. Factories moved. People didn’t.
Post-1980, three things changed speed — but not all at the same speed:

Capital mobility — money moves in seconds; hard for any one state to tax or regulate it alone
Trade and production mobility — manufacturing moved to wherever labour was cheapest
Labour did not move nearly as freely — people are much stickier than money or factories


That mismatch — capital and goods globalising fast, labour staying put — is where the backlash comes from.

This is the mechanism, not just the description — make sure it lands as why some places lost and others didn’t, not just “globalisation happened.” Rust Belt Ohio and industrial northern England didn’t move to where the jobs went; the jobs moved away from them.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Who lost, and what they voted for
text:
Who lost, and what they voted for

Manufacturing regions that lost jobs to cheaper production elsewhere, with no comparable replacement industry
Wages stagnant for decades even as national GDP kept rising — the gains went somewhere, just not evenly
The political response: Brexit, Trump, the rise of parties on the populist right and left across Europe


You’ve already met the shape of this — Lecture 6’s populism, the thin ideology that attaches to whoever’s angriest. This is one of the engines that fed it.

IMAGE — a specific, concrete photo tied to this case: the Sunderland Nissan plant (a real Brexit-and-trade flashpoint) or a Rust Belt factory-closure photo with a visible “for sale”/shutdown sign. Source: Wikimedia Commons / news-agency archive (check licensing before use).


Deliberately keeping this to a one-line callback rather than re-running the populism material — Lecture 6 already owns “the people vs. the corrupt elite” as a frame. Here the point is narrower and economic: where the grievance came from, not what ideology it attached to.


Good moment for a current, non-US/UK example if you have one by delivery time — the brief flags every current-events beat needs a lecturer-supplied refresh, textbook stops mid-2024. A recent European election result with a strong “left behind by trade” component would land better than recycling Brexit/Trump again for the fourth time this term.


Noah: 75 words — dense, but one tight causal chain, so left whole with .breathe rather than split. Same call as “State capacity callback” and “The compensation hypothesis” below.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
State capacity callback (Lecture 4)
Here’s the twist: globalisation didn’t make states smaller. It changed what they do.


2008 financial crisis: states didn’t shrink, they bailed out banks worth hundreds of billions
Covid: states closed borders, ran furlough schemes, bought vaccines by the hundreds of millions
Every “globalised, powerless” state above still had the capacity to act — fast, and at enormous scale



Same tool as Lecture 4: capacity is not the same axis as how open or closed an economy is.

IMAGE — chart comparing 2008 bank bailout spending (e.g. US TARP, ~$700bn) against Covid fiscal-response spending by major economies, bar chart. Source: IMF Fiscal Monitor / Our World in Data Covid government-response tracker.


This is the direct payoff of the state-capacity concept from Lecture 4 — say the callback out loud, don’t just gesture at it. The point: “globalisation shrank the state” is a story about choices, not about states losing the physical ability to act. They chose to deregulate finance; they were fully capable of re-regulating it, or bailing it out, the moment the politics demanded it.


Noah: 74 words — dense, but one tight causal chain, left whole with .breathe rather than split. Same call as “Who lost…” above and “The compensation hypothesis” below.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: How do we know that? Did globalisation shrink the welfare state?
text:
How do we know that? Did globalisation shrink the welfare state?
The intuitive story: open economies compete on cost, so they cut taxes and welfare to stay competitive — the race to the bottom hypothesis.

Check it against the data: the most open economies — the Nordics, the Netherlands, even Ireland — often have bigger welfare states, not smaller.

The race-to-the-bottom hypothesis predicts that as economies open up to trade and capital mobility, governments come under pressure to cut taxes, deregulate and shrink welfare provision in order to stay competitive with lower-cost rivals. It’s an intuitive story, and it’s the one most people reach for first. But when you actually look at the cross-national data, the pattern runs the other way: small, highly trade-dependent economies — the Nordic countries, the Netherlands, Ireland — tend to have among the largest welfare states in the world, not the smallest. Openness and welfare-state size are, if anything, positively correlated.


IMAGE — scatter plot: trade openness (exports+imports as % GDP, x-axis) against social spending (% GDP, y-axis) across OECD countries, with Nordics/Netherlands/Ireland highlighted in the high-openness, high-spending corner. Source: Our World in Data or OECD Social Expenditure Database.


This is the lecture’s dedicated “how do we know that” autopsy slot — deliberately placed here rather than as the opener, because it needs the backlash material already on the table to land as a genuine surprise rather than an abstract claim. Cold-call before revealing: “if you had to bet, more open economy = bigger or smaller welfare state?” Most will guess smaller. Let the wrong guess sit for a second.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The compensation hypothesis
David Cameron’s answer (1978), developed by Peter Katzenstein: small, trade-exposed states build bigger safety nets because they’re exposed.


If your economy lives or dies on trade, workers bear risk they didn’t choose — a currency swing, an offshored factory, an undercutting competitor
A generous welfare state is the domestic insurance policy against that external risk
Voters in exposed economies often demand more openness because the state promises to catch them



So: openness didn’t shrink the welfare state — in many cases, it’s why the welfare state got built this big.

The compensation logic in full: when a national economy depends heavily on international trade, individual workers are exposed to risks they had no hand in creating and cannot manage alone — a currency appreciation that prices an export sector out of a market overnight, a multinational relocating its factory to a cheaper country, a foreign competitor undercutting an entire domestic industry. None of that is something a worker can insure against through savings or private choices alone. A generous welfare state — unemployment insurance, retraining, healthcare not tied to a job — is the collective insurance policy against exactly that risk. That’s why, on Cameron and Katzenstein’s account, voters in small open economies don’t just tolerate a big state alongside an open economy; they often want both, because the two are doing complementary jobs.


IMAGE — simple two-box diagram illustrating the insurance-policy metaphor: “Trade exposure → individual risk” on one side, “Welfare state → collective insurance” on the other, joined by an arrow labelled “compensates for.” Build in Keynote/Canva rather than sourced — this is a concept diagram, not a photo.


This is the falsification beat the brief asks for — a clean, intuitive theory (race to the bottom) that mostly doesn’t survive contact with the evidence. Don’t oversell it as fully settled; there ARE places where openness did coincide with retrenchment (this is genuinely contested in the literature) — the point is that the simple story is wrong often enough that you can’t just assume it. That intellectual honesty (“ask yourselves whether this fits everywhere”) is exactly the register the brief wants.


Cameron/Katzenstein compensation hypothesis is the standard political-economy answer here and isn’t claimed by Comp A’s Wk11–12 (which runs on Acemoglu & Robinson institutions-and-growth territory, not welfare-state comparative political economy) — safe ground. One-line Acemoglu namecheck below keeps the guard-rail explicit without building anything around it.


Noah: 87 words — the densest slide in the deck. One four-step argument that didn’t split cleanly, so left whole with .breathe rather than trimmed further. Flagging as deliberately dense.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: So did states lose, or just change jobs?
text:
So did states lose, or just change jobs?
If capital can move overnight but voters still expect their government to catch them when it doesn’t work out — who’s actually in charge here?

Push them past a simple “states won” / “markets won” answer — the honest answer is that the bargain changed: states gave up some direct control over capital in exchange for still being the ones voters hold responsible when things go wrong. That’s not weakness, that’s a different kind of power. (One-line acknowledgement, if it comes up: “why do some countries get richer and stay richer than others” is a huge question in its own right — that’s Acemoglu & Robinson’s territory, which second-year covers properly.)

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Key term: collective action problem (third outing)
text:
Key term: collective action problem (third outing)

Collective action problem (Olson, 1965): everyone is better off if everyone cooperates — and each person is better off free-riding. So nobody cooperates, and everybody agrees they should.


Third time you’ve seen this shape. Lecture 14: corruption. Lecture 18: median-voter redistribution. Now: climate.

Olson’s full formulation, from The Logic of Collective Action (1965): a group would be better off if everyone in it cooperated, but each individual member is better off free-riding on everyone else’s effort — so cooperation doesn’t happen, even though every member “agrees” that it should.


Say the callback out loud, don’t just gesture at it — “if you take one tool out of this entire course, it’s this one.” Ask who remembers the corruption version (bribery is individually rational, collectively corrosive) before you move on.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Olson’s actual argument
Olson’s twist wasn’t just “people free-ride” — it was about group size.

Small groups organise — big benefit share, visible free-riders, peer pressure bites
Large groups don’t — one contribution barely moves it; free-riding is invisible
Climate is the largest group there is: eight billion, one unowned atmosphere


Small, organised interests beat large, diffuse ones — easier to organise, not more right.

Olson’s insight was that free-riding gets worse, not better, as a group grows. In a small group each member’s share of the collective benefit is large enough to make cooperating worth it, defectors are easy to spot, and social pressure can enforce cooperation. In a very large group, an individual’s contribution moves the outcome by an imperceptible amount, monitoring becomes impossible, and free-riding is effectively invisible. Climate change confronts humanity with the largest possible version of this problem: roughly eight billion people, the overwhelming majority of whom will never meet or coordinate with one another, sharing a single atmosphere that none of them owns or controls.


IMAGE — inline .absolute, contrast pair. A small, close-knit meeting or committee room next to a vast crowd or stadium — visualising “small groups organise, large groups struggle.” Generic imagery, not climate-specific, since this is the structural Olson slide that survives any case-swap. Source: Unsplash.


Noah: this slide is fairly earnest/dry (theory, no case yet) — good spot for a one-line joke or aside before you move to Ireland. E.g. something about how eight billion people trying to coordinate is basically a group WhatsApp chat trying to pick a restaurant, except the restaurant is the atmosphere. Your call on the bit.


This slide is the hinge of the whole lecture — everything from here (democracies under-supplying the future, Irish agriculture) is this one mechanism applied at different scales. Don’t rush it.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The clock problem
Democracies run on election cycles. Climate runs on a much longer clock.

A government elected for 4–5 years is judged by the next election
The costs of climate policy land now
The benefits (a liveable 2070) land on a timescale no government will ever be judged against


Politicians aren’t ignoring the science — the institution has no mechanism for rewarding a 30-year bet.

Elections create a specific time horizon: governments are judged on outcomes voters can feel before the next vote, typically four or five years away. Climate policy inverts that timing — the costs are felt immediately, while the benefits of avoiding the worst warming accrue on a thirty- to fifty-year horizon that no government currently in office will ever be electorally judged against. The mismatch is structural, not a failure of political will: a well-intentioned government inside a badly-timed institution still produces badly-timed policy.


Specific cost examples, if a student asks “like what?”: higher fuel prices, land-use limits, disruption to carbon-intensive industries.


Resist the temptation to make this a “politicians are short-termist and bad” rant — the point is structural, not moral. Good people inside a badly-timed institution still produce bad-timed outcomes.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
The intergenerational franchise problem
Sharpest version yet: the people with the biggest stake in 2070 can’t vote.

A baby born this year lives through the worst of it, with no vote at all
Anyone born after 2070 can never lobby, protest or vote on it. Ever.
Every other problem in this course had affected parties who were alive.


Farmers, ideologues, ethnic groups, voters — every group we’ve studied could at least organise. The future cannot.

This is the line that should make first-years sit up: it’s not that future generations organise badly, it’s that organising is definitionally impossible for people who don’t exist yet. That’s a genuinely different, harder collective action problem than corruption or redistribution.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: States free-ride too. One slide on that, then back to Ireland.
text:
States free-ride too. One slide on that, then back to Ireland.

Every country gains if emissions fall — and gains individually from cheap growth now
No world government to force compliance the way a state forces citizens
Paris (2015): voluntary pledges, enforced by embarrassment


That’s the global layer. Domestic from here.

Paris Agreement, spelled out: the textbook international-relations case of a large group failing to bind itself, same free-rider logic as the rest of this lecture, just scaled up to states.


The same collective-action logic runs at the international level: every country benefits if global emissions fall, but every country individually benefits from cheap fossil-fuelled growth right now. Unlike a state, no world government can force compliance — there is no higher authority to coerce two hundred sovereign states the way a state coerces its own citizens. The Paris Agreement (2015) is the clearest illustration: its pledges are voluntary and its enforcement is reputational rather than legal, a textbook case of a large group failing to bind itself. This course keeps that international layer to one slide and stays domestic for the rest of the lecture — the state-level politics of who blocks a climate target is where the more interesting, more testable politics is.


IMAGE — chart, inline .absolute. Global CO2 emissions over time with the Paris Agreement (2015) marked on the timeline, showing the gap between pledged and actual trajectories. Source: Our World in Data (“CO2 emissions” chart) or the UNEP Emissions Gap Report’s headline figure.


Deliberately keeping the international-relations layer to a single slide per PLAN §3 (“keep it DOMESTIC”). There’s a much longer lecture available here (free-riding among states, the tragedy-of-the-commons framing, treaty design) — that’s Comparative/IR territory, not this course’s job. Resist the pull to expand this slide.


Say explicitly you’re choosing not to go deep here — “there’s a whole international-relations course in this one slide, and we’re not doing it today.” Keeps the domestic pivot feeling deliberate rather than like you ran out of time.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
text:
Ireland’s cows
The clearest collective action problem in Irish politics — and it’s not housing.

IMAGE — full-bleed divider background. Irish dairy or beef cattle in a green field, ideally with a farmhouse or hedgerow visible — the deck’s central case image. Source: Unsplash / Teagasc press images (check licensing). Use as ## Ireland's cows {background-image="w12-lec19-img/cows.jpg"}.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Ireland’s emissions don’t look like anyone else’s
text:
Ireland’s emissions don’t look like anyone else’s

Agriculture is about 38% of national emissions — cattle methane, and nitrogen fertiliser
Nowhere near a normal figure for a rich economy: most peers run on energy and transport
The EU sets Ireland binding sectoral ceilings, agriculture included, with real money attached


So Ireland can’t do climate in the abstract. It has to decide, out loud, how many fewer cows.

IMAGE — chart, inline .absolute. Ireland’s emissions by sector (pie or stacked bar), agriculture’s share highlighted against energy/transport/industry, ideally with an EU-peer-average comparison alongside. Source: EPA Ireland or Climate Change Advisory Council annual report figures.


Figure verified 2026-09-03: the EPA puts agriculture at 37.9% of Ireland’s national greenhouse-gas emissions for 2024 in its provisional inventory (EPA, “Agriculture”, epa.ie; provisional GHG report 1990–2024, published July 2025), and 36.9% in the final 1990–2024 inventory (March 2026). Both round to “about 38%” / “well over a third” — I’ve used the vaguer form on the slide so it can’t go stale mid-term. Emissions from the sector fell 1.7% in 2024, mainly on a 2.9% drop in cattle numbers. Sources: epa.ie agriculture page; EPA news release “Ireland’s Greenhouse Gas Emissions decrease by 2 per cent in 2024”.


Currency check before delivery: the sectoral ceiling figure (agriculture’s required reduction by 2030 under the Climate Action Plan) and the latest Climate Change Advisory Council / EPA projection of whether Ireland is on track are deliberately not on this slide — insert the live numbers close to delivery rather than risk a stale target.


This is the case that makes the abstract Olson logic concrete for eighteen-year-olds who’ve maybe never thought about agriculture as a political actor at all.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: The IFA: a textbook Olsonian small group
text:
The IFA: a textbook Olsonian small group
The IFA is the case study you’d invent to teach Olson.

Small and well-defined — everyone knows who’s in, and what’s at stake
Geographically concentrated — in the constituencies TDs need to win
Already organised — the lobbying infrastructure was paid for decades ago
Large personal stake — herd, land, income, the family farm


Compare: diffuse beneficiaries — everyone, a little, eventually — no association, no lobbyist, barely notice.

The Irish Farmers’ Association meets all four of the conditions Olson identifies for successful collective organisation. Farmers are a small, well-defined group — everyone in it knows exactly who else is in it and what they individually stand to lose. They are geographically concentrated in specific rural constituencies, which matters enormously to TDs defending local seats. They are already organised, with a standing association, annual conventions and direct lines into government — the fixed costs of organising were paid decades ago. And each farmer’s stake in the outcome is large and personal: herd size, land use, household income, sometimes the family farm itself. Compare the other side of the ledger: the diffuse beneficiaries of lower emissions are everyone, a little, eventually. They have no association, no annual convention, no lobbyist — and each of them individually barely notices the difference either way.


IMAGE — inline .absolute. IFA tractor rally or protest outside Leinster House / the Dáil — a concrete, organised-small-group image to sit alongside the bullet list. Source: press photo (RTÉ, Irish Times, Irish Farmers Journal); check licensing before use.


Explicit callback: “this is Lecture 14’s small-group logic — corruption, again, structurally. Small organised group, concentrated stake, versus a diffuse public that can’t be bothered to show up for a cause that benefits them by a rounding error each.”

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Concentrated interests beat diffuse interests — again
text:
Concentrated interests beat diffuse interests — again
The asymmetry that keeps reappearing this term, now with cows in it.

Farmers are concentrated: identifiable, organised, a lot at stake per head, right now
Everyone else is diffuse: marginally better outcomes, shared by billions, decades away
The concentrated side organises, lobbies, shows up. The diffuse side does none of those things.


Same asymmetry as Lecture 18’s housing veto players — concentrated interests beating diffuse ones. Ireland keeps producing this exact structure.

Lecture 18 parallel spelled out: existing homeowners are concentrated, organised, vocal; future renters are diffuse, absent from the room. Same asymmetry, different policy — in both cases a small group with a lot at stake per head beats a large group with little at stake per head, whether the concentrated side is extracting a cost or defending a benefit.


Explicit collective-action callback (4th use of the concept this term, counting the “third outing” framing earlier in this deck as outing #3 and this as reinforcement rather than a new #4 — word this however feels cleanest live; the plan and the stub disagree slightly on the count, not worth losing sleep over, the logic is what matters).


Fixed per fresh-eyes review (2026-09-03, §1 item 5 / §7 item 2): this slide’s title and Lecture 18 cross-reference previously used “concentrated costs, diffuse benefits” and claimed “same shape” as Lecture 18’s housing case — but Lecture 18 had framed its own case as “concentrated benefit, diffuse cost” and explicitly called it “the mirror image, flipped direction” from Lecture 14, contradicting this slide’s “same asymmetry” claim. Standardised both decks on the canonical phrasing “concentrated interests beat diffuse interests” (a small, organised group with high per-head stakes beats a large, diffuse group with low per-head stakes, regardless of which side is the one bearing a cost vs. claiming a benefit) so the cross-reference is now actually true. The cows/IFA example is unchanged.


Land the housing parallel hard — it’s the single best “you already have this tool” moment in the lecture, and it rewards anyone who was paying attention two lectures ago.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Who can actually block the target?
text:
Who can actually block the target?
Bring back Lecture 15’s question: who can stop whom?

Partisan veto power — need rural seats to govern, so listen or lose
Caught between green voters (who want targets) and rural voters (who punish delivery)
Set high, negotiated down, missed, re-set — the fight never resolves, it defers


Small country, binding EU targets, nowhere to hide.

Bring back Lecture 15’s veto-player logic. Farmers hold partisan veto power through coalition arithmetic: any party that depends on rural seats to form a government has to listen to the IFA, or risk losing office. That leaves government caught between two constituencies it needs simultaneously — urban and green-leaning voters who want ambitious climate targets, and rural voters who will punish a government that actually delivers them. The result is a familiar pattern: targets get set ambitiously on paper, then negotiated down in practice, then missed, then re-negotiated — the underlying veto-player conflict never resolves, it just gets deferred to the next round. Ireland, unlike a larger economy, cannot quietly absorb the political cost of missing a target or negotiate a longer compliance runway with Brussels: it is a small country with legally binding EU targets and nowhere to hide.


IMAGE — inline .absolute. Coalition government press conference or the Dáil chamber during a vote — visualising “who can stop whom” in institutional terms. Source: press photo (RTÉ, Oireachtas TV); check licensing before use.


Veto players (Lec 15) is the second portable concept doing work in this lecture, alongside collective action — say both names out loud so the “concept spine” is audible, not just structurally present.


Live poll — final wording (this deck’s one poll): “Ireland will miss its 2030 agricultural emissions target. (a) Agree, (b) Disagree, (c) It’ll be renegotiated so that technically we won’t.” Option (c) is the teaching point, and it usually wins. Tool still undecided (TCDpolls/Vevox available institutionally); wording is locked.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: How do we know? Does protest actually change climate policy?
text:
How do we know? Does protest actually change climate policy?
An honest evidence question, not a rhetorical one.

Easy to assume marches move policy — they’re visible and satisfying to be part of
Much harder to show it: opinion shift? elite attention? neither? timing isn’t causation
A different mechanism: deliberation — random citizens, evidence, months in a room


Ireland ran that experiment: the Citizens’ Assembly (2016–18) took up climate as one of its topics in 2017 and recommended stronger action than government proposed — some of it reached later legislation.

This is an honest evidence question, not a rhetorical one. It is easy to assume that marches and school strikes move policy — they are visible and emotionally satisfying to take part in. It is much harder to actually demonstrate it: protest could shift public opinion, or elite attention, or neither, and the timing of protest and policy change rarely lines up cleanly enough to establish causation rather than coincidence. A different mechanism worth testing is deliberation rather than protest: put a random, representative sample of citizens in a room with evidence and expert witnesses for months, and see what they recommend. Ireland actually ran that experiment — the Citizens’ Assembly (2016–18) took “How the State can make Ireland a leader in tackling climate change” as one of its five topics in 2017, and recommended stronger action than the government of the day was proposing, and some (not all) of its recommendations did later show up in legislation.


IMAGE — inline .absolute. Photo of the Citizens’ Assembly in session (round-table format, the format itself is the visual point) — pairs with the cc-flagged HDWKT caution below on the causal claim. Source: Citizens’ Assembly official press photos / RTÉ coverage.


Candidate case for the HDWKT beat — cc-flagging as requested rather than committing: Ireland’s Citizens’ Assembly on climate is the nice non-obvious Irish angle (avoids “civics-class Ireland”), but the causal claim (“assembly recommendation → actual legislative change”) needs a real citation before this goes on a slide as fact, not just “some of it did show up.” If Noah wants the protest-movements version instead (Fridays for Future, XR), that’s a different literature (e.g. work on protest and legislative attention) — his call which thread to run with live.


Fixed per fresh-eyes review (2026-09-03, §1 item 5): there was no body called the “Citizens’ Assembly on Climate Change (2016–18).” Ireland’s actual Citizens’ Assembly (2016–18) covered five topics; climate was one of them — “How the State can make Ireland a leader in tackling climate change,” considered in 2017 — alongside the Eighth Amendment, an ageing population, referendum fixed dates, and how the Dáil holds government to account. Corrected the name and dated the climate topic to 2017 within the Assembly’s 2016–18 run. Source: web search / Ireland’s Citizens’ Assembly official record of its topics and timeline.


This is the HDWKT segment for this lecture — it’s about THIS lecture’s own claim (does activism/deliberation work), not autopsying a previous lecture’s claim, because the plan’s spec for lec19 is self-contained. Keep it honest: we genuinely don’t have a clean answer, and that’s the point — it models the scepticism the course has been building toward Lecture 20.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: Can you escape a collective action problem?
text:
Can you escape a collective action problem?
Three levers show up in every version of this problem:

Coercion — a state (or the EU) sets a binding rule and penalises breaking it
Incentives — change the prices, so cooperating costs less than defecting
Norms — change what people want, not just what’s rational for them


Ireland: EU targets are lever one, carbon tax lever two. Whether norms are shifting fast enough is contested.

Three levers keep recurring across every version of a collective action problem this course has covered. Coercion: a state, or a supra-state body like the EU, sets a binding rule and penalises non-compliance. Incentives: change the relative prices people face — carbon taxes, subsidies for low-emission farming — so that cooperating becomes cheaper than defecting. Norms: change what people actually want, not just what is individually rational for them — a genuine shift in what farming, or flying, or eating, is supposed to look like. In the Irish case, the EU emissions ceilings are lever one and the carbon tax is lever two; whether norms are shifting fast enough, at scale, to matter is genuinely contested, and the honest answer is that nobody fully knows yet.


IMAGE — simple three-icon graphic (not a photo): a gavel for coercion, a euro/coin for incentives, a group of people for norms. Generic and swap-safe — this slide is the portable-concept payoff and should carry over to any case. Easy to build directly in Keynote from a stock icon set (e.g. Noun Project, licensed).


Noah: coercion lever — this is a natural spot for a quick authoritarian-state contrast if you want one (e.g. a state that can just ban something, Russia/China-style, versus Ireland negotiating with the IFA for a decade). Not required, but it’s the kind of “here’s the other model” aside that livens up an otherwise structural slide.


Don’t oversell lever three — students will want a hopeful ending, but the honest answer is norms move slowly and unevenly, and the lecture shouldn’t paper over that with a feel-good close.

title: POU11011: Introduction to Political Science
section: If future generations could vote, what would change?
text:
If future generations could vote, what would change?
Not “should they be able to” — assume they somehow could. What, concretely, would a government do differently on day one?

Let this run properly — it’s the emotional and intellectual payoff of the intergenerational-franchise point from earlier. Don’t rush to an answer; a few genuinely different answers (carbon budgets with teeth, infrastructure choices, land-use planning) are all defensible. The point is making the absence of that franchise felt, not resolving it.

title: POU11011 — Discussion points and tutorials
text:
Why this exists
Four tutorials is not many. If people turn up having skimmed the reading on the walk over, the session becomes me-by-proxy: your TA talks, twenty students nod. That is a waste of the one hour in this module where you get to argue with somebody.
So the deal is that you arrive having already written down what you want to argue about. Your TA reads the submissions beforehand and builds the session around them. The points are the agenda, not a hoop.
There is a second reason, and I will be straight about it: writing something about the reading a week after the lecture is the only thing in this module that makes you retrieve the material before December. Students who do this consistently do better on the essay. That is not a motivational line, it is what the marks look like.

title: POU11011 — Discussion points and tutorials
text:
What to write
Three numbered points. Each at most a paragraph. One page in total.
You are not being asked for a polished analysis, and there is no thesis statement to construct. You are being asked to raise something worth twenty minutes of argument.
Things that work:

What is the argument actually claiming, and what would have to be true for it to hold?
Where does the argument fit the cases badly? Name the case.
Something in the news this month that the reading explains — or fails to.
Do you believe it? What is the alternative explanation?
Two readings that disagree, and what the disagreement turns on.

Things that do not work: a summary of the reading; three variations on “this was interesting”; a point that could have been written without opening the text.
Write it in whatever register you like. Nobody is marking your prose here.

title: POU11011 — Discussion points and tutorials
text:
The mechanics
Which tutorials. Discussion points attach to tutorials 2, 3 and 4. Tutorial 1 is orientation — how the module works, how to read a political science article, what your TA expects — and carries no submission. Attend it anyway; it is where the group is set up.
[DECISION for Noah — default applied: points attach to tutorials 2, 3 and 4, with tutorial 1 as orientation. The alternative is to let students choose any three of the four, which is friendlier but means tutorial 1 has no prepared room and tutorial 4 gets skipped by everyone who has banked three passes.]
Deadline: 20:00 the evening before your tutorial meets. Not the start of the tutorial. Your TA needs to read twenty of these and plan a session around them, and cannot do that at 9am.
[DECISION for Noah — default applied: 20:00 the evening before. Last year’s Intro said “before the tutorial”; Comparative A says “midnight before”. 20:00 is the version that actually gives the TA a working evening.]
Late points are not accepted. Not at 21:00, not on the morning of. The whole point is that your TA has read them. Papers cannot be accepted after the tutorial has taken place, and there is no late-penalty ladder here — it is in or it is not.
Marking. Pass/fail. Two points for each tutorial you attend with an accepted submission, to a maximum of six points across the three tutorials, which is this 10% component. Your TA can reject a submission that is too short, or that makes no genuine attempt to engage with the reading. That is the only quality bar.
[DECISION for Noah — default applied: pass/fail, two points per tutorial, max six. This mirrors Comparative A exactly. The alternative — grading them — is not survivable at n≈500 with four TAs.]
The 80 cap. Departmental policy: this component is capped at 80. Full attendance with three accepted submissions earns a mark of 80 for the component, with reductions proportional to that. This reflects the realities of the Trinity marking scale, and it applies across the department, not just here.
[DECISION for Noah — default applied: the 80-cap applies, as it does in Comparative A. Confirm it is departmental policy for first-year modules too.]
The Assignment Submission Form. Discussion points are exempt. The School form is required for the blog post and the final essay, not for a one-page pass/fail submission.
[DECISION for Noah — default applied: exempt. The syllabus currently implies the form is needed on every written submission; recommendation is to exempt these explicitly, which is what this handout does. Make the two agree.]

title: POU11011 — Discussion points and tutorials

Attendance
Attendance at tutorials is compulsory and it is half of this component. Submitting without attending earns nothing; attending without submitting earns nothing.
If you need an absence excused for certified medical reasons, your College Tutor must contact both your TA and me. Only requests from College Tutors are considered. If you want the credit for that tutorial, the discussion points must still be submitted — at or before the next tutorial, or within one week of the end of term if it was the last one. Tutorials are a place for open, warm and sometimes contentious discussion. People in the room have different backgrounds and different personal stakes in these questions. Engage seriously with the arguments and generously with the people making them.

Direct AI content — not permitted.

A rough, obviously human page is worth more here than a smooth one.

title: POU11011 — Marking rubric
text: This is how the blog post and the final essay are marked. Read it before you write. It applies to both pieces; where the two differ, the difference is noted.

title: POU11011 — Marking rubric
text:
The five criteria

Argument — a claim a reasonable person could disagree with, defended.
Use of concepts — are the module’s concepts doing work, or being described?
Evidence — real, specific details from real cases, supporting the argument rather than decorating it.
Structure and writing — can the reader follow it, and is it in the right register? (For the blog post that means blog, not essay: hook, short paragraphs, headings and links that earn their place.)
Referencing — accurate, consistent, and only sources you have actually read.

Criteria 1–3 carry most of the mark. Criterion 5 carries the least, but sloppy referencing is visible and it costs. The gap between a II.2 and a II.1 is almost always the gap between describing a concept and using it; the gap between a II.1 and a first is almost always answering the strongest objection to your own case.

title: POU11011 — Marking rubric
text:
The bands
Marks follow Trinity’s scale, as set out in the School’s marking descriptors.









Band

Evidence
Structure, writing, referencing




I — 70+First
A clear, independent argument that answers the question directly. Concepts are integrated with evidence rather than reported; there is real critical evaluation, and at least one original connection between ideas the lectures did not make for you. Handles the strongest objection to its own case.
Well-chosen, precise, drawn from more than the set readings. Cases are compared, not listed.
Lucid. Every paragraph earns its place. Referencing accurate and consistent throughout. Above 79: independence of judgement, imagination and originality throughout.


II.1 — 60–69Upper second
Sound and well-organised, with a clear position and no significant errors. Deals completely with the question. Evaluation is present but largely derivative — it follows the readings’ own arguments rather than pressing beyond them. Not necessarily excellent in any one area.
Accurate and relevant, mostly from the module readings, and genuinely supports the claims.
Coherent and cogent; the reader is never lost. Referencing sound, minor slips only.


II.2 — 50–59Lower second
Substantially correct and shows understanding of the basic principles, but the argument is not really developed. Concepts are defined accurately and then applied thinly, or applied to a case that is too large to say anything specific about. Draws largely on the textbook and lecture notes.
Present but general. Cases are described more than analysed.
Clear enough, but organisation is loose or the register is wrong for the genre. Referencing inconsistent or incomplete.


III — 40–49Third
Basic understanding of the main issues, but the piece is descriptive only and does not answer the question directly. Assertions are not supported by argument or evidence. Key points missing; some serious inaccuracies.
Sparse, vague, or not connected to the claims.
Hard to follow; no clear line. Referencing minimal or erratic.


F — below 40Fail
Misunderstands basic material, or fails to answer the question set. Information inadequate; presentation incoherent. (Below 30: virtually no appropriate material.)
Absent or wrong.
Incoherent. Absent or unusable referencing.



Two rules markers apply consistently across all TAs:

A good piece of writing that strays from the question set is normally capped in the II.2 band, however well written it is.
A piece that would otherwise be a II.1 but is too short, rushed, unfinished or badly organised is normally marked at the top of the II.2 band.

Penalties, applied after the band mark: three per cent for exceeding the word limit; five marks per day, to a maximum of twenty, for late submission. Both are set out in the module outline.

title: POU11011 — Marking rubric
text:
Discussion points — pass/fail
Discussion points are not marked against the bands above. They are pass/fail, and the bar is genuine engagement, not quality.







Pass
Three numbered points, at most a page, submitted on time. Each point engages with the actual reading or lecture material and raises something arguable — a question, a challenge, a connection, a case that fits badly. Rough prose is fine.


Fail
Substantially short of the required length; a summary of the reading with no point of your own; generic remarks that could have been written without opening the text; or submitted after the deadline.



Two points per tutorial attended with an accepted submission, to a maximum of six across three tutorials. Attendance without a submission, or a submission without attendance, earns nothing for that tutorial. Full detail: discussion points handout.
